CAUSALPY_FILES = {
    "banks": "banks.csv",
    "covid": "deaths_and_temps_england_wales.csv",
    "drinking": "drinking.csv",
    "risk": "AJR2001.csv",
    "schoolReturns": "schoolingReturns.csv",
    "california_prop99": "california_prop99.csv",
}

def load_causalpy(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load a CausalPy example dataset.

    Uses causalpy.load_data when that package is installed. Otherwise reads
    the same CSV from the CausalPy GitHub data directory.
    """
    try:
        import causalpy as cp
        frame = cp.load_data(name)
        print(f"Loaded {name!r} with causalpy.load_data. Shape {frame.shape}.")
        return frame
    except ImportError:
        url = (
            "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pymc-labs/CausalPy/main/causalpy/data/"
            + CAUSALPY_FILES[name]
        )
        frame = pd.read_csv(url)
        print(f"CausalPy is not installed. Loaded {name!r} from")
        print(url)
        print("Install the package with: pip install 'pycausalml[causalpy]'")
        print(f"Shape {frame.shape}.")
        return frame

title: 8.5 Bayesian Causal Inference for Quasi-Experimental Data
text:
Posterior draws
Every quasi-experimental estimator stores draws_ and a summary() without those draws. The histogram is the posterior the interval is read from.


Code
def show_draws(model, title, rope=None):
    draws = np.asarray(model.draws_, dtype=float)
    summary = model.summary()
    print(pd.Series({k: summary[k] for k in summary if k != "rope_probability"}).round(3))
    if rope is not None:
        print(f"ROPE {rope}: {rope_probability(draws, rope[0], rope[1]):.3f}")
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.4))
    ax.hist(draws, bins=30, color="#4C78A8", edgecolor="white")
    ax.axvline(model.effect_, color="#E45756", lw=2, label="Estimate")
    lo, hi = np.quantile(draws, [0.025, 0.975])
    ax.axvline(lo, color="gray", ls="--")
    ax.axvline(hi, color="gray", ls="--", label="95% interval")
    if rope is not None:
        ax.axvspan(rope[0], rope[1], color="#F2C14E", alpha=0.35, label="ROPE")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend()
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

title: 8.5 Bayesian Causal Inference for Quasi-Experimental Data
section: Part 1: Linear CATE on a simulation
text:
Part 1: Linear CATE on a simulation
The conditional effect is \(1.5 + 0.8 x_0\). Treatment is binary and depends on \(x_0\). BayesianLinearCATE cross-fits the outcome and the propensity, builds doubly robust scores, and puts a ridge-normal posterior on a linear function of \(X\).


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 900, 4
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
propensity = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.4 * X[:, 0])))
treatment = rng.binomial(1, propensity)
true_cate = 1.5 + 0.8 * X[:, 0]
outcome = 2 + 0.5 * X[:, 1] + treatment * true_cate + rng.normal(size=n)

cate = BayesianLinearCATE(prior_precision=1.0, n_splits=2, random_state=0)
cate.fit(X, treatment, outcome, feature_names=["x0", "x1", "x2", "x3"])
print("Average treatment effect from the doubly robust scores:")
print({k: round(v, 3) for k, v in cate.average_treatment_effect().items()})
print(f"Mean predicted CATE: {cate.predict(X).mean():.3f}")
print(f"Mean true CATE: {true_cate.mean():.3f}")

lo, hi = cate.credible_interval(X[:4])
preview = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "x0": X[:4, 0],
        "predicted": cate.predict(X[:4]),
        "true": true_cate[:4],
        "ci_lower": lo,
        "ci_upper": hi,
    }
)
print(preview.round(3))

8.5 Bayesian Causal Inference for Quasi-Experimental Data
text:
Part 2: Difference-in-differences, banking closures
banks records banks in business in the 6th and 8th Federal Reserve districts, 1929–1934 (Richardson and Troost; Angrist and Pischke, Mastering Metrics). The 6th district is treated. The post period starts in 1931, matching CausalPy’s intervention at 1930.5. The ROPE is a change of fewer than 5 banks, used here only as a scale for “small.”


Code
banks = load_causalpy("banks")
yearly = (
    banks.filter(items=["bib6", "bib8", "year"])
    .rename(columns={"bib6": "sixth", "bib8": "eighth"})
    .groupby("year")
    .median()
    .reset_index()
)
long = yearly.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="district", value_name="banks_open")
long["treated"] = (long["district"] == "sixth").astype(float)
long["post"] = (long["year"] >= 1931).astype(float)
did = DifferenceInDifferences(n_boot=400, rope=(-5, 5), random_state=0)
did.fit(long["banks_open"], long["treated"], long["post"])
show_draws(did, "DiD: 6th minus 8th district after 1930", rope=(-5, 5))

title: 8.5 Bayesian Causal Inference for Quasi-Experimental Data
text:
Part 3: Synthetic control, California Proposition 99
california_prop99 is annual per-capita cigarette sales, 1970–2000 (Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller, 2010). California adopted the tax in 1989. Donor weights are nonnegative and sum to one. The point estimate uses the original pre-period. Bootstrap draws that match California less well can move the gap, so the posterior mean need not equal that point estimate.


Code
prop = load_causalpy("california_prop99").set_index("Year").sort_index().astype(float)
pre = prop.index < 1989
donors = prop.drop(columns=["California"])
scm = SyntheticControl(n_boot=40, random_state=0)
scm.fit(
    donors.loc[pre].to_numpy(),
    prop.loc[pre, "California"].to_numpy(),
    donors.loc[~pre].to_numpy(),
    prop.loc[~pre, "California"].to_numpy(),
)
weights = pd.Series(scm.weights_, index=donors.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)
print("Largest donor weights:")
print(weights.head(6).round(3))
show_draws(scm, "Proposition 99: post-period gap in packs per capita")

section: Part 5: Interrupted time series, deaths in England and Wales
text:
Part 5: Interrupted time series, deaths in England and Wales
covid is the CausalPy monthly series of deaths and temperature. pre is true through December 2019. Temperature and calendar month are removed using coefficients fit on the pre-period only, so the post-period level is not absorbed into the seasonal fit. InterruptedTimeSeries then estimates the level shift at the first post-period month. This is a design illustration. It is not an estimate of the pandemic’s mortality toll: the interruption coincides with many other changes.


Code
deaths = load_causalpy("covid")
deaths["date"] = pd.to_datetime(deaths["date"])
y = deaths["deaths"].to_numpy(float)
t = deaths["t"].to_numpy(float)
pre_mask = deaths["pre"].to_numpy(bool)
month = pd.get_dummies(deaths["month"], drop_first=True).to_numpy(float)
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), deaths["temp"].to_numpy(float), month])
season = np.linalg.lstsq(design[pre_mask], y[pre_mask], rcond=None)[0]
residual = y - design @ season
intervention = float(t[~pre_mask][0])
its = InterruptedTimeSeries(n_boot=300, random_state=0)
its.fit(t, residual, intervention)
print(f"Intervention index: {intervention:.0f} ({deaths.loc[~pre_mask, 'date'].iloc[0].date()})")
show_draws(its, "Level shift in seasonally adjusted deaths")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax.plot(deaths["date"], residual, color="#4C78A8")
ax.axvline(deaths.loc[~pre_mask, "date"].iloc[0], color="red", ls="--", label="January 2020")
ax.set_ylabel("Deaths, seasonally adjusted")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 8.5 Bayesian Causal Inference for Quasi-Experimental Data
text:
Part 6: Instrumental variables, colonial origins
risk is the Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson (2001) country sample (AJR2001.csv). Log GDP per capita is the outcome, protection against expropriation (risk) is the endogenous treatment, and log settler mortality (logmort0) is the instrument. The exclusion restriction — settler mortality affects present income only through institutions — is contested. The posterior below is the 2SLS coefficient under that assumption, not a settled answer.


Code
ajr = load_causalpy("risk").dropna(subset=["loggdp", "risk", "logmort0"])
iv = InstrumentalVariable(n_boot=300, random_state=0)
iv.fit(ajr["loggdp"].to_numpy(), ajr["risk"].to_numpy(), ajr["logmort0"].to_numpy())
show_draws(iv, "AJR: log GDP on expropriation protection")

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Overview

The Core Idea
When treatment is assigned by a threshold on a continuous score, units immediately above and below the cutoff are essentially identical except for treatment status. This creates a local randomization around the threshold, enabling causal effect estimation.
For example:

Customers with credit score ≥ 700 get approved for a loan
Students with test score ≥ 80 pass the exam
Stores with performance score below 50 get a turnaround program
Orders over $50 get free shipping

The key insight is that whether a unit ends up just above or just below the cutoff is effectively random — it depends on small fluctuations in the running variable. Comparing outcomes in a narrow window around the cutoff identifies the local average treatment effect (LATE) at the threshold.


Business Setting
RDD is ideal when:

Treatment is assigned by a clear threshold on a continuous score
The threshold is known and rule-based (not manipulated)
Units cannot precisely manipulate their score to sort around the cutoff
You have sufficient data near the cutoff for estimation

Common business examples:

Credit scoring: loan approval based on credit score thresholds
Pricing: discounts for orders above a certain amount
Performance management: interventions for underperforming stores/employees
Churn prevention: retention calls for customers above a churn-risk threshold
Academic testing: scholarships for students above a test score cutoff



The Identifying Assumptions
RDD relies on two key assumptions:

Continuity of potential outcomes: Potential outcomes \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) are continuous functions of the running variable at the cutoff. Nothing else jumps at the threshold except treatment status.
No precise manipulation: Units cannot precisely control their score to end up on one side of the cutoff. While they may influence their score generally, they cannot fine-tune it to fall just above or below the threshold.



Key Advantages

Internal validity: RDD is often considered the most credible quasi-experimental design after RCTs
Transparent: The cutoff is observable and the assumption of local randomization is intuitive
Visual: The discontinuity in outcomes at the cutoff is directly visible in plots
Local effect: Estimates the effect at the margin — exactly the policy-relevant question for threshold decisions
Falsifiable: The assumptions can be tested with density tests and covariate continuity checks

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Implementation in Python
RegressionDiscontinuity fits a local linear model \(Y = a + b(R-c) + \tau D + d(R-c)D\) inside a bandwidth around the cutoff. \(\tau\) is the jump. The interval is a Bayesian bootstrap of the rows inside that window.
The setup matches the other PyCausalML tutorials: find the repository, import the package, and install the editable checkout only if the import fails.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Simulated Example: Churn-Risk Threshold
We’ll simulate a scenario where customers with churn-risk score ≥ 0.7 receive a retention call. This lets us know the true effect and verify that RDD recovers it.


Code
n = 6000
score = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)  # churn-risk score
cutoff = 0.7
D = (score >= cutoff).astype(int)  # treatment: retention call

TRUE_RD = 6.5  # true effect: call adds $6.5 in customer value

# Outcome: customer value depends on score (quadratic) + treatment
y = 40 - 25*score + 8*score**2 + TRUE_RD*D + rng.normal(0, 5, n)

rd = pd.DataFrame(dict(score=score, D=D, y=y))

print(rd.head())
print(f"\nTrue effect at cutoff: ${TRUE_RD}")


   score  D      y
0  0.774  1 26.758
1  0.439  0 32.982
2  0.859  1 27.895
3  0.697  0 18.211
4  0.094  0 36.279

True effect at cutoff: $6.5

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Visualize with Binned Means
Always plot first — a discontinuity you can’t see in a binned scatter is rarely robust. Binning reduces noise and makes the pattern visible.


Code
# Bin the data and compute means
rd["bin"] = pd.cut(rd.score, bins=40)
binned = rd.groupby("bin", observed=True).agg(
    x=("score", "mean"), 
    y=("y", "mean")
)

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 4))
plt.scatter(binned.x, binned.y, s=18)
plt.axvline(cutoff, color="red", ls="--", label="Cutoff")
plt.xlabel("Churn-risk score")
plt.ylabel("Customer value ($)")
plt.title("Binned Scatter: Check for Discontinuity at Cutoff")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









You should see a jump at the cutoff (score = 0.7). If there’s no visible discontinuity, RDD is unlikely to find a significant effect.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Local Linear Estimation
The estimator fits a straight line on each side of the cutoff, inside a bandwidth, and reads the jump at the cutoff. A narrower window reduces bias from curvature. A wider window uses more rows and tightens the interval. The summary reports the jump and a 95% Bayesian bootstrap interval.


Code

bandwidth = 0.15
rd_fit = RegressionDiscontinuity(cutoff=cutoff, bandwidth=bandwidth, n_boot=200, random_state=0)
rd_fit.fit(rd["score"].to_numpy(), rd["y"].to_numpy())
print(pd.Series(rd_fit.summary()).round(3))
print(f"True effect at cutoff: ${TRUE_RD}")


estimate         6.871
ci_lower         5.929
ci_upper         7.845
posterior_mean   6.890
dtype: float64
True effect at cutoff: $6.5


The summary reports:

estimate: the jump at the cutoff
ci_lower and ci_upper: the 95% interval from the Bayesian bootstrap
posterior_mean: the mean of those draws

The estimate should sit near the true effect of $6.5.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
RDD Plot
Binned means show the raw pattern. Local linear fits on each side show the jump the estimator uses.


Code

def local_line(x, y, c, bandwidth, right):
    if right:
        mask = (x >= c) & (x <= c + bandwidth)
    else:
        mask = (x < c) & (x >= c - bandwidth)
    design = np.column_stack([np.ones(mask.sum()), x[mask] - c])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y[mask], rcond=None)[0]
    grid = np.linspace(x[mask].min(), x[mask].max(), 40)
    return grid, beta[0] + beta[1] * (grid - c)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.scatter(binned.x, binned.y, s=18, label="Binned mean")
for right, name in [(False, "Below cutoff"), (True, "Above cutoff")]:
    grid, pred = local_line(rd.score.to_numpy(), rd.y.to_numpy(), cutoff, bandwidth, right)
    ax.plot(grid, pred, lw=2, label=name)
ax.axvline(cutoff, color="red", ls="--", label="Cutoff")
ax.set_xlabel("Churn-risk score")
ax.set_ylabel("Customer value ($)")
ax.set_title("RDD Plot: Local Linear Fits")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The plot shows binned means and a local linear fit on each side of the cutoff. The vertical gap between those lines at the cutoff is the RDD estimate. The numerical interval is in the summary above.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Validity Checks
RDD assumptions are falsifiable — we can test them with several diagnostic checks.

1. Manipulation Test (McCrary Density Test)
If units can precisely manipulate their scores to end up on one side of the cutoff, the density of the running variable will jump at the threshold. The McCrary test checks for this.


Code

window = 0.05
left_n = int(((rd.score >= cutoff - window) & (rd.score < cutoff)).sum())
right_n = int(((rd.score >= cutoff) & (rd.score < cutoff + window)).sum())
print(f"Rows in [{cutoff - window:.2f}, {cutoff}): {left_n}")
print(f"Rows in [{cutoff:.2f}, {cutoff + window:.2f}): {right_n}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.hist(rd.score, bins=40, color="#4C78A8", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(cutoff, color="red", ls="--", label="Cutoff")
ax.set_xlabel("Churn-risk score")
ax.set_ylabel("Count")
ax.set_title("Running-variable density")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Rows in [0.65, 0.7): 303
Rows in [0.70, 0.75): 275









The null hypothesis is no manipulation (no jump in density). A significant p-value suggests manipulation, which would violate RDD assumptions.
Note: In our simulated data, there should be no manipulation (p-value > 0.05).


2. Covariate Continuity
Pre-treatment covariates should not jump at the cutoff. If they do, it suggests that units above and below the cutoff differ systematically, violating the local randomization assumption.
Let’s add a covariate (customer tenure) and test its continuity:


Code

rd["tenure"] = 3 + 2 * rd.score + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
tenure_fit = RegressionDiscontinuity(cutoff=cutoff, bandwidth=bandwidth, n_boot=150, random_state=1)
tenure_fit.fit(rd["score"].to_numpy(), rd["tenure"].to_numpy())
print("Covariate continuity (tenure should not jump):")
print(pd.Series(tenure_fit.summary()).round(3))


Covariate continuity (tenure should not jump):

ci_upper          0.083
posterior_mean   -0.016

The effect on tenure should be statistically insignificant (close to zero). If it’s significant, it suggests the cutoff divides different types of customers.


3. Placebo Cutoffs
Estimate the effect at fake cutoffs (e.g., 0.5, 0.6, 0.8). Effects at these placebo cutoffs should be approximately zero.

        f"Cutoff {fake:.2f}: estimate = {summary['estimate']:.3f}, "
        f"interval = [{summary['ci_lower']:.3f}, {summary['ci_upper']:.3f}]"

Check whether the estimate is stable across different bandwidth choices. The estimate should not change dramatically with reasonable bandwidth variations.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Fuzzy RDD
In a sharp RDD, treatment status is deterministic at the cutoff (all units above are treated, all below are untreated). In a fuzzy RDD, crossing the threshold only increases the probability of treatment — some units above may not be treated, and some below may be treated.
For example: - Customers with score ≥ 0.7 should get a call, but not all do (some agents skip calls) - Some customers below the threshold still get calls (exceptions)
In fuzzy RDD, the cutoff becomes an instrument for treatment, and the estimand is a LATE at the cutoff (effect on compliers whose treatment status is moved by the cutoff).


Code

n_fuzzy = 4000
score_fuzzy = rng.uniform(0, 1, n_fuzzy)
p_treat = np.where(score_fuzzy >= cutoff, 0.8, 0.2)
D_fuzzy = rng.binomial(1, p_treat)
y_fuzzy = 40 - 25 * score_fuzzy + 8 * score_fuzzy**2 + TRUE_RD * D_fuzzy + rng.normal(0, 5, n_fuzzy)

jump_y = RegressionDiscontinuity(cutoff=cutoff, bandwidth=bandwidth, n_boot=120, random_state=0)
jump_y.fit(score_fuzzy, y_fuzzy)
jump_d = RegressionDiscontinuity(cutoff=cutoff, bandwidth=bandwidth, n_boot=120, random_state=1)
jump_d.fit(score_fuzzy, D_fuzzy.astype(float))
late = jump_y.effect_ / jump_d.effect_
print(f"Jump in the outcome: {jump_y.effect_:.2f}")
print(f"Jump in treatment probability: {jump_d.effect_:.2f}")
print(f"Fuzzy LATE (ratio of the jumps): {late:.2f}")
print(f"True effect: {TRUE_RD}")


Jump in the outcome: 4.18
Jump in treatment probability: 0.59
Fuzzy LATE (ratio of the jumps): 7.06
True effect: 6.5


The fuzzy RDD estimate is the LATE for compliers — units whose treatment status is actually moved by crossing the cutoff.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Manipulation of the Running Variable
If units can precisely control their score to end up on one side of the cutoff, the local randomization assumption fails.
Examples: - Teachers inflating test scores to get students above a passing threshold - Salespeople nudging order amounts just above a discount threshold
Solution: Compare how many units sit just above and just below the cutoff. A one-sided pile-up means the running variable was manipulated and RDD is not credible.


2. Other Discontinuities at the Cutoff
If other variables jump at the cutoff (e.g., a policy change affecting both treatment and outcome), the effect may be confounded.
Solution: Test covariate continuity and check for co-occurring policy changes.


3. Insufficient Data Near the Cutoff
With too few observations near the cutoff, estimates are unstable and bandwidths become very large (far from local).
Solution: Ensure sufficient sample size. Consider wider cutoff definition or alternative methods.


4. Wrong Functional Form
Using a linear fit when the true relationship is highly non-linear can bias estimates, especially with wide bandwidths.
Solution: Keep the local linear fit and check that the estimate is stable across bandwidths.


5. Extrapolating Beyond the Cutoff
RDD estimates the local effect at the cutoff. It does not license claims about effects far from the threshold.
Example: Finding that a retention call is worth $6.5 for customers at score 0.7 does not mean it’s worth $6.5 for customers at score 0.9 or 0.5.
Solution: Be explicit with stakeholders that the effect is local to the cutoff.

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
When to Use RDD
RDD is the right choice when:

Treatment is assigned by a clear threshold on a continuous score
The threshold is rule-based and transparent
Units cannot precisely manipulate their scores
You have sufficient data near the cutoff
You care about the local effect at the margin (e.g., should we move the threshold?)

Consider alternatives when:

No clear threshold → DiD, SCM, IV
Manipulation is detected → Instrumental variables or other methods
Effect far from cutoff is needed → Extrapolate cautiously or use other methods
Insufficient data near cutoff → Aggregate or use alternative designs

title: 8.3 Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)
text:
Summary
Regression Discontinuity Design is one of the most credible quasi-experimental methods, providing rigorous causal effect estimates when treatment is assigned by a threshold. Its strength lies in the transparency of the local randomization assumption and the extensive falsification tests available.
Key takeaways:

RDD exploits threshold-based treatment assignment to estimate local effects
Units just above and below the cutoff are as good as randomized
Always visualize with binned means before estimation
Fit the local linear jump with RegressionDiscontinuity and check the bandwidth
Run validity checks: manipulation test, covariate continuity, placebo cutoffs
Be explicit that effects are local to the cutoff, not generalizable
Fuzzy RDD handles cases where the cutoff only increases treatment probability

Scientific Terminology
Plain-language definitions for the terms in this tutorial are in the scientific terminology glossary.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text: Python Banner

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Overview

The Core Idea
DiD removes two kinds of bias simultaneously:

Level differences between treated and control groups (e.g., flagship markets are naturally larger)
Common time shocks (seasonality, macro conditions, company-wide changes)

The basic DiD estimator is:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{DiD} = \big(\bar{Y}^{T}_{post} - \bar{Y}^{T}_{pre}\big) - \big(\bar{Y}^{C}_{post} - \bar{Y}^{C}_{pre}\big)
\]
This is literally the difference in differences: the treated group’s change minus the control group’s change.


Business Setting
DiD is ideal when:

Treatment is assigned to some groups (markets, stores, customer segments) at a known point in time
Other groups remain untreated throughout the observation period
You have pre- and post-period outcomes for both groups

Common business examples:

A new store format launches in select markets
A pricing change applies to certain product categories
A marketing campaign runs in specific regions
A training program is rolled out to some departments



The Identifying Assumption: Parallel Trends
The critical assumption for DiD is parallel trends: absent the treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trajectory over time. Level differences are fine — they cancel out when we take differences. But differential trends are fatal.
Important: Parallel trends cannot be proven — it is a claim about an unobservable counterfactual. However, we can probe it by checking that the groups moved in parallel during the pre-treatment period and that divergence occurs precisely at the intervention date.


When DiD Breaks
DiD fails when:

Treated and control groups had different pre-treatment trends (e.g., a struggling division gets the intervention)
Something else happens to only the treated group at the same time as the intervention (common in business where events cluster geographically)
Treatment timing is staggered (groups adopt at different times) with dynamic effects — standard two-way fixed effects regression can produce biased estimates in this case (see the note on staggered adoption below. Chapter 6.5 puts a Bayesian interval on this same regression)



Key Advantages

Intuitive: Easy to explain to non-technical stakeholders
Transparent: The parallel trends assumption is clear and can be visually checked
Flexible: Works with panel data (multiple units over time) and repeated cross-sections
Robust: Handles many confounders as long as they affect both groups similarly over time

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Implementation in Python
DifferenceInDifferences fits \(Y = a + b\,\mathrm{treated} + c\,\mathrm{post} + \tau\,\mathrm{treated}\times\mathrm{post}\) and returns a Bayesian bootstrap interval for \(\tau\). A two-way within estimator is also computed on the simulated panel, because store and week shocks are part of that design. The bootstrap resamples rows. It does not replace clustering at the market, which still matters when only a few markets are treated.
The setup matches the other PyCausalML tutorials: find the repository, import the package, and install the editable checkout only if the import fails.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Simulated Example: Store-Level Rollout
We’ll simulate a retail scenario where a new program launches in some markets but not others. This lets us know the true effect and verify that DiD recovers it.


Code
def make_panel(
    n_stores=120,
    n_markets=12,
    n_weeks=104,                # 2 years of weekly data
    treat_markets=(0, 1, 2, 3), # which markets get the program
    treat_week=60,              # program launch week
    true_effect=8.0,            # true lift in weekly revenue ($k)
    effect_ramp=6,              # weeks for the effect to reach full size
    seed=42,
):
    """Simulate store-week panel data with a known treatment effect."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    stores = np.arange(n_stores)
    markets = stores % n_markets
    
    # Store and market fixed effects
    store_fe = rng.normal(100, 15, n_stores)
    market_fe = rng.normal(0, 8, n_markets)
    store_trend = rng.normal(0.05, 0.03, n_stores)
    
    rows = []
    market_shock = rng.normal(0, 3, (n_markets, n_weeks))
    
    for w in range(n_weeks):
        season = 6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * w / 52)  # yearly seasonality
        for s in stores:
            m = markets[s]
            treated_unit = m in treat_markets
            post = w >= treat_week
            
            # Treatment effect ramps in over effect_ramp weeks
            if treated_unit and post:
                ramp = min(1.0, (w - treat_week + 1) / effect_ramp)
                tau = true_effect * ramp
            else:
                tau = 0.0
            
            # Revenue outcome
            y = (store_fe[s] + market_fe[m] + store_trend[s] * w
                 + season + market_shock[m, w]
                 + tau + rng.normal(0, 4))
            
            rows.append((s, m, w, int(treated_unit), int(post),
                         int(treated_unit and post), y))
    
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[
        "store", "market", "week", "treated", "post", "D", "revenue"])

# Generate the panel
panel = make_panel()
print(panel.head())
print("\nTrue effect at full ramp: $8k/week")

0      0       0     0        1     0  0   99.304
1      1       1     0        1     0  0   84.039
2      2       2     0        1     0  0  119.259
3      3       3     0        1     0  0  129.004
4      4       4     0        0     0  0   75.000

Key columns:

treated — 1 if the store belongs to a market that ever receives the program
post — 1 for weeks at or after launch
D = treated × post — the actual treatment status in each store-week

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
The 2×2 DiD Estimator
Let’s start with the simplest approach: compute the 2×2 table of means and take the difference in differences.


Code
# Group by treatment status and time period
g = (panel.groupby(["treated", "post"]).revenue.mean()
          .unstack("post"))
g.columns = ["pre", "post"]
g["change"] = g["post"] - g["pre"]

print(g)

# DiD estimate
did_2x2 = g.loc[1, "change"] - g.loc[0, "change"]
print(f"\n2×2 DiD estimate: ${did_2x2:.2f}k/week")
print("(True effect at full ramp: $8k/week)")


            pre    post  change
treated                        
0        99.069 101.205   2.136
1       101.875 110.678   8.803

2×2 DiD estimate: $6.67k/week
(True effect at full ramp: $8k/week)


Note that the estimate is below $8k because the effect ramps up over 6 weeks — the post-period average effect is diluted by the ramp. This is realistic: business interventions rarely hit full strength instantly.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
section: Regression DiD with Two-Way Fixed Effects
text:
Regression DiD with Two-Way Fixed Effects
The regression form generalizes the 2×2, allows covariates, and produces standard errors:
\[
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau \, D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
\]
where: - \(\alpha_i\) are store fixed effects (controls for time-invariant differences between stores) - \(\lambda_t\) are week fixed effects (controls for time shocks affecting all stores) - \(D_{it}\) is the store-week treatment indicator - \(\tau\) is the DiD coefficient — our causal effect estimate


Code

did = DifferenceInDifferences(n_boot=200, rope=(-1.0, 1.0), random_state=0)
did.fit(panel["revenue"].to_numpy(), panel["treated"].to_numpy(), panel["post"].to_numpy())
print("Regression DiD:")
print(pd.Series(did.summary()).round(3))


def twfe_coefficient(frame, y, d, unit, time):
    """Treatment coefficient after removing unit means and time means."""
    work = frame[[y, d, unit, time]].copy()
    work["y_dm"] = (
        work[y]
        - work.groupby(unit)[y].transform("mean")
        - work.groupby(time)[y].transform("mean")
        + work[y].mean()
    )
    work["d_dm"] = (
        work[d]
        - work.groupby(unit)[d].transform("mean")
        - work.groupby(time)[d].transform("mean")
        + work[d].mean()
    )
    yd = work["y_dm"].to_numpy()
    dd = work["d_dm"].to_numpy()
    return float(np.dot(dd, yd) / np.dot(dd, dd))


tau_twfe = twfe_coefficient(panel, "revenue", "D", "store", "week")
print(f"Two-way fixed-effects coefficient: ${tau_twfe:.2f}k/week")
print("True full-ramp effect: $8k/week. The post-period average is smaller because the effect ramps in.")
print("The row bootstrap does not cluster by market. With four treated markets, read the interval as optimistic.")


Regression DiD:
estimate           6.668
ci_lower           5.484
ci_upper           7.809
posterior_mean     6.677
rope_probability   0.000
dtype: float64
Two-way fixed-effects coefficient: $6.67k/week
True full-ramp effect: $8k/week. The post-period average is smaller because the effect ramps in.
The row bootstrap does not cluster by market. With four treated markets, read the interval as optimistic.



Three Practical Points

Cluster standard errors at the level of treatment assignment — here, the market, not the store. Treatment varies at the market level, so store-level errors within a market are correlated. Clustering at the store level would dramatically overstate precision.
Few treated clusters is a real problem. With only 4 treated markets, asymptotic clustered SEs are unreliable. Consider randomization/permutation inference or aggregate to the market level.
Covariates should be pre-treatment or time-invariant. Never add post-treatment variables (mediators) — this would bias the estimate by blocking part of the treatment effect.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Testing Parallel Trends
Parallel trends cannot be tested directly — it’s a statement about an unobserved counterfactual. But we can check pre-period trends: if the groups diverged before treatment, parallel trends is violated.


Code
# Compute mean weekly revenue by group
trend = (panel.groupby(["week", "treated"]).revenue.mean()
              .unstack("treated"))

# Plot
ax = trend.plot(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.axvline(60, color="red", ls="--", label="Launch")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean weekly revenue ($k)")
ax.set_xlabel("Week")
ax.legend(["Control markets", "Treated markets", "Launch"])
plt.title("Pre-trend Check: Parallel Trends?")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The pre-period (weeks 0-59) should show the two lines moving in parallel. If they diverge before week 60, parallel trends is violated and DiD is biased.
A formal pre-trend test can be done by interacting the treatment indicator with leads (time before treatment):


Code

pre = panel[panel["post"] == 0]
slopes = {}
for flag, group in pre.groupby("treated"):
    means = group.groupby("week")["revenue"].mean()
    slopes[int(flag)] = float(np.polyfit(means.index.to_numpy(float), means.to_numpy(), 1)[0])

print(f"Pre-period slope, control markets: {slopes[0]:.4f}")
print(f"Pre-period slope, treated markets: {slopes[1]:.4f}")
print(f"Slope gap (treated - control): {slopes[1] - slopes[0]:.4f}")
print("A gap near zero is the pre-period check on parallel trends.")


Pre-period slope, control markets: -0.0559
Pre-period slope, treated markets: -0.0779
Slope gap (treated - control): -0.0220
A gap near zero is the pre-period check on parallel trends.


If the lead coefficients are statistically significant, it suggests pre-existing divergence — a red flag for parallel trends.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Staggered Adoption and Event Studies
In practice, business programs often roll out in waves, not all at once. This is called staggered adoption. With staggered timing and dynamic effects, the standard two-way fixed effects regression can produce biased estimates because it uses already-treated units as controls — introducing “forbidden comparisons.”
Modern practice uses event-study DiD, which estimates effects at each time point relative to the intervention. This serves two purposes:

Pre-trend test: Leads (coefficients before treatment) should be near zero
Dynamic trajectory: Lags trace how the effect evolves over time

Chapter 6.5 fits this regression with the same Bayesian interval on a real banking panel. The pre-trend plot in this notebook is the event-study check for a single adoption date.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Violation of Parallel Trends
If treated and control groups were on different trajectories before treatment, DiD is biased. This often happens when struggling units get the intervention (negative selection) or high-performing units get it first (positive selection).
Solution: Use pre-trend checks and consider alternative methods (synthetic control, RDD) if parallel trends fails.


2. Contemporaneous Shocks
If something else happens to the treated group at the same time as the intervention (e.g., a competitor exits, a local event), DiD will attribute the combined effect to the intervention.
Solution: Maintain an intervention calendar and check for co-occurring events. Use multiple control groups or synthetic control to triangulate.


3. Wrong Clustering Level
Clustering at the wrong level (e.g., store instead of market) leads to incorrect standard errors.
Solution: Always cluster at the level of treatment assignment.


4. Including Post-Treatment Covariates
Adding variables that change after treatment (mediators) blocks part of the treatment effect and biases the estimate.
Solution: Only include pre-treatment or time-invariant covariates.


5. Few Treated Clusters
With few treated groups (< ~40), clustered standard errors are unreliable.
Solution: Use wild-cluster bootstrap, permutation tests, or aggregate to the treatment level.

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
When to Use DiD
DiD is the right choice when:

Treatment is assigned to clear groups at known times
You have pre- and post-period data for both treated and control groups
The parallel trends assumption is plausible (supported by pre-trend checks)
Treatment timing is simultaneous (or you use event-study methods for staggered adoption)

Consider alternatives when:

Parallel trends is violated → Synthetic control, RDD
Treatment is assigned by a threshold → RDD
Treatment is self-selected with confounding → IV, propensity methods
Only one treated unit → Synthetic control

title: 8.1 Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
text:
Summary
DiD is a powerful and intuitive method for estimating causal effects when treatment is assigned to groups at known times. Its strength lies in the transparency of the parallel trends assumption and the ease of communicating results to stakeholders.
Key takeaways:

DiD estimates the difference in changes between treated and control groups
The identifying assumption is parallel trends — check it with pre-trend visualizations and formal tests
Cluster standard errors at the level of treatment assignment
Be cautious with staggered adoption — already-treated units are poor controls when effects change over time
Chapter 6.5 reports the Bayesian interval for this estimator on the CausalPy banking panel
Always probe the assumption with falsification tests

title: 7.3 Policy Forest
text:
Overview

What is Policy Forest?
PyCausalML’s DRPolicyForest is an ensemble of policy trees that:

Learns multiple policy trees on different bootstrap samples or feature subsets
Aggregates predictions across trees to reduce variance and improve stability
Provides uncertainty quantification through bootstrap distributions
Handles complex heterogeneity better than single trees



Key Features

Ensemble method: Combines multiple trees for robustness
Reduced variance: Aggregation reduces overfitting and improves generalization
Uncertainty quantification: Bootstrap provides confidence intervals
Flexible ML models: Can use any scikit-learn compatible model
Robust policy learning: More stable than single policy trees
Visualization: Can plot individual trees for interpretation



Business Setting
Policy Forest is ideal when:

Robustness needed: Single policy trees may overfit
Complex heterogeneity: Treatment effects vary in complex ways
Uncertainty quantification: Need confidence intervals for policy decisions
Large datasets: Sufficient data to support ensemble methods
Binary treatment: Treatment is yes/no

Common business applications:

Large-scale customer targeting
Credit scoring with robust policies
Marketing campaign optimization
Healthcare treatment allocation

def create_policy_data(n_samples=1000, n_features=5, random_state=42):
    """
    Create synthetic data for policy learning.
    
    Treatment effect depends on covariates:
    - Positive effect for high values of X1
    - Negative effect for high values of X2
    """
    np.random.seed(random_state)
    
    # Generate covariates
    X = np.random.normal(0, 1, (n_samples, n_features))
    
    # True CATE: heterogeneous treatment effect
    tau = 2 * X[:, 0] - 1.5 * X[:, 1] + 0.5 * X[:, 2]
    
    # Treatment assignment (depends on covariates)
    propensity = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.5 * X[:, 0] + 0.3 * X[:, 1])))
    T = np.random.binomial(1, propensity)
    
    # Outcome
    Y = 10 + np.sum(X[:, :3], axis=1) + tau * T + np.random.normal(0, 1, n_samples)
    
    # Create DataFrame
    feature_names = [f'X{i}' for i in range(n_features)]
    df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=feature_names)
    df['T'] = T
    df['Y'] = Y
    df['tau_true'] = tau  # true CATE for evaluation
    
    return df

title: 7.3 Policy Forest
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Too Few Trees
With too few trees, the ensemble may not reduce variance sufficiently.
Solution: Use at least 50-100 trees for reliable variance reduction.


2. Overfitting Individual Trees
If individual trees are too deep, they may overfit, and the ensemble may inherit this bias.
Solution: Limit tree depth, increase min_samples_leaf, or use stronger regularization.


3. Computational Cost
Policy forests can be computationally expensive with many trees and large datasets.
Solution: Use fewer trees, limit tree depth, or use subsampling.

Binary treatment: Treatment is yes/no

Small datasets → Single policy tree or simpler methods
Interpretability is paramount → Single policy tree
Computational constraints → Fewer trees or shallower depth
Multi-armed treatment → Multi-arm policy methods

title: 7.1 Policy Tree
text:
Overview

What is the policy tree?
PyCausalML’s DRPolicyTree learns a deterministic binary treatment policy. It cross-fits outcome and propensity models, builds a doubly robust score for each unit, and grows a classification tree on the sign of that score, weighted by its absolute value. Leaves assign treatment where the score is positive.


Key Features

Deterministic policies: Assigns treatment with certainty (0 or 1)
Interpretable rules: Tree structure provides clear decision rules
Based on the IRM score: Uses the same doubly robust score as an interactive regression model
Flexible: Can use any subset of covariates for policy learning
Visualization: The fitted tree can be drawn with scikit-learn



Business Setting
A policy tree is ideal when:

Clear decision rules needed: Stakeholders need interpretable policies
Heterogeneous effects: Treatment effects vary across customer segments
IRM scores are available: You already estimate effects with a doubly robust model
Binary treatment: Treatment is yes/no (not multi-armed)

Common business applications:

Customer targeting for marketing campaigns
Credit approval decisions
Feature rollout decisions
Retention offer targeting

text:
Example: Synthetic Group Effects
The design follows the DoubleML group-effect example. Treatment effects depend on two covariates, with a different effect in each region.


Code
def group_effect(x):
    """Define group-specific treatment effects."""
    if x[0] <= -0.3:
        te = 2.2
    elif (x[0] >= 0.2) & (x[1] >= 0.4):
        te = 2
    else:
        te = -2
    return te

def create_synthetic_group_data(n_samples=200, n_w=10, support_size=5):
    """
    Creates a simple synthetic example for group effects.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    n_samples : int
        Number of samples.
    n_w : int
        Dimension of covariates.
    support_size : int
        Number of relevant covariates.
    
    Returns
    -------
    data : pd.DataFrame
        A data frame with covariates, treatment, and outcome.
    covariates : list
        List of covariate column names.
    """
    np.random.seed(42)
    
    # Outcome support
    support_w = np.random.choice(np.arange(n_w), size=support_size, replace=False)
    coefs_w = np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=support_size)
    epsilon_sample = lambda n: np.random.uniform(-1, 1, size=n_samples)
    
    # Treatment support
    support_t = np.random.choice(np.arange(n_w), size=support_size, replace=False)
    coefs_t = np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=support_size)
    eta_sample = lambda n: np.random.uniform(-1, 1, size=n_samples)

    # Generate covariates
    w = np.random.normal(0, 1, size=(n_samples, n_w))
    
    # Group treatment effect
    te = np.apply_along_axis(group_effect, axis=1, arr=w)
    
    # Treatment assignment
    log_odds = np.dot(w[:, support_t], coefs_t) + eta_sample(n_samples)
    t_sigmoid = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-log_odds))
    t = np.array([np.random.binomial(1, p) for p in t_sigmoid])
    
    # Outcome
    y = te * t + np.dot(w[:, support_w], coefs_w) + epsilon_sample(n_samples)

    # Build dataset
    y_df = pd.DataFrame({'y': y})
    t_df = pd.DataFrame({'t': t})
    w_df = pd.DataFrame(data=w, index=np.arange(w.shape[0]),
                        columns=[f'w_{i}' for i in range(1, w.shape[1] + 1)])

    data = pd.concat([y_df, t_df, w_df], axis=1)
    covariates = list(w_df.columns.values)

    return data, covariates

# Generate data

n_w = 10
support_size = 5

# The same generator, called again, draws a new sample

    n_samples=n_samples, n_w=n_w, support_size=support_size
)
pred = policy_tree.predict(new_data[["w_1", "w_2"]])
pred_df = new_data[["w_1", "w_2", "t", "y"]].copy()
pred_df["pred_treatment"] = pred

print("Policy predictions:")
print(pred_df.head(10))
print(f"Treatment rate: {pred_df['pred_treatment'].mean():.3f}")

title: 7.1 Policy Tree
text:
Understanding the Policy
The policy tree provides interpretable rules:

Leaf nodes: Indicate whether to treat (1) or not treat (0)
Splits: Show the covariate thresholds that define treatment regions
Samples: Number of training samples in each region

In our example, the tree correctly identifies the regions where treatment is beneficial (positive CATE) vs. harmful (negative CATE).

title: 7.1 Policy Tree
text:
Hyperparameter Tuning
Key hyperparameters for policy learning:

depth: Tree depth (controls complexity)
min_samples_leaf: Minimum samples per leaf (controls overfitting)
max_features: Features to consider for splits

Deeper trees can capture more complex patterns but may overfit. Shallower trees are more interpretable but may miss important heterogeneity.


Code
for depth in [2, 3, 4, 5]:
    pt = DRPolicyTree(
        max_depth=depth,
        n_splits=2,
        nuisance="gbr",
        n_estimators=30,
        random_state=42,
    )
    pt.fit(features, t, y)
    rate = pt.predict(features).mean()
    print(
        f"Depth {depth}: treatment rate = {rate:.3f}, "
        f"policy value = {pt.training_policy_value():.3f}"
    )

title: 7.1 Policy Tree
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Overfitting
Deep trees may overfit to noise in the CATE estimates.
Solution: Use shallower trees, cross-validation, or ensemble methods (policy forests).


2. Wrong Feature Selection
Using irrelevant features can lead to poor policies.
Solution: Use domain knowledge or feature importance from the IRM model to select relevant features.


3. Ignoring Uncertainty
Policy trees don’t account for uncertainty in CATE estimates.
Solution: Use policy forests (ensembles) or bootstrap to quantify uncertainty.

title: 7.1 Policy Tree
section: When to use a policy tree
text:
When to use a policy tree
DRPolicyTree is the right choice when:

Interpretable rules needed: Stakeholders need clear decision rules
IRM scores are enough: A single tree on the doubly robust score is the decision rule you want
Binary treatment: Treatment is yes/no
Moderate heterogeneity: Effects vary but not extremely complex

Consider alternatives when:

Complex heterogeneity → Policy forests or neural policies
Multi-armed treatment → Policy forests with multi-arm support
Uncertainty quantification needed → Bootstrap or Bayesian methods

title: 7.1 Policy Tree

Summary
PyCausalML’s policy tree is a simple, interpretable way to turn doubly robust scores into a treatment rule.
Key takeaways:

Policy trees learn deterministic treatment rules from the sign of the doubly robust score
InteractiveRegressionDML estimates the average effect; DRPolicyTree assigns treatment
Provide interpretable decision rules through tree structure
Can use any subset of covariates for policy learning
Deeper trees capture more complexity but may overfit
Always validate policies on held-out data
Consider policy forests for more robust policies

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Overview
Each class reports the same summary keys: estimate (the posterior mean of the point fit’s target coefficient), posterior_mean, ci_lower, ci_upper, and std. Draws stay on draws_. A region of practical equivalence can be passed as rope=(low, high) where the constructor accepts it; the summary then adds the posterior probability that the effect sits inside that band.

What this tutorial covers

The regression or weighting formula for each design, and the posterior attached to it
A simulation in which the design parameter is known, for all five classes
Banks in business in the 6th and 8th Federal Reserve districts, as a difference-in-differences and as a single-series interruption
Age-cell mortality at the minimum legal drinking age
Settler mortality as an instrument for expropriation protection (Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson, 2001)
California Proposition 99 and a synthetic donor pool (Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller, 2010)

The real series are the CausalPy tables in the CausalPy data directory, Apache License 2.0.

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
The algorithms
Throughout, a conjugate Gaussian posterior means the following. The conditional mean is linear, \(Y = X\beta + \varepsilon\), and the prior on the slopes is a ridge of precision \(\lambda\) (prior_precision, default \(10^{-4}\)). The intercept column is almost unpenalized. The posterior of \(\beta\) given the residual variance is normal:
\[
\beta \mid \sigma^2,\; Y \sim N\!\left(\hat\beta,\; \sigma^2 (X^\top X + \Lambda)^{-1}\right),
\]
where \(\Lambda\) is diagonal with \(\lambda\) on the penalized entries and \(\hat\beta\) is the ridge estimate. \(\sigma^2\) is plugged in as the residual variance. Credible intervals are quantiles of draws from that normal. Difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, and interrupted time series use this posterior. The reported effect is one coordinate of \(\beta\).
A Bayesian bootstrap draws Dirichlet weights on the rows and refits the whole procedure under those weights. Instrumental variables and synthetic control use it, so a first-stage or a donor-weight estimation step is inside every draw.

1. Difference-in-differences
For a binary group indicator \(D_i\) and a binary post indicator \(P_t\),
\[
Y_{it} = a + b D_i + c P_t + \tau D_i P_t + \varepsilon_{it}.
\]
Under parallel trends, \(\tau\) is the average treatment effect on the treated: the change in the treated group’s mean, minus the change in the control group’s mean. fit(y, treated, post) builds the four columns and stores the posterior of \(\tau\) (effect_index 3). The class does not add unit fixed effects or cluster the residuals. With many units and a large between-unit variance, the interval describes the residual variance of this saturated regression. Aggregating to the group-time means, or using a two-group panel such as the bank districts below, matches the regression the class actually fits.


2. Regression discontinuity
Let \(R\) be the running variable, \(c\) the cutoff, and \(D = 1\{R \ge c\}\) when treatment is not supplied. Center \(R_c = R - c\). The local linear model is
\[
Y = a + b R_c + \tau D + d R_c D + \varepsilon.
\]
\(\tau\) is the jump at the cutoff. Rows with \(|R_c| > h\) are dropped when bandwidth is set. The window must contain at least four rows. The posterior is the Gaussian posterior of \(\tau\) inside that window. Units that can set \(R\) exactly onto one side of \(c\) violate the design; the posterior does not test that.


3. Interrupted time series
For a single series and an intervention time \(t^\star\),
\[
Y_t = a + b\, t + \tau\, 1\{t \ge t^\star\} + d\, (t - t^\star)_+ + \varepsilon_t,
\]
where \((t - t^\star)_+ = \max(t - t^\star, 0)\). The reported effect is the immediate level shift \(\tau\). The slope change \(d\) is stored as slope_change_. A level shift is identified from the break in the mean after the pre-period trend is partialled out. A second shock that arrives at \(t^\star\) is absorbed into \(\tau\). That is why a control series, when one exists, belongs in the difference-in-differences specification rather than in a second copy of this regression.


4. Instrumental variables
The first stage and the second stage are
\[
\begin{aligned}
D &= \alpha_0 + Z^\top \alpha_1 + X^\top \alpha_2 + \varepsilon_D, \\
Y &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat D + X^\top \beta_2 + \varepsilon_Y.
\end{aligned}
\]
fit(y, treatment, instrument, X=None) runs weighted least squares twice. The point estimate uses equal weights. Each posterior draw draws a Dirichlet weight vector and repeats both stages. \(\beta_1\) is the structural effect, a local average treatment effect when the instrument is binary and the usual monotonicity condition holds. A weak first stage shows up as a wide posterior, because reweighting the rows moves \(\hat D\).
predict(treatment, X) evaluates the second-stage equation at an intervened treatment level. It does not re-solve the first stage.


5. Synthetic control
One treated unit has a pre-period vector \(Y^{\mathrm{pre}}\) and a post-period vector \(Y^{\mathrm{post}}\). Donor matrices \(X^{\mathrm{pre}}\) and \(X^{\mathrm{post}}\) have one column per donor. Weights \(w\) solve
\[
\min_{w \ge 0,\; \sum_j w_j = 1} \sum_{t \in \mathrm{pre}} \omega_t \left(Y^{\mathrm{pre}}_t - X^{\mathrm{pre}}_{t} w\right)^2.
\]
The point fit uses \(\omega_t = 1\). The synthetic post-period path is \(X^{\mathrm{post}} w\), and the reported effect is the mean gap
\[
\hat\tau = \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{post}}} \sum_{t \in \mathrm{post}} \left(Y^{\mathrm{post}}_t - X^{\mathrm{post}}_{t} w\right).
\]
Posterior draws replace \(\omega\) with a Dirichlet draw on the pre-period dates and re-solve the weights. The donor pool is part of the design. Changing it after seeing \(\hat\tau\) changes the target.

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Setup
Estimators are imported from pycausalml.bayesian_causalML. Real datasets are loaded with causalpy.load_data when CausalPy is installed, and from the same CSV on GitHub otherwise.


Code
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

def _repo_root() -> Path:
    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for cand in [here, *here.parents]:
        if (cand / "pyproject.toml").is_file() and (cand / "src" / "pycausalml").is_dir():
            return cand
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "PyCausalML repository was not found. Run this notebook from the repository."
    )

root = _repo_root()
data_dir = root / "Data"
if not data_dir.is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "The Data directory was not found. It should sit next to pyproject.toml."
    )

try:
    import pycausalml  # noqa: F401
    print("PyCausalML ready.")
except ImportError:
    subprocess.check_call(
        [sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "-e", f"{root}[plot]"],
    )
    print("PyCausalML installed.")
print("Data directory:", data_dir)




Code

%matplotlib inline
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from pycausalml.bayesian_causalML import (
    BayesianDifferenceInDifferences,
    BayesianInstrumentalVariable,
    BayesianInterruptedTimeSeries,
    BayesianRegressionDiscontinuity,
    BayesianSyntheticControl,
)
from pycausalml.data import make_iv_data

plt.rcParams["axes.spines.top"] = False
plt.rcParams["axes.spines.right"] = False
CAUSALPY_FILES = {
    "banks": "banks.csv",
    "drinking": "drinking.csv",
    "risk": "AJR2001.csv",
    "schoolReturns": "schoolingReturns.csv",
    "california_prop99": "california_prop99.csv",
}

def load_causalpy(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load a CausalPy example dataset.

    Uses causalpy.load_data when that package is installed. Otherwise reads
    the same CSV from the CausalPy GitHub data directory.
    """
    try:
        import causalpy as cp
        frame = cp.load_data(name)
        print(f"Loaded {name!r} with causalpy.load_data. Shape {frame.shape}.")
        return frame
    except ImportError:
        url = (
            "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pymc-labs/CausalPy/main/causalpy/data/"
            + CAUSALPY_FILES[name]
        )
        frame = pd.read_csv(url)
        print(f"CausalPy is not installed. Loaded {name!r} from")
        print(url)
        print("Install the package with: pip install 'pycausalml[causalpy]'")
        print(f"Shape {frame.shape}.")
        return frame


def show_posterior(draws, estimate, title, truth=None, xlabel="Effect"):
    draws = np.asarray(draws, dtype=float).ravel()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    ax.hist(draws, bins=30, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.9, density=True)
    ax.axvline(estimate, color="#8B1E3F", lw=2, label=f"estimate {estimate:.3f}")
    low, high = np.quantile(draws, [0.025, 0.975])
    ax.axvspan(low, high, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.18, label="95% credible interval")
    if truth is not None:
        ax.axvline(truth, color="black", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"known effect {truth:.3f}")
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Getting started with simulated data
Each simulation writes the design parameter into the outcome and then asks the matching class to recover it. The random number generator is fixed so a second run reprints the same interval.

Difference-in-differences
Half the units are treated. The post period is the second half of a two-period layout, woven through the sample. The interaction equals \(1.5\) and the residual scale is \(0.15\).


Code

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 240
treated = np.repeat([0.0, 1.0], n // 2)
post = np.tile([0.0, 1.0], n // 2)
y_did = 1.0 + 0.2 * treated + 0.3 * post + 1.5 * treated * post + rng.normal(scale=0.15, size=n)
did = BayesianDifferenceInDifferences(n_draws=400, random_state=0)
did.fit(y_did, treated, post)
print(pd.Series(did.summary()).round(3))
show_posterior(did.draws_, did.effect_, "Simulated difference-in-differences", truth=1.5)




Regression discontinuity
The running variable is uniform on \([-1, 1]\). Treatment begins at \(0\). The jump is \(1.2\) and the slope on either side is \(0.4\).


Code

running = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=400)
jump = (running >= 0).astype(float)
y_rd = 0.4 * running + 1.2 * jump + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=400)
rd = BayesianRegressionDiscontinuity(cutoff=0.0, n_draws=400, random_state=0)
rd.fit(running, y_rd)
print(pd.Series(rd.summary()).round(3))
show_posterior(rd.draws_, rd.effect_, "Simulated regression discontinuity", truth=1.2)

grid = np.linspace(-1, 1, 200)
# Local linear mean using the fitted coefficients: intercept, slope, jump, slope change.
coef = rd.coef_
center = grid - rd.cutoff
treated_grid = (grid >= rd.cutoff).astype(float)
mean = coef[0] + coef[1] * center + coef[2] * treated_grid + coef[3] * center * treated_grid
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(running, y_rd, s=10, alpha=0.35, c="#4C72B0")
ax.plot(grid, mean, color="#8B1E3F", lw=2)
ax.axvline(0.0, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Running variable")
ax.set_ylabel("Outcome")
ax.set_title("Jump at the cutoff")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Interrupted time series
Eighty dates. The pre-period slope is \(0.05\). At date 40 the level jumps by \(2\) and the slope does not change.


Code

time = np.arange(80, dtype=float)
y_its = 0.05 * time + np.where(time >= 40, 2.0, 0.0) + rng.normal(scale=0.05, size=80)
its = BayesianInterruptedTimeSeries(n_draws=400, random_state=0)
its.fit(time, y_its, intervention_time=40)
print(pd.Series(its.summary()).round(3))
print("Slope change:", round(its.slope_change_, 3))
show_posterior(its.draws_, its.effect_, "Simulated interrupted time series", truth=2.0)




Instrumental variables
make_iv_data builds a confounded treatment, a valid instrument, and covariates. The structural coefficient in that generator is \(1.5\). The bootstrap uses 80 draws so the notebook stays short; a published interval can use more.


Code

iv_data = make_iv_data(n=800, random_state=1)
iv = BayesianInstrumentalVariable(n_draws=80, random_state=1)
iv.fit(iv_data["Y"], iv_data["W"], iv_data["Z"], iv_data["X"])
print(pd.Series(iv.summary()).round(3))
show_posterior(iv.draws_, iv.effect_, "Simulated instrumental variable", truth=1.5)




Synthetic control
Three donors with weights \((0.2, 0.5, 0.3)\) reproduce the treated pre-period exactly. The post-period gap is a constant \(1\).


Code

pre = rng.normal(size=(12, 3))
weights = np.array([0.2, 0.5, 0.3])
treated_pre = pre @ weights
post_donors = rng.normal(size=(6, 3))
treated_post = post_donors @ weights + 1.0
sc = BayesianSyntheticControl(n_draws=20, random_state=0)
sc.fit(pre, treated_pre, post_donors, treated_post)
print("Donor weights:", np.round(sc.weights_, 3), "sum", round(float(sc.weights_.sum()), 3))
print(pd.Series(sc.summary()).round(3))
show_posterior(sc.draws_, sc.effect_, "Simulated synthetic control", truth=1.0)

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Use case: Federal Reserve districts, 1929–1934
banks records banks in business in the 6th and 8th Federal Reserve districts (Richardson and Troost; Angrist and Pischke, Mastering Metrics). The 6th district changed policy. The 8th district is the comparison. The post period starts in 1931, matching an intervention placed at 1930.5 in the CausalPy notes. The table is aggregated to one median per district-year so each row is the series the design describes.
The difference-in-differences uses both districts. The interrupted time series uses the 6th district alone, on purpose: the Depression is a second shock at the same dates, and a single series folds that shock into the level shift. The contrast between the two fits is the reason to prefer the control district when it exists.


Code

banks = load_causalpy("banks")
yearly = (
    banks.filter(items=["bib6", "bib8", "year"])
    .rename(columns={"bib6": "sixth", "bib8": "eighth"})
    .groupby("year")
    .median()
    .reset_index()
    .sort_values("year")
)
long = yearly.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="district", value_name="banks_open")
long["treated"] = (long["district"] == "sixth").astype(float)
long["post"] = (long["year"] >= 1931).astype(float)
print(yearly.round(1))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(yearly["year"], yearly["sixth"], marker="o", label="6th district", color="#8B1E3F")
ax.plot(yearly["year"], yearly["eighth"], marker="o", label="8th district", color="#4C72B0")
ax.axvline(1930.5, color="black", ls="--", lw=1, label="Intervention")
ax.set_ylabel("Banks in business")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_title("Two Federal Reserve districts")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Code

banks_did = BayesianDifferenceInDifferences(n_draws=400, rope=(-5, 5), random_state=0)
banks_did.fit(long["banks_open"], long["treated"], long["post"])
print("Difference-in-differences, 6th minus 8th after 1930:")
print(pd.Series(banks_did.summary()).round(3))
show_posterior(
    banks_did.draws_,
    banks_did.effect_,
    "Banks in business: DiD",
    xlabel="Change in banks in business",
)

banks_its = BayesianInterruptedTimeSeries(n_draws=400, random_state=0)
banks_its.fit(yearly["year"].to_numpy(float), yearly["sixth"].to_numpy(float), intervention_time=1931)
print("Interrupted series, 6th district alone:")
print(pd.Series(banks_its.summary()).round(3))
print("Slope change:", round(banks_its.slope_change_, 3))
show_posterior(
    banks_its.draws_,
    banks_its.effect_,
    "Banks in business: ITS on the 6th district",
    xlabel="Level shift",
)


Read the DiD posterior as the interaction in a six-year, two-district regression. The ROPE of \(\pm 5\) banks is a scale for “small” relative to a district that has on the order of a hundred banks in business. It is not a clinical or regulatory margin. The ITS level shift on the 6th district does not subtract the path of the 8th. If the two posteriors disagree, the design difference is the reason.

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Use case: mortality at age 21
drinking is the age-cell mortality series from the CausalPy regression-discontinuity example. The running variable is agecell, the midpoint of each age cell in years. The cutoff is the minimum legal drinking age, 21. The outcome is the all-cause death rate all. The bandwidth is one year, so the local linear fit uses cells in \([20, 22]\).


Code

drinking = load_causalpy("drinking")
print("Columns include agecell and all. Age runs from",
      round(float(drinking["agecell"].min()), 2), "to",
      round(float(drinking["agecell"].max()), 2))
rdd = BayesianRegressionDiscontinuity(cutoff=21, bandwidth=1.0, n_draws=400, random_state=0)
rdd.fit(drinking["agecell"].to_numpy(float), drinking["all"].to_numpy(float))
print("Rows inside the one-year window:", rdd.n_window_)
print(pd.Series(rdd.summary()).round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(drinking["agecell"], drinking["all"], s=18, c="#4C72B0")
ax.axvline(21, color="#8B1E3F", ls="--", label="Age 21")
ax.set_xlabel("Age")
ax.set_ylabel("All-cause death rate")
ax.set_title("Death rate by age cell")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
show_posterior(rdd.draws_, rdd.effect_, "Jump in the death rate at age 21", xlabel="Jump at 21")


The jump is the vertical gap between the two local lines at 21, in death-rate units. Ages outside \([20, 22]\) do not enter the posterior. A bandwidth is a design choice: a wider window uses more cells and leans harder on the linear slope.

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Use case: colonial origins
risk is the Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson (2001) country table (AJR2001.csv). Log settler mortality logmort0 is the instrument. Protection against expropriation risk is the endogenous treatment. Log GDP per capita loggdp is the outcome. The exclusion restriction — settler mortality affects present income only through institutions — is disputed. The posterior below is the two-stage least squares posterior under that restriction. It is not a test of the restriction.


Code

ajr = load_causalpy("risk").dropna(subset=["loggdp", "risk", "logmort0"])
print("Countries:", len(ajr))
ajr_iv = BayesianInstrumentalVariable(n_draws=200, random_state=0)
ajr_iv.fit(ajr["loggdp"].to_numpy(float), ajr["risk"].to_numpy(float), ajr["logmort0"].to_numpy(float))
print(pd.Series(ajr_iv.summary()).round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.scatter(ajr["logmort0"], ajr["risk"], s=28, c="#4C72B0")
ax.set_xlabel("Log settler mortality")
ax.set_ylabel("Expropriation protection")
ax.set_title("First-stage cloud")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
show_posterior(
    ajr_iv.draws_,
    ajr_iv.effect_,
    "Log GDP on expropriation protection",
    xlabel="IV coefficient",
)

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Use case: California Proposition 99
california_prop99 is annual per-capita cigarette sales for 39 states, 1970–2000 (Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller, 2010). California raised the cigarette tax in 1989. The other states are the donor pool. Weights are nonnegative and sum to one. The point estimate matches the pre-1989 path with equal date weights. Bootstrap draws that match California less well on some pre-period years can move the mean gap, so the posterior mean need not equal the point estimate.


Code

prop = load_causalpy("california_prop99").set_index("Year").sort_index().astype(float)
treated_name = "California"
pre_years = prop.index < 1989
donors = prop.drop(columns=[treated_name])
synth = BayesianSyntheticControl(n_draws=25, random_state=0)
synth.fit(
    donors.loc[pre_years].to_numpy(),
    prop.loc[pre_years, treated_name].to_numpy(),
    donors.loc[~pre_years].to_numpy(),
    prop.loc[~pre_years, treated_name].to_numpy(),
)
weights = pd.Series(synth.weights_, index=donors.columns, name="weight")
print(weights.sort_values(ascending=False).head(8).round(3))
print("Average post-1988 gap, packs per capita:")
print(pd.Series(synth.summary()).round(2))

synth_pre = donors.loc[pre_years].to_numpy() @ synth.weights_
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(prop.index, prop[treated_name], label="California", color="#8B1E3F")
ax.plot(
    list(prop.index[pre_years]) + list(prop.index[~pre_years]),
    np.concatenate([synth_pre, synth.synth_post_]),
    label="Synthetic California",
    color="#4C72B0",
)
ax.axvline(1989, color="black", ls="--", lw=1, label="Proposition 99")
ax.set_ylabel("Cigarette packs per capita")
ax.set_title("California and its synthetic control")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
show_posterior(
    synth.draws_,
    synth.effect_,
    "Mean post-1988 gap",
    xlabel="Packs per capita",
)



How to read a quasi-experimental posterior

The interval is the uncertainty of the design coefficient under the likelihood the class uses. Parallel trends, no manipulation of the running variable, a isolated interruption, a valid instrument, and a fixed donor pool are outside that likelihood.
Difference-in-differences here is the four-term regression. It does not cluster by state or county and it does not fit staggered adoption.
A synthetic-control posterior recenters donor weights. It does not add a new donor.
Pre-period fit, density at the cutoff, and the first-stage coefficient are the checks that decide whether the posterior is worth quoting.

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Summary and conclusion
The five classes share a summary and differ in the column they call the effect. Difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, and interrupted time series draw that column from a ridge-normal posterior. Instrumental variables and synthetic control redraw the whole procedure under Dirichlet weights so the first stage, or the donor weights, moves with the data.
Simulations with a known jump, level shift, IV coefficient, interaction, and post-period gap recover those constants inside the plotted intervals. The bank panel shows the same years as a two-district interaction and as a single-series level shift. The drinking-age jump, the AJR two-stage coefficient, and the Proposition 99 gap are the same summaries on the CausalPy tables, each with the design assumption written next to the histogram.

title: 6.4 Bayesian Quasi-Experiments
text:
Scientific terminology







Term
Meaning in this notebook




ATT
Average treatment effect on the treated. In the DiD regression it is \(\tau\) on \(D \times P\).


Parallel trends
Absent treatment, the treated and control means would have changed by the same amount.


Running variable
The score that assigns treatment when it crosses a cutoff.


Bandwidth
The window around the cutoff that enters the local linear fit.


Level shift
The immediate change in the mean at an intervention date, after the pre-period slope.


LATE
Local average treatment effect: the IV coefficient for units whose treatment responds to the instrument.


Bayesian bootstrap
Dirichlet weights on rows or on pre-period dates. Each weighted refit is one draw.


Donor pool
The untreated units allowed a positive weight in the synthetic control.


ROPE
A band of effects treated as practically small. The summary reports the posterior probability of that band.
