title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
Overview

Why start with a graph?
Regression of \(Y\) on \(T\) estimates \(E[Y \mid T]\). An intervention asks for \(E[Y \mid do(T)]\). Those two agree when every open path from \(T\) to \(Y\) is a directed causal path. A common cause, a conditioned collider, or a mediator left out of the graph changes the functional.
The graph in this module is a directed acyclic graph. An edge (parent, child) means the parent is a direct cause of the child. Once the graph is drawn, identification treats it as causally sufficient: a latent confounder has to appear as a node, or the adjustment set is the adjustment set of a different system. A cycle raises ValueError.


What this tutorial covers

d-separation on the chain, the fork, and the collider
The backdoor criterion, the frontdoor criterion, and the definition of an instrument
A linear-Gaussian network whose total effect is known, compared with the naive regression
A discrete network in which do(T) and conditioning on \(T\) answer different questions
The frontdoor functional, computed from \((T, M, Y)\) alone and checked against a do query
Backdoor regression and graph-based instrumental variables on simulated systems with a known effect
The Sachs flow-cytometry measurements in Data/sachs_data.csv, with a published protein-signaling skeleton

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
The algorithms

1. d-separation
Let \(G\) be a DAG. A path between \(X\) and \(Y\) is blocked by a conditioning set \(Z\) when one of these holds:

the path contains a chain \(A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C\) or a fork \(A \leftarrow B \rightarrow C\) and \(B \in Z\)
the path contains a collider \(A \rightarrow B \leftarrow C\) and neither \(B\) nor any descendant of \(B\) is in \(Z\)

\(X\) and \(Y\) are d-separated by \(Z\) when every path between them is blocked. CausalGraph.d_separated implements the equivalent moral-graph test: take the ancestors of \(X \cup Y \cup Z\), moralize that subgraph (join co-parents, drop arrowheads), delete \(Z\), and ask whether any node of \(X\) still meets any node of \(Y\).
The three canonical graphs fix the reading of every later criterion.









Graph
Edges
\(A \perp C\) with \(Z = \emptyset\)
\(A \perp C\) given \(B\)




Chain
\(A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C\)
open
blocked


Fork
\(A \leftarrow B \rightarrow C\)
open
blocked


Collider
\(A \rightarrow B \leftarrow C\)
blocked
open



Conditioning on a collider, or on a descendant of a collider, opens a path that was closed.


2. Backdoor adjustment
A set \(Z\) satisfies the backdoor criterion for \((T, Y)\) when

\(Z\) contains neither \(T\) nor \(Y\)
no node of \(Z\) is a descendant of \(T\)
\(Z\) blocks every path from \(T\) to \(Y\) in the graph with the arrows out of \(T\) removed

Condition 3 is d-separation in the mutilated graph. Removing the arrows out of \(T\) deletes the causal paths, so the test only looks at backdoor paths.
When \(Z\) qualifies and the conditional expectations exist,
\[
E[Y \mid do(T=t)] = \sum_z E[Y \mid T=t, Z=z] \, P(Z=z).
\]
adjustment_sets searches the empty set, the parents of \(T\), and other subsets of the non-descendants of \(T\). It returns the inclusion-minimal sets that pass the criterion. minimal_adjustment_set returns one smallest set. An empty result means the observed graph does not identify the effect by adjustment.


3. Frontdoor criterion
A mediator set \(M\) satisfies Pearl’s frontdoor criterion for \((T, Y)\) when

\(M\) intercepts every directed path from \(T\) to \(Y\)
there is no unblocked backdoor path from \(T\) to \(M\)
\(T\) blocks every backdoor path from \(M\) to \(Y\)

The identifying functional uses only the observational distribution of \((T, M, Y)\):
\[
P(y \mid do(t)) = \sum_m P(m \mid t) \sum_{t'} P(y \mid m, t') \, P(t').
\]
frontdoor_sets returns mediator sets that meet the criterion. The class identifies the set. The notebook computes the functional from the sample, because a latent common cause of \(T\) and \(Y\) is not entered into the regression.


4. Instruments read from the graph
A node \(Z\) is an instrument for \((T, Y)\) when there is a directed path from \(Z\) to \(T\), and \(Z\) is d-separated from \(Y\) in the graph with \(T\) removed. The second clause is the exclusion restriction as drawn: every directed path from \(Z\) to \(Y\) goes through \(T\). instruments returns those nodes. A direct edge \(Z \rightarrow Y\) removes \(Z\) from the list.


5. Linear-Gaussian Bayesian network
Each node has the structural assignment
\[
X_i = a_i + \sum_{j \in \mathrm{pa}(i)} \beta_{ij} X_j + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma_i^2),
\]
with independent noise across equations. GaussianBayesianNetwork.fit places a weak ridge prior on the slopes (the intercept is almost unpenalized) and returns the conjugate normal posterior of each equation. The noise variance is the residual variance, so the coefficient posterior is the usual conditional normal posterior given that variance.
A hard intervention \(do(T=t)\) replaces the equation for \(T\) with the constant \(t\). In a linear system the average treatment effect is the total derivative along directed paths:
\[
E[Y \mid do(T=t_1)] - E[Y \mid do(T=t_0)] = (t_1 - t_0) \sum_{\text{paths } T \rightsquigarrow Y} \prod_{(j \rightarrow i) \in \text{path}} \beta_{ij}.
\]
ate evaluates that derivative by a topological accumulation, once at the posterior means and once for each draw of the coefficient vector. sample(do=...) draws from the posterior-mean equations with the intervened node clamped. The draws are a predictive check of the same linear effect. They are not a second posterior.


6. Discrete Bayesian network
Each conditional distribution is categorical. With a Dirichlet prior of concentration \(\alpha\) on every parent configuration, the posterior mean of a cell is
\[
\hat P(X_i = k \mid \mathrm{pa}(i) = j) = \frac{n_{jk} + \alpha}{n_{j\cdot} + \alpha \, |\mathcal{X}_i|}.
\]
query marginalizes this conditional probability table. Exact enumeration is used when the joint table has at most exact_limit cells (default 8192). Larger joints use likelihood weighting. A do map replaces that node’s conditional with a point mass and does not multiply the query weight by the observational conditional. An evidence map keeps the conditional and reweights by it. A node cannot be both.
For a numeric outcome,
\[
\mathrm{ATE} = E[Y \mid do(T=t_1)] - E[Y \mid do(T=t_0)].
\]
ate returns that contrast. It does not return a posterior interval: the conditional probabilities are posterior means, and the query is a function of those means.


7. Naive adjustment and naive instrumental variables
NaiveAdjustmentRegressor calls minimal_adjustment_set and fits
\[
Y = a + \tau T + Z^\top \gamma + \varepsilon
\]
with the same ridge-normal posterior. The reported effect is the posterior of \(\tau\). Under the graph, linearity, and constant effects, \(\tau\) is \(E[Y \mid do(T=1)] - E[Y \mid do(T=0)]\).
NaiveIVRegressor calls instruments. If the list is empty it raises ValueError. Otherwise it fits Bayesian two-stage least squares: Dirichlet weights on the rows, weighted least squares of \(T\) on \(Z\), then weighted least squares of \(Y\) on the fitted \(\hat T\). The first-stage uncertainty is inside the second-stage draws. This is the native counterpart of pgmpy’s NaiveIVRegressor. Covariates that are not instruments are not entered; a confounder that the graph says must be controlled belongs in NaiveAdjustmentRegressor or in BayesianStructuralSCM.

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
Setup
This notebook fits the graph and network classes from PyCausalML (pycausalml.bayesian_causalML). The setup finds the repository, imports the package, and installs the editable checkout only if the import fails.


Code
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

def _repo_root() -> Path:
    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for cand in [here, *here.parents]:
        if (cand / "pyproject.toml").is_file() and (cand / "src" / "pycausalml").is_dir():
            return cand
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "PyCausalML repository was not found. Run this notebook from the repository."
    )

root = _repo_root()
data_dir = root / "Data"
if not data_dir.is_dir():
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        "The Data directory was not found. It should sit next to pyproject.toml."
    )

try:
    import pycausalml  # noqa: F401
    print("PyCausalML ready.")
except ImportError:
    subprocess.check_call(
        [sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "-e", f"{root}[plot]"],
    )
    print("PyCausalML installed.")
print("Data directory:", data_dir)




Code

%matplotlib inline
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from pycausalml.bayesian_causalML import (
    CausalGraph,
    DiscreteBayesianNetwork,
    GaussianBayesianNetwork,
    NaiveAdjustmentRegressor,
    NaiveIVRegressor,
)

plt.rcParams["axes.spines.top"] = False
plt.rcParams["axes.spines.right"] = False


def show_posterior(draws, estimate, title, truth=None):
    draws = np.asarray(draws, dtype=float).ravel()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    ax.hist(draws, bins=30, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.9, density=True)
    ax.axvline(estimate, color="#8B1E3F", lw=2, label=f"posterior mean of the fit {estimate:.3f}")
    low, high = np.quantile(draws, [0.025, 0.975])
    ax.axvspan(low, high, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.18, label="95% credible interval")
    if truth is not None:
        ax.axvline(truth, color="black", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"known effect {truth:.3f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Effect")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    return pd.Series({"estimate": estimate, "ci_lower": low, "ci_upper": high})

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
section: Getting started: identification on the canonical graphs
text:
Getting started: identification on the canonical graphs
The first checks have no data. They confirm that CausalGraph blocks and opens the paths the criteria use.


Code

chain = CausalGraph([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")])
fork = CausalGraph([("B", "A"), ("B", "C")])
collider = CausalGraph([("A", "B"), ("C", "B")])

rows = [
    ("chain", chain.d_separated("A", "C"), chain.d_separated("A", "C", "B")),
    ("fork", fork.d_separated("A", "C"), fork.d_separated("A", "C", "B")),
    ("collider", collider.d_separated("A", "C"), collider.d_separated("A", "C", "B")),
]
print(pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["graph", "separated_without_B", "separated_given_B"]).to_string(index=False))

confounded = CausalGraph([("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")])
print("Backdoor sets for T -> Y:", confounded.adjustment_sets("T", "Y"))
print("Smallest set:", confounded.minimal_adjustment_set("T", "Y"))
print("Empty set is a backdoor set:", confounded.satisfies_backdoor("T", "Y", []))

frontdoor = CausalGraph([("U", "T"), ("U", "Y"), ("T", "M"), ("M", "Y")])
print("Frontdoor sets:", frontdoor.frontdoor_sets("T", "Y"))

instrument = CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("U", "T"), ("U", "Y"), ("T", "Y")])
leaked = CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("T", "Y"), ("Z", "Y")])
print("Instruments when Z is excluded from Y:", instrument.instruments("T", "Y"))
print("Instruments when Z also points at Y:", leaked.instruments("T", "Y"))


The chain and the fork are open until \(B\) is conditioned on. The collider is closed until \(B\) is conditioned on. In the confounded graph the smallest backdoor set is \(\{C\}\). The empty set fails because \(C\) leaves \(T \leftarrow C \rightarrow Y\) open. In the frontdoor graph \(\{M\}\) is the mediator set, and \(U\) is not an instrument. Adding \(Z \rightarrow Y\) removes \(Z\) from the instrument list.

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
section: Getting started: a linear-Gaussian network with a known effect
text:
Getting started: a linear-Gaussian network with a known effect
The structural assignments are
\[
C \sim N(0,1), \qquad T = 0.5\, C + \varepsilon_T, \qquad Y = 1.5\, T - 0.7\, C + \varepsilon_Y,
\]
with \(\varepsilon_T, \varepsilon_Y \sim N(0, 0.4^2)\). The interventional effect of a unit change in \(T\) is \(1.5\). The observational regression of \(Y\) on \(T\) also picks up the backdoor through \(C\), so its slope is not \(1.5\).


Code

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 3000
confounder = rng.normal(size=n)
treatment = 0.5 * confounder + rng.normal(scale=0.4, size=n)
outcome = 1.5 * treatment - 0.7 * confounder + rng.normal(scale=0.4, size=n)
frame = pd.DataFrame({"C": confounder, "T": treatment, "Y": outcome})

naive = np.linalg.lstsq(
    np.column_stack([np.ones(n), treatment]), outcome, rcond=None
)[0][1]

gauss = GaussianBayesianNetwork(
    [("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")], n_draws=300, random_state=0
)
gauss.fit(frame)
ate = gauss.ate("T", "Y", treated=1.0, control=0.0)
print(f"Naive slope of Y on T: {naive:.3f}")
print("Gaussian network ATE:")
print(pd.Series(ate).round(3))
show_posterior(gauss.draws_, ate["estimate"], "Linear-Gaussian network", truth=1.5)

do1 = gauss.sample(4000, do={"T": 1.0}, random_state=1)
do0 = gauss.sample(4000, do={"T": 0.0}, random_state=2)
print(f"Sample contrast E[Y|do(T=1)] - E[Y|do(T=0)]: {(do1['Y'].mean() - do0['Y'].mean()):.3f}")


The posterior interval covers \(1.5\). The naive slope does not. sample clamps \(T\) and redraws \(C\) and \(Y\) from the fitted equations, so the Monte Carlo contrast estimates the same linear effect.

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
Getting started: intervention versus conditioning
Binary variables with a fork at \(C\):
\[
P(T=1 \mid C=1) = 0.9, \quad P(T=1 \mid C=0) = 0.1,
\]
\[
P(Y=1 \mid T, C) = 0.1 + 0.2\, T + 0.6\, C.
\]
The interventional contrast \(E[Y \mid do(T=1)] - E[Y \mid do(T=0)]\) equals \(0.2\), because \(do(T)\) deletes the arrow \(C \rightarrow T\) and the remaining coefficient on \(T\) is \(0.2\). Conditioning on \(T=1\) leaves \(C\) associated with \(T\), so \(P(Y=1 \mid T=1)\) is larger than \(P(Y=1 \mid do(T=1))\).


Code

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 8000
confounder = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, size=n)
treatment = rng.binomial(1, np.where(confounder == 1, 0.9, 0.1))
probability = 0.1 + 0.2 * treatment + 0.6 * confounder
outcome = rng.binomial(1, probability)
binary = pd.DataFrame({"C": confounder, "T": treatment, "Y": outcome})

discrete = DiscreteBayesianNetwork(
    [("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")], alpha=0.5, random_state=0
)
discrete.fit(binary)
print("ATE from do-queries:")
print(pd.Series(discrete.ate("T", "Y", treated=1, control=0)).round(3))

interventional = discrete.query("Y", do={"T": 1})["distributions"]["Y"][1]
conditional = discrete.query("Y", evidence={"T": 1})["distributions"]["Y"][1]
print(f"P(Y=1 | do(T=1)) = {interventional:.3f}")
print(f"P(Y=1 | T=1)     = {conditional:.3f}")
print("Query method:", discrete.query("Y", do={"T": 1})["method"])
print(discrete.cpd("Y").round(3))

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
Getting started: the frontdoor functional
Simulate the graph \(U \rightarrow T\), \(U \rightarrow Y\), \(T \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\), with no direct arrow \(T \rightarrow Y\). The do query on a network that still contains \(U\) is the target. The frontdoor formula is then computed from the counts of \((T, M, Y)\) only.


Code

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 8000
latent = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, size=n)
treatment = rng.binomial(1, np.where(latent == 1, 0.8, 0.2))
mediator = rng.binomial(1, np.where(treatment == 1, 0.85, 0.15))
y_prob = np.where(mediator == 1, 0.15 + 0.55 * latent, 0.05 + 0.15 * latent)
outcome = rng.binomial(1, y_prob)
front = pd.DataFrame({"U": latent, "T": treatment, "M": mediator, "Y": outcome})

front_graph = CausalGraph([("U", "T"), ("U", "Y"), ("T", "M"), ("M", "Y")])
print("Frontdoor sets:", front_graph.frontdoor_sets("T", "Y"))

full = DiscreteBayesianNetwork(
    [("U", "T"), ("U", "Y"), ("T", "M"), ("M", "Y")], alpha=0.5, random_state=0
)
full.fit(front)
target = full.ate("T", "Y", treated=1, control=0)["estimate"]


def frontdoor_ate(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    # Pearl's frontdoor contrast for binary T, M, Y. The latent U is not used.
    t = data["T"].to_numpy()
    m = data["M"].to_numpy()
    y = data["Y"].to_numpy()

    def pt(value):
        return float(np.mean(t == value))

    def pm_given_t(m_value, t_value):
        selected = t == t_value
        return float(np.mean(m[selected] == m_value))

    def py_given_mt(y_value, m_value, t_value):
        selected = (m == m_value) & (t == t_value)
        return float(np.mean(y[selected] == y_value))

    def mean_y(t_value):
        total = 0.0
        for m_value in (0, 1):
            inner = 0.0
            for t_prime in (0, 1):
                inner += py_given_mt(1, m_value, t_prime) * pt(t_prime)
            total += pm_given_t(m_value, t_value) * inner
        return total

    return mean_y(1) - mean_y(0)


print(f"ATE from the network that still contains U: {target:.3f}")
print(f"ATE from the frontdoor formula on (T, M, Y): {frontdoor_ate(front):.3f}")

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
section: Getting started: adjustment and instrumental variables
text:
Getting started: adjustment and instrumental variables
Two linear systems with effect \(1.5\). The first is the backdoor graph \(C \rightarrow T\), \(C \rightarrow Y\), \(T \rightarrow Y\). The second is \(Z \rightarrow T \rightarrow Y\) with a latent common cause of \(T\) and \(Y\) that is present in the data-generating process and absent from \(Z\)’s exclusion path.


Code

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2500
confounder = rng.normal(size=n)
treatment = 0.8 * confounder + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)
outcome = 1.5 * treatment + 1.2 * confounder + rng.normal(scale=0.4, size=n)
adjust_frame = pd.DataFrame({"C": confounder, "T": treatment, "Y": outcome})
adjusted = NaiveAdjustmentRegressor(
    CausalGraph([("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")]),
    "T",
    "Y",
    n_draws=400,
    random_state=0,
)
adjusted.fit(adjust_frame)
print("Adjustment set:", adjusted.adjustment_set_)
print(pd.Series(adjusted.summary_).round(3))
show_posterior(adjusted.draws_, adjusted.effect_, "Naive adjustment", truth=1.5)

instrument = rng.normal(size=n)
latent = rng.normal(size=n)
endogenous = 0.9 * instrument + 0.7 * latent + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
response = 1.5 * endogenous + 0.8 * latent + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
iv_frame = pd.DataFrame({"Z": instrument, "T": endogenous, "Y": response})
iv_graph = CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("T", "Y")])
print("Instruments on the drawn graph:", iv_graph.instruments("T", "Y"))
naive_iv = NaiveIVRegressor(iv_graph, "T", "Y", n_draws=80, random_state=0)
naive_iv.fit(iv_frame)
print("Instruments:", naive_iv.instruments_)
print(pd.Series(naive_iv.summary_).round(3))
show_posterior(naive_iv.draws_, naive_iv.effect_, "Naive IV", truth=1.5)



Key parameters








Parameter
Class
Role




edges
graph, both networks
(parent, child) pairs. A cycle is rejected.


prior_precision
Gaussian network, adjustment
Ridge penalty on slopes. The default is a weak prior.


n_draws
Gaussian network, adjustment, IV
Number of posterior draws for the interval.


alpha
discrete network
Dirichlet concentration added to every cell.


exact_limit
discrete network
Largest joint table that is summed exactly.


random_state
all stochastic fits
Seed for posterior draws and likelihood weighting.

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
section: Use case: the Sachs protein-signaling network
text:
Use case: the Sachs protein-signaling network
The measurements are the flow-cytometry sample shipped as Data/sachs_data.csv: 11 phosphoproteins and phospholipids, one row per cell. Sachs et al. (2005) introduced this system as a Bayesian-network benchmark. This notebook does not rediscover the edges. It conditions on a standard published skeleton — the same directed edges used with the Sachs sample in the bnlearn documentation — and asks two questions the classes are built to answer.

Which observed proteins form a backdoor set for the effect of Mek on Erk?
What is the posterior of that total effect on the log scale, and how does the single-protein regression compare?

Proteins are analyzed as \(\log x\). The Gaussian effect is then a log-log slope: the percent change in Erk associated with a one-percent interventional change in Mek, along the directed paths in this skeleton. Erk’s other parent in the skeleton is PKA, and every backdoor from Mek into Erk passes through PKA, so the smallest adjustment set is {pka}.

Data
Eleven columns: raf, mek, plc, pip2, pip3, erk, akt, pka, pkc, p38, jnk. Values are continuous abundances. There is no treatment indicator in the file. The intervention is the do operator on the fitted structural equations.


Code

sachs = pd.read_csv(data_dir / "sachs_data.csv")
print("Shape:", sachs.shape)
print(sachs.describe().T[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(2))

proteins = ["plc", "pip2", "pip3", "pkc", "pka", "raf", "mek", "erk", "akt", "p38", "jnk"]
sachs_log = np.log(sachs[proteins].clip(lower=1e-6))
sachs_log.describe().T[["mean", "std"]].round(3)




Data visualization


Code

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].scatter(sachs_log["mek"], sachs_log["erk"], s=6, alpha=0.25, c="#4C72B0")
axes[0].set_xlabel("log Mek")
axes[0].set_ylabel("log Erk")
axes[0].set_title("Observational cloud")
axes[1].scatter(sachs_log["pka"], sachs_log["erk"], s=6, alpha=0.25, c="#8B1E3F")
axes[1].set_xlabel("log PKA")
axes[1].set_ylabel("log Erk")
axes[1].set_title("PKA is Erk's other parent in the skeleton")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()




The skeleton and the adjustment set
Edges point from the upstream kinase or phospholipid to its published target. CausalGraph rejects the list if it contains a cycle.


Code

sachs_edges = [
    ("pkc", "pka"), ("pkc", "raf"), ("pkc", "mek"), ("pkc", "jnk"), ("pkc", "p38"),
    ("pka", "raf"), ("pka", "mek"), ("pka", "erk"), ("pka", "akt"), ("pka", "jnk"), ("pka", "p38"),
    ("raf", "mek"), ("mek", "erk"),
    ("plc", "pkc"), ("plc", "pip3"), ("plc", "pip2"),
    ("pip3", "pip2"), ("pip2", "pkc"), ("pip3", "akt"),
]
sachs_graph = CausalGraph(sachs_edges)
print("Nodes in topological order:", sachs_graph.nodes)
print("Parents of Mek:", sachs_graph.parents("mek"))
print("Parents of Erk:", sachs_graph.parents("erk"))
print("Minimal backdoor set, Mek -> Erk:", sachs_graph.minimal_adjustment_set("mek", "erk"))
print("All minimal backdoor sets:", sachs_graph.adjustment_sets("mek", "erk"))
print("Instruments for Mek -> Erk:", sachs_graph.instruments("mek", "erk"))
print("Frontdoor sets:", sachs_graph.frontdoor_sets("mek", "erk"))

adjacency = sachs_graph.adjacency()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 5.5))
image = ax.imshow(adjacency.to_numpy(), cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(adjacency.columns)))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(adjacency.index)))
ax.set_xticklabels(adjacency.columns, rotation=90)
ax.set_yticklabels(adjacency.index)
ax.set_title("Adjacency: row child, column parent")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The instrument list is empty: no protein reaches Mek only through a path that is blocked from Erk once Mek is deleted. The frontdoor list is empty: Mek’s only directed path to Erk is the direct edge, and that edge is not a mediator set. Identification is by adjustment. The smallest set is PKA.


Gaussian network and backdoor regression


Code

sachs_net = GaussianBayesianNetwork(sachs_edges, n_draws=300, random_state=0)
sachs_net.fit(sachs_log)
sachs_ate = sachs_net.ate("mek", "erk")
print("Total effect of log Mek on log Erk:")
print(pd.Series(sachs_ate).round(3))

erk_equation = sachs_net.equations_["erk"]
print("Erk equation features:", erk_equation["feature_names"])
print("Erk posterior-mean coefficients:", np.round(erk_equation["coef"], 3))

naive_slope = np.linalg.lstsq(
    np.column_stack([np.ones(len(sachs_log)), sachs_log["mek"]]),
    sachs_log["erk"],
    rcond=None,
)[0][1]
print(f"Naive slope of log Erk on log Mek: {naive_slope:.3f}")

sachs_adj = NaiveAdjustmentRegressor(
    sachs_graph, "mek", "erk", n_draws=400, random_state=0
)
sachs_adj.fit(sachs_log)
print("Backdoor set:", sachs_adj.adjustment_set_)
print(pd.Series(sachs_adj.summary_).round(3))
show_posterior(
    sachs_net.draws_,
    sachs_ate["estimate"],
    "Sachs skeleton: total effect of Mek on Erk",
)


Mek’s only child in this skeleton is Erk, so the total effect equals the direct coefficient on Mek in the Erk equation. The backdoor regression of Erk on Mek and PKA estimates that same coefficient. The single-protein slope is close to it in this sample: the observational association of Mek and Erk is not dominated by the PKA backdoor. Closeness is a result about these measurements. It is not a reason to skip the graph. A different skeleton, or a different pair of proteins, moves the two numbers apart, as the simulated fork did.


A discrete slice of the same cells
Dichotomize PKA, Mek, and Erk at their medians and fit the fork pka → mek, pka → erk, mek → erk. The outcome is a 0/1 label, so ate is a difference in probabilities, not a log-abundance slope. The comparison that matters is do(mek=1) against conditioning on mek=1.


Code

discrete_sachs = pd.DataFrame({
    "pka": (sachs_log["pka"] >= sachs_log["pka"].median()).astype(int),
    "mek": (sachs_log["mek"] >= sachs_log["mek"].median()).astype(int),
    "erk": (sachs_log["erk"] >= sachs_log["erk"].median()).astype(int),
})
slice_net = DiscreteBayesianNetwork(
    [("pka", "mek"), ("pka", "erk"), ("mek", "erk")], alpha=1.0, random_state=0
)
slice_net.fit(discrete_sachs)
print(pd.Series(slice_net.ate("mek", "erk", treated=1, control=0)).round(3))
print(
    "P(Erk high | do(Mek high)) =",
    round(slice_net.query("erk", do={"mek": 1})["distributions"]["erk"][1], 3),
)
print(
    "P(Erk high | Mek high)     =",
    round(slice_net.query("erk", evidence={"mek": 1})["distributions"]["erk"][1], 3),
)




How to read the Sachs fit
In the median-split slice, \(P(\text{Erk high} \mid do(\text{Mek high}))\) and \(P(\text{Erk high} \mid \text{Mek high})\) are nearly the same. The simulated fork is the case where those two probabilities separate. The dichotomized Sachs slice is a weak fork, which is a result about the split, not a reason to skip the comparison.

The adjacency matrix is an assumption. ate propagates coefficient uncertainty through that assumption. It does not propagate uncertainty about which edges exist.
The credible interval is a statement about the linear coefficients given the skeleton and the ridge prior. A nonlinear dependence among the proteins is outside the model.
Median splits throw away the abundance scale. Use them to compare do with conditioning. Use the Gaussian network for the log-log effect.
An empty instrument list is a finding about this skeleton. It says the file, under these edges, does not contain a protein that can be an instrument for Mek.

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
Summary and conclusion
CausalGraph answers the identification question before any likelihood is fit: which set blocks the backdoors, which mediators satisfy the frontdoor criterion, and which nodes are instruments. GaussianBayesianNetwork turns a linear skeleton into a posterior for \(E[Y \mid do(T)]\). DiscreteBayesianNetwork keeps the distinction between clamping a node and conditioning on it. NaiveAdjustmentRegressor and NaiveIVRegressor are the two regressions those criteria license, with a normal or Bayesian-bootstrap posterior on the coefficient.
On the simulated fork the naive slope and the interventional effect separate cleanly, and the posterior covers the known value \(1.5\). On the Sachs skeleton the smallest backdoor set for Mek on Erk is PKA, the total effect equals the direct coefficient, and the interval sits on a small negative log-log slope. The graph is an input. The posterior describes the coefficients given that input.

title: 6.2 Graphs and Bayesian Networks
text:
Scientific terminology







Term
Meaning in this notebook




DAG
A directed graph with no directed cycles.


d-separation
A graphical criterion for conditional independence in a DAG.


Backdoor path
A path from treatment to outcome that starts with an arrow into the treatment.


Adjustment set
A covariate set that blocks every backdoor and contains no descendant of treatment.


Frontdoor
Identification through a mediator when treatment and outcome share an unobserved common cause.


\(do(T=t)\)
A hard intervention that replaces the structural equation for \(T\) with the constant \(t\).


Total effect
The sum of the products of coefficients along every directed path from \(T\) to \(Y\).


Credible interval
The central 95% of posterior draws of the effect.


Dirichlet prior
A prior on a probability vector. The posterior mean shrinks the empirical frequencies toward a uniform table.

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
text: Python Banner

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
text:
Overview

Why Bayesian Causal Inference?
Bayesian methods offer several advantages for causal inference:

Explicit Uncertainty Quantification: Bayesian methods provide full posterior distributions for causal effects, not just point estimates and confidence intervals. This is crucial for decision-making under uncertainty.
Incorporation of Prior Knowledge: When data is limited or we have domain expertise, Bayesian methods allow us to encode prior beliefs and update them with data.
Flexibility: Bayesian models can handle complex hierarchical structures, missing data, and non-standard likelihoods that are difficult for frequentist methods.
Propagating Uncertainty: In multi-stage causal analyses (e.g., propensity score estimation followed by outcome modeling), Bayesian methods naturally propagate uncertainty through all stages.
Small Sample Performance: With informative priors, Bayesian methods can produce reliable estimates even with small sample sizes.



The Bayesian Framework
In Bayesian statistics, we treat unknown parameters as random variables with probability distributions. The key components are:

Prior Distribution: \(p(\theta)\) — our beliefs about parameters before seeing data
Likelihood: \(p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\) — how likely the data is given parameters
Posterior Distribution: \(p(\theta \mid \text{data}) \propto p(\text{data} \mid \theta) \times p(\theta)\) — updated beliefs after seeing data

For causal inference, the parameters of interest are typically treatment effects (ATE, ATT, CATE, etc.). The posterior distribution gives us a full picture of our uncertainty about these effects.


Bayesian vs. Frequentist Causal Inference








Aspect
Frequentist
Bayesian




Parameters
Fixed unknown constants
Random variables with distributions


Uncertainty
Confidence intervals (long-run coverage)
Credible intervals (probability statements)


Prior Knowledge
Cannot incorporate naturally
Explicitly encoded in priors


Small Samples
Relies on asymptotics
Can use informative priors


Computation
Often faster
Requires MCMC/variational inference


Interpretation
“If we repeated this experiment…”
“Given the data, the probability is…”





Methods Covered in This Section
This section introduces Bayesian approaches to core causal inference methods:









Method
Chapter
Business Setting
Key Advantage




Bayesian A/B Testing
6.1
Randomized experiments with small samples
Natural incorporation of prior knowledge, sequential updating


Bayesian DiD
6.2
Treatment assigned to groups at known times
Full uncertainty for treatment effects, handles sparse data


Bayesian ITS
6.3
Company-wide interventions with time series
Flexible time-series modeling, propagates parameter uncertainty


Bayesian IV
6.4
Treatment confounded by unobservables with instrument
Full posterior for LATE, handles weak instruments better


Bayesian Propensity Methods
6.5
Self-selected treatment with rich covariates
Propagates uncertainty from propensity to outcome estimation





Where Bayesian CausalML fits
The table above is the PyMC sequence in notebooks 6.1–6.5. This notebook also documents pycausalml.bayesian_causalML, the package interface for Bayesian causal graphs, structural models, and the same quasi-experimental designs. Bayesian CausalML specifies what each class identifies, which posterior it returns, and how to call it.


Key Tools

PyMC samples a joint posterior with the NUTS algorithm. The randomized experiment in this notebook, and notebooks 6.1–6.5, use it when the likelihood or the prior is one you want to write yourself.
ArviZ reads those MCMC draws: R-hat, effective sample size, trace plots, and posterior plots.
pycausalml.bayesian_causalML is the native Bayesian CausalML module. A conjugate Gaussian posterior or a Bayesian bootstrap supplies the interval for a graph, a structural model, or a quasi-experiment.
CausalPy is the reference for the quasi-experimental layouts and for the structural treatment–outcome model. The module implements those layouts with NumPy and SciPy.



When to Use Bayesian Causal Methods
Bayesian causal inference is particularly valuable when:

Sample sizes are small: Informative priors can stabilize estimates
Prior knowledge exists: You have domain expertise to encode
Uncertainty quantification is critical: Decision-makers need probability statements
Models are complex: Hierarchical structures, missing data, or non-standard likelihoods
Sequential analysis: You want to update beliefs as new data arrives
Propagating uncertainty: Multi-stage analyses where uncertainty should flow through



Key Concepts

Prior Distributions
Priors encode our beliefs before seeing data. Common choices:

Weakly informative priors: Wide distributions that let data speak (e.g., Normal(0, 10))
Informative priors: Narrow distributions based on domain knowledge
Hierarchical priors: Priors on priors for multi-level models



Posterior Distributions
The posterior is our updated belief after seeing data. For causal effects, we get:

Point estimates: Posterior mean or median
Uncertainty intervals: Credible intervals (e.g., 95% highest posterior density)
Probability statements: P(effect > 0) = 0.95



Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
MCMC algorithms (e.g., NUTS in PyMC) sample from the posterior distribution when analytical solutions are intractable. Key diagnostics:

Convergence: R-hat statistics near 1
Effective sample size: Sufficient independent samples
Trace plots: Visual inspection of chains




Advantages in Business Contexts
In business settings, Bayesian methods are particularly valuable because:

Natural communication: “There’s a 95% probability the lift is between 3% and 7%” is more intuitive than frequentist confidence intervals
Sequential decision-making: As new data arrives (e.g., ongoing A/B tests), we can update our posteriors incrementally
Incorporating business knowledge: Historical results, expert judgment, and business constraints can be encoded as priors
Risk assessment: Posterior distributions enable Value at Risk (VaR) and other risk metrics
Small experiments: Pilot programs and early-stage tests often have limited data — Bayesian methods handle this gracefully



Connection to Other Sections
This section complements other causal inference approaches in this tutorial:

Tree-Based Models (Section 5.1): Frequentist heterogeneous treatment effects
Meta-Learners (Section 5.2): ML-based frequentist CATE estimation
DoubleML (Section 5.4): Frequentist double/debiased machine learning
DeepCausalML (Section 5.5): Neural network-based causal methods

Bayesian methods provide an alternative paradigm that excels when uncertainty quantification, prior knowledge, or small samples are important.
Bayesian CausalML is the package side of that comparison. Tree-based models, meta-learners, and double machine learning return a point estimate or a frequentist interval for a conditional average treatment effect. Bayesian CausalML returns a posterior for an effect that a graph or a design has identified. Deep causal models are the neural counterpart when the assignment mechanism is a learned representation, a generative model, or a learned DAG.

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
section: Simple Example: Bayesian Treatment Effect Estimation
text:
Simple Example: Bayesian Treatment Effect Estimation
Let’s start with a simple example: estimating the average treatment effect in a randomized experiment.


Code
# Simulate a simple A/B test
np.random.seed(42)
n_control = 100
n_treatment = 100

# True effect: treatment increases outcome by 5 units
true_effect = 5

# Control group: mean 100, std 15
y_control = np.random.normal(100, 15, n_control)

# Treatment group: mean 105, std 15
y_treatment = np.random.normal(100 + true_effect, 15, n_treatment)

print(f"Control mean: {y_control.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Treatment mean: {y_treatment.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Observed difference: {y_treatment.mean() - y_control.mean():.2f}")


Now let’s estimate the treatment effect using Bayesian methods:


Code
with pm.Model() as model:
    # Priors for group means (weakly informative)
    mu_control = pm.Normal("mu_control", mu=100, sigma=20)
    mu_treatment = pm.Normal("mu_treatment", mu=100, sigma=20)
    
    # Prior for standard deviation (half-normal)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=20)
    
    # Treatment effect (difference in means)
    tau = pm.Deterministic("tau", mu_treatment - mu_control)
    
    # Likelihood for control group
    pm.Normal("y_control", mu=mu_control, sigma=sigma, observed=y_control)
    
    # Likelihood for treatment group
    pm.Normal("y_treatment", mu=mu_treatment, sigma=sigma, observed=y_treatment)
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)


Let’s examine the posterior distribution of the treatment effect:


Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95)




Code
# Plot posterior
az.plot_posterior(trace, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95)
plt.title("Posterior Distribution of Treatment Effect")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The posterior gives us:

Point estimate: Posterior mean of τ
Credible interval: 95% HDI (highest density interval)
Probability statements: P(τ > 0) from the posterior

This is much richer information than a single number with a confidence interval!

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
text:
Model Diagnostics
Before trusting our results, we should check MCMC diagnostics:


Code
# Check convergence (R-hat should be close to 1)
print("R-hat statistics:")
print(az.rhat(trace))

# Trace plots
az.plot_trace(trace, var_names=["tau"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Good MCMC diagnostics:

R-hat < 1.01: Chains have converged
Trace plots: Look like “fuzzy caterpillars” (good mixing)
Effective sample size: Large enough for stable estimates

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
text:
Incorporating Prior Knowledge
One of Bayesian methods’ strengths is incorporating prior knowledge. Let’s see how informative priors affect the estimate:


Code
with pm.Model() as model_informative:
    # Informative priors based on domain knowledge
    # We believe the effect is around 3 with uncertainty ±2
    mu_control = pm.Normal("mu_control", mu=100, sigma=10)
    mu_treatment = pm.Normal("mu_treatment", mu=103, sigma=10)
    
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=15)
    
    tau = pm.Deterministic("tau", mu_treatment - mu_control)
    
    pm.Normal("y_control", mu=mu_control, sigma=sigma, observed=y_control)
    pm.Normal("y_treatment", mu=mu_treatment, sigma=sigma, observed=y_treatment)
    
    trace_informative = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)

# Compare weakly informative vs informative priors
print("Weakly informative priors:")
print(az.summary(trace, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95))

print("\nInformative priors:")
print(az.summary(trace_informative, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95))


With informative priors, the posterior is “shrunk” toward the prior. This is particularly useful with small samples or when we have strong domain knowledge.

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
text:
Bayesian CausalML
The PyMC example above writes a likelihood and samples it. Bayesian CausalML is the module that answers the next question: given a causal graph or a study design, what is the posterior of the identified effect?
from pycausalml.bayesian_causalML import (
    CausalGraph,
    GaussianBayesianNetwork,
    DiscreteBayesianNetwork,
    BayesianStructuralSCM,
    BayesianTimeSeriesSCM,
)
The module lives at pycausalml.bayesian_causalML. It uses NumPy, SciPy, and NetworkX. The identification rules match the operations in pgmpy’s causal inference helpers (backdoor adjustment, frontdoor sets, naive adjustment, naive instrumental variables). The structural equations match the treatment–outcome model in the CausalPy structural-model notes. Both are implemented in this module, so a fit does not import those packages.

Three families








Family
Classes
Question




Graphs and Bayesian networks
CausalGraph, GaussianBayesianNetwork, DiscreteBayesianNetwork, NaiveAdjustmentRegressor, NaiveIVRegressor
Which observed variables identify the effect, and what is \(E[Y \mid do(T)]\)?


Structural models
BayesianStructuralSCM, BayesianTimeSeriesSCM, simulate_structural_scm
What is the structural coefficient on an endogenous treatment, in a cross-section or in a lagged system?


Quasi-experiments
BayesianDifferenceInDifferences, BayesianRegressionDiscontinuity, BayesianInterruptedTimeSeries, BayesianInstrumentalVariable, BayesianSyntheticControl
What is the design parameter (ATT, cutoff jump, level shift, IV coefficient, synthetic-control gap), with a posterior interval?



Each family has a detail notebook: the identifying formula, a simulation with a known effect, and a fit on Data/ or a CausalPy table.

6.6 Graphs and Bayesian networks
6.7 Structural models
6.8 Quasi-experiments

pycausalml.bayesian_causal_inference is a second module. It holds BayesianLinearCATE and an earlier set of quasi-experimental estimators. The classes in this section are the Bayesian CausalML API added in PyCausalML 0.2.0: those designs, plus networks and structural time series, with one summary format.


How uncertainty is represented
Every numeric estimator uses one of two posteriors.
Conjugate Gaussian posterior. The conditional mean is linear, and the prior on the slopes is a weak ridge: a small penalty, with the intercept left almost unpenalized. The coefficient posterior is then normal. Its mean is the ridge estimate. Its covariance is the residual variance times the inverse of the penalized Gram matrix. Credible intervals are quantiles of draws from that normal. Difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, interrupted time series, each equation of a linear-Gaussian network, naive adjustment, and each equation of the time-series model use this posterior.
Bayesian bootstrap. A draw reweights the sample with a Dirichlet \((1,\ldots,1)\) vector and refits the estimator. The collection of refits is the posterior. Instrumental variables, synthetic control, and the cross-sectional structural model use it. A two-stage estimator is refit from scratch under each weight vector, so uncertainty from the first stage is inside the interval.
summary() returns:







Key
Meaning




estimate
Point fit of the causal contrast (ridge estimate or unweighted estimator)


posterior_mean
Mean of the stored draws


ci_lower, ci_upper
2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of draws_


std
Standard deviation of the draws


rope_probability
Included when the constructor received rope=(low, high): the share of draws inside that region of practical equivalence



The draws stay on draws_. They are omitted from summary() so a printed summary stays small.
A discrete network is the exception worth remembering. DiscreteBayesianNetwork.ate contrasts interventional expectations under the posterior-mean conditional probability tables. It returns that contrast, the treated mean, and the control mean. It does not return a quantile interval. query is the method that returns the interventional distribution.


From a graph to an interval

Write the causal contrast. For a binary intervention this is \(E[Y \mid do(T=1)] - E[Y \mid do(T=0)]\). In a design it is the parameter that equals that contrast: the DiD interaction, the jump at a cutoff, the IV coefficient.
Write the graph, or name the design assumption (parallel trends, continuity at the cutoff, an exclusion restriction).
Read off an adjustment set, a frontdoor set, or an instrument. If the graph has none, the effect is not identified from the observed variables.
Fit the structural equations or the design regression.
Report the posterior of the contrast.

Observing the treatment and intervening on it are different queries. \(P(Y \mid T=1)\) still travels along any open backdoor. \(P(Y \mid do(T=1))\) deletes the arrows into \(T\) and then propagates. The discrete-network example prints both numbers from one fitted model.


Code
from IPython.display import display

from pycausalml.bayesian_causalML import (
    BayesianDifferenceInDifferences,
    BayesianStructuralSCM,
    BayesianTimeSeriesSCM,
    CausalGraph,
    DiscreteBayesianNetwork,
    GaussianBayesianNetwork,
    NaiveAdjustmentRegressor,
    NaiveIVRegressor,
    simulate_structural_scm,
)




1. Causal graphs and identification
CausalGraph stores a directed acyclic graph. The edge (parent, child) means the parent is a direct cause of the child. Every common cause you are willing to use has to appear as a node: once the graph is drawn, identification treats it as causally sufficient. A cycle raises ValueError.
d-separation is the test the rest of the rules are built from.








Graph
Edges
What the criterion says




Chain
A → B → C
A and C are d-separated by B


Fork
A ← B → C
A and C are d-separated by B


Collider
A → B ← C
A and C are d-separated when nothing is conditioned on. Conditioning on B opens the path



Backdoor criterion. A set \(Z\) identifies the effect of \(T\) on \(Y\) when all three of the following hold.

\(Z\) contains neither \(T\) nor \(Y\).
No member of \(Z\) is a descendant of \(T\). A descendant can sit on a causal path, or it can be a collider that opens a non-causal path.
In the graph with the arrows out of \(T\) removed, \(Z\) d-separates \(T\) and \(Y\). Removing those arrows leaves the non-causal paths, which is what an adjustment set has to block.

minimal_adjustment_set(treatment, outcome) returns one smallest valid set, as a sorted list of names. adjustment_sets returns every inclusion-minimal set among the empty set, the parents of treatment, and subsets of the non-descendants up to max_size. If no observed set works, minimal_adjustment_set raises ValueError.
Frontdoor criterion. A mediator set \(M\) identifies the effect when four things hold.

\(M\) is non-empty and contains neither treatment nor outcome.
Every directed path from treatment to outcome passes through \(M\).
Treatment and \(M\) have no open backdoor. They are d-separated once the arrows out of treatment are removed.
Every backdoor from \(M\) to the outcome is blocked by treatment.

frontdoor_sets(treatment, outcome) returns those mediator sets. This is the identification result used when the confounder is latent and a mediator on the causal path is observed. The graph names the mediator. A discrete network can then evaluate the interventional distribution with query.
Instruments. instruments(treatment, outcome) lists observed nodes that have a directed path into the treatment and are d-separated from the outcome after the treatment node is removed. A node with its own arrow into the outcome fails that test and is left out. A latent confounder of treatment and outcome does not, by itself, remove an instrument: if the instrument has no arrow into the outcome and no connection to the confounder except through treatment, exclusion still holds.
adjacency() returns a DataFrame with A.loc[child, parent] = 1. parents, children, ancestors, and descendants expose the same graph for inspection.


Code
chain = CausalGraph([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")])
fork = CausalGraph([("B", "A"), ("B", "C")])
collider = CausalGraph([("A", "B"), ("C", "B")])

print("Chain: A ⊥ C | B ", chain.d_separated("A", "C", "B"))
print("Chain: A ⊥ C     ", chain.d_separated("A", "C"))
print("Fork:  A ⊥ C | B ", fork.d_separated("A", "C", "B"))
print("Collider: A ⊥ C  ", collider.d_separated("A", "C"))
print("Collider: A ⊥ C | B", collider.d_separated("A", "C", "B"))

# Engagement C confounds a loyalty offer T and spend Y.
confounded = CausalGraph([("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")])
print("Backdoor set:", confounded.minimal_adjustment_set("T", "Y"))
print("Empty set is valid:", confounded.satisfies_backdoor("T", "Y", []))
print("Adjusting for C is valid:", confounded.satisfies_backdoor("T", "Y", ["C"]))

# A mediator M of the offer is a descendant. It is not a backdoor set.
mediated = CausalGraph([("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "M"), ("M", "Y")])
print("Adjustment set with a mediator in the graph:", mediated.minimal_adjustment_set("T", "Y"))
print("Adjusting for the mediator is valid:", mediated.satisfies_backdoor("T", "Y", ["M"]))

# Latent U confounds T and Y. M sits on the only causal path.
frontdoor = CausalGraph([("U", "T"), ("U", "Y"), ("T", "M"), ("M", "Y")])
print("Frontdoor sets:", frontdoor.frontdoor_sets("T", "Y"))

instrument = CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("T", "Y")])
leaked = CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("T", "Y"), ("Z", "Y")])
print("Instrument when Z is excluded from Y:", instrument.instruments("T", "Y"))
print("Instrument when Z also points at Y:", leaked.instruments("T", "Y"))

confounded.adjacency()


The prints are the identification checklist in miniature.

In the chain and the fork, the middle node blocks the path. In the collider, the path is blocked until you condition on the collision node. That is why a descendant of treatment is a dangerous control.
With \(C \rightarrow T\), \(C \rightarrow Y\), and \(T \rightarrow Y\), the smallest backdoor set is \(\{C\}\). The empty set leaves the fork open.
Adding the mediator \(T \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\) does not put \(M\) into the adjustment set. satisfies_backdoor rejects \(\{M\}\) because \(M\) is a descendant of treatment and lies on the causal path.
In the frontdoor graph the confounder \(U\) is latent, so it cannot be an adjustment covariate. The mediator \(M\) still satisfies the frontdoor criterion, and the effect remains identified.
\(Z\) is an instrument when the only way it reaches \(Y\) is through \(T\). An extra arrow \(Z \rightarrow Y\) removes it from instruments.

The adjacency matrix uses the package convention A.loc[child, parent] = 1: the row is the effect, the column is the cause.


2. Linear-Gaussian Bayesian network
GaussianBayesianNetwork turns the graph into a structural equation for every node:
\[
X_j = a_j + \sum_{k \in \mathrm{pa}(j)} \beta_{jk} X_k + \varepsilon_j,
\qquad \varepsilon_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_j^2).
\]
fit(data) expects a data frame with one column per node and estimates a separate Gaussian posterior for each equation. Parents are taken from the graph, so a column that the graph does not name as a parent stays out of that equation.
ate(treatment, outcome, treated=1, control=0) is the posterior of
\[
E[Y \mid do(T = \texttt{treated})] - E[Y \mid do(T = \texttt{control})].
\]
In a linear system that contrast equals the total effect times treated - control. The total effect sums the products of structural coefficients along every directed path from treatment to outcome. Each posterior draw perturbs every equation’s coefficients, then recomputes the path sum, so the interval includes uncertainty in the confounder equations as well as in the outcome equation.
sample(n, do={"T": 1.0}) draws from the posterior-mean equations in topological order. A node listed in do is clamped to that value and its parents are ignored for that node. The difference between the outcome mean under do(T=1) and under do(T=0) is a simulation estimate of the same total effect.
Call summary() after ate. The draws of the total effect are on draws_.
The simulation below is a loyalty offer. Prior engagement \(C\) pushes customers into the offer and also shifts spend. The structural effect of the offer on spend is \(+2\). A regression of spend on the offer alone leaves the engagement fork open, so its slope mixes the offer with engagement. The network includes both arrows out of \(C\) and recovers the structural slope.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
engagement = rng.normal(size=n)
offer = 0.8 * engagement + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)
spend = 2.0 * offer - 1.1 * engagement + rng.normal(scale=0.6, size=n)
frame = pd.DataFrame({"C": engagement, "T": offer, "Y": spend})

naive = np.linalg.lstsq(
    np.column_stack([np.ones(n), offer]), spend, rcond=None
)[0][1]

network = GaussianBayesianNetwork(
    [("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")],
    n_draws=500,
    random_state=0,
)
network.fit(frame)
ate = network.ate("T", "Y", treated=1.0, control=0.0)

print(f"Naive slope of spend on offer: {naive:.3f}")
print("Network posterior of the total effect:")
display(pd.Series(ate))

do_offer = network.sample(5000, do={"T": 1.0}, random_state=1)
do_control = network.sample(5000, do={"T": 0.0}, random_state=2)
print(
    "Simulated E[Y | do(T=1)] - E[Y | do(T=0)]:",
    f"{do_offer['Y'].mean() - do_control['Y'].mean():.3f}",
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.0))
ax.hist(network.draws_, bins=40, density=True, color="C0", alpha=0.85)
low, high = np.quantile(network.draws_, [0.025, 0.975])
ax.axvspan(low, high, color="C0", alpha=0.18, label="95% credible interval")
ax.axvline(2.0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label="structural effect = 2")
ax.set_xlabel("total effect of the offer on spend")
ax.set_ylabel("posterior density")
ax.set_title(r"Gaussian Bayesian network: $E[Y \mid do(T=1)] - E[Y \mid do(T=0)]$")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The naive slope sits away from 2 because engagement is inside both the offer and spend. The network posterior concentrates on the structural value 2: the backdoor through engagement is in the graph, so it is removed from the offer equation and the spend equation before the path product is formed. The do samples land on the same contrast. Clamping T cuts the arrow from engagement into the offer, which is the intervention the total effect refers to.


3. Discrete Bayesian network
DiscreteBayesianNetwork is the same graph with categorical conditionals. For a node with states \(\mathcal{X}\) and Dirichlet concentration alpha (the default is 1, one pseudo-count per state), the posterior mean of a conditional probability is
\[
\hat P(x \mid \mathrm{pa})
  = \frac{n(x, \mathrm{pa}) + \alpha}{n(\mathrm{pa}) + \alpha \, |\mathcal{X}|}.
\]
fit builds one such table for every parent configuration that appears in the data. cpd(node) returns that table as a data frame.
query(variables, evidence=None, do=None) returns marginal distributions.

do={node: value} replaces that node’s conditional with a point mass at value. Parents of the node no longer affect it. This is an intervention.
evidence={node: value} conditions on the observed value and still uses the node’s conditional. This is association.
A node cannot appear in both maps.

The joint is enumerated exactly when its size is at most exact_limit cells (default 8192). The result then has "method": "exact". Larger joints use likelihood weighting and "method": "likelihood_weighting". Probabilities are keyed by the original state labels.
ate(treatment, outcome, treated=1, control=0) is defined when the outcome labels are numeric. It subtracts \(E[Y \mid do(T=\mathrm{control})]\) from \(E[Y \mid do(T=\mathrm{treated})]\). String labels need query rather than ate.
Two processes follow. Both use binary nodes, so the exact enumerator applies.
A chain. \(T \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\), with \(P(M=1 \mid T) = 0.2 + 0.6\,T\) and \(P(Y=1 \mid M) = 0.1 + 0.8\,M\). There is no backdoor. The interventional contrast is
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y \mid do(T=1)] &= 0.8 \times 0.9 + 0.2 \times 0.1 = 0.74, \\
E[Y \mid do(T=0)] &= 0.2 \times 0.9 + 0.8 \times 0.1 = 0.26,
\end{aligned}
\]
so the average treatment effect is \(0.48\). Conditioning on \(T\) agrees with intervening on \(T\), because nothing confounds the chain.
A confounder. \(C\) causes both \(T\) and \(Y\), and \(T\) also causes \(Y\), with
\[
P(Y=1 \mid T, C) = 0.1 + 0.2\,T + 0.6\,C
\]
and \(P(C=1) = 1/2\). Under an intervention the confounder stays at its marginal, so
\[
E[Y \mid do(T=1)] = 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.60.
\]
Conditioning on \(T=1\) over-samples \(C=1\), because the confounder is what produced treatment. \(P(Y=1 \mid T=1)\) is therefore larger than the interventional probability. That gap is the confounding the graph removes.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 8000

# Chain: the offer changes redemption, and redemption changes purchase.
treatment = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, size=n)
mediator = rng.binomial(1, np.where(treatment == 1, 0.8, 0.2))
outcome = rng.binomial(1, np.where(mediator == 1, 0.9, 0.1))
chain_frame = pd.DataFrame({"T": treatment, "M": mediator, "Y": outcome})

chain_net = DiscreteBayesianNetwork(
    [("T", "M"), ("M", "Y")], alpha=0.5, random_state=0
)
chain_net.fit(chain_frame)
print("Chain ATE (structural value 0.48):")
display(pd.Series(chain_net.ate("T", "Y", treated=1, control=0)))
print("CPD of the mediator:")
display(chain_net.cpd("M"))

# Confounded offer: engagement drives both take-up and purchase.
confounder = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, size=n)
treatment = rng.binomial(1, np.where(confounder == 1, 0.9, 0.1))
probability = 0.1 + 0.2 * treatment + 0.6 * confounder
outcome = rng.binomial(1, probability)
confounded_frame = pd.DataFrame({"C": confounder, "T": treatment, "Y": outcome})

confounded_net = DiscreteBayesianNetwork(
    [("C", "T"), ("C", "Y"), ("T", "Y")], alpha=0.5, random_state=0
)
confounded_net.fit(confounded_frame)
interventional = confounded_net.query("Y", do={"T": 1})
conditional = confounded_net.query("Y", evidence={"T": 1})
print("Query method:", interventional["method"])
print("P(Y=1 | do(T=1)):", f"{interventional['distributions']['Y'][1]:.3f}")
print("P(Y=1 | T=1):    ", f"{conditional['distributions']['Y'][1]:.3f}")
print("Confounded-graph ATE:")
display(pd.Series(confounded_net.ate("T", "Y", treated=1, control=0)))


On the chain, the fitted average treatment effect sits on 0.48, and the mediator’s conditional probability table reproduces the two assignment probabilities, about 0.2 and 0.8. On the confounded graph, \(P(Y=1 \mid do(T=1))\) sits on 0.60, while \(P(Y=1 \mid T=1)\) is pulled upward by the customers whose engagement both triggered the offer and raised purchase. Reporting the conditional probability as the effect of the offer would credit the offer for engagement. The do query leaves engagement at its population mix.
The printed ATE is about 0.20, which is the coefficient on \(T\) in the probability formula. The control interventional mean is \(E[Y \mid do(T=0)] = 0.1 + 0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.40\), and \(0.60 - 0.40 = 0.20\).


4. Adjustment and instrumental variables from the graph
The network classes estimate every structural equation. Two thinner estimators skip the equations you do not need and read the identifying set from a CausalGraph.
NaiveAdjustmentRegressor(graph, treatment, outcome) calls minimal_adjustment_set and fits the Bayesian outcome regression
\[
Y = a + \tau \, T + Z^{\top}\gamma + \varepsilon.
\]
Under the graph and a linear outcome model, \(\tau\) is the average treatment effect. summary() includes adjustment_set. predict(data) evaluates the fitted mean. The posterior on \(\tau\) is the conjugate Gaussian posterior from the ridge regression.
NaiveIVRegressor(graph, treatment, outcome) calls instruments and runs Bayesian two-stage least squares. summary() includes instruments. If instruments returns an empty list, fit raises ValueError.
The graph you hand the estimator is the identifying assumption.

For adjustment, draw every confounder you can condition on. The class uses the smallest backdoor set and ignores mediators that fail the backdoor criterion.
For an instrument, draw \(Z \rightarrow T \rightarrow Y\). A latent confounder of \(T\) and \(Y\) can stay off the drawn graph: the assumption encoded by that picture is that \(Z\) reaches \(Y\) only through \(T\), and that \(Z\) is independent of the latent confounder. Adding an arrow \(Z \rightarrow Y\) is an exclusion failure, instruments returns [], and the regressor refuses to fit.

The adjustment example reuses the loyalty-offer frame from the Gaussian network, where the structural effect is 2 and the adjustment set is engagement. The instrumental-variable example is a separate draw: an encouragement \(Z\) shifts take-up, a latent shock confounds take-up and the outcome, and the structural effect is 1.5. Ordinary least squares of the outcome on take-up is biased. Two-stage least squares, with \(Z\) read off the graph, targets 1.5.


Code
adjusted = NaiveAdjustmentRegressor(confounded, "T", "Y", n_draws=800, random_state=0)
adjusted.fit(frame)
print("Backdoor regression on the loyalty-offer frame:")
display(pd.Series(adjusted.summary()))

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n_iv = 3000
encouragement = rng.normal(size=n_iv)
latent = rng.normal(size=n_iv)
takeup = 0.9 * encouragement + 0.7 * latent + rng.normal(scale=0.2, size=n_iv)
response = 1.5 * takeup + 0.8 * latent + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n_iv)
iv_frame = pd.DataFrame({"Z": encouragement, "T": takeup, "Y": response})

ols_iv = np.linalg.lstsq(
    np.column_stack([np.ones(n_iv), takeup]), response, rcond=None
)[0][1]
print(f"OLS slope of response on take-up: {ols_iv:.3f}")

iv_graph = CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("T", "Y")])
print("Instruments on the exclusion graph:", iv_graph.instruments("T", "Y"))
print(
    "Instruments after adding Z → Y:",
    CausalGraph([("Z", "T"), ("T", "Y"), ("Z", "Y")]).instruments("T", "Y"),
)

iv_model = NaiveIVRegressor(iv_graph, "T", "Y", n_draws=200, random_state=0)
iv_model.fit(iv_frame)
print("Bayesian IV posterior (structural effect 1.5):")
display(pd.Series(iv_model.summary()))




5. Structural causal model for an endogenous treatment
BayesianStructuralSCM writes the treatment and the outcome as a pair of structural assignments:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T &= a_T + X_T^{\top}\beta_T + V, \\
Y &= \alpha \, T + a_Y + X_Y^{\top}\beta_Y + U,
\qquad \mathrm{Corr}(U, V) = \rho.
\end{aligned}
\]
When \(\rho \neq 0\), the treatment residual \(V\) is inside \(T\). Ordinary least squares of \(Y\) on \(T\) and the covariates is then biased for \(\alpha\), because the regression can partial out \(X\) and still leave \(V\) in the treatment. The residual correlation is unobserved confounding.
Exclusion restrictions split the columns of \(X\):



Role
Argument
Where it enters




Instrument
instruments
Treatment equation only


Outcome covariate
outcome_only
Outcome equation only


Confounder
every remaining column
Both equations



Column indices or column names both work. fit(X, treatment, y, instruments=..., outcome_only=...) runs two-stage least squares and stores a Bayesian bootstrap of both stages. identified_by_ is "instrumental_variable" when instruments are passed. Omit instruments only when treatment is conditionally ignorable given \(X\): the fit is then a Bayesian outcome regression and identified_by_ is "conditional_ignorability".
Under \(do(T = t)\) the outcome equation is evaluated at that value of \(t\). The treatment residual is an estimation device. It is not part of the intervened assignment. Three prediction methods use that intervened equation:

predict(X, treatment) returns the mean outcome at the supplied treatment values.
predict_interval(X, treatment, level=0.95) adds a pointwise credible band from the coefficient draws.
potential_outcomes(X) returns \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\). With a homogeneous \(\alpha\), the row-wise contrast equals the structural effect.

simulate_structural_scm(n, alpha, rho) builds a known version of this design. Five standardized covariates are returned in X: columns 0 and 1 are confounders, columns 2 and 3 are instruments, and column 4 predicts the outcome only. Treatment and outcome errors are bivariate normal with correlation rho. The structural effect is alpha. The dictionary also returns instruments, outcome_only, and feature_names, which can be passed straight into fit.


Code
data = simulate_structural_scm(n=2500, alpha=3.0, rho=0.6, random_state=0)
ols_design = np.column_stack(
    [np.ones(len(data["y"])), data["treatment"], data["X"]]
)
ols_alpha = np.linalg.lstsq(ols_design, data["y"], rcond=None)[0][1]

scm = BayesianStructuralSCM(n_draws=200, random_state=0)
scm.fit(
    data["X"],
    data["treatment"],
    data["y"],
    instruments=data["instruments"],
    outcome_only=data["outcome_only"],
    feature_names=data["feature_names"],
)

print(f"OLS coefficient on treatment: {ols_alpha:.3f}")
print(f"Identification: {scm.identified_by_}")
print("Structural posterior (true alpha = 3):")
display(pd.Series(scm.summary()))

y0, y1 = scm.potential_outcomes(data["X"][:5])
print("Y(1) - Y(0) on five rows (homogeneous effect):")
print(np.round(y1 - y0, 3))


Ordinary least squares is pulled off 3 by the correlated residuals. The structural fit, which keeps the instruments out of the outcome equation and the outcome-only covariate out of the treatment equation, puts the posterior on 3. Because \(\alpha\) is homogeneous, \(Y(1) - Y(0)\) is the same number on every row, and that number is the posterior point fit of \(\alpha\).


6. Structural time series
BayesianTimeSeriesSCM is the structural model on a multivariate series. Contemporaneous parents form a DAG, passed as edges. Each equation also contains its own lags and the lags of those parents, up to lag (the default is 1). An empty edge list is a system of separate autoregressions. Every equation has its own Gaussian coefficient posterior.
Two interventions answer two different questions.
A hard intervention replaces an equation for the whole horizon. The clamped series does not consult its parents or its lags. counterfactual(horizon, interventions, baseline=None, history=None) subtracts a baseline rollout from the intervened rollout.

interventions maps a variable to a scalar or to a horizon-length sequence.
baseline=None is the observational forecast from forecast.
baseline={"X": 0.0} together with interventions={"X": 1.0} is the sustained contrast of \(do(X=1)\) against $do(X=0)`.

The returned dictionary holds names, counterfactual, baseline, effect, effect_lower, and effect_upper. The last two are pointwise 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles across coefficient draws.
An impulse adds a shock to the structural residual for one period, then lets every equation run as fitted. impulse_response(variable, shock=1, horizon=10) returns response, baseline, and effect. A clamp answers “what if this series is held at a value.” An impulse answers “what if this series is hit once and then reacts.”
summary(node) returns that equation’s feature_names, posterior-mean coef, and residual variance sigma2. Names look like X[t], Y[t-1], and X[t-1]: the [t] term is the contemporaneous parent, and the lag terms are the node’s own past and its parents’ past.
history has one column per series, in the order of names_ (topological order), and at least lag rows. Leave it out to start from the end of the fitted sample. The example below starts from a zero history so the contrast is the effect of the intervention rather than a continuation of a particular sample path.
The data-generating process is a weekly demand series. A driver \(X\) is autoregressive with coefficient 0.4. Demand \(Y\) loads on the current driver with coefficient 0.8 and on its own lag with coefficient 0.2. There is no direct lag from \(X\) into \(Y\) beyond what the contemporaneous arrow and \(Y\)’s own lag induce.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_weeks = 1200
driver = np.zeros(n_weeks)
demand = np.zeros(n_weeks)
for t in range(1, n_weeks):
    driver[t] = 0.4 * driver[t - 1] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.5)
    demand[t] = 0.8 * driver[t] + 0.2 * demand[t - 1] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.3)

ts = BayesianTimeSeriesSCM(edges=[("X", "Y")], lag=1, n_draws=150, random_state=0)
ts.fit(pd.DataFrame({"X": driver, "Y": demand}))
equation = ts.summary("Y")
print("Posterior mean of the demand equation (structural loading on X[t] is 0.8):")
display(pd.Series(equation["coef"], index=equation["feature_names"], name="coef"))

history = np.zeros((ts.lag, len(ts.names_)))
impulse = ts.impulse_response("X", shock=1.0, horizon=8, history=history)
y_index = impulse["names"].index("Y")
print(f"One-period response of Y: {impulse['effect'][0, y_index]:.3f}")

contrast = ts.counterfactual(
    24, {"X": 1.0}, baseline={"X": 0.0}, history=history
)
y_index = contrast["names"].index("Y")
horizon = np.arange(contrast["effect"].shape[0])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.0))
axes[0].plot(impulse["effect"][:, y_index], marker="o", color="C0")
axes[0].axhline(0.0, color="0.5", linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set_title("Impulse: unit shock to X, then the system reacts")
axes[0].set_xlabel("weeks after the shock")
axes[0].set_ylabel("effect on Y")

axes[1].plot(horizon, contrast["effect"][:, y_index], color="C0", label="posterior mean")
axes[1].fill_between(
    horizon,
    contrast["effect_lower"][:, y_index],
    contrast["effect_upper"][:, y_index],
    color="C0",
    alpha=0.2,
    label="95% credible band",
)
axes[1].set_title(r"Hard intervention: $do(X=1)$ against $do(X=0)$")
axes[1].set_xlabel("weeks from a zero history")
axes[1].set_ylabel("effect on Y")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The demand equation’s coefficient on X[t] recovers the contemporaneous loading 0.8, and the coefficient on Y[t-1] recovers the own lag 0.2. The coefficient on X[t-1] stays near 0, which is the lag the simulation did not include.
The impulse plot jumps by that contemporaneous loading in week 0 and then decays: after the shock, \(X\) and \(Y\) follow their fitted dynamics. The hard-intervention plot rises toward the steady gap between holding the driver at 1 and holding it at 0. With loading 0.8, own lag 0.2, and no parent lag, that gap is \(0.8 / (1 - 0.2) = 1\). The credible band is the posterior uncertainty in the coefficients, rolled forward under both interventions.


7. Quasi-experimental posteriors
Five classes encode a study design directly, for the case where the design itself is the identification argument and a unit-level graph is unnecessary. Notebooks 6.2–6.4 rebuild difference-in-differences, interrupted time series, and instrumental variables in PyMC, which is the tool to open when you want a hierarchical likelihood, a custom prior, or a posterior predictive check. The classes here are the ones to call from pycausalml when the design in the table is the design you have.








Class
Call
Causal parameter




BayesianDifferenceInDifferences
fit(y, treated, post)
\(\tau\) in \(Y = a + b\,\mathrm{treated} + c\,\mathrm{post} + \tau\,\mathrm{treated}\times\mathrm{post}\). This is the average treatment effect on the treated under parallel trends. treated and post are 0/1 indicators.


BayesianRegressionDiscontinuity
fit(running, y, treatment=None)
Jump at cutoff in the local linear design \(1,\ (R-c),\ D,\ (R-c)D\). Rows with \(\lvert R-c\rvert\) above bandwidth are dropped when a bandwidth is set. If treatment is omitted, \(D = 1\{R \ge c\}\). The number of rows kept is n_window_.


BayesianInterruptedTimeSeries
fit(time, y, intervention_time)
Immediate level shift in \(Y = a + b\,\mathrm{time} + \tau\,\mathrm{post} + d\,\mathrm{time\ since}\). The slope change \(d\) is stored on slope_change_.


BayesianInstrumentalVariable
fit(y, treatment, instrument, X=None)
Second-stage coefficient on fitted treatment. instrument may have several columns. X holds covariates that enter both stages. Draws are a Bayesian bootstrap of both stages.


BayesianSyntheticControl
fit(control_pre, treated_pre, control_post, treated_post)
Mean post-period gap for one treated unit. Donor weights are non-negative and sum to one. control_pre has shape (n_pre, n_donors). The post-period gap path is effect_path_; effect_ is its mean.



The linear designs and the instrumental-variable class accept rope=(low, high). The summary then includes rope_probability, the posterior probability that the effect sits inside an interval you would treat as negligible for the decision.
The fit below is a two-group, two-period panel with a true interaction of 1.5. The region of practical equivalence is \((-0.25, 0.25)\): effects inside that band would not change the decision.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_panel = 400
treated = np.repeat([0.0, 1.0], n_panel // 2)
post = np.tile([0.0, 1.0], n_panel // 2)
outcome = (
    1.0
    + 0.2 * treated
    + 0.3 * post
    + 1.5 * treated * post
    + rng.normal(scale=0.25, size=n_panel)
)

did = BayesianDifferenceInDifferences(
    n_draws=1000, rope=(-0.25, 0.25), random_state=0
)
did.fit(outcome, treated, post)
print("Coefficient names:", did.feature_names_)
print("Posterior of the treated × post interaction (true value 1.5):")
display(pd.Series(did.summary()))


treated_x_post is the causal parameter. Its posterior sits on 1.5, and rope_probability is the share of draws inside \(\pm 0.25\). A near-zero rope probability is the Bayesian statement that the ATT is large enough to act on, under the parallel-trends assumption built into the interaction.
The other four classes return the same summary keys from the calls in the table. Pass random_state so the draws repeat, and keep n_draws at a few hundred: these intervals are quantiles of a normal or of a bootstrap, and they settle quickly.


Choosing an estimator







You have
Call




An observed confounder and a linear outcome
GaussianBayesianNetwork or NaiveAdjustmentRegressor


Categorical variables and a query under do
DiscreteBayesianNetwork


A latent confounder and an observed mediator that meets the frontdoor criterion
CausalGraph.frontdoor_sets, then DiscreteBayesianNetwork.query


An instrument named by the graph
NaiveIVRegressor


An instrument and covariates, without building a graph
BayesianInstrumentalVariable


Exclusion restrictions on a covariate matrix
BayesianStructuralSCM


Two groups and a known adoption date, with parallel trends
BayesianDifferenceInDifferences


A cutoff on a running variable
BayesianRegressionDiscontinuity


One series and an intervention date
BayesianInterruptedTimeSeries


One treated unit and a donor pool
BayesianSyntheticControl


A multivariate series, and either a hard intervention or a one-period shock
BayesianTimeSeriesSCM



Use the PyMC notebooks when the likelihood is hierarchical, the prior is something other than a weak ridge, or you want a posterior predictive check of the outcome distribution. Use this module when the graph or the design above is the model and the deliverable is a posterior interval for the identified contrast.

title: 6. Bayesian Causal Machine Learning
text:
What You’ll Learn
By the end of this section, you will:

Know when a posterior for a causal effect is the quantity a decision needs
Fit a Bayesian average treatment effect in PyMC and read the posterior, the credible interval, and the MCMC diagnostics
Encode domain knowledge as a prior and see how it moves the posterior
Build a causal graph and read off a backdoor set, a frontdoor set, or an instrument

title: 5.4.5 Graph Neural Network (GNN) Causal Models
text:
Part 1: Theoretical Foundation

Why GNNs for Causal Discovery?
A GNN treats variables as nodes and causal relationships as edges in a graph
\[\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}).\]
Message passing makes the causal structure explicit and inspectable:
\[
\mathbf{h}_i^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{UPDATE}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(\ell)},\ \mathrm{AGGREGATE}\left(\{\mathbf{h}_j^{(\ell)}:j\in\mathcal{N}(i)\}\right)\right).
\]
Unlike RNNs/Transformers where causal effects are implicit in hidden states, in GNN causal models the graph itself is a first-class object that can be regularized, inspected, and interpreted.

title: 5.4.5 Graph Neural Network (GNN) Causal Models
text:
Part 2: The Three Models

1) GVAR — Graph Vector Autoregression
GVAR extends classical VAR with a learned graph and nonlinear feature transforms:
\[
X_i^{(t)}=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{d}A_{ij}^{(k)}\,\phi\!\left(X_j^{(t-k)}\right)+\epsilon_i^{(t)}.
\]

\(A^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\): lag-specific adjacency (learned)
\(\phi(\cdot)\): nonlinear transform (GNN feature map)
sparsity via L1/group-LASSO style penalties



2) CausalGNN / CD-GNN
Two-stage joint learning:

Graph learner outputs soft adjacency \(\hat{G}\) with NOTEARS acyclicity

\[
h(\mathbf{A})=\mathrm{tr}(e^{\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{A}})-d=0
\]

Dynamics learner propagates messages along parents:

\[
\mathbf{m}_{j\rightarrow i}^{(t)}=\mathrm{MSG}(\mathbf{h}_j^{(t)},\mathbf{h}_i^{(t)},e_{ij}),\quad
\mathbf{h}_i^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{UPDATE}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(t)},\sum_{j\in\mathrm{Pa}(i)}\mathbf{m}_{j\rightarrow i}^{(t)}\right).
\]


3) CUTS / CUTS+
Designed for unevenly sampled or missing time series:

causal-aware imputation network
variational posterior over graphs: \(q(G)\approx\prod_{ij}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij})\)
joint optimization of reconstruction + imputation + graph regularization

A common ELBO form is:
\[
\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}[\log p(X_{\mathrm{obs}}\mid G,X_{\mathrm{miss}})]
+\mathbb{E}[\log p(X_{\mathrm{miss}}\mid G)]
-\mathrm{KL}[q(G)\|p(G)].
\]

In this notebook, we explored neural network-based approaches for causal discovery in financial time series.
Key steps and findings: - We simulated or loaded multivariate time series and constructed three causal discovery models: 1. GVAR (Graphical VAR): A sparse linear baseline estimating Granger-causal dependencies via a regularized VAR. 2. CausalGNN: A neural architecture learning directed dependencies in a data-driven manner, potentially modeling nonlinearity. 3. CUTS+-like: A lightweight, attention-based model inspired by the CUTS+ method (here for teaching), which leverages neural attention to infer causal structure. - For each model, we visualized the learned adjacency (causal) matrices and compared their dominant dependencies via heatmaps. - We further extracted and printed the top-weighted causal edges, making the results interpretable and highlighting important directed relationships.
Conclusions: - Neural causal discovery methods like CausalGNNs can flexibly recover both linear and nonlinear dependencies, offering richer modeling power than purely linear baselines. - Visualization and ranking of discovered edges can help practitioners interpret learned causal graphs and guide further hypothesis testing or domain validation. - For robust application in real finance data, additional techniques (regularization, thresholding, validation, bootstrapping) are essential to avoid spurious findings.
