title: 1.8 Boosted Multi-Arm Causal Model
text:
Overview
A Boosted Multi-Arm Causal Model estimates heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE) in settings with more than two treatment options — for example, a placebo arm alongside two or more active interventions. Rather than fitting a single causal model across all arms simultaneously, it adopts a T-learner strategy: one outcome model per arm, each capturing the arm-specific relationship between covariates and outcomes. Treatment effects are then recovered as contrasts between arm predictions, relative to a chosen baseline.
The “boosted” label refers to the learner: each contrast is a boosted X-learner (CXGBoost). That brings XGBoost’s tabular strengths — nonlinear interactions, robustness to irrelevant features, and stable fits on moderate samples — to each arm contrast.
This approach trades off some efficiency (arm models share no parameters) for simplicity and flexibility: it makes no assumptions about how treatment effects relate across arms, and each arm model can be tuned independently.

When to Use It
The Boosted Multi-Arm Causal Model is appropriate when:

There are \(K \geq 3\) treatment conditions (including control/placebo), and binary causal forest methods do not apply directly.
The relationship between covariates and outcomes is likely nonlinear or involves interactions that regression-based methods would miss.
The primary goal is individual-level treatment effect estimation — identifying which arm benefits which subgroup — rather than population-average inference.
Observational data requires covariate adjustment, and a binary treatment model does not match the design.

Typical applications include clinical trials comparing multiple drug regimens against placebo, policy evaluations with several intervention variants, and marketing experiments with multiple campaign conditions.


Key Concepts
T-learner. The T-learner (or “treatment-specific learner”) fits a separate outcome model for each arm \(k\):
\[\hat{\mu}_k(x) \approx E[Y \mid X = x,\, W = k], \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, K-1\]
where arm \(k = b\) (typically \(k = 0\), placebo or control) serves as the baseline. Each model is trained only on units assigned to arm \(k\), so the models are entirely independent of one another.
Treatment contrasts. The conditional average treatment effect (CATE) for arm \(k\) relative to baseline \(b\) is:
\[\tau_{k \leftarrow b}(x) = \hat{\mu}_k(x) - \hat{\mu}_b(x)\]
For \(K\) arms, this yields \(K - 1\) contrast surfaces over the covariate space. For example, with arms \(\{\)placebo, drug A, drug B\(\}\), the model returns \(\hat{\tau}_{A \leftarrow \text{placebo}}(x)\) and \(\hat{\tau}_{B \leftarrow \text{placebo}}(x)\) for each individual.
Pairwise contrasts. Any two non-baseline arms can also be compared directly:
\[\tau_{k \leftarrow j}(x) = \hat{\mu}_k(x) - \hat{\mu}_j(x)\]
This is straightforward since all \(\hat{\mu}_k\) are defined over the full covariate space.
Propensity scores. A multiclass propensity model estimates \(\hat{e}_k(x) = P(W = k \mid X = x)\) for all arms jointly, typically using a probability forest or multinomial model. These propensity scores are not incorporated into the outcome model training (the approach is not doubly robust), but serve three diagnostic purposes: detecting covariate imbalance across arms, flagging low-overlap regions where counterfactual predictions are unreliable, and enabling inverse probability weighting (IPW) for population-level ATE estimation if needed.
Identification assumptions. Like all observational causal methods, the T-learner requires:

Consistency — the observed outcome for a unit assigned to arm \(k\) equals its potential outcome \(Y(k)\).
Ignorability — conditional on \(X\), treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes: \(W \perp (Y(0), \ldots, Y(K-1)) \mid X\). There must be no unmeasured confounders.
Overlap — every unit has a non-zero probability of receiving any arm: \(P(W = k \mid X = x) > 0\) for all \(k\) and all \(x\) in the support.



Known Limitations
T-learner bias in small arms. When one arm has few observations, its outcome model is poorly estimated, which degrades the contrast estimates for that arm disproportionately. S-learner or X-learner variants can partially mitigate this by sharing information across arms.
No regularization toward a common effect. Unlike the Multi-Arm/Multi-Outcome Causal Forest (which uses a joint splitting criterion), T-learner arm models are fully independent. If treatment effects are genuinely similar across arms, a joint model would be more efficient.
Not doubly robust. Propensity scores are estimated but not used in the outcome model training. Misspecification of \(\hat{\mu}_k\) is not corrected by a well-estimated propensity model.
Extrapolation risk. Each \(\hat{\mu}_k\) must produce predictions for all units regardless of arm assignment — including covariate regions where that arm had few or no training observations. Low-propensity regions should be interpreted cautiously.


Pipeline: Five Steps



Boosted multi-arm causal model


A few things worth emphasizing from the pipeline:
Step 2 extrapolation is the central challenge. Each arm model is trained on only the units assigned to that arm, but must predict \(\hat{\mu}_k(x)\) for every unit in the dataset — including those from other arms. In regions of covariate space where arm \(k\) is rare (low propensity), the model is extrapolating from very little data. The propensity scores in step 4 directly diagnose this risk: wherever \(\hat{e}_k(x)\) is near zero, the corresponding \(\hat{\mu}_k(x)\) estimates should be treated with caution.
Step 3’s “best arm” output is operationally the most useful in personalized treatment settings. For each individual, the model returns \(\text{argmax}_k\, \hat{\tau}_{k \leftarrow b}(x)\), identifying which arm delivers the largest estimated benefit. This is the basis for individualized treatment rules (ITRs) — policies that assign different arms to different subgroups based on predicted effect heterogeneity. That said, uncertainty around CATE estimates should be factored in before acting on these assignments; small margin differences between arms may not be reliable.
Step 4 propensity scores serve three distinct roles that are worth keeping separate: (1) diagnostics — visualizing covariate overlap across arms to identify extrapolation risk; (2) ATE correction — IPW-adjusted averages account for non-random arm assignment in observational data; and (3) sensitivity analysis — comparing naive and propensity-weighted ATEs reveals how sensitive conclusions are to the observational design.

title: 1.8 Boosted Multi-Arm Causal Model
text:
Implementation in Python
MultiArmCausalBoost in PyCausalML fits one boosted contrast model per non-baseline arm. The implementation is designed for flexibility and interpretability, with the following features:

Outcome models: one CXGBoost model per contrast against the baseline.
Propensity model: a logistic regression inside each contrast model, used to combine the arm-specific effect estimates.
Prediction output: predict(X) returns one contrast column per non-baseline arm.

title: 1.8 Boosted Multi-Arm Causal Model

Setup
This notebook fits MultiArmCausalBoost from PyCausalML (pycausalml.tree_based_models).
fit(X, treatment, y) returns the fitted estimator. predict returns a NumPy array of conditional average treatment effects. A fitted model also exposes explain and plot_shap.
Install the package from this repository, with the plotting and boosting extras.
The three-arm example is built with make_patient_multiarm from Data/patients.csv, the same design as the multi-arm causal forest tutorial. One boosted model is fit for each outcome. Arm labels are coded placebo=0, A=1, B=2, and the baseline arm is 0.

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

def _repo_root() -> Path:

Imported PyCausalML



Prepare the patient dataset
The example is built from Data/patients.csv: real age, comorbidity, baseline risk, and sex, a simulated three-arm treatment (placebo, A, B), observed log length of stay, and a simulated binary clinical response that improves under A and more so under B.
make_patient_multiarm builds that design from Data/patients.csv:

Draws a three-level treatment (placebo, A, B) with probabilities 40%, 30%, and 30%.
Keeps observed log length of stay (log_los) as the first outcome. Treatment is randomized, so its effect on length of stay is null.
Simulates a binary clinical response that is higher under arm A and higher still under arm B.

Train MultiArmCausalBoost on log_los and response
MultiArmCausalBoost fits one boosted contrast per non-baseline arm. This notebook fits a separate model for each outcome, log_los and response.

Key choices you control:

These plots explain the predicted log-length-of-stay contrasts against placebo. explain_cate uses a subsample of the test rows so the permutation explainer stays small.


Code
class _Contrast:
    def __init__(self, model, column):
        self.model = model
        self.column = column
        self.feature_names_ = feature_names

    def predict(self, new_x):
        return np.asarray(self.model.predict(new_x))[:, self.column]

sv_A = explain_cate(_Contrast(model_los, 0), X_test, feature_names=feature_names, max_samples=30, random_state=1)
sv_B = explain_cate(_Contrast(model_los, 1), X_test, feature_names=feature_names, max_samples=30, random_state=1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
for ax, sv, title in (
    (axes[0], sv_A, "log_los: A vs placebo"),
    (axes[1], sv_B, "log_los: B vs placebo"),
):
    order = np.argsort(sv.importance())
    ax.barh(np.array(feature_names)[order], sv.importance()[order], color="#4C72B0")
    ax.set_title(title)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 1.8 Boosted Multi-Arm Causal Model
text:
Notes and limitations

Each contrast is a boosted X-learner against placebo, fit only on the baseline arm and that arm.
Propensity scores are used inside each contrast. The averages above are means of predicted contrasts, not a doubly robust score.
Each arm needs enough rows, because that arm’s outcome model is trained only on units assigned to it.
The two outcomes are fit separately. The models do not share an outcome-correlation structure.
SHAP explains the predicted contrast. That is the structural effect only when the identification assumptions hold.

text:

title: 2.1 Meta-Learner with Binary Treatments
text:
Overview
Meta-learners are flexible, modular frameworks designed to estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) by decomposing the causal estimation problem into one or more supervised learning sub-problems. Rather than requiring a purpose-built causal model, meta-learners treat any regression or classification algorithm — such as random forests, gradient boosting machines, LASSO, or neural networks — as a plug-in “base learner,” making them highly adaptable to a wide range of data settings. This separation of concerns between the causal structure and the predictive machinery is one of the defining advantages of the meta-learning approach.
For binary treatments, where \(W_i \in \{0, 1\}\) indicates whether unit \(i\) received the treatment, the central challenge is to recover individual-level treatment effect heterogeneity from observed outcomes. The key idea across all binary-treatment meta-learners is to leverage the treatment indicator in structurally different ways — either by fitting separate outcome models for each treatment arm, by modeling the treatment propensity directly, or by constructing pseudo-outcomes that isolate the treatment effect signal. These design choices lead to a family of estimators that differ substantially in their assumptions, bias-variance tradeoffs, and sensitivity to model misspecification.
Binary treatment meta-learners are particularly consequential in observational studies, where treatment assignment is not randomized and is instead driven by observed (and potentially unobserved) covariates. In such settings, naive comparisons between treated and control units conflate the treatment effect with confounding — systematic differences in baseline characteristics between the two groups. Meta-learners address confounding through unconfoundedness (or ignorability) assumptions, combined with careful modeling of the outcome and/or treatment assignment process. The quality of CATE estimates therefore depends critically on the richness of the observed covariate set and the adequacy of the base learner in capturing the relevant data structure.
The most widely studied meta-learners for binary treatments include:

The S-Learner (Single learner), which fits a single outcome model including the treatment indicator as a feature, and recovers the CATE as the difference in predicted outcomes under \(W = 1\) versus \(W = 0\). Its simplicity makes it computationally attractive, but it can suffer from regularization bias if the base learner shrinks the treatment indicator coefficient toward zero.
The T-Learner (Two-model learner), which fits separate outcome models for the treated and control groups and estimates the CATE as their difference. This approach naturally allows treatment effect heterogeneity but can exhibit high variance when the two groups are imbalanced in size or covariate distribution.
The X-Learner, which extends the T-Learner by constructing imputed treatment effects for each unit using the other group’s fitted model, and then combining these estimates via a weighting function, often based on the propensity score. The X-Learner is especially effective in settings with significant imbalance between treatment and control group sizes.
The R-Learner (Robinson decomposition learner), which builds on the partial linear residualization idea of Robinson (1988) to orthogonalize both the outcome and the treatment before fitting the CATE. It is designed to target the CATE directly, and enjoys favorable theoretical properties under cross-fitting, connecting closely to the double/debiased machine learning literature.
The DR-Learner (Doubly Robust learner), which leverages augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) to construct doubly robust pseudo-outcomes. An estimator is doubly robust in the sense that it remains consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity score model is correctly specified — though not necessarily both.

Each meta-learner embodies a different set of implicit assumptions and practical tradeoffs. Their performance is highly sensitive to characteristics of the data, including: (i) the degree of treatment group imbalance, which can destabilize estimators that rely heavily on extrapolation across groups; (ii) the smoothness and complexity of the underlying CATE function, which determines how well the base learner can approximate it; (iii) the signal-to-noise ratio in the outcome, which affects variance of effect estimates; and (iv) the overlap in covariate distributions between treated and control units, which is a prerequisite for identification in observational settings. Understanding these sensitivities is essential for selecting an appropriate meta-learner in practice, and motivates the use of simulation studies and cross-validated evaluation strategies.

N_EST = 25

def ate_row(name, model, X):
    cate = np.asarray(model.predict(X), dtype=float)
    info = model.average_treatment_effect(X)
    est = float(info["estimate"])
    se = float(info["std.err"])
    if not np.isfinite(se):
        se = float(np.std(cate, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(cate)))
        est = float(np.mean(cate))
    return {
        "learner": name,
        "ate": est,
        "se": se,
        "ci_lower": est - 1.96 * se,
        "ci_upper": est + 1.96 * se,
    }

def abs_pct_ate(pred, truth):
    denom = abs(float(np.mean(truth)))
    if denom < 1e-8:
        return np.nan
    return 100.0 * abs(float(np.mean(pred) - np.mean(truth))) / denom

def kl_divergence(pred, truth, bins=15):
    pred = np.asarray(pred, dtype=float)
    truth = np.asarray(truth, dtype=float)
    lo = float(min(pred.min(), truth.min()))
    hi = float(max(pred.max(), truth.max()))
    if not np.isfinite(lo) or hi <= lo:
        return np.nan
    hp, _ = np.histogram(pred, bins=bins, range=(lo, hi))
    hq, _ = np.histogram(truth, bins=bins, range=(lo, hi))
    hp = hp.astype(float) + 1e-3
    hq = hq.astype(float) + 1e-3
    hp /= hp.sum()
    hq /= hq.sum()
    return float(np.sum(hp * np.log(hp / hq)))

def cumulative_gain(y, w, score):
    order = np.argsort(-np.asarray(score, dtype=float))
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)[order]
    w = np.asarray(w)[order]
    n = len(y)
    frac = np.arange(1, n + 1) / n
    gain = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        ww = w[: i + 1]
        yy = y[: i + 1]
        n1 = int((ww == 1).sum())
        n0 = int((ww == 0).sum())
        gain[i] = 0.0 if n1 == 0 or n0 == 0 else (yy[ww == 1].mean() - yy[ww == 0].mean()) * (i + 1) / n
    return frac, gain

text:
Summary and Conclusions
This notebook demonstrates how to use PyCausalML to implement meta-learners (S-, T-, X-, R-learners) for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (CATE/ITE) on synthetic data. We validate the meta-learners’ performance using train/validation splits and report metrics like Abs % Error of ATE, MSE, KL Divergence, and AUUC. The results show how different meta-learners and base regressors perform in estimating CATE, with visualizations of predicted vs actual CATE distributions and scatter plots. Part C uses SHAP (via explain_cate(), permutation SHAP, and PyCausalML SHAP plots) to summarize which covariates drive each meta-learner’s predicted CATE on a held subset of units, optionally in parallel using future (multisession) and parallel = TRUE in permshap. Part D fits S-, T-, X-, and R-learners on the abortion dataset with treatment coded as "Control" / "Treated", reports training-set ATE estimates and predicted-CATE histograms, and applies the same SHAP workflow to a training subsample for interpretability.

title: 2.3. Meta-Learners with Continuous Treatments
text:
Overview
When the treatment variable is continuous — such as a drug dosage, an exposure duration, a price, or a policy intensity — the binary and multi-arm frameworks of the preceding sections no longer apply directly. There is no finite set of contrasts to estimate, and the treatment effect cannot be summarized as a difference between two discrete potential outcomes. Instead, the quantity of interest is a dose-response function that describes how the expected outcome, and its rate of change, varies jointly with the treatment level \(d\) and the covariate vector \(x\).

Estimands
Two complementary estimands are commonly targeted in the continuous treatment setting.
The Conditional Average Dose Response (CADR) function characterizes the full outcome surface as a function of dose:
\[\mu(d, x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(d) \mid X = x]\]
and the treatment effect at dose level \(d\) relative to a reference dose \(d_0\) (often zero or the observed minimum) is:
\[\tau(d, x) = \mu(d, x) - \mu(d_0, x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(d) - Y(d_0) \mid X = x]\]
This is the natural generalization of the binary CATE: rather than a single scalar effect per unit, we obtain a curve — one contrast value for each point on a pre-specified dose grid \(\mathcal{D} = \{d_1, d_2, \dots, d_m\}\).
The Marginal Structural Derivative (or dose-response slope) targets the local rate of change in the outcome with respect to the treatment:
\[\tau'(d, x) = \frac{\partial}{\partial d} \mathbb{E}[Y(d) \mid X = x]\]
This is useful when the practitioner is interested in marginal effects — whether increasing the dose slightly from its current level improves or worsens outcomes — rather than in cumulative contrasts against a baseline. In practice, \(\tau'(d, x)\) is often approximated by finite differences on the estimated CADR surface.
Both estimands require identification via a generalized unconfoundedness assumption:
\[Y(d) \perp D \mid X \quad \text{for all } d \in \mathcal{D}\]
along with a positivity (or overlap) condition requiring that the generalized propensity score \(f(d \mid x)\) — the conditional density of treatment given covariates — is bounded away from zero across the support of \(D\):
\[f(d \mid x) > 0 \quad \text{for all } (d, x) \text{ in the support}\]
Violations of positivity are more likely and harder to detect in the continuous setting, since the support of \(D\) is infinite-dimensional relative to any finite sample. Overlap diagnostics should therefore be conducted carefully, for example by inspecting the distribution of the generalized propensity score across subgroups.


The Generalized Propensity Score
In the binary setting, the propensity score \(e(x) = P(T=1 \mid X=x)\) is a scalar probability. For continuous treatments, it is replaced by the generalized propensity score (GPS):
\[r(d, x) = f_{D \mid X}(d \mid x)\]
the conditional density of receiving dose \(d\) given covariates \(x\). The GPS plays the same role as the binary propensity score in balancing covariate distributions and enabling doubly robust estimation, but its estimation is substantially more demanding. Common approaches include:

Parametric GPS: Assume \(D \mid X \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat{m}(x), \hat{\sigma}^2)\) where \(\hat{m}(x)\) is a regression of \(D\) on \(X\). The GPS is then evaluated as the normal density at the observed dose.
Nonparametric GPS: Use kernel density estimation or normalizing flows conditioned on \(X\) to estimate \(f(d \mid x)\) without distributional assumptions.
Residual-based GPS: In the R-Learner, the GPS enters implicitly through the treatment residual \(D - \hat{m}(X)\), avoiding the need to estimate the full conditional density.

Misspecification of the GPS can introduce substantial bias into propensity-weighted and doubly robust estimators, and this risk is heightened in the continuous case relative to binary treatments.


Adapting Meta-Learner Variants to Continuous Treatments

S-Learner
The S-Learner fits a single outcome model \(\hat{\mu}(x, d)\) on the full sample, treating the continuous dose \(D\) as an additional continuous feature alongside \(X\):
\[\hat{\tau}(d, x) = \hat{\mu}(x, d) - \hat{\mu}(x, d_0)\]
The dose-response curve is recovered by evaluating \(\hat{\mu}(x, \cdot)\) on the dose grid \(\mathcal{D}\) at any covariate value of interest. This is the most straightforward extension and imposes no particular structure on the dose-response shape, relying entirely on the base learner to capture the joint \((X, D)\) surface. Flexible base learners such as gradient boosting or neural networks can represent nonlinear and non-monotone dose-response relationships naturally. The key limitation is the same as in the binary case: if the base learner imposes strong smoothness or regularization in the \(D\) direction, the estimated dose-response curve may be overly flat and fail to capture meaningful heterogeneity.


T-Learner
The T-Learner generalizes to the continuous setting by discretizing the dose into \(m\) bins or grid points \(\{d_1, \dots, d_m\}\) and fitting a separate outcome model \(\hat{\mu}_j(x)\) for each bin \(j\):
\[\hat{\tau}(d_j, x) = \hat{\mu}_j(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\]
where \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\) corresponds to the reference dose bin. This approach is intuitive but has significant practical drawbacks. The choice of binning scheme is arbitrary and can meaningfully affect results. Fine grids produce sparse bins, each with few observations, leading to high-variance arm-specific models — essentially the same sparsity problem that affects multi-arm T-Learners, but now potentially at much larger scale. For this reason, the T-Learner is generally the least preferred meta-learner for continuous treatments unless the dose variable is naturally near-discrete in its distribution.


X-Learner
The X-Learner can be adapted to continuous treatments by applying the cross-fitting logic locally on the dose grid: for each grid point \(d_j\), units near \(d_j\) and units at the reference dose \(d_0\) are selected, and the binary X-Learner pipeline is run on this local subsample using an arm-specific propensity model. The resulting local estimates are then assembled into a dose-response curve. This approach inherits the X-Learner’s efficiency advantages under imbalance — which is common in continuous treatment settings where the dose distribution may be concentrated in certain regions — but introduces sensitivity to the bandwidth or neighborhood definition used to select units near each grid point.


R-Learner
The R-Learner is particularly well-suited to the continuous treatment setting and is the method implemented in r_learner_continuous() in PyCausalML. It extends Robinson’s (1988) partial linear residualization to the continuous case by orthogonalizing both the outcome and the treatment against their respective conditional expectations:

Estimate nuisance functions:

\(\hat{m}(x) = \mathbb{E}[D \mid X = x]\) (dose regression on covariates)
\(\hat{\mu}(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]\) (outcome regression on covariates, marginalizing over dose)

Compute residuals:

Outcome residual: \(\tilde{Y}_i = Y_i - \hat{\mu}(X_i)\)
Treatment residual: \(\tilde{D}_i = D_i - \hat{m}(X_i)\)

Estimate \(\tau(d, x)\) by solving:

\[\min_{\tau} \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( \tilde{Y}_i - \tau(D_i, X_i) \cdot \tilde{D}_i \right)^2 \right]\]
The orthogonalization ensures that errors in the nuisance estimates \(\hat{m}(x)\) and \(\hat{\mu}(x)\) enter the CATE estimation problem only at second order, providing robustness to moderate nuisance misspecification. Under regularity conditions, the R-Learner achieves near-oracle convergence rates for \(\tau(d, x)\) (Nie & Wager, 2021). In r_learner_continuous(), the final step is implemented by evaluating the fitted \(\hat{\tau}(\cdot, x)\) on the dose grid \(\mathcal{D}\), yielding a discretized dose-response curve for each unit or covariate profile.


DR-Learner
The DR-Learner generalizes to continuous treatments by constructing doubly robust pseudo-outcomes using the generalized propensity score. For a contrast at dose level \(d\) versus reference \(d_0\), the AIPW-style pseudo-outcome for unit \(i\) is:
\[\hat{\phi}_i(d) = \frac{\mathbf{1}[D_i \approx d]}{r(d, X_i)} \left(Y_i - \hat{\mu}(d, X_i)\right) - \frac{\mathbf{1}[D_i \approx d_0]}{r(d_0, X_i)} \left(Y_i - \hat{\mu}(d_0, X_i)\right) + \hat{\mu}(d, X_i) - \hat{\mu}(d_0, X_i)\]
where \(r(d, x) = f(d \mid x)\) is the generalized propensity score and the indicator \(\mathbf{1}[D_i \approx d]\) selects units with doses in a neighborhood of \(d\). Regressing \(\hat{\phi}_i(d)\) on \(X_i\) for each grid point \(d \in \mathcal{D}\) yields the DR-Learner dose-response estimate. The doubly robust property holds pointwise on the grid: at each dose level \(d\), the estimate is consistent if either the outcome model \(\hat{\mu}(d, x)\) or the GPS \(r(d, x)\) is correctly specified. However, the localization step introduces a bandwidth choice, and the pseudo-outcome construction is sensitive to extreme GPS values — a risk that is heightened in the continuous setting because near-zero densities can occur in any region of the dose support.



Single-Vector Summaries with treatment_type = "continuous"
In many applied settings, the practitioner does not need the full dose-response curve. Instead, a single-vector CATE summary — one scalar effect estimate per unit — is sufficient, typically representing the effect of moving from the observed dose to a target dose, or the local slope of the dose-response at the observed dose. The meta-learners in PyCausalML with treatment_type = "continuous" are designed for this use case. Rather than evaluating \(\hat{\tau}(d, x)\) on a full grid, they return:
\[\hat{\tau}_i = \hat{\tau}(D_i^*, X_i)\]
where \(D_i^*\) is a user-specified target dose (e.g., the population mean dose, the maximum tolerated dose, or a policy-relevant threshold). This produces a unit-level treatment effect vector of the same form as in the binary CATE setting, enabling the same downstream analyses — effect heterogeneity visualization, policy targeting, subgroup discovery — without committing to a full dose-response curve estimation.


Practical Considerations
Continuous treatment settings require additional care relative to binary and multi-arm settings along several dimensions:

Dose grid selection: The resolution of \(\mathcal{D}\) involves a bias-variance tradeoff. Fine grids yield smoother curves but thinner local samples; coarser grids are more stable but may obscure nonlinearities. Adaptive grids based on the observed dose distribution are often preferable to uniform spacing.
GPS estimation quality: The generalized propensity score is harder to estimate well than a binary propensity score, and GPS misspecification propagates into weighted and doubly robust estimators. Residual diagnostics — checking whether \(\tilde{D}_i = D_i - \hat{m}(X_i)\) is approximately uncorrelated with \(X_i\) after adjustment — are a useful sanity check.
Extrapolation risk: Unlike binary treatments where predictions are made at \(W \in \{0, 1\}\), continuous treatment estimators must extrapolate \(\hat{\mu}(d, x)\) to dose values not observed near a given covariate profile. This is particularly problematic at the tails of the dose distribution and in regions of thin overlap.
Monotonicity and shape constraints: When domain knowledge supports a monotone or concave dose-response relationship, incorporating shape constraints into the base learner can substantially reduce estimation variance at the cost of flexibility.

Part A: Meta-learners with synthetic data
We simulate a continuous treatment and a smooth dose–response surface so we can compare estimates to a known benchmark.

Data Generation for Continuous Treatment


Code
%matplotlib inline
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from pathlib import Path

from pycausalml import (
    DRLearner,
    DomainAdaptationLearner,
    LinearDML,
    RLearner,
    SLearner,
    SparseLinearDML,
    TLearner,
    XLearner,
    explain_cate,
    synthetic_data,
)
from pycausalml.data import make_multiarm_data
from pycausalml.double_machine_learning import CausalForestDML, PartiallyLinearDML

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110
N_EST = 25
print("Imported PyCausalML")

rng = np.random.default_rng(123)
n, p = 1000, 6
X = rng.normal(size=(n, p))
dose = np.clip(rng.normal(1.4 + 0.35 * X[:, 0], 0.55, size=n), 0.05, 4.0)
modifier = 1.0 + 0.45 * X[:, 0]
# Marginal slope (1.15 - 0.30 * d) * modifier. Outcome is the integral plus noise.
y = (
    0.5 * X[:, 1]
    + dose * modifier * (1.15 - 0.15 * dose)
    + rng.normal(scale=0.45, size=n)
)
true_slope = (1.15 - 0.30 * dose) * modifier
names = [f"X{i+1}" for i in range(p)]
grid = np.linspace(np.quantile(dose, 0.08), np.quantile(dose, 0.92), 11)
print(X.shape, "dose mean", round(float(dose.mean()), 3))


Imported PyCausalML
(1000, 6) dose mean 1.411




Estimand: Conditional Average Dose Response (CADR)
For continuous treatment \(D\) (e.g., dosage), we estimate:
\[\tau(d, x) = \frac{\partial}{\partial d} \mathbb{E}[Y(d) \mid X = x]\]
This is the marginal effect of an infinitesimal dose increase at level \(d\) for units with covariates \(x\).


Generalized R-Learner for Continuous Treatments
Extends Robinson transformation to continuous treatments using kernel smoothing. The implementation lives in PyCausalML as r_learner_continuous() (cross-fitted learner="rf" nuisances and local weighted lm, with cross-fitted gradient-boosting nuisances and a local weighted slope):


Average Dose-Response Curve


Code
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

mu = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=N_EST, max_depth=2, random_state=0)
mu.fit(np.column_stack([X, dose]), y)
level = [float(mu.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.full(len(X), d)])).mean()) for d in grid]

m_y = np.zeros(len(y))
m_d = np.zeros(len(y))
rng_fold = np.random.default_rng(0)
fold = rng_fold.integers(0, 2, size=len(y))
for k in (0, 1):
    tr, te = fold != k, fold == k
    fy = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=N_EST, max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
    fd = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=N_EST, max_depth=2, random_state=1).fit(X[tr], dose[tr])
    m_y[te] = fy.predict(X[te])
    m_d[te] = fd.predict(X[te])
y_res, d_res = y - m_y, dose - m_d
bw = 1.06 * np.std(dose) * len(dose) ** (-0.2)

def local_slope(mask=None):
    dd = dose if mask is None else dose[mask]
    yr = y_res if mask is None else y_res[mask]
    dr = d_res if mask is None else d_res[mask]
    out = []
    for g in grid:
        wt = np.exp(-0.5 * ((dd - g) / bw) ** 2)
        out.append(float(np.sum(wt * dr * yr) / np.sum(wt * dr ** 2)))
    return np.asarray(out)

slope_hat = local_slope()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
axes[0].plot(grid, level, marker="o")
axes[0].set_title("S-learner average dose response")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Dose")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Mean predicted outcome")
axes[1].plot(grid, slope_hat, marker="o", label="R-learner")
axes[1].plot(grid, [((1.15 - 0.30 * g) * modifier).mean() for g in grid], color="black", label="True average slope")
axes[1].set_title("Average marginal slope")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Dose")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Heterogeneous Dose-Response: Effect Modification
Visualize how dose-response varies by key covariate (X1):


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.8))
for mask, label in ((X[:, 0] > 0, "X1 > 0"), (X[:, 0] <= 0, "X1 ≤ 0")):
    ax.plot(grid, local_slope(mask), marker="o", label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Dose")
ax.set_ylabel("Local slope")
ax.set_title("Dose-response slope by X1")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Native S/T/X/R/DR with a continuous dose (synthetic)
PyCausalML now accepts continuous treatment for SLearner, TLearner, XLearner, RLearner, and DRLearner via a continuous dose. This is not the same object as r_learner_continuous() (which returns a dose grid \(\times\) units surface for CADR): here you get a single \(\hat{\tau}(X)\) vector per specification (e.g., S-learner contrast \(\mu(X,d_1)-\mu(X,d_0)\) at training quartiles of \(D\); T/X high-vs-low dose at the median; R-learner Robinson partial effect; DR continuous pseudo-outcome). The chunk below is a minimal sanity check on the same simulated data as above.


Code
d0, d1 = np.quantile(dose, [0.25, 0.75])
s_mu = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=N_EST, max_depth=2, random_state=2)
s_mu.fit(np.column_stack([X, dose]), y)
s_contrast = s_mu.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.full(len(X), d1)])) - s_mu.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.full(len(X), d0)]))
high = (dose > np.median(dose)).astype(int)
native_rows = [{"learner": "S contrast (q75-q25)", "mean": float(s_contrast.mean())}]
for label, cls in (("T median split", TLearner), ("X median split", XLearner), ("DR median split", DRLearner)):
    model = cls(learner="gbr", n_estimators=N_EST, random_state=2)
    model.fit(X, high, y, feature_names=names)
    native_rows.append({"learner": label, "mean": float(np.mean(model.predict(X)))})
plr = PartiallyLinearDML(discrete_treatment=False, model_y="gbr", n_estimators=N_EST, random_state=2)
plr.fit(X, dose, y, feature_names=names)
native_rows.append({"learner": "Partially linear DML slope", "mean": float(plr.effect())})
print(pd.DataFrame(native_rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("True mean slope", round(float(true_slope.mean()), 3))


                   learner  mean
      S contrast (q75-q25) 0.597
            T median split 0.849
            X median split 0.695
           DR median split 0.720
Partially linear DML slope 0.699
True mean slope 0.683




Diagnostics & Validation Protocol
Diagnostics help ensure that dose-response estimates are not driven by lack of overlap, covariate imbalance, or miscalibration. Below we implement overlap checks, balance assessment before/after weighting, and a CATE calibration plot.

Overlap Diagnostics
For continuous treatments, overlap means that the conditional support of \(D\) given \(X\) has sufficient density across the dose range we care about. We check the marginal distribution of \(D\) and the distribution of the conditional expectation \(E[D|X]\) (estimated via a regression of \(D\) on \(X\)) to assess common support.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(dose, bins=30, color="#2E86AB")
axes[0].set_title("Marginal dose")
axes[1].hist(m_d, bins=30, color="#1F4E79")
axes[1].set_title("Estimated E[D | X]")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

quartiles = pd.qcut(dose, 4, labels=["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"])
rows = []
for q in ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]:
    mask = quartiles == q
    ref = quartiles == "Q1"
    for j, name in enumerate(names):
        rows.append({
            "quartile": q,
            "covariate": name,
            "smd_vs_q1": float((X[mask, j].mean() - X[ref, j].mean()) / (X[:, j].std() + 1e-8)),
        })
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index="covariate", columns="quartile", values="smd_vs_q1").round(3))









quartile    Q1     Q2     Q3     Q4
covariate                          
X1         0.0  0.400  0.849  1.312
X2         0.0 -0.025  0.046  0.003
X3         0.0  0.081  0.018  0.058
X4         0.0  0.120  0.072  0.005
X5         0.0 -0.103 -0.126  0.014
X6         0.0  0.032 -0.031  0.074


Interpretation: substantial overlap across covariate strata (e.g., E[D|X] distributions by X1 quartile) supports estimation of dose-response over the observed dose range; narrow or separated supports suggest limited overlap and cautious interpretation.


Balance Assessment (Before/After Weighting)
We stratify units by dose quartiles and assess standardized mean differences (SMD) of covariates across strata. We then compute stabilized inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) for continuous \(D\) using a normal approximation: \(w_i = f(D_i) / f(D_i|X_i)\), with \(f(D|X)\) from \(D|X \sim N(\hat{e}(X), \hat{\sigma}^2)\), and reassess balance after weighting.


CATE Calibration Plot
We bin units by their predicted marginal effect at a reference dose (median dose) and plot mean predicted effect vs. mean observed outcome (residualized by baseline) in each bin. A well-calibrated estimator should show a positive alignment between predicted effect and realized outcomes.


Code
ref = float(np.median(dose))
pred_at_ref = np.array([
    local_slope()[np.argmin(np.abs(grid - ref))]
] * len(X))
# unit-level slope proxy: residual ratio, shrunk
unit_slope = y_res * d_res / (d_res ** 2 + 0.15)
bins = pd.qcut(unit_slope, 6, duplicates="drop")
tab = pd.DataFrame({"pred": unit_slope, "actual": true_slope, "bin": bins}).groupby("bin", observed=True).mean()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.8))
ax.plot(tab.pred, tab.actual, marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel("Mean residual slope proxy")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean true slope")
ax.set_title("Calibration of the local slope proxy")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()












Decision Framework: Which Meta-Learner to Use?
For continuous treatments, the choice of approach depends on data structure and goals:







Criterion
Recommendation




Target
Full curve \(\tau(d,x)\) on a grid → r_learner_continuous(). Single-vector heterogeneous “effects” with continuous \(D\) in PyCausalML → SLearner / TLearner / XLearner / RLearner / DRLearner with treatment_type = "continuous" (see help text for each estimand).


Overlap
Ensure sufficient density of \(D\) across \(X\); trim or restrict to common support if needed.


Curvature
If effect is linear in \(d\) → local linear R-Learner or parametric DR model; if nonlinear → kernel smoothing, splines, or generalized random forests.


Bandwidth
Use cross-validation to choose bandwidth for kernel weights; Silverman-type rules are a starting point.


Alternatives
Generalized random forests (generalized random forests) for continuous treatment; double ML with series expansion in \(d\); causal BART with continuous treatment.



Use the R-Learner when you want a debiased, flexible estimator that leverages ML for nuisances and residualization; use GRF or BART when you prefer a single forest that directly targets the dose-response.

Part B: Use case — NMES (nmes_data from this tutorial (data/nmes_data.csv))
nmes_data comes from the 1987 National Medical Expenditure Survey (NMES) and is bundled in this tutorial (data/nmes_data.csv) (data/nmes_data.csv). It is widely used for continuous treatment / dose-response methods (e.g., Imai & van Dyk, 2004). The extract has 9,708 observations and 12 variables (complete cases in the packaged version).








Role
Variable
Description




Outcome
TOTALEXP
Total annual medical expenditures (USD)


Treatment
packyears
Pack-years: (cigarettes per day / 20) × years smoked


Covariates
AGESMOKE
Age when started smoking



LASTAGE
Age at last interview



MALE
Sex (indicator)



RACE3
Race (coded)



educate
Education



marital
Marital status



SREGION
Census region



POVSTALB
Poverty status



beltuse
Seat belt use



HSQACCWT
Sampling weight (include as covariate here for simplicity; full survey inference would use design-based weights)



Inference is only as credible as unconfoundedness and overlap over the support of packyears.

Explore treatment and outcome


Prepare analysis data and fit generalized R-learner
We map TOTALEXP \(\to\) Y, packyears \(\to\) D, and use the covariates above. The dose grid spans the 5th–95th percentiles of packyears to limit extrapolation.


Code
def tutorial_file(name: str):
    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for cand in [here, *here.parents]:
        path = cand / "Tutorials" / "05_02_Meta_Learners" / "data" / name
        if path.is_file():
            return path
    raise FileNotFoundError(name)

nmes = pd.read_csv(tutorial_file("nmes_data.csv"))
print(nmes.shape)
print(nmes[["packyears", "TOTALEXP"]].describe().round(2))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(nmes["packyears"], bins=30, color="#2E86AB")
axes[0].set_title("Pack-years")
axes[1].hist(np.log1p(nmes["TOTALEXP"]), bins=30, color="#1F4E79")
axes[1].set_title("log(1 + total expenditure)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
take = rng.choice(len(nmes), size=1200, replace=False)
sub = nmes.iloc[take].reset_index(drop=True)
covars = [c for c in sub.columns if c not in ("TOTALEXP", "packyears")]
Xn = sub[covars].to_numpy(dtype=float)
dn = sub["packyears"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
yn = np.log1p(sub["TOTALEXP"].to_numpy(dtype=float))
nmes_names = covars
grid_n = np.linspace(np.quantile(dn, 0.05), np.quantile(dn, 0.95), 9)
mu_n = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=N_EST, max_depth=2, random_state=4)
mu_n.fit(np.column_stack([Xn, dn]), yn)
level_n = [float(mu_n.predict(np.column_stack([Xn, np.full(len(Xn), d)])).mean()) for d in grid_n]
print("NMES subsample", len(sub), "covariates", covars)

count    9708.00    9708.00

NMES subsample 1200 covariates ['AGESMOKE', 'LASTAGE', 'MALE', 'RACE3', 'beltuse', 'educate', 'marital', 'SREGION', 'POVSTALB', 'HSQACCWT']




Average estimated local slope vs pack-years (NMES)


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.6))
ax.plot(grid_n, level_n, marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel("Pack-years")
ax.set_ylabel("Mean predicted log expenditure")
ax.set_title("NMES: S-learner average dose response")
fig.tight_layout()

Quick overlap check (continuous treatment)
We plot the marginal distribution of packyears and the distribution of \(\hat{E}[D \mid X]\) (random forest) by sex, as a simple overlap diagnostic.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.6))
axes[0].hist(dn, bins=30, color="#2E86AB")
axes[0].set_title("Pack-years in the subsample")
male = sub["MALE"].to_numpy()
axes[1].hist(dn[male == 0], bins=25, density=True, histtype="step", label="Female")
axes[1].hist(dn[male == 1], bins=25, density=True, histtype="step", label="Male")
axes[1].set_title("Dose by sex")
axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()











Meta-learners on NMES: continuous packyears and binary median split
For compute time when rendering, we fit meta-learners on a random subsample of up to 3,000 rows (the r_learner_continuous() fit above still uses all complete cases).
1. Native continuous treatment. Pass packyears as treatment with treatment_type = "continuous". S-Learner contrasts predicted outcome at the 25th vs. 75th percentile of training \(D\) (override with dose_values = c(d0, d1)). T- / X-Learner use the sample median of \(D\) as high-vs-low split (override with dose_split). R-Learner uses Robinson-style \(\mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[D|X]\) nuisances. DR-Learner uses a continuous cross-fitted pseudo-outcome (see package documentation). Covariates exclude raw packyears so dose enters only through treatment.
2. Binary median split. For a classic ATE of high vs. low exposure and for SHAP below, we also fit binary learners on
\[W_i = \mathbf{1}\{\texttt{packyears}_i > \mathrm{median}(\texttt{packyears})\}.\]
We still do not put raw packyears in \(X\) when using \(W\) (overlap).


Code
high = (dn > np.median(dn)).astype(int)
rows = []
stored = {}
for label, cls in (("S", SLearner), ("T", TLearner), ("X", XLearner), ("R", RLearner), ("DR", DRLearner)):
    model = cls(learner="gbr", n_estimators=N_EST, random_state=4)
    model.fit(Xn, high, yn, feature_names=nmes_names)
    stored[label] = model
    rows.append({"learner": f"{label} high vs low pack-years", "mean_cate": float(np.mean(model.predict(Xn)))})
plr_n = PartiallyLinearDML(discrete_treatment=False, model_y="gbr", n_estimators=N_EST, random_state=4)
plr_n.fit(Xn, dn, yn, feature_names=nmes_names)
rows.append({"learner": "Partially linear DML (per pack-year)", "mean_cate": float(plr_n.effect())})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))


                             learner  mean_cate
            S high vs low pack-years      0.000
            T high vs low pack-years      0.040
            X high vs low pack-years     -0.042
            R high vs low pack-years     -0.110
           DR high vs low pack-years     -0.069
Partially linear DML (per pack-year)      0.000


The mean predicted column averages \(\hat{\tau}(X)\) from predict(); ate_plugin uses estimate_ate()’s internal variance formulas (continuous rows use high-vs-low-\(D\) logic where applicable). Interpret S as a dose contrast at training quartiles, T/X as above-median vs. below, R as a Robinson-type effect, and DR as the continuous DR CATE surface aggregated to a mean—comparability across columns is limited.


Use case: Double machine learning on NMES (DML)
We reuse the same subsample (X_meta, d_meta = packyears, y_meta = TOTALEXP) and fit partially linear DML with random forests nuisances: LinearDML (OLS final stage on residual interactions), SparseLinearDML (Lasso final stage), and CausalForestDML (a causal forest on residuals). All three target \(\hat{\theta}(X)\) in \(\tilde{Y} \approx \tilde{D}\cdot\theta(X)\) with continuous \(\tilde{D}\) (see pycausalml.double_machine_learning). There is no ground-truth CATE on NMES, so we compare (i) ATE with a large-sample normal CI, (ii) holdout RMSE of the cross-fitted \(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid X]\) on a 30% test split (models refit on 70% train only), and (iii) Spearman correlation between predicted \(\hat{\theta}(X)\) on the full subsample (agreement of rankings across methods).


Code
lin = LinearDML(discrete_treatment=False, n_estimators=N_EST, model_y="gbr", random_state=4)
lin.fit(Xn, dn, yn, feature_names=nmes_names)
sparse = SparseLinearDML(discrete_treatment=False, n_estimators=N_EST, model_y="gbr", random_state=4, alpha=0.05)
sparse.fit(Xn, dn, yn, feature_names=nmes_names)
forest = CausalForestDML(num_trees=40, n_splits=2, random_state=4)
forest.fit(Xn, high, yn, feature_names=nmes_names)
rows = []
for label, model in (("LinearDML", lin), ("SparseLinearDML", sparse), ("CausalForestDML (median split)", forest)):
    info = model.average_treatment_effect()
    rows.append({"learner": label, "ate": info["estimate"], "se": info["std.err"]})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))
spear = pd.DataFrame({
    "linear": lin.predict(Xn),
    "sparse": sparse.predict(Xn),
    "forest": forest.predict(Xn),
}).corr(method="spearman")
print("Spearman correlation of predicted effects")
print(spear.round(3))


                       learner    ate    se
                     LinearDML  0.005 0.004
               SparseLinearDML  0.005 0.004
CausalForestDML (median split) -0.182 0.177
Spearman correlation of predicted effects
        linear  sparse  forest
linear   1.000   0.995   0.410
sparse   0.995   1.000   0.406
forest   0.410   0.406   1.000


Interpretation: ATE rows aggregate \(\hat{\theta}(X)\); intervals use the notebook’s default large-sample standard error for the mean CATE (not debiased DML inference). RMSE_EY_holdout measures how well the cross-fitted outcome nuisance predicts \(Y\) out of sample—higher overlap and smoother \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\) often yield lower RMSE. Spearman shows whether heterogeneity rankings agree across linear, sparse, and forest final stages.


SHAP for predicted CATE (DML, NMES)
As in § NMES SHAP for meta-learners, we attribute predicted \(\hat{\theta}(X)\) (not necessarily causal structure) using explain_cate(..., use_permshap = TRUE) and the PyCausalML SHAP plots, on the full-subsample DML fits above.


SHAP interpretability for predicted CATE (NMES)
SHAP attributes predicted \(\hat{\tau}(X)\) to covariates. We use explain_cate() with use_permshap = TRUE, smaller explain/background samples, and relaxed max_iter / tol so the document renders in reasonable time. The X-Learner is fit without a fixed propensity vector so predict() evaluates learned \(e(X)\) on any newdata, as required when permutation SHAP perturbs features.
We run SHAP for S-, T-, X-, and R-learners only: DR-learner predictions require multiple cross-fitted surfaces per call, so permutation SHAP at this sample size is prohibitively slow; the DR row remains in the binary ATE table above. (You can run explain_cate() on tl_nmes_c or other continuous fits similarly if needed; we keep SHAP on binary fits here for cost and a single estimand.)


Code
exp_t = explain_cate(stored["T"], Xn, max_samples=20, n_permutations=5, feature_names=nmes_names, random_state=4)
print(pd.Series(exp_t.importance(), index=exp_t.feature_names).round(3).sort_values(ascending=False).to_string())

MALE        0.228
beltuse     0.135
HSQACCWT    0.116
AGESMOKE    0.056
POVSTALB    0.023
RACE3       0.019
SREGION     0.010
educate     0.000
marital     0.000




SHAP beeswarm and waterfall for the T-Learner surrogate


Code
exp_t.plot_importance(title="NMES T-Learner SHAP (high vs low pack-years)")
plt.show()
exp_t.plot_waterfall(row=int(np.argmax(np.abs(exp_t.predictions))))

title: 2.3. Meta-Learners with Continuous Treatments
text:
Summary and Conclusions
This notebook demonstrated meta-learners for continuous treatments (Part A: synthetic \(D\) with known CADR; Part B: NMES nmes_data with TOTALEXP, packyears, and covariates from this tutorial (data/nmes_data.csv)). Key takeaways:

CADR: For continuous treatment \(D\), a natural target is \(\tau(d,x) = \frac{\partial}{\partial d}\mathbb{E}[Y(d)|X=x]\), the marginal effect of dose at \(d\) given \(x\), estimated on a dose grid by r_learner_continuous().
Native continuous meta-learners: SLearner, TLearner, XLearner, RLearner, and DRLearner accept treatment_type = "continuous" and numeric treatment (e.g. packyears); estimands differ (quartile contrast, median split, Robinson, continuous DR, etc.—see Details in each function’s documentation).
R-Learner for continuous (grid): Cross-fit outcome and treatment (E[D|X]) models, form residuals, then use local linear regression with kernel weights over a dose grid to estimate \(\tau(d,x)\) (or population averages).
Bandwidth: Silverman-type rule used here; in practice choose via cross-validation. Local linear regression reduces boundary bias vs. kernel averaging.
Heterogeneity: Stratifying by covariates (e.g., X1) shows how dose-response differs across subgroups; the R-Learner output can be used for subgroup-specific curves.
SHAP: Because r_learner_continuous() returns a dose \(\times\) unit surface, we explain variation in \(\hat{\tau}(d_{\mathrm{ref}}, x)\) across units by permutation SHAP on a ranger surrogate of those slopes at a fixed reference dose. Interpret as attribution for model-estimated heterogeneity, not as causal Shapley effects for the true DGP.
Diagnostics: Overlap (distribution of \(D\) and \(E[D|X]\)), balance (SMD before/after stabilized IPTW), and CATE calibration (predicted vs residualized outcome by quintile) support the validity of dose-response estimates.
Decision framework: Use the R-Learner for debiased, flexible dose-response estimation; consider GRF or causal BART when a single forest or Bayesian approach is preferred. Always check overlap and balance.
NMES (Part B): Continuous r_learner_continuous() curve for packyears; S/T/X/R/DR with treatment_type = "continuous" on raw packyears (native API); binary median-split S/T/X/R/DR for discrete ATE and SHAP; LinearDML / SparseLinearDML / CausalForestDML on the same subsample with ATE, holdout RMSE for \(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y\mid X]\), Spearman agreement of predicted CATE, and permutation SHAP for \(\hat{\theta}(X)\); learner="rf" in nuisances where used. Interpret under unconfoundedness; use survey weights properly in real reporting.

For a full dose–response surface on a grid, use r_learner_continuous() or methods such as GRF. For a single vector of heterogeneous effects with continuous \(D\), use treatment_type = "continuous" on the standard meta-learners and read each learner’s estimand in the package help. Validate bandwidth and overlap in \(D\) given \(X\); use SHAP on an explicit target (here, surrogate predictions at \(d_{\mathrm{ref}}\) or binary \(\hat{\tau}(X)\)) when reporting interpretability.

title: 2.5. Domain Adaptation Learner (DA-Learner)

title: 2.5. Domain Adaptation Learner (DA-Learner)
text:
Overview
The Domain Adaptation Learner (DA-Learner, implemented as DomainAdaptationLearner in EconML) is a meta-learner for estimating the Conditional Average Treatment Effect:
\[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]\]
from observational data. It is designed specifically for settings where the covariate distributions of the treated and control groups differ substantially — a condition variously described as covariate shift, domain shift, or selection bias — and where standard meta-learners consequently produce biased counterfactual predictions.

Motivation
The T-Learner fits separate outcome models \(\hat{\mu}_1(x)\) and \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\) on the treated and control subsamples, then estimates the CATE as their difference. This works well when the two groups are exchangeable in covariate distribution. In observational studies, however, treatment assignment is typically confounded: units that receive treatment are systematically different from those that do not. When covariate distributions diverge, the outcome model trained on one group must extrapolate to predict counterfactuals for the other group — a region of the covariate space it has not seen during training. This extrapolation degrades prediction quality and biases the resulting CATE estimates.
The DA-Learner addresses this by reweighting each group’s training distribution to resemble the other group’s distribution before fitting the outcome models, making counterfactual predictions more reliable. In this sense it is best understood as a distribution-aligned extension of the T-Learner, closely related in spirit to the X-Learner but with an explicit domain adaptation motivation.



Algorithm

Step 1: Propensity Score Estimation
Estimate the propensity score \(\hat{g}(x) = \hat{P}(T = 1 \mid X = x)\) using any classifier — logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting. The propensity score quantifies how similar or different the two groups are at each point in the covariate space and serves as the basis for the importance weights in the next step.


Step 2: Domain-Adaptive Outcome Model Estimation
This is the defining step of the DA-Learner. Rather than fitting \(\hat{\mu}_0\) and \(\hat{\mu}_1\) on their respective raw subsamples, each model is trained with importance weights that tilt its training distribution toward the opposite group:
Control outcome model \(\hat{\mu}_0\): fit on control units (\(T_i = 0\)) with sample weights
\[w_i^0 = \frac{\hat{g}(X_i)}{1 - \hat{g}(X_i)}\]
Multiplying control observations by \(\hat{g}/(1-\hat{g})\) — the odds of treatment — upweights control units whose covariates resemble the treated population and downweights those that are unrepresentative of it. The resulting model is calibrated to predict \(Y(0)\) accurately for individuals whose covariate profiles are typical of the treated group, which is precisely what is needed for counterfactual imputation.
Treatment outcome model \(\hat{\mu}_1\): fit on treated units (\(T_i = 1\)) with sample weights
\[w_i^1 = \frac{1 - \hat{g}(X_i)}{\hat{g}(X_i)}\]
Symmetrically, this tilts the treated training distribution toward the control population, improving counterfactual accuracy for control units.
Any ML regressor may be used for both models. The importance-weighting scheme is an instance of covariate shift correction from the domain adaptation literature: when the source domain (the group used for training) and the target domain (the group for which predictions are needed) have different marginal distributions over \(X\), reweighting training observations by the density ratio \(p_{\text{target}}(x) / p_{\text{source}}(x)\) recovers consistency of the trained model on the target distribution. The propensity-score-based weights are proportional to this density ratio under standard regularity conditions.


Step 3: Pseudo-Effect Imputation
Using the domain-adapted outcome models, impute a treatment effect residual for each observed unit:
\[\hat{D}_i^1 = Y_i - \hat{\mu}_0(X_i) \quad \text{for treated units } (T_i = 1)\]
\[\hat{D}_i^0 = \hat{\mu}_1(X_i) - Y_i \quad \text{for control units } (T_i = 0)\]
Each residual approximates the individual treatment effect for that unit: \(\hat{D}_i^1\) is the excess outcome of a treated unit above what the adapted control model predicts they would have experienced under control; \(\hat{D}_i^0\) is the gain a control unit would have obtained had they been treated, according to the adapted treatment model. These pseudo-effects play the same structural role as the imputed treatment effects in the X-Learner, but benefit from the distribution alignment performed in Step 2.


Step 4: Final CATE Model
Pool the pseudo-effects and their associated covariates across both groups and fit a single regression model \(\hat{\tau}\):
\[\hat{\tau} = M_3\!\left(\{\hat{D}_i^0, X_i\}_{T_i=0} \cup \{\hat{D}_i^1, X_i\}_{T_i=1}\right)\]
This final model directly estimates \(\tau(x)\) as a smooth function of \(x\), combining information from both groups. Any flexible regressor may be used for \(M_3\).




Full Formulation
The complete procedure in compact notation:
\[\hat{\mu}_0 = M_1\!\left(Y \sim X,\ \text{weights} = \frac{\hat{g}(X)}{1 - \hat{g}(X)},\ T=0\right)\]
\[\hat{\mu}_1 = M_2\!\left(Y \sim X,\ \text{weights} = \frac{1 - \hat{g}(X)}{\hat{g}(X)},\ T=1\right)\]
\[\hat{D}^1 = Y^1 - \hat{\mu}_0(X^1), \qquad \hat{D}^0 = \hat{\mu}_1(X^0) - Y^0\]
\[\hat{\tau} = M_3\!\left(\hat{D} \sim X,\ \text{data} = \{(X^0, \hat{D}^0)\} \cup \{(X^1, \hat{D}^1)\}\right)\]
where \(M_1, M_2, M_3\) are arbitrary ML regressors and \(\hat{g}(x)\) is the estimated propensity score.



Relationship to Other Meta-Learners
The DA-Learner occupies a natural position in the meta-learner family. Like the T-Learner, it fits separate outcome models per arm. Like the X-Learner, it constructs pseudo-effects by cross-imputing counterfactuals and regresses them onto covariates in a final stage. Its distinguishing feature is the explicit use of importance weighting to align training distributions before outcome model fitting — a step that neither the T-Learner nor the standard X-Learner performs.
Relative to the R-Learner and DR-Learner, the DA-Learner does not directly target an orthogonalized or doubly robust objective. It does not enjoy the Neyman-orthogonality property that makes the R-Learner robust to nuisance misspecification, nor the formal double robustness guarantee of the DR-Learner. Its practical advantage lies instead in robustness to distributional mismatch: when covariate shift is severe and extrapolation by un-reweighted outcome models is the primary source of bias, the domain adaptation weighting provides a more targeted correction than generic orthogonalization.


Practical Considerations

Propensity score quality: The importance weights \(\hat{g}/(1-\hat{g})\) and \((1-\hat{g})/\hat{g}\) can become extreme when the propensity score is near 0 or 1. In such regions, a small number of observations receive very large weights, destabilizing the outcome model fit. Weight trimming or clipping — replacing extreme weights with a fixed upper bound — is standard practice and can substantially improve stability with minimal bias cost.
Overlap assumption: The DA-Learner, like all meta-learners, requires that both treatment and control units are observed across the relevant covariate support. In regions where \(\hat{g}(x) \approx 0\) or \(\hat{g}(x) \approx 1\), counterfactual predictions are extrapolations regardless of weighting, and CATE estimates in those regions should be interpreted with caution.
Choice of base learners: The weighting scheme changes the effective training distribution seen by \(M_1\) and \(M_2\), which can interact with the regularization behavior of the base learner. Tree-based methods are generally robust to this, but linear models with strong regularization may still underfit the reweighted distribution in high-curvature regions.

def ate_row(name, model, X):
    cate = np.asarray(model.predict(X), dtype=float)
    info = model.average_treatment_effect(X)
    est = float(info["estimate"])
    se = float(info["std.err"])
    if not np.isfinite(se):
        se = float(np.std(cate, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(cate)))
        est = float(np.mean(cate))
    return {
        "learner": name,
        "ate": est,
        "se": se,
        "ci_lower": est - 1.96 * se,
        "ci_upper": est + 1.96 * se,
    }

def abs_pct_ate(pred, truth):
    denom = abs(float(np.mean(truth)))
    if denom < 1e-8:
        return np.nan
    return 100.0 * abs(float(np.mean(pred) - np.mean(truth))) / denom

def kl_divergence(pred, truth, bins=15):
    pred = np.asarray(pred, dtype=float)
    truth = np.asarray(truth, dtype=float)
    lo = float(min(pred.min(), truth.min()))
    hi = float(max(pred.max(), truth.max()))
    if not np.isfinite(lo) or hi <= lo:
        return np.nan
    hp, _ = np.histogram(pred, bins=bins, range=(lo, hi))
    hq, _ = np.histogram(truth, bins=bins, range=(lo, hi))
    hp = hp.astype(float) + 1e-3
    hq = hq.astype(float) + 1e-3
    hp /= hp.sum()
    hq /= hq.sum()
    return float(np.sum(hp * np.log(hp / hq)))

def cumulative_gain(y, w, score):
    order = np.argsort(-np.asarray(score, dtype=float))
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)[order]
    w = np.asarray(w)[order]
    n = len(y)
    frac = np.arange(1, n + 1) / n
    gain = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        ww = w[: i + 1]
        yy = y[: i + 1]
        n1 = int((ww == 1).sum())
        n0 = int((ww == 0).sum())
        gain[i] = 0.0 if n1 == 0 or n0 == 0 else (yy[ww == 1].mean() - yy[ww == 0].mean()) * (i + 1) / n
    return frac, gain

title: 3. Uplift Learners
text:
Summary and Conclusion
Uplift trees are a powerful tool for estimating individual treatment effects, going beyond traditional predictive modeling to directly target causal impact. By using specialized splitting criteria that focus on maximizing the difference in outcomes between treated and control groups, uplift trees can identify who will respond positively to an intervention — not just who is likely to convert. This makes them invaluable for personalized marketing, clinical decision-making, and any scenario where understanding the causal effect of an action is crucial.

title: 3. Uplift Learners
text:
Resources

CausalML implements the Uplift Tree approach based on the following paper: Sołtys, M., Jaroszewicz, S., & Rzepakowski, P. (2015). Ensemble methods for uplift modeling. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery, 29(6), 1531–1559. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10618-015-0424-8
Piotr Rzepakowski and Szymon Jaroszewicz. Decision trees for uplift modeling with single and multiple treatments. Knowl. Inf. Syst., 32(2):303–327, August 2012.
Pierre Gutierrez and Jean-Yves Gerardy. Causal inference and uplift modeling a review of the literature. JMLR: Workshop and Conference Proceedings 67, 2016.

title: 3.2 Uplift Tree-Regression
text:
Overview
Uplift modeling with continuous outcomes — often called uplift regression or heterogeneous treatment effect regression — estimates how the causal effect of a treatment varies across individuals when the outcome of interest is a real-valued metric rather than a binary event. Examples include exam scores, revenue per customer, time spent on a platform, blood pressure reduction, or any other quantity that varies continuously across individuals and could plausibly be affected by an intervention.
The estimand is the Conditional Average Treatment Effect:
\[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1, X=x] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0, X=x]\]
where \(T=1\) denotes treatment, \(T=0\) control, \(Y \in \mathbb{R}\) the continuous outcome, and \(x\) the individual’s covariate vector. As in the binary case, the goal is to estimate \(\tau(x)\) accurately across the covariate space — but now the effect is a real-valued quantity rather than a probability difference, and the splitting criteria, leaf estimators, and evaluation metrics must be adapted accordingly.


From Classification to Regression
In the binary uplift setting, the tree maximizes divergence between the treated and control outcome distributions within each leaf — a natural criterion when outcomes are categorical. With continuous outcomes, distributional divergence is replaced by criteria that directly measure treatment effect heterogeneity in terms of the conditional mean outcome.
The core logic remains the same: find splits that create child nodes where the within-node treatment effect \(\hat{\tau}(x)\) is as homogeneous and as far from zero as possible, while the between-node treatment effects are as different as possible. What changes is how this is measured. For continuous outcomes, the natural criterion is based on the variance reduction in the treatment effect, or equivalently, on the increase in explained variance of \(Y\) attributable to the treatment-by-covariate interaction after the split.



Splitting Criterion
The standard regression uplift tree criterion evaluates a candidate split \(s\) by the gain in treatment effect variance explained:
\[\text{gain}(s) = \frac{n_\ell}{n} \cdot \hat{\tau}(\phi_\ell)^2 + \frac{n_r}{n} \cdot \hat{\tau}(\phi_r)^2 - \hat{\tau}(\phi)^2\]
where \(\hat{\tau}(\phi_j) = \bar{Y}^{(1)}_{\phi_j} - \bar{Y}^{(0)}_{\phi_j}\) is the difference in sample means between treated and control units in node \(\phi_j\). This criterion selects splits that maximize the weighted sum of squared treatment effects in the children, analogously to how variance reduction in CART maximizes homogeneity of \(Y\) within leaves. A large gain indicates that the split successfully separates individuals with substantially different treatment effect magnitudes.
An alternative formulation evaluates the split by the reduction in mean squared error of the treatment effect:
\[\text{gain}_{\text{MSE}}(s) = \text{MSE}(\phi) - \frac{n_\ell}{n} \cdot \text{MSE}(\phi_\ell) - \frac{n_r}{n} \cdot \text{MSE}(\phi_r)\]
where \(\text{MSE}(\phi_j)\) measures the residual variance of \(Y - \hat{\tau}(\phi_j) \cdot T\) within node \(\phi_j\). This penalizes splits that reduce treatment effect heterogeneity at the cost of poor within-leaf fit.



Leaf Estimation
Each terminal leaf \(\ell\) contains both treated (\(\mathcal{I}_\ell^1\)) and control (\(\mathcal{I}_\ell^0\)) units. The leaf-level CATE estimate is:
\[\hat{\tau}(\ell) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_\ell^1|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\ell^1} Y_i - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_\ell^0|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\ell^0} Y_i = \bar{Y}_\ell^{(1)} - \bar{Y}_\ell^{(0)}\]
For a new individual with covariates \(x\), the tree routes them to a leaf \(\ell(x)\) and outputs \(\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\tau}(\ell(x))\) as the predicted treatment effect. The prediction is therefore a step function over the covariate space — piecewise constant within each leaf region, and varying discontinuously at split boundaries.
In randomized experiments, this estimator is unbiased for \(\tau(x)\) within each leaf under the assumption that the treatment effect is homogeneous within the leaf. In observational studies, a propensity-score adjustment may be applied within each leaf to correct for residual confounding:
\[\hat{\tau}_{\text{adj}}(\ell) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\ell^1} w_i^1 Y_i - \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\ell^0} w_i^0 Y_i\]
where \(w_i^t \propto 1/\hat{e}_t(X_i)\) are inverse propensity weights normalized to sum to one within each arm.



Regularization
The same three regularization adjustments applied in the classification setting carry over directly:

Gain normalization by \(H(T \mid \phi)\) corrects for treatment imbalance within the node.
Sample-size penalty \(\frac{n_\ell n_r}{(n_\ell + n_r)^2}\) discourages lopsided splits with few observations in one child.
Treatment-imbalance penalty \(\alpha \sum_t |\hat{\pi}_\phi(t) - \hat{\pi}(t)|\) penalizes nodes where the local treatment mix deviates from the global experimental design.

These adjustments are especially important in the regression setting, where small leaves can produce highly variable \(\bar{Y}^{(1)} - \bar{Y}^{(0)}\) estimates simply due to sampling noise in the continuous outcome.



Regression vs. Classification Uplift Trees








Aspect
Classification (Binary \(Y\))
Regression (Continuous \(Y\))




Estimand
\(P(Y=1\mid T=1,X=x) - P(Y=1\mid T=0,X=x)\)
\(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=1,X=x] - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid T=0,X=x]\)


Split criterion
Distributional divergence (KL, ED, \(\chi^2\)) or CTS
Treatment effect variance gain or MSE reduction


Leaf value
Difference in treatment/control proportions
Difference in treatment/control sample means


Scale
Probability difference \(\in [-1, 1]\)
Real-valued; scale depends on outcome units


Evaluation
Qini curve, uplift AUC
CATE RMSE, treatment effect \(R^2\)

title: 3.2 Uplift Tree-Regression
text:
Motivating Example
Consider a tutoring program (treatment) designed to improve student exam scores (continuous outcome). A randomized study assigns students to receive tutoring or not, and an uplift regression tree is fitted to estimate the heterogeneous treatment effect across student profiles.
For a particular student profile \(x\) — defined, say, by prior GPA, study hours per week, and subject difficulty:

Predicted score without tutoring: \(\hat{\mu}_0(x) = 72\)
Predicted score with tutoring: \(\hat{\mu}_1(x) = 79\)
Estimated CATE: \(\hat{\tau}(x) = 79 - 72 = \mathbf{+7\ \text{points}}\)

This means students with this profile are expected to score 7 points higher on the exam because of the tutoring program — not merely because they are high-achieving students who would score well regardless. A standard regression model predicting exam scores from student characteristics cannot make this distinction; it would assign high predicted scores to high-ability students whether they receive tutoring or not, and would provide no guidance on who benefits most from the intervention.
The uplift tree goes further by partitioning the student population into segments with distinct estimated CATEs. A student in a leaf with \(\hat{\tau}(x) = +12\) benefits substantially from tutoring and should be prioritized for enrollment. A student in a leaf with \(\hat{\tau}(x) = +1\) benefits minimally, and tutoring resources allocated to them may yield greater returns if redirected to higher-uplift students. A student with \(\hat{\tau}(x) < 0\) — perhaps a student who performs worse under the pressure of structured tutoring — would be actively harmed by the program and should be excluded.
This kind of individualized resource allocation, guided by estimated treatment effects rather than predicted outcomes, is the central use case for uplift regression trees in education, healthcare, marketing, and policy settings alike.

def make_uplift_classification(
    treatment_name=("control", "treatment1", "treatment2", "treatment3"),
    y_name="conversion",
    n_samples=2000,
    n_classification_features=10,
    n_classification_informative=5,
    n_uplift_increase_dict=None,
    n_uplift_decrease_dict=None,
    delta_uplift_increase_dict=None,
    delta_uplift_decrease_dict=None,
    random_seed=111,
):
    """Synthetic multi-arm classification data for uplift trees.

    Informative features shift the baseline conversion probability. A separate
    block of features raises or lowers the uplift of each treatment arm.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_seed)
    names = list(treatment_name)
    arms = names[1:]
    X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_classification_features))
    beta = np.zeros(n_classification_features)
    n_info = min(n_classification_informative, n_classification_features)
    beta[:n_info] = 0.55
    baseline = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(X @ beta)))
    arm_id = rng.integers(0, len(names), size=n_samples)
    uplift = np.zeros(n_samples)
    for j, arm in enumerate(arms):
        n_inc = int(n_uplift_increase_dict[arm])
        n_dec = int(n_uplift_decrease_dict[arm])
        d_inc = float(delta_uplift_increase_dict[arm])
        d_dec = float(delta_uplift_decrease_dict[arm])
        inc = (X[:, :n_inc] > 0).mean(axis=1)
        dec = (X[:, n_inc : n_inc + n_dec] > 0).mean(axis=1)
        uplift[arm_id == (j + 1)] = d_inc * inc[arm_id == (j + 1)] + d_dec * dec[arm_id == (j + 1)]
    probability = np.clip(baseline + uplift, 0.02, 0.98)
    y = rng.binomial(1, probability)
    columns = [f"x{i}" for i in range(n_classification_features)]
    frame = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=columns)
    frame["treatment_group_key"] = np.asarray(names)[arm_id]
    frame[y_name] = y
    return frame, columns


def make_uplift_regression(
    treatment_name=("control", "treatment1", "treatment2", "treatment3"),
    y_name="outcome",
    n_samples=2000,
    n_regression_features=10,
    n_regression_informative=5,
    n_uplift_increase_dict=None,
    n_uplift_decrease_dict=None,
    delta_uplift_increase_dict=None,
    delta_uplift_decrease_dict=None,
    sigma=1.0,
    random_seed=111,
):
    """Synthetic multi-arm regression data. Same feature blocks as classification."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_seed)
    names = list(treatment_name)
    arms = names[1:]
    X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_regression_features))
    beta = np.zeros(n_regression_features)
    n_info = min(n_regression_informative, n_regression_features)
    beta[:n_info] = 0.8
    baseline = X @ beta
    arm_id = rng.integers(0, len(names), size=n_samples)
    uplift = np.zeros(n_samples)
    for j, arm in enumerate(arms):
        n_inc = int(n_uplift_increase_dict[arm])
        n_dec = int(n_uplift_decrease_dict[arm])
        d_inc = float(delta_uplift_increase_dict[arm])
        d_dec = float(delta_uplift_decrease_dict[arm])
        inc = (X[:, :n_inc] > 0).mean(axis=1)
        dec = (X[:, n_inc : n_inc + n_dec] > 0).mean(axis=1)
        uplift[arm_id == (j + 1)] = d_inc * inc[arm_id == (j + 1)] + d_dec * dec[arm_id == (j + 1)]
    y = baseline + uplift + rng.normal(0.0, sigma, size=n_samples)
    columns = [f"x{i}" for i in range(n_regression_features)]
    frame = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=columns)
    frame["treatment_group_key"] = np.asarray(names)[arm_id]
    frame[y_name] = y
    return frame, columns


def fit_multi(df, x_names, y_name, factory, control="control"):
    models = {}
    for arm in [a for a in df["treatment_group_key"].unique() if a != control]:
        sub = df[df["treatment_group_key"].isin([control, arm])]
        model = factory()
        model.fit(
            sub[x_names].to_numpy(),
            (sub["treatment_group_key"].to_numpy() != control).astype(int),
            sub[y_name].to_numpy(),
            feature_names=x_names,
        )
        models[arm] = model
    return models


def predict_multi(models, X, kind="uplift"):
    frame = {}
    for i, (arm, model) in enumerate(models.items()):
        if kind == "rates" and hasattr(model, "predict_rates"):
            p_control, p_treat = model.predict_rates(X)
            if i == 0:
                frame["control"] = p_control
            frame[arm] = p_treat
        elif kind == "means" and hasattr(model, "mu0_"):
            if i == 0:
                frame["control"] = np.asarray(model.mu0_.predict(X), dtype=float)
            frame[arm] = np.asarray(model.mu1_.predict(X), dtype=float)
        else:
            frame[arm] = np.asarray(model.predict(X), dtype=float)
    return pd.DataFrame(frame)


def plot_forest(forest, title="Uplift forest", n_show=4):
    n_show = min(n_show, len(forest.trees_))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
    for ax, tree in zip(np.ravel(axes), forest.trees_[:n_show]):
        plot_uplift_tree(tree, title=tree.criterion.upper() if hasattr(tree, "criterion") else "Tree", ax=ax)
    for ax in np.ravel(axes)[n_show:]:
        ax.set_axis_off()
    fig.suptitle(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

Interpretation notes

Positive SHAP pushes the predicted CATE up; negative SHAP pushes it down.
Explanations target heterogeneity in \(\hat{\tau}(X)\), not the raw outcome margin \(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\).
explain is model-agnostic: it calls predict on the T-learner and attributes the predicted CATE.

title: 3.2 Uplift Tree-Regression
text:
Summary
With a continuous outcome, a TLearner (or UpliftXGBoost) estimates \(\hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\) separately in each arm. InteractionTree and CausalTree publish the partition. The Qini curve and explain are the same evaluation tools as in the classification notebook, with the outcome column outcome instead of conversion.
