title: 3.4 Uplift XGBoost Regression
text:
Overview
A standard predictive model asks: “What outcome do we expect for this unit?”
An uplift model asks a different question:

“How much would the outcome change because of the treatment for this unit, given their covariates?”

That quantity is the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE). For a unit with covariates \(X = x\) and a continuous outcome \(Y\):
\[\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 1, X = x] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 0, X = x]\]
where \(T = 1\) is treated and \(T = 0\) is control. Heterogeneity means \(\tau(x)\) varies with \(x\): some subgroups benefit strongly, others barely, and some may be harmed.
For binary outcomes (e.g. conversion yes/no), the CATE is:
\[\tau(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid T = 1, X = x) - P(Y = 1 \mid T = 0, X = x)\]

title: 3.4 Uplift XGBoost Regression
text:
Why gradient boosting for uplift?
UpliftXGBoost is a T-learner with gradient-boosted trees as the base learner:

Fit one ensemble on control units (\(T = 0\)) to estimate \(\hat{\mu}_0(x)\).
Fit a separate ensemble on treated units (\(T = 1\)) to estimate \(\hat{\mu}_1(x)\).
Predict CATE as the difference:

\[\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)\]








Aspect
Uplift random forest
Uplift XGBoost




Class
UpliftRandomForest
UpliftXGBoost


Base learner
Bagged uplift trees
Gradient-boosted trees


Splitting rule
Squared CATE gap
T-learner only


Strengths
Treatment-aware splits; individual trees can be drawn
Flexible nonlinear surfaces



The model output is \(\hat{\tau}(x)\) on the scale of \(Y\). Here \(Y\) is lnr, so a CATE of \(-0.12\) is a 0.12 log-point lower gonorrhea rate for that profile.

From ATE to targeted policy








CATE region
Interpretation
Targeting decision




High positive \(\tau(x)\)
Large expected benefit from treatment
Priority targets


Near zero
Treatment adds little
Skip / low priority


Negative \(\tau(x)\)
Treatment may worsen outcomes
Actively avoid treating



The abortion dataset has a single policy indicator (repeal), so this notebook stays on the binary path.

    qini_curve,
)

plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110


def f_filter(X, y, w, names, order=1):
    """Rank features by the partial F statistic of treatment interactions.

    Order 1 tests ``Y ~ X + W + X:W``. Higher orders add powers of ``X`` and
    the matching treatment interactions, following the F-filter idea in
    Zhao et al. (2020).
    """
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(w, dtype=float)
    rows = []
    for j, name in enumerate(names):
        xj = np.asarray(X[:, j], dtype=float)
        scale = float(np.std(xj))
        if scale < 1e-8:
            rows.append({"feature": name, "score": np.nan})
            continue
        xj = (xj - float(np.mean(xj))) / scale
        main = [np.ones(len(y)), w, xj]
        for power in range(2, order + 1):
            main.append(xj ** power)
        n_main = len(main)
        interactions = [w * (xj ** power) for power in range(1, order + 1)]
        design = np.column_stack(main + interactions)
        try:
            full = sm.OLS(y, design).fit()
            restricted = sm.OLS(y, design[:, :n_main]).fit()
            q = design.shape[1] - n_main
            score = ((restricted.ssr - full.ssr) / q) / (full.ssr / full.df_resid)
        except Exception:
            score = np.nan
        rows.append({"feature": name, "score": float(score)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)


def plot_qini_models(y, treatment, scores, title):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))
    table = []
    for name, score in scores.items():
        curve = qini_curve(y, treatment, score)
        ax.plot(curve["fraction"], curve["qini"], label=name)
        table.append({"model": name, "qini": qini_coefficient(y, treatment, score)})
    ax.set_xlabel("Fraction targeted")
    ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative incremental gain")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig, pd.DataFrame(table)

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
text:
Overview
ML models predict well but produce biased causal estimates because regularization (for example, a shallow random forest or a penalized regression) distorts the coefficients we care about. The table below summarizes the three challenges DML addresses and how it addresses each one.








Challenge
Why it matters
DML’s response




Regularization bias
ML shrinks nuisance fits, which contaminates \(\hat{\theta}\)
Neyman-orthogonal scores (partialling-out or IV-type) make \(\hat{\theta}\) insensitive to first-order nuisance errors


Overfitting bias
Using the same data for ML nuisances and for estimating \(\theta\) inflates apparent fit
Sample splitting: train nuisances on one fold, estimate \(\theta\) on another


High-dimensional confounders
Classical OLS breaks down when \(p \gg n\) or relationships are non-linear
Flexible learners (random forests, gradient boosting, lasso) estimate \(g_0(X)\) and \(m_0(X)\)



Cross-fitting combines both halves of the sample split by rotating roles across \(K\) folds, so no observations are wasted.

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
text:
The Partially Linear Regression (PLR) Model
Both parts of this notebook use the partially linear regression (PLR) model, which separates the linear treatment effect \(\theta_0\) from the nonparametric confounding functions \(g_0\) and \(m_0\):
\[Y = D\,\theta_0 + g_0(X) + \zeta, \quad \mathbb{E}(\zeta \mid D, X) = 0\]
\[D = m_0(X) + V, \quad \mathbb{E}(V \mid X) = 0\]



Symbol
Role




\(Y\)
Outcome variable


\(D\)
Treatment variable


\(X\)
High-dimensional confounders


\(\theta_0\)
Causal parameter (ATE)


\(g_0(X),\, m_0(X)\)
Nuisance functions estimated by ML


\(\zeta,\, V\)
Stochastic errors

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization

Implementation in Python
Throughout this notebook the causal estimators come from PyCausalML. Part A writes the three scores explicitly — non-orthogonal, IV-type, and partialling-out — so the source of the bias is visible. The cross-fitted partialling-out estimator is the same construction as PartiallyLinearDML. Part B calls PartiallyLinearDML and LinearDML directly on Data/data_401k.csv.

section: Part A: Diagnosing Bias with Synthetic Data
text:
Part A: Diagnosing Bias with Synthetic Data
Part A uses Monte Carlo simulation to make the bias problems visible. We draw replications of the partially linear model from Chernozhukov et al. (2018) and compare the distribution of the rescaled estimator \((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0) / \hat{\text{se}}\) against \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) under three approaches. A valid estimator produces a histogram that matches the standard normal; deviations expose regularization or overfitting bias.
The data-generating process is:
\[y_i = \theta_0\, d_i + g_0(x_i) + \zeta_i, \quad \zeta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\]
\[d_i = m_0(x_i) + v_i, \quad v_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\]
Covariates \(x_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)\) with \(\Sigma_{kj} = 0.7^{|j-k|}\). The true causal parameter is \(\theta_0 = 0.5\). Nuisance functions:
\[m_0(x_i) = x_{i,1} + \frac{1}{4}\frac{\exp(x_{i,3})}{1 + \exp(x_{i,3})}\]
\[g_0(x_i) = \frac{\exp(x_{i,1})}{1 + \exp(x_{i,1})} + \frac{1}{4}x_{i,3}\]
Each replication draws \(n = 500\) observations with \(p = 20\) covariates. The extra coordinates are pure noise, which is what makes a regularized forest shrink \(g_0\). The Monte Carlo uses 30 replications so the notebook finishes in one pass; increase n_rep for a tighter histogram.

A.1 Generate Simulated Data


Code
def make_plr_ccddhnr2018(n_obs, dim_x, alpha, rng):
    """Partially linear DGP from Chernozhukov et al. (2018)."""
    index = np.arange(dim_x)
    cov = 0.7 ** np.abs(index[:, None] - index[None, :])
    x = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(dim_x), cov, size=n_obs)
    m0 = x[:, 0] + 0.25 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x[:, 2]))
    g0 = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x[:, 0])) + 0.25 * x[:, 2]
    d = m0 + rng.normal(size=n_obs)
    y = alpha * d + g0 + rng.normal(size=n_obs)
    columns = [f"X{j + 1}" for j in range(dim_x)]
    frame = pd.DataFrame(x, columns=columns)
    frame["d"] = d
    frame["y"] = y
    return frame


def forest(seed):
    return RandomForestRegressor(
        n_estimators=40,
        max_depth=4,
        min_samples_leaf=5,
        random_state=seed,
        n_jobs=1,
    )


def _predict_nuisance(X, target, n_splits, seed, cross_fit):
    if not cross_fit:
        model = forest(seed)
        model.fit(X, target)
        return model.predict(X)
    pred = np.zeros(len(target))
    splitter = KFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    for fold, (tr, te) in enumerate(splitter.split(X)):
        model = forest(seed + fold)
        model.fit(X[tr], target[tr])
        pred[te] = model.predict(X[te])
    return pred


def plr_estimate(X, d, y, score, cross_fit, seed, n_splits=2):
    """Return (theta, se) for one PLR score.

    score='nonorth' uses only the outcome nuisance and a single sample split.
    score='iv' residualizes Y with g(X) and instruments D with D - m(X).
    score='partial' residualizes both Y and D (the PartiallyLinearDML score).
    """
    if score == "nonorth":
        splitter = KFold(n_splits=2, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
        tr, te = next(splitter.split(X))
        model = forest(seed)
        model.fit(X[tr], y[tr])
        g_hat = model.predict(X[te])
        d_te, y_te = d[te], y[te]
        theta = float(np.dot(d_te, y_te - g_hat) / np.dot(d_te, d_te))
        resid = d_te * (y_te - g_hat - theta * d_te)
        se = float(np.std(resid, ddof=1) / (np.sqrt(len(te)) * np.mean(d_te ** 2)))
        return theta, se

    g_hat = _predict_nuisance(X, y, n_splits, seed, cross_fit)
    m_hat = _predict_nuisance(X, d, n_splits, seed + 17, cross_fit)
    if score == "iv":
        v_hat = d - m_hat
        u_hat = y - g_hat
        denom = float(np.dot(v_hat, d))
        theta = float(np.dot(v_hat, u_hat) / denom)
        psi = v_hat * (u_hat - theta * d) / np.mean(v_hat * d)
    elif score == "partial":
        y_res = y - g_hat
        d_res = d - m_hat
        denom = float(np.dot(d_res, d_res))
        theta = float(np.dot(d_res, y_res) / denom)
        psi = d_res * (y_res - theta * d_res) / np.mean(d_res ** 2)
    else:
        raise ValueError(score)
    se = float(np.std(psi, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(psi)))
    return theta, se


def replicate(datasets, score, cross_fit, seed):
    theta = np.empty(len(datasets))
    se = np.empty(len(datasets))
    for i, frame in enumerate(datasets):
        x_cols = [c for c in frame.columns if c.startswith("X")]
        theta[i], se[i] = plr_estimate(
            frame[x_cols].to_numpy(),
            frame["d"].to_numpy(),
            frame["y"].to_numpy(),
            score=score,
            cross_fit=cross_fit,
            seed=seed + i,
        )
    return theta, se

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
text:
A.3 Approach 1 — Naive ML (Non-Orthogonal Score)
A naive estimator splits the sample in two, fits \(\hat{g}_0(X)\) with ML on one half, then uses the other half to compute:
\[\hat{\theta}_0 = \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I} D_i^2\Bigr)^{-1}
  \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I} D_i\bigl(Y_i - \hat{g}_0(X_i)\bigr)\]
This uses a non-orthogonal score. Regularization bias from estimating \(g_0\) with ML does not vanish; \(\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}_0 - \theta_0)\) does not stay bounded.

A.3.1 Define Non-Orthogonal Score
The score below uses only \(\hat{g}(X)\) to residualize \(Y\), ignoring \(D\)’s dependence on \(X\). The moment condition is therefore not orthogonal.


A.3.2 Fit Naive ML Over Replications


Code
theta_nonorth, se_nonorth = replicate(datasets, score="nonorth", cross_fit=False, seed=1111)
print("Mean theta:", round(float(np.mean(theta_nonorth)), 4))


Mean theta: 0.2824




A.3.3 Plot Distribution — Non-Orthogonal
Under valid inference, \((\hat{\theta} - \theta_0) / \hat{\text{se}}\) should follow \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). For the naive estimator it does not: the histogram is shifted and spread, revealing regularization bias from the forest’s shrinkage of \(g_0(X)\).


Code
def plot_t_hist(values, title, color, label):
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    values = values[np.isfinite(values)]
    grid = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
    ax.hist(values, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.35, color=color, edgecolor=color, label=label)
    ax.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), color="black", lw=1.2, label="N(0,1)")
    ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlim(-6, 6)
    ax.set_xlabel("Rescaled estimate")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig




Code
t_nonorth = (theta_nonorth - alpha) / se_nonorth
plot_t_hist(t_nonorth, "Naive ML: Regularization Bias", "darkblue", "Non-orthogonal ML")

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
section: A.4 Approach 2 — Orthogonalized ML, No Sample Splitting
text:
A.4 Approach 2 — Orthogonalized ML, No Sample Splitting
Orthogonalization removes the leading regularization bias by partialling \(X\) out of \(D\) as well. Let \(\hat{V} = D - \hat{m}(X)\) and use the IV-type score:
\[\check{\theta}_0 = \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I} \hat{V}_i D_i\Bigr)^{-1}
  \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in I} \hat{V}_i\bigl(Y_i - \hat{g}_0(X_i)\bigr)\]
With nuisances and the final estimate computed on the same data, overfitting bias is not eliminated by sample splitting.

A.4.1 Fit IV-Type Score, No Sample Splitting


Code
theta_orth_nosplit, se_orth_nosplit = replicate(datasets, score="iv", cross_fit=False, seed=2222)
print("Mean theta:", round(float(np.nanmean(theta_orth_nosplit)), 4))


Mean theta: 0.4167




A.4.2 Plot Distribution — Orthogonal, No Sample Splitting


Code
t_orth_nosplit = (theta_orth_nosplit - alpha) / se_orth_nosplit
plot_t_hist(
    t_orth_nosplit,
    "Orthogonal Score, No Sample Splitting: Overfitting Bias",
    "darkorange",
    "DML (no sample splitting)",
)
















Even with an orthogonal score, omitting sample splitting allows overfitting bias to persist. Extreme or non-finite t-values (filtered in the histogram) are a characteristic symptom.

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
section: A.5 Approach 3 — Full DML with Cross-Fitting (IV-Type Score)
text:
A.5 Approach 3 — Full DML with Cross-Fitting (IV-Type Score)
Cross-fitting completes the fix. With two folds, nuisances are trained on one fold and \(\theta\) estimated on the held-out fold; the roles are then swapped and the estimates combined. This eliminates both regularization bias (orthogonal score) and overfitting bias (sample splitting) while using all observations.

A.5.1 Fit DML with Cross-Fitting (IV-Type)


Code
theta_dml, se_dml = replicate(datasets, score="iv", cross_fit=True, seed=3333)
print("Mean theta:", round(float(np.mean(theta_dml)), 4))


Mean theta: 0.4888




A.5.2 Plot Distribution — DML with Cross-Fitting


Code
t_dml = (theta_dml - alpha) / se_dml
plot_t_hist(t_dml, "Full DML with Cross-Fitting: Valid Inference", "darkgreen", "DML with cross-fitting")
















The rescaled estimates now sit much closer to \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), confirming that combining an orthogonal score with cross-fitting restores valid inference.

section: A.6 Comparison: All Three IV-Type Approaches
text:
A.6 Comparison: All Three IV-Type Approaches


Code

grid = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400)
specs = [
    (t_nonorth, "darkblue", "Non-orthogonal ML"),
    (t_orth_nosplit, "darkorange", "DML (no sample splitting)"),
    (t_dml, "darkgreen", "DML with cross-fitting"),
]
for values, color, label in specs:
    finite = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    finite = finite[np.isfinite(finite)]
    ax.hist(finite, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.28, color=color, label=label)
ax.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), color="black", lw=1.2, label="N(0,1)")
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlim(-6, 6)
ax.set_xlabel("Rescaled estimate")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_title("Comparison of All Three Approaches")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()









The three histograms make the progression concrete: naive ML (blue) is shifted and spread; orthogonal without splitting (orange) is better but still distorted; full DML with cross-fitting (green) is the one that lines up with \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
text:
A.7 Partialling-Out Score
The partialling-out score is the most common choice in practice. It uses \(\ell_0(X) = \mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) and \(m_0(X) = \mathbb{E}[D|X]\) directly. The orthogonal moment condition is:
\[\psi(W;\,\theta,\eta) := \bigl[Y - \ell(X) - \theta(D - m(X))\bigr](D - m(X))\]
PartiallyLinearDML solves this score. We repeat the no-splitting versus cross-fitting comparison to confirm that the result holds independently of which orthogonal score is used.

A.7.1 Partialling-Out, No Sample Splitting


Code
theta_po_nosplit, se_po_nosplit = replicate(datasets, score="partial", cross_fit=False, seed=4444)
print("Mean theta:", round(float(np.mean(theta_po_nosplit)), 4))


Mean theta: 0.4833




A.7.2 Partialling-Out with Cross-Fitting


Code
theta_dml_po, se_dml_po = replicate(datasets, score="partial", cross_fit=True, seed=5555)
# The same score, called through PyCausalML on the first replication.
frame0 = datasets[0]
x_cols = [c for c in frame0.columns if c.startswith("X")]
package_fit = PartiallyLinearDML(
    discrete_treatment=False, n_splits=2, model_y="rf", n_estimators=40, random_state=5555,
)
package_fit.fit(frame0[x_cols], frame0["d"], frame0["y"], feature_names=x_cols)
print("Manual cross-fit mean theta:", round(float(np.mean(theta_dml_po)), 4))
print("PartiallyLinearDML on replication 1:", package_fit.average_treatment_effect())

PartiallyLinearDML on replication 1: {'estimate': 0.39925797346729136, 'std.err': 0.04753551277103456, 'ci_lower': 0.3060900804494199, 'ci_upper': 0.49242586648516284}




A.7.3 Plot Distribution — Partialling-Out with Cross-Fitting


Code
t_dml_po = (theta_dml_po - alpha) / se_dml_po
plot_t_hist(
    t_dml_po,
    "Partialling-Out Score with Cross-Fitting: Valid Inference",
    "darkgreen",
    "DML (partialling out)",
)


















A.7.4 Comparison: Partialling-Out vs IV-Type (with Cross-Fitting)


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 4.4))
grid = np.linspace(-6, 6, 400)
for values, color, label in [
    (t_dml, "darkgreen", "DML — IV-type"),
    (t_dml_po, "steelblue", "DML — partialling out"),
]:
    finite = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    finite = finite[np.isfinite(finite)]
    ax.hist(finite, bins=30, density=True, alpha=0.3, color=color, label=label)
ax.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), color="black", lw=1.2, label="N(0,1)")
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlim(-6, 6)
ax.set_xlabel("Rescaled estimate")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_title("IV-Type vs Partialling-Out Score (both with cross-fitting)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()









Both scores achieve approximately valid inference when combined with cross-fitting. The two distributions are close in practice, which supports using whichever score is computationally simpler for a given problem.

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
section: Part B: Real-World Application — 401(k) Eligibility and Net Financial Assets
text:
Part B: Real-World Application — 401(k) Eligibility and Net Financial Assets
Part B applies DML to the 401(k) dataset (Chernozhukov et al., 2020), stored as Data/data_401k.csv, to estimate the average causal effect of employer-sponsored 401(k) eligibility (e401) on net total financial assets (net_tfa), controlling for age, income, education, family structure, and other background variables.
The workflow has four stages: (1) an 80/20 stratified train–test split; (2) causal estimation with PartiallyLinearDML on the training fold; (3) out-of-sample validation of the nuisance models on the held-out test fold; and (4) SHAP interpretation of treatment-effect heterogeneity with LinearDML. Formal PLR inference applies to the training sample. The test fold is used for predictive checks of the nuisance regressions.

B.2 Outcome, Treatment, Covariates, and Train–Test Split
The split is stratified on e401 (80% train / 20% test) so both folds retain similar treatment prevalence.


Code
x_cols_401k = ["age", "inc", "fsize", "educ", "db", "marr", "twoearn", "pira", "hown"]
X_401k = df_401k[x_cols_401k].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y_401k = df_401k["net_tfa"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
t_401k = df_401k["e401"].to_numpy(dtype=int)

rng_split = np.random.default_rng(3141)
train_parts = []
for arm in (0, 1):
    pool = np.flatnonzero(t_401k == arm)
    take = max(1, int(np.floor(0.8 * len(pool))))
    train_parts.append(rng_split.choice(pool, size=take, replace=False))
train_idx = np.sort(np.concatenate(train_parts))
test_idx = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(t_401k)), train_idx)
X_tr, X_te = X_401k[train_idx], X_401k[test_idx]
y_tr, y_te = y_401k[train_idx], y_401k[test_idx]
t_tr, t_te = t_401k[train_idx], t_401k[test_idx]
print(
    "Train n =", len(train_idx),
    "| Test n =", len(test_idx),
    "| mean(e401) train =", round(float(t_tr.mean()), 3),
    "test =", round(float(t_te.mean()), 3),
)

title: 4.1. Double ML: Bias, Orthogonalization
section: B.6 Holdout Validation of Nuisance Models
text:
B.6 Holdout Validation of Nuisance Models
To check that the nuisance models generalize beyond the training fold, we refit random forests on the training data only and evaluate them on the held-out test set. We report RMSE for the outcome regression \(\hat{\ell}(X) \approx \mathbb{E}[Y|X]\) and the Brier score for the treatment propensity \(\hat{m}(X) \approx \mathbb{E}[D|X]\). Lower values indicate better out-of-sample nuisance fit. This is a predictive sanity check — it does not replace the PLR assumptions, but a severely poor fit would signal that the nuisance models are misspecified.


Code
rf_y = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=80, max_depth=5, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=1, n_jobs=1)
rf_d = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=80, max_depth=5, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=1, n_jobs=1)
rf_y.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
rf_d.fit(X_tr, t_tr)
y_hat = rf_y.predict(X_te)
p_hat = rf_d.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
rmse_y = float(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_te, y_hat)))
brier_d = float(brier_score_loss(t_te, p_hat))
validation_tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "Metric": ["RMSE of Y (net_tfa)", "Brier score for D (e401)"],
    "Value": [round(rmse_y, 2), round(brier_d, 4)],
})

section: B.7 SHAP Interpretation of Treatment Effect Heterogeneity
text:
B.7 SHAP Interpretation of Treatment Effect Heterogeneity
PartiallyLinearDML estimates a single scalar \(\hat{\theta}\), which is not a function of \(X\) and therefore cannot be explained by SHAP. To explore which covariates drive heterogeneity, we fit LinearDML on the training fold (random-forest first stage, OLS on the residual-on-residual design). This produces a CATE prediction \(\hat{\tau}(X)\) that varies with \(X\). Permutation SHAP is computed with explain_cate on a subsample of the test rows.


Code
ldml_401k = LinearDML(
    discrete_treatment=True, n_splits=3, model_y="rf", n_estimators=40, random_state=3143,
)
ldml_401k.fit(X_tr, t_tr, y_tr, feature_names=x_cols_401k)
explanation = explain_cate(
    ldml_401k, X_te, feature_names=x_cols_401k,
    max_samples=48, n_permutations=8, random_state=3143,
)
print("ATE from the linear CATE:", ldml_401k.average_treatment_effect())
explanation.plot_importance(title="SHAP importance for predicted CATE (LinearDML)")


ATE from the linear CATE: {'estimate': 8183.038050910903, 'std.err': 1515.9678873491396, 'ci_lower': 5211.795589987316, 'ci_upper': 11154.28051183449}


















Code

Reading the plots. SHAP values here are contributions to \(\hat{\tau}(X)\) from LinearDML — a descriptive heterogeneity model, not the same object as the PLR scalar \(\hat{\theta}\) in B.4–B.5. Use them to explore which covariates are associated with larger or smaller estimated treatment effects under this specification.


Code

2
Cross-fitting
Train on \(K-1\) folds, predict on the held-out fold


3
Orthogonal score
\(\psi_i = \big(\frac{D_i}{\bar{p}} - \frac{(1-D_i)\hat{e}(X_i)}{\bar{p}(1-\hat{e}(X_i))}\big)(\Delta Y_i - \hat{\ell}(X_i))\)


4
Final estimation
\(\hat{\theta} = n^{-1}\sum_i \psi_i\), with an influence-function standard error











Challenge
Linear DiD
DML-DiD




Many controls
OLS is noisy or infeasible when \(p\) is large
ML fits the nuisances


Nonlinear confounding
A linear \(g(X)\) is misspecified
Forests and boosting approximate \(g\)


Inference
Valid under correct linear specification
Valid if the nuisances converge and the score is orthogonal



The group-time estimand \(\mathrm{ATT}(g,t)\) is the effect at calendar time \(t\) for the cohort first treated at \(g\), using not-yet-treated and never-treated units as controls (Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021). The score above is the doubly robust DiD score of Sant’Anna and Zhao (2020) applied to \(\Delta Y\).

Code
def _classifier(kind, seed):
    if kind == "logit":
        return LogisticRegression(max_iter=400)
    if kind == "rf":
        return RandomForestClassifier(
            n_estimators=40, max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1,
        )
    return GradientBoostingClassifier(
        n_estimators=30, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.08, random_state=seed,
    )


def _regressor(kind, seed):
    if kind == "ridge":
        return Ridge(alpha=1.0)
    if kind == "rf":
        return RandomForestRegressor(
            n_estimators=40, max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1,
        )
    return GradientBoostingRegressor(
        n_estimators=30, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.08, random_state=seed,
    )


def dr_att(X, d, dy, learner="linear", seed=0, n_splits=2):
    """Doubly robust ATT for a first-differenced 2×2 comparison."""
    d = np.asarray(d, dtype=int)
    dy = np.asarray(dy, dtype=float)
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    if X.ndim == 1:
        X = X.reshape(-1, 1)
    n = len(d)
    e_hat = np.full(n, float(d.mean()))
    mu0 = np.full(n, float(dy[d == 0].mean()) if np.any(d == 0) else 0.0)
    kind_c = {"linear": "logit", "rf": "rf", "gbr": "gbr"}[learner]
    kind_r = {"linear": "ridge", "rf": "rf", "gbr": "gbr"}[learner]
    splitter = KFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    for fold, (tr, te) in enumerate(splitter.split(X)):
        if len(np.unique(d[tr])) < 2 or np.sum(d[tr] == 0) < 8:
            continue
        clf = _classifier(kind_c, seed + fold)
        clf.fit(X[tr], d[tr])
        e_hat[te] = clf.predict_proba(X[te])[:, 1]
        reg = _regressor(kind_r, seed + fold)
        ctrl = tr[d[tr] == 0]
        reg.fit(X[ctrl], dy[ctrl])
        mu0[te] = reg.predict(X[te])
    e_hat = np.clip(e_hat, 0.05, 0.95)
    p_hat = float(np.mean(d))
    psi = (d / p_hat - (1 - d) * e_hat / (p_hat * (1 - e_hat))) * (dy - mu0)
    theta = float(np.mean(psi))
    se = float(np.std(psi, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n))
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((dy[d == 0] - mu0[d == 0]) ** 2)))
    acc = float(np.mean((e_hat >= 0.5).astype(int) == d))
    return {"att": theta, "se": se, "rmse_mu0": rmse, "propensity_acc": acc}


def simulate_panel(n_units=700, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    cohort = rng.choice([0, 2, 3, 4], size=n_units, p=[0.45, 0.2, 0.2, 0.15])
    x = rng.normal(size=(n_units, 2))
    rows = []
    for period in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        treated_now = ((cohort > 0) & (period >= cohort)).astype(float)
        exposure = np.where(treated_now == 1, period - cohort, 0)
        outcome = (
            0.4 * x[:, 0]
            + 0.15 * period
            + treated_now * (1.0 + 0.4 * exposure)
            + 0.25 * x[:, 1] * treated_now
            + rng.normal(scale=0.45, size=n_units)
        )
        rows.append(pd.DataFrame({
            "id": np.arange(n_units),
            "period": period,
            "G": cohort,
            "Y": outcome,
            "treat": treated_now.astype(int),
            "x1": x[:, 0],
            "x2": x[:, 1],
        }))
    return pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)

Group-time ATT with three nuisance learners
For each cohort \(g \in \{2,3,4\}\) and time \(t \ge g\), the pre-period is \(g-1\) and the control group is never-treated units. The outcome in the score is \(\Delta Y = Y_t - Y_{g-1}\).


Code
def group_time_table(frame, id_col, time_col, cohort_col, y_col, x_cols, learner):
    cohorts = sorted(g for g in frame[cohort_col].unique() if g > 0)
    rows = []
    for g in cohorts:
        pre = int(g) - 1
        for t in sorted(frame[time_col].unique()):
            if t < g or pre not in set(frame[time_col]):
                continue
            post = frame[frame[time_col] == t][[id_col, y_col, cohort_col, *x_cols]]
            base = frame[frame[time_col] == pre][[id_col, y_col]].rename(columns={y_col: "y_pre"})
            merged = post.merge(base, on=id_col)
            treated = merged[cohort_col] == g
            control = merged[cohort_col] == 0
            sample = merged[treated | control]
            if sample[cohort_col].eq(g).sum() < 15 or sample[cohort_col].eq(0).sum() < 15:
                continue
            result = dr_att(
                sample[x_cols].to_numpy(),
                (sample[cohort_col] == g).astype(int).to_numpy(),
                (sample[y_col] - sample["y_pre"]).to_numpy(),
                learner=learner,
                seed=int(g) * 10 + int(t),
            )
            result.update({"G": int(g), "time": int(t), "learner": learner, "target": 1.0 + 0.4 * (int(t) - int(g))})
            rows.append(result)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Group-time fits do not have a single predict surface. To show SHAP we take the 2004 cohort against never-treated counties, build \(\Delta Y = \text{lemp}_{2004} - \text{lemp}_{2003}\), and fit LinearDML on lpop plus a second copy of the covariate so the CATE can vary. These values describe that slice, not the group-time table.

pre = mpdta[mpdta["year"] == 2003][["countyreal", "lemp"]].rename(columns={"lemp": "lemp0"})
slice_s = post.merge(pre, on="countyreal")
slice_s = slice_s[slice_s["first.treat"].isin([0, 2004])].copy()
dy = (slice_s["lemp"] - slice_s["lemp0"]).to_numpy()
treat = (slice_s["first.treat"] == 2004).astype(int).to_numpy()
# Two columns so a linear CATE is not forced to a constant.
xs = np.column_stack([
    slice_s["lpop"].to_numpy(),
    (slice_s["lpop"] - slice_s["lpop"].mean()) ** 2,
])

title: 4.5 Dynamic Double Machine Learning
text:
Overview
The panel for one unit is a short history of controls and treatments and a final outcome \(Y\). With a linear effect of each period’s treatment,
\[Y = \sum_{t=1}^{m} \theta_t T_t + \gamma^\top W + \eta.\]
Cross-fitting residualizes \(Y\) and every \(T_t\) on the controls. The final stage regresses the outcome residual on the treatment residuals, one coefficient per period. When the effect also depends on baseline covariates \(X\),
\[\theta_t(X) = a_t + X^\top b_t,\]
the same residuals are interacted with \((1, X)\).
A policy contrast compares a baseline path (all zeros) with a target path (all ones). For a constant effect the contrast is the sum of the period coefficients. For a heterogeneous effect it is \(\sum_t \hat\theta_t(X_i)\) for each unit.

def cross_fit_predict(X, y, n_splits, seed, kind="ridge"):
    """Out-of-fold predictions. kind is 'ridge', 'rf', or 'gbr'."""
    pred = np.zeros(len(y), dtype=float)
    splitter = KFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    for fold, (tr, te) in enumerate(splitter.split(X)):
        model = _nuisance(kind, seed + fold)
        model.fit(X[tr], y[tr])
        pred[te] = model.predict(X[te])
    return pred


def _nuisance(kind, seed):
    if kind == "ridge":
        return Ridge(alpha=1.0)
    if kind == "lasso":
        return Lasso(alpha=0.02, max_iter=8000)
    if kind == "rf":
        return RandomForestRegressor(
            n_estimators=40, max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1,
        )
    if kind == "gbr":
        return GradientBoostingRegressor(
            n_estimators=40, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.08, random_state=seed,
        )
    raise ValueError(kind)


def plot_beeswarm(explanation, title, max_display=8):
    imp = explanation.importance()
    order = np.argsort(imp)[-max_display:]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 0.42 * len(order) + 1.3))
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for i, j in enumerate(order):
        vals = explanation.values[:, j]
        raw = explanation.data[:, j]
        span = float(np.ptp(raw)) or 1.0
        color = (raw - np.min(raw)) / span
        jitter = rng.uniform(-0.16, 0.16, size=len(vals))
        ax.scatter(vals, np.full(len(vals), i) + jitter, c=color, cmap="coolwarm", s=18, alpha=0.9)
    ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(order)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([explanation.feature_names[j] for j in order])
    ax.axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("SHAP value")
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

def fit_dynamic(T, controls, y, X=None, kind="ridge", n_splits=2, seed=0):
    """Period-specific linear effects of the columns of T on the final outcome."""
    T = np.asarray(T, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    y_res = y - cross_fit_predict(controls, y, n_splits, seed, kind)
    t_res = np.column_stack([
        T[:, j] - cross_fit_predict(controls, T[:, j], n_splits, seed + 1 + j, kind)
        for j in range(T.shape[1])
    ])
    if X is None:
        coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(t_res, y_res, rcond=None)
        return np.asarray(coef, dtype=float)
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
    phi = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
    design = np.column_stack([t_res[:, j:j + 1] * phi for j in range(T.shape[1])])
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y_res, rcond=None)
    return np.asarray(beta, dtype=float).reshape(T.shape[1], phi.shape[1])


def simulate_dynamic(n=900, m=4, seed=0, heterogeneous=False):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    controls = rng.normal(size=(n, 3))
    baseline = rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
    treatment = rng.binomial(1, 0.45, size=(n, m)).astype(float)
    gamma = np.array([0.5, -0.3, 0.2])
    if not heterogeneous:
        theta = np.linspace(0.4, 1.3, m)
        outcome = treatment @ theta + controls @ gamma + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)
        return treatment, controls, baseline, outcome, theta
    intercepts = np.linspace(0.3, 1.0, m)
    slopes = np.linspace(0.2, 0.7, m)
    effect = intercepts + baseline[:, 0:1] * slopes
    outcome = np.sum(treatment * effect, axis=1) + controls @ gamma + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=n)
    return treatment, controls, baseline, outcome, intercepts, slopes

title: 4.7 Cluster Robust Double Machine Learning
text:
Overview
The score is the partially linear IV moment. After cross-fitting,
\[\hat\theta = \frac{\sum_i \tilde Z_i \tilde Y_i}{\sum_i \tilde Z_i \tilde D_i}, \qquad
\psi_i = \frac{\tilde Z_i(\tilde Y_i - \hat\theta \tilde D_i)}{\overline{\tilde Z\tilde D}}.\]
The cluster-robust standard error replaces \(\psi_i\) with \(\Psi_c = \sum_{i \in c} \psi_i\). The asymptotics need many clusters, not just many rows. A working rule is 30 or more clusters in each dimension you cluster on.








Design
Correlation
Variance




One-way
Rows that share one id
Variance of that id’s score totals


Two-way
Rows that share either of two ids
Sum of the two one-way variances, minus the cell variance

Part 1 simulates a two-way grid in the spirit of Chiang et al. (2021). Part 2 turns the second shock off. Code
def fold_ids(labels, n_folds, seed):
    labels = np.asarray(labels)
    uniq = np.unique(labels)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    order = rng.permutation(uniq)
    mapping = {label: i % n_folds for i, label in enumerate(order)}
    return np.array([mapping[label] for label in labels])


def cross_fit_lasso(X, y, folds, alpha=0.05):
    pred = np.zeros(len(y), dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    for fold in np.unique(folds):
        te = folds == fold
        tr = ~te
        if tr.sum() < 10 or te.sum() == 0:
            pred[te] = np.mean(y[tr]) if tr.any() else np.mean(y)
            continue
        scaler = StandardScaler()
        Xtr = scaler.fit_transform(X[tr])
        model = Lasso(alpha=alpha, max_iter=8000)
        model.fit(Xtr, y[tr])
        pred[te] = model.predict(scaler.transform(X[te]))
    return pred


def cluster_variance(psi, clusters):
    totals = pd.DataFrame({"psi": psi, "c": clusters}).groupby("c")["psi"].sum().to_numpy()
    g = len(totals)
    return (g / (g - 1.0)) * np.sum(totals ** 2) / (len(psi) ** 2)


def twoway_se(psi, cluster_i, cluster_j):
    pair = pd.Series(np.asarray(cluster_i).astype(str)) + ":" + pd.Series(np.asarray(cluster_j).astype(str))
    variance = cluster_variance(psi, cluster_i) + cluster_variance(psi, cluster_j) - cluster_variance(psi, pair.to_numpy())
    return float(np.sqrt(max(variance, 0.0)))


def pliv(X, y, d, z, folds, alpha=0.05):
    y_res = y - cross_fit_lasso(X, y, folds, alpha)
    d_res = d - cross_fit_lasso(X, d, folds, alpha)
    z_res = z - cross_fit_lasso(X, z, folds, alpha)
    denom = float(np.mean(z_res * d_res))
    theta = float(np.dot(z_res, y_res) / np.dot(z_res, d_res))
    psi = z_res * (y_res - theta * d_res) / denom
    iid_se = float(np.std(psi, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(psi)))
    return theta, psi, iid_se


def make_cluster_pliv(n_i=20, n_j=20, p=25, theta=1.0, seed=0, one_way=False):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ii, jj = np.meshgrid(np.arange(n_i), np.arange(n_j), indexing="ij")
    cluster_i, cluster_j = ii.ravel(), jj.ravel()
    n = len(cluster_i)
    shock_i = rng.normal(size=n_i)
    shock_j = np.zeros(n_j) if one_way else rng.normal(size=n_j)
    X = rng.normal(scale=0.4, size=(n, p))
    X[:, 0] += shock_i[cluster_i] + shock_j[cluster_j]
    eps = rng.normal(size=n) + 0.8 * (shock_i[cluster_i] + shock_j[cluster_j])
    instrument = 0.8 * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(size=n)
    treatment = 0.7 * instrument + 0.3 * X[:, 2] + 0.5 * eps + rng.normal(scale=0.3, size=n)
    outcome = theta * treatment + 0.8 * X[:, 0] + eps
    return X, outcome, treatment, instrument, cluster_i, cluster_j

title: 5. Deep Causal Learning
section: Types of Deep Causal Learning Models
text:
Types of Deep Causal Learning Models
Deep Causal Learning models can be categorized based on their primary objective: are they trying to estimate an effect, discover a graph, learn robust representations, or make sequential decisions?
Here is a detailed breakdown of the different types of Deep Causal Learning models, organized by their function and architecture.

1. Causal Effect Estimation Models
Goal: Estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) or Individual Treatment Effect (ITE) from high-dimensional observational data.
Problem: Standard regression fails due to confounding bias and selection bias.

Representation Learning Networks (TARNet / CFRNet)

Architecture: A neural network learns a representation \(\Phi(X)\) of the covariates. This representation is fed into two separate “heads” (networks): one predicts the outcome for the treated group, one for the control group.
Key Mechanism: Balancing Loss. The model is penalized if the distribution of representations \(\Phi(X)\) differs between the treated and control groups. This mimics propensity score matching but in a latent space.
Use Case: Clinical trials with high-dimensional patient data.



Propensity-Adjusted Networks (DragonNet)

Architecture: Similar to TARNet but adds a third output head that predicts the propensity score \(P(T=1|X)\).
Key Mechanism: Targeted Regularization. By forcing the lower layers to predict the treatment assignment accurately, the network is encouraged to learn sufficient statistics for the propensity score, which theoretically reduces bias in the effect estimate (based on the theory of Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation).
Use Case: When selection bias is strong and known covariates drive treatment assignment.



Generative Counterfactual Models (CEVAE / GANITE)

Architecture:

CEVAE (Causal Effect VAE): Uses a Variational Autoencoder to infer latent confounders \(Z\) from proxy variables \(X\), then estimates effects using \(Z\).
GANITE: Uses a Generative Adversarial Network. The generator imputes missing counterfactuals (e.g., generating the outcome for a treated patient as if they were untreated), and the discriminator tries to distinguish real factual data from generated counterfactuals.

Key Mechanism: Imputation. Explicitly modeling the joint distribution \(P(X, T, Y)\) to sample counterfactual outcomes.
Use Case: When there are unobserved confounders that can be proxied by high-dimensional data (e.g., images, text).




2. Causal Structure Learning Models
Goal: Discover the causal graph (DAG) from data without prior knowledge of the edges.
Problem: Traditional constraint-based methods (PC Algorithm) struggle with non-linear relationships and high dimensions.

Continuous Optimization Models (NOTEARS)

Architecture: Treats the adjacency matrix of the graph as a learnable parameter matrix \(W\).
Key Mechanism: Acyclicity Constraint. Instead of a discrete search, it uses a smooth mathematical constraint (trace of matrix exponential) to ensure the learned graph has no cycles, allowing gradient descent to find the DAG.
Use Case: Learning non-linear causal relationships in tabular data.



Variational Graph Models (DAG-GNN)

Architecture: Combines a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a graphical model. The adjacency matrix is learned as part of the VAE’s latent structure.
Key Mechanism: Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Maximizes the likelihood of the data under the constraint that the underlying structure is a DAG.
Use Case: When data is noisy or contains latent variables.



Neural Structural Equation Models (GraN-DAG)

Architecture: Each node in the graph is parameterized by a neural network (an MLP) that takes its parents as input.
Key Mechanism: Functional Mechanism Learning. Instead of just finding edges, it learns the specific non-linear function \(X_i = f_i(Pa_i) + \epsilon_i\) for each node.
Use Case: Complex systems where causal mechanisms are highly non-linear.




3. Causal Representation Learning Models
Goal: Map low-level observations (pixels, audio) to high-level causal variables (objects, forces).
Problem: Standard deep learning learns correlated features, not causal factors.

Identifiable VAEs (iVAE)

Architecture: A VAE that conditions the latent prior on an auxiliary variable (e.g., domain index or time segment).
Key Mechanism: Weak Supervision. By observing how the latent distribution changes with the auxiliary variable, the model can mathematically guarantee (under assumptions) that the latents correspond to the true causal factors.
Use Case: Disentangling object position, color, and shape in images.



CausalVAE

Architecture: Integrates a Structural Causal Model (SCM) layer into the latent space of a VAE.
Key Mechanism: Causal Mask. The latent variables interact via a causal mask matrix before being decoded into the observation.
Use Case: Video generation where objects move according to physical causal laws.



Independent Mechanism Networks

Architecture: Enforces that the conditional distribution of a cause given its effect is independent of the distribution of the effect.
Key Mechanism: Independence Penalties. Regularization terms that minimize the mutual information between learned mechanisms.
Use Case: Domain adaptation and transfer learning.




4. Invariant & Robust Learning Models
Goal: Learn predictors that generalize across different environments (domains) by relying on causal features rather than spurious correlations.
Problem: Models fail when test data distribution differs from training data (OOD generalization).

Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM)

Architecture: A feature extractor \(\Phi\) and a classifier \(w\). Trained on multiple environments (e.g., data from different hospitals).
Key Mechanism: Invariance Constraint. Finds a representation \(\Phi\) such that the optimal classifier \(w\) is the same across all training environments. This forces the model to ignore features that correlate with the label only in specific environments.
Use Case: Medical diagnosis across different scanner types; autonomous driving in different weather.



Risk Extrapolation (REx)

Architecture: Similar to IRM but focuses on variance.
Key Mechanism: Variance Regularization. Penalizes the variance of the risk (loss) across different training environments. If the loss is stable across environments, the features are likely causal.
Use Case: Robust classification tasks.




5. Causal Time-Series Models
Goal: Discover causality or estimate effects in sequential data.
Problem: Temporal dependencies and lagged effects complicate standard causal assumptions.

Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF)

Architecture: Uses Attention-based Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).
Key Mechanism: Attention Interpretation. The attention weights indicate which time series and which time lags are causally influencing the target.
Use Case: Financial market analysis, gene regulatory networks.



Recurrent Structural Causal Models

Architecture: Uses RNNs or LSTMs to model the structural equations \(X_t = f(X_{t-1}, \epsilon_t)\).
Key Mechanism: Temporal SCMs. Extends the SCM framework to include time steps, allowing for counterfactual reasoning in time series (e.g., “What would the stock price be today if interest rates hadn’t risen last month?”).
Use Case: Climate modeling, economic forecasting.




6. Causal Reinforcement Learning (Causal RL)
Goal: Agents that learn policies by understanding the causal structure of the environment.
Problem: Standard RL learns correlations between actions and rewards, leading to poor transfer.

Model-Based Causal RL

Architecture: The agent learns a causal model of the transition dynamics \(P(S_{t+1} | S_t, A_t)\) rather than a black-box transition function.
Key Mechanism: Interventional Planning. The agent plans by simulating interventions (\(do(A_t)\)) on the learned causal model.
Use Case: Robotics where physical laws are invariant but textures/lighting change.



Counterfactual Data Augmentation

Architecture: Standard RL algorithm (e.g., PPO, DQN) augmented with a generative model.
Key Mechanism: Counterfactual Generation. Generates synthetic experiences (“What if I took action B instead of A?”) to enrich the replay buffer and reduce sample complexity.
Use Case: Environments where data collection is expensive or dangerous.

Which Model Should You Choose?

If you have a known graph and want to estimate effects: Use Deep DML or TARNet.
If you don’t have a graph and want to find one: Use NOTEARS (for tabular) or TCDF (for time-series).
If you have images/text and want causal features: Use CausalVAE or iVAE.
If your test data differs from training data: Use IRM.
If you suspect hidden confounders: Use CEVAE (if you have proxy data).

title: 5. Deep Causal Learning
text:
Summary and Conclusion
Deep causal learning represents a powerful fusion of deep learning and causal inference, enabling models to uncover cause-and-effect relationships from complex, high-dimensional data. By leveraging architectures like VAEs, GANs, and attention mechanisms, these models can estimate treatment effects, discover causal graphs, learn robust representations, and handle temporal dynamics. While challenges remain in identifiability and scalability, ongoing research continues to push the boundaries of what deep causal learning can achieve across domains like healthcare, robotics, and economics. For practitioners, the choice of model depends on the specific causal question, data type, and assumptions about the underlying causal structure. As the field evolves, we can expect more sophisticated models that blend symbolic reasoning with deep learning for even greater causal understanding.

Foundational Papers

Representation Learning for Causal Inference

“Estimating individual treatment effect: generalization bounds and algorithms” — Shalit, Johansson & Sontag (2017). The paper that introduced TARNet and CFRNet. Establishes the theoretical IPM bound. proceedings.mlr.press
“Adapting Neural Networks for the Estimation of Treatment Effects” — Shi, Blei & Veitch (2019). Introduces DragonNet — propensity-integrated architecture with targeted regularization. arxiv.org
“A Primer on Deep Learning for Causal Inference” — Koch, Sainburg et al. (2021, updated 2023). The most comprehensive survey of deep learning methods under the potential outcomes framework. arxiv.org



Causal Discovery

“DAGs with NO TEARS: Continuous Optimization for Structure Learning” — Zheng et al. (2018). The foundational paper for differentiable DAG learning. arxiv.org
“DYNOTEARS: Structure Learning from Time-Series Data” — Pamfil et al. (2020). Extends NOTEARS to temporal/lagged causal graphs. arxiv.org
“Neural Granger Causality” — Tank et al. (2022). Introduces cMLP and cLSTM with group LASSO for nonlinear Granger causal discovery. arxiv.org
“Temporal Causal Discovery Framework” — Nauta et al. (2019). Attention-based discovery of causal relationships in multivariate time series. arxiv.org



Double Machine Learning & Semiparametric Methods

“Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Structural Parameters” — Chernozhukov et al. (2018). The DML paper — cross-fitting + Neyman orthogonality. arxiv.org
“Quasi-oracle estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects” — Nie & Wager (2021). Introduces the R-Learner — a flexible meta-learning approach compatible with any ML model. arxiv.org



Causal Reinforcement Learning & Counterfactual Forecasting

text: Python Banner

title: 5.1.1 TARNet (Treatment-Agnostic Representation Network)
text:
Overview
TARNet is a neural network architecture for causal inference, specifically designed to estimate individualized treatment effects (ITE) from observational data. It was introduced by Shalit, Johansson, and Sontag (2017) in “Estimating individual treatment effects: generalization bounds and algorithms.”

title: 5.1.1 TARNet (Treatment-Agnostic Representation Network)
text:
Architecture
Two core challenges motivate TARNet’s design:

The fundamental problem of causal inference: For any individual, only one potential outcome is ever observed.
Selection bias: In observational data, treatment assignment is rarely random — sicker patients may be more likely to receive treatment, confounding naive effect estimates.

title: 5.1.1 TARNet (Treatment-Agnostic Representation Network)
text:
Why “Treatment-Agnostic”?
The shared encoder Φ is trained to be agnostic to treatment assignment — encoding a patient’s underlying features, not which group they belonged to.
The related CFRNet variant extends TARNet by adding an IPM regularizer that explicitly penalizes distributional divergence between treated and control representations.

title: 5.1.1 TARNet (Treatment-Agnostic Representation Network)
text:
TARNet vs. Other Approaches








Approach
Key idea
Limitation




S-Learner
Single model; treatment as a feature
Treatment effect can be smoothed away


T-Learner
Separate models per treatment arm
No shared learning; high variance


TARNet
Shared representation + separate heads
Balances shared features with arm-specific prediction


CFRNet
TARNet + IPM regularizer
More aggressive covariate shift correction

section: Load data and prepare (X, t, y)
text:
Load data and prepare (X, t, y)
We use NSW (nsw_mixtape) from causaldata: treatment treat, outcome re78, covariates age, educ, black, hisp, marr, nodegree, re74, re75. After dropping incomplete rows, we split into training and test sets (80/20); covariates are standardized using the training mean and SD only.


Code
from pathlib import Path
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet, LogisticRegression, LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold


def load_nsw_mixtape() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load NSW (Lalonde) mixtape data (same variables as causaldata::nsw_mixtape)."""
    try:
        import causaldata.nsw_mixtape.data as nsw_data
        dta = Path(nsw_data.__file__).parent / "nsw_mixtape.dta"
        return pd.read_stata(dta)
    except Exception:
        pass
    url = (
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NickCH-K/causaldata/master/"
        "data-raw/nsw_mixtape.dta"
    )
    return pd.read_stata(url)


def propensity_elastic_net(X: np.ndarray, treatment: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    model = LogisticRegression(
        penalty="elasticnet", solver="saga", l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=2000
    )
    model.fit(X, treatment)
    return model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]


class SLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger"):
        self.learner = learner

    def fit(self, X, t, y):
        Xt = np.column_stack([X, t])
        if self.learner == "lm":
            self.model_ = LinearRegression().fit(Xt, y)
        else:
            self.model_ = RandomForestRegressor(
                n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
            ).fit(Xt, y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        y0 = self.model_.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.zeros(len(X))]))
        y1 = self.model_.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.ones(len(X))]))
        return y1 - y0


class TLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger"):
        self.learner = learner

    def fit(self, X, t, y):
        t = t.astype(int)
        if self.learner == "lm":
            self.m0_ = LinearRegression().fit(X[t == 0], y[t == 0])
            self.m1_ = LinearRegression().fit(X[t == 1], y[t == 1])
        else:
            self.m0_ = RandomForestRegressor(
                n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
            ).fit(X[t == 0], y[t == 0])
            self.m1_ = RandomForestRegressor(
                n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
            ).fit(X[t == 1], y[t == 1])
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.m1_.predict(X) - self.m0_.predict(X)


class XLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger"):
        self.learner = learner

    def _reg(self):
        if self.learner == "lm":
            return LinearRegression()
        return RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

    def fit(self, X, t, y, p=None):
        t = t.astype(int)
        p = propensity_elastic_net(X, t) if p is None else p
        m0, m1 = self._reg(), self._reg()
        m0.fit(X[t == 0], y[t == 0])
        m1.fit(X[t == 1], y[t == 1])
        d1 = y[t == 1] - m0.predict(X[t == 1])
        d0 = m1.predict(X[t == 0]) - y[t == 0]
        tau1 = self._reg().fit(X[t == 1], d1)
        tau0 = self._reg().fit(X[t == 0], d0)
        self.p_, self.tau0_, self.tau1_ = p, tau0, tau1
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.p_ * self.tau0_.predict(X) + (1 - self.p_) * self.tau1_.predict(X)


class RLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger", n_fold: int = 3):
        self.learner = learner
        self.n_fold = n_fold

    def _reg(self):
        if self.learner == "lm":
            return LinearRegression()
        return RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

    def fit(self, X, t, y, p=None):
        t = t.astype(int).astype(float)
        p = propensity_elastic_net(X, t) if p is None else p
        e = t - p
        m = self._reg()
        kf = KFold(n_splits=self.n_fold, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
        y_hat = np.zeros_like(y, dtype=float)
        for tr, va in kf.split(X):
            m.fit(X[tr], y[tr])
            y_hat[va] = m.predict(X[va])
        resid = y - y_hat
        tau = self._reg()
        tau.fit(X, resid / (e + 1e-6), sample_weight=e**2)
        self.tau_ = tau
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.tau_.predict(X)


def get_cumgain(df_preds, outcome_col="y", treatment_col="w", treatment_effect_col="tau", normalize=True):
    """Cumulative gain curve (CausalML-style AUUC helper)."""
    y = df_preds[outcome_col].to_numpy()
    w = df_preds[treatment_col].to_numpy()
    tau = df_preds[treatment_effect_col].to_numpy()
    model_cols = [c for c in df_preds.columns if c not in {outcome_col, treatment_col, treatment_effect_col}]
    n = len(df_preds)
    out = {}
    for col in model_cols:
        scores = df_preds[col].to_numpy()
        order = np.argsort(-scores)
        cum = []
        treated_so_far = control_so_far = 0.0
        for i, idx in enumerate(order, start=1):
            if w[idx] == 1:
                treated_so_far += y[idx]
            else:
                control_so_far += y[idx]
            lift = treated_so_far / max((w[order[:i]] == 1).sum(), 1) - control_so_far / max(
                (w[order[:i]] == 0).sum(), 1
            )
            cum.append(lift)
        curve = np.array(cum)
        if normalize and curve[-1] != 0:
            curve = curve / np.abs(curve[-1])
        out[col] = curve
    out[treatment_effect_col] = out.get(treatment_effect_col, out[model_cols[0]])
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


def plot_gain(df_preds, outcome_col="y", treatment_col="w", treatment_effect_col="tau", model_cols=None, main="", normalize=True):
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    gain = get_cumgain(df_preds, outcome_col, treatment_col, treatment_effect_col, normalize)
    model_cols = model_cols or [c for c in gain.columns]
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    for col in model_cols:
        if col in gain.columns:
            plt.plot(gain[col].values, label=col)
    plt.xlabel("Population fraction targeted")
    plt.ylabel("Cumulative gain" + (" (normalized)" if normalize else ""))
    plt.title(main)
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def load_ihdp(replications: int = 2, random_state: int = 1):
    base_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uber/causalml/master/docs/examples/data"
    cols = ["treatment", "y_factual", "y_cfactual", "mu0", "mu1"] + [f"X{i}" for i in range(25)]
    parts = []
    for i in range(1, 10):
        url = f"{base_url}/ihdp_npci_{i}.csv"
        tmp = pd.read_csv(url, header=None)
        tmp.columns = cols[: tmp.shape[1]]
        parts.append(tmp)
    df = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
    if replications > 1:
        df = pd.concat([df] * replications, ignore_index=True)
    binfeats = [f"X{i}" for i in range(6, 25)]
    contfeats = [f"X{i}" for i in range(6)]
    xcols = binfeats + contfeats
    X = df[xcols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    treatment = df["treatment"].to_numpy(dtype=int)
    y = df["y_factual"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    tau = np.where(
        treatment == 1,
        df["y_factual"] - df["y_cfactual"],
        df["y_cfactual"] - df["y_factual"],
    )
    n = len(X)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    val_idx = rng.choice(n, size=int(0.2 * n), replace=False)
    train_idx = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), val_idx)
    return df, X, treatment, y, tau, train_idx, val_idx


def simulate_hidden_confounder(n=2000, p=5, sigma=1.0, adj=0, random_state=42):
    """Synthetic DGP with latent confounder (CausalML-style benchmark)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    z = rng.normal(size=n)
    X = np.column_stack([z + rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=n) for _ in range(p)])
    e = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(adj + 0.5 * z)))
    w = rng.binomial(1, e)
    b = 2 * z + rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=n)
    tau = 0.5 + 0.3 * z
    y = b + w * tau + rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=n)
    return {"X": X, "y": y, "w": w, "tau": tau, "b": b, "e": e}


def result_table(df_preds, tau_true):
    model_cols = [c for c in ["S", "T", "X", "R", "GANITE", "CEVAE"] if c in df_preds.columns]
    methods = model_cols + ["actual"]
    ate = [df_preds[m].mean() for m in model_cols] + [float(tau_true.mean())]
    mae = [float(np.mean(np.abs(df_preds[m] - tau_true))) for m in model_cols] + [np.nan]
    gain = get_cumgain(df_preds)
    auuc = [float(gain[m].mean()) if m in gain.columns else np.nan for m in model_cols]
    auuc.append(float(gain["tau"].mean()) if "tau" in gain.columns else np.nan)
    return pd.DataFrame({"Method": methods, "ATE": ate, "MAE": mae, "AUUC": auuc})


def synthetic_summary(preds, tau_ref, actual_ate):
    rows = []
    for name, p in preds.items():
        rows.append({
            "Method": name,
            "ATE": p.mean(),
            "MSE": np.mean((p - tau_ref) ** 2),
            "AbsPctErrorATE": abs(p.mean() / actual_ate - 1) if actual_ate != 0 else np.nan,
        })
    rows.append({"Method": "Actuals", "ATE": actual_ate, "MSE": np.nan, "AbsPctErrorATE": np.nan})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

import os
from pathlib import Path
from pydeepcausalml.effect import TARNet

FAST_RUN = os.getenv("PYDEEPCAUSALML_FAST_RENDER", "true").lower() == "true"
EPOCHS = 30 if FAST_RUN else 100
NUM_TREES = 100 if FAST_RUN else 500

set_seed(42)
df = load_nsw_mixtape()
y_col, t_col = "re78", "treat"
x_cols = ["age", "educ", "black", "hisp", "marr", "nodegree", "re74", "re75"]
df = df.dropna(subset=[y_col, t_col] + x_cols).copy()
df[t_col] = df[t_col].astype(int)

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
idx = rng.choice(len(df), size=int(0.8 * len(df)), replace=False)
mask = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
mask[idx] = True
df_train, df_test = df[mask], df[~mask]

X_train_raw = df_train[x_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
X_test_raw = df_test[x_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
cm = X_train_raw.mean(axis=0)
cs = X_train_raw.std(axis=0)
cs[cs == 0] = 1.0
X_train = (X_train_raw - cm) / cs
X_test = (X_test_raw - cm) / cs
t_train = df_train[t_col].to_numpy(dtype=int)
y_train = df_train[y_col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
t_test = df_test[t_col].to_numpy(dtype=int)
y_test = df_test[y_col].to_numpy(dtype=float)

print(f"Train n = {len(X_train)} | Test n = {len(X_test)} | p = {X_train.shape[1]}")

Fit TARNet, S-Learner, and T-Learner
TARNet trains with mini-batches on the training fold. S-Learner and T-Learner use random forests on the same scaled covariates — a standard tree-based baseline.

fit_tarnet = TARNet(
    repr_dim=100,
    head_dim=64,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    batch_size=64,

    standardize=False,

).fit(X_train, t_train, y_train)

fit_sl = SLearner(learner="ranger").fit(X_train, t_train, y_train)
fit_tl = TLearner(learner="ranger").fit(X_train, t_train, y_train)

section: Predict and validate on the test set
text:
Predict and validate on the test set
For each unit, \(\hat{\tau}(x) = \hat{Y}(1 \mid x) - \hat{Y}(0 \mid x)\). Because NSW has no counterfactual labels, we also report factual outcome MSE on the test set.


Code
def factual_mse_tarnet(est, X, t, y):
    y0, y1 = est.predict_potential_outcomes(X)
    y_hat = np.where(t.astype(bool), y1, y0)
    return float(np.mean((y - y_hat) ** 2))


def factual_mse_sl(est, X, t, y):
    y0 = est.model_.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.zeros(len(X))]))
    y1 = est.model_.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.ones(len(X))]))
    y_hat = np.where(t.astype(bool), y1, y0)
    return float(np.mean((y - y_hat) ** 2))


def factual_mse_tl(est, X, t, y):
    y_hat = np.where(t.astype(bool), est.m1_.predict(X), est.m0_.predict(X))
    return float(np.mean((y - y_hat) ** 2))


ite_tarnet = fit_tarnet.predict_cate(X_test)
ite_sl = fit_sl.predict(X_test)
ite_tl = fit_tl.predict(X_test)

compare_tbl = pd.DataFrame({
    "Learner": ["TARNet", "S-Learner (ranger)", "T-Learner (ranger)", "Naive diff-in-means"],
    "ATE_test": [ite_tarnet.mean(), ite_sl.mean(), ite_tl.mean(),
                 y_test[t_test == 1].mean() - y_test[t_test == 0].mean()],
    "Factual_MSE_test": [
        factual_mse_tarnet(fit_tarnet, X_test, t_test, y_test),
        factual_mse_sl(fit_sl, X_test, t_test, y_test),
        factual_mse_tl(fit_tl, X_test, t_test, y_test),

})

Permutation-based feature importance (TARNet)
We measure how much predicted CATE depends on each covariate using permutation importance on the test fold.

n_rep = 8
rng = np.random.default_rng(4343)
ite_base = fit_tarnet.predict_cate(X_test)
imp = []
for j in range(X_test.shape[1]):

title: 5.1.3 DragonNet: Propensity-Adjusted Networks for Causal Inference
text: Python Banner

title: 5.1.3 DragonNet: Propensity-Adjusted Networks for Causal Inference
text:
Overview
DragonNet is a deep learning architecture that explicitly incorporates propensity score estimation into the training process. It consists of a shared representation layer followed by three separate heads: one for predicting the propensity score and two for predicting potential outcomes under treatment and control. The key innovation is a targeted regularization term derived from the theory of targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE), which encourages the model to learn representations that are sufficient for causal estimation. The result is a model that can achieve doubly-robust ATE estimation — meaning that even if either the outcome model or the propensity model is misspecified, the ATE estimate remains consistent.

The DragonNet Architecture
The shared representation Φ(x) feeds into three heads:



The Core Insight: Why Propensity Matters
The propensity score e(x) = P(T=1 | X=x) is the probability that a unit receives treatment, given its covariates. It is the fundamental tool in classical causal inference for de-confounding observational data.
The key theoretical result behind DragonNet comes from the sufficient representation theorem (Shi et al., 2019):

If a representation Φ(x) is sufficient for predicting the propensity score, it is also sufficient for estimating any causal quantity.

In plain terms: you don’t need to capture all of X — you only need to capture the parts of X that are relevant to treatment assignment. Any other variation in X is irrelevant noise for causal estimation and can be discarded. This is a much more targeted form of dimension reduction than TARNet or CFRNet apply.


How DragonNet Works
Step 1 — Shared backbone. All patients are passed through the shared deep network Φ(x), producing a learned representation. This is structurally identical to TARNet’s shared layer, but the training signal it receives is fundamentally different.
Step 2 — Three-headed output. The representation feeds three separate heads simultaneously: - \(g(\Phi(x))\) — the propensity head, which outputs a sigmoid probability \(\hat{e}(x) = \hat{P}(T=1 \mid x)\). This is a binary classifier trained on treatment assignment. - \(Q_0(\Phi(x))\) — the control outcome head - \(Q_1(\Phi(x))\) — the treated outcome head
Step 3 — Targeted regularization. This is DragonNet’s unique contribution. Rather than just adding a propensity prediction loss on top, DragonNet applies a targeted regularization term derived from the theory of targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). The regularizer nudges the outcome predictions \(Q_0\) and \(Q_1\) toward being doubly robust — meaning that even if either the outcome model or the propensity model is slightly wrong, the final ATE estimate remains consistent.
Step 4 — Joint backpropagation. The combined loss flows back through all three heads and through the shared backbone simultaneously. Because the propensity head and the outcome heads share Φ, the backbone is forced to learn features that are predictive of both treatment assignment and outcomes — and the targeted regularizer ensures these features align with what is causally necessary.
Step 5 — ITE at inference. \(\text{ITE}(x) = \hat{Q}_1(\Phi(x)) - \hat{Q}_0(\Phi(x))\). The propensity head is discarded — it was only needed during training to shape the representation.


The Targeted Regularization Term
The targeted regularization is the most mathematically novel part. Here is what it computes:

from pathlib import Path
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet, LogisticRegression, LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold


def load_nsw_mixtape() -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load NSW (Lalonde) mixtape data (same variables as causaldata::nsw_mixtape)."""
    try:
        import causaldata.nsw_mixtape.data as nsw_data
        dta = Path(nsw_data.__file__).parent / "nsw_mixtape.dta"
        return pd.read_stata(dta)
    except Exception:
        pass
    url = (
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NickCH-K/causaldata/master/"
        "data-raw/nsw_mixtape.dta"
    )
    return pd.read_stata(url)


def propensity_elastic_net(X: np.ndarray, treatment: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    model = LogisticRegression(
        penalty="elasticnet", solver="saga", l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=2000
    )
    model.fit(X, treatment)
    return model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]


class SLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger"):
        self.learner = learner

    def fit(self, X, t, y):
        Xt = np.column_stack([X, t])
        if self.learner == "lm":
            self.model_ = LinearRegression().fit(Xt, y)
        else:
            self.model_ = RandomForestRegressor(
                n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
            ).fit(Xt, y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        y0 = self.model_.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.zeros(len(X))]))
        y1 = self.model_.predict(np.column_stack([X, np.ones(len(X))]))
        return y1 - y0


class TLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger"):
        self.learner = learner

    def fit(self, X, t, y):
        t = t.astype(int)
        if self.learner == "lm":
            self.m0_ = LinearRegression().fit(X[t == 0], y[t == 0])
            self.m1_ = LinearRegression().fit(X[t == 1], y[t == 1])
        else:
            self.m0_ = RandomForestRegressor(
                n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
            ).fit(X[t == 0], y[t == 0])
            self.m1_ = RandomForestRegressor(
                n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1
            ).fit(X[t == 1], y[t == 1])
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.m1_.predict(X) - self.m0_.predict(X)


class XLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger"):
        self.learner = learner

    def _reg(self):
        if self.learner == "lm":
            return LinearRegression()
        return RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

    def fit(self, X, t, y, p=None):
        t = t.astype(int)
        p = propensity_elastic_net(X, t) if p is None else p
        m0, m1 = self._reg(), self._reg()
        m0.fit(X[t == 0], y[t == 0])
        m1.fit(X[t == 1], y[t == 1])
        d1 = y[t == 1] - m0.predict(X[t == 1])
        d0 = m1.predict(X[t == 0]) - y[t == 0]
        tau1 = self._reg().fit(X[t == 1], d1)
        tau0 = self._reg().fit(X[t == 0], d0)
        self.p_, self.tau0_, self.tau1_ = p, tau0, tau1
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.p_ * self.tau0_.predict(X) + (1 - self.p_) * self.tau1_.predict(X)


class RLearner:
    def __init__(self, learner: str = "ranger", n_fold: int = 3):
        self.learner = learner
        self.n_fold = n_fold

    def _reg(self):
        if self.learner == "lm":
            return LinearRegression()
        return RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)

    def fit(self, X, t, y, p=None):
        t = t.astype(int).astype(float)
        p = propensity_elastic_net(X, t) if p is None else p
        e = t - p
        m = self._reg()
        kf = KFold(n_splits=self.n_fold, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
        y_hat = np.zeros_like(y, dtype=float)
        for tr, va in kf.split(X):
            m.fit(X[tr], y[tr])
            y_hat[va] = m.predict(X[va])
        resid = y - y_hat
        tau = self._reg()
        tau.fit(X, resid / (e + 1e-6), sample_weight=e**2)
        self.tau_ = tau
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.tau_.predict(X)


def get_cumgain(df_preds, outcome_col="y", treatment_col="w", treatment_effect_col="tau", normalize=True):
    """Cumulative gain curve (CausalML-style AUUC helper)."""
    y = df_preds[outcome_col].to_numpy()
    w = df_preds[treatment_col].to_numpy()
    tau = df_preds[treatment_effect_col].to_numpy()
    model_cols = [c for c in df_preds.columns if c not in {outcome_col, treatment_col, treatment_effect_col}]
    n = len(df_preds)
    out = {}
    for col in model_cols:
        scores = df_preds[col].to_numpy()
        order = np.argsort(-scores)
        cum = []
        treated_so_far = control_so_far = 0.0
        for i, idx in enumerate(order, start=1):
            if w[idx] == 1:
                treated_so_far += y[idx]
            else:
                control_so_far += y[idx]
            lift = treated_so_far / max((w[order[:i]] == 1).sum(), 1) - control_so_far / max(
                (w[order[:i]] == 0).sum(), 1
            )
            cum.append(lift)
        curve = np.array(cum)
        if normalize and curve[-1] != 0:
            curve = curve / np.abs(curve[-1])
        out[col] = curve
    out[treatment_effect_col] = out.get(treatment_effect_col, out[model_cols[0]])
    return pd.DataFrame(out)


def plot_gain(df_preds, outcome_col="y", treatment_col="w", treatment_effect_col="tau", model_cols=None, main="", normalize=True):
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    gain = get_cumgain(df_preds, outcome_col, treatment_col, treatment_effect_col, normalize)
    model_cols = model_cols or [c for c in gain.columns]
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
    for col in model_cols:
        if col in gain.columns:
            plt.plot(gain[col].values, label=col)
    plt.xlabel("Population fraction targeted")
    plt.ylabel("Cumulative gain" + (" (normalized)" if normalize else ""))
    plt.title(main)
    plt.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def load_ihdp(replications: int = 2, random_state: int = 1):
    base_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uber/causalml/master/docs/examples/data"
    cols = ["treatment", "y_factual", "y_cfactual", "mu0", "mu1"] + [f"X{i}" for i in range(25)]
    parts = []
    for i in range(1, 10):
        url = f"{base_url}/ihdp_npci_{i}.csv"
        tmp = pd.read_csv(url, header=None)
        tmp.columns = cols[: tmp.shape[1]]
        parts.append(tmp)
    df = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
    if replications > 1:
        df = pd.concat([df] * replications, ignore_index=True)
    binfeats = [f"X{i}" for i in range(6, 25)]
    contfeats = [f"X{i}" for i in range(6)]
    xcols = binfeats + contfeats
    X = df[xcols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    treatment = df["treatment"].to_numpy(dtype=int)
    y = df["y_factual"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    tau = np.where(
        treatment == 1,
        df["y_factual"] - df["y_cfactual"],
        df["y_cfactual"] - df["y_factual"],
    )
    n = len(X)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    val_idx = rng.choice(n, size=int(0.2 * n), replace=False)
    train_idx = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), val_idx)
    return df, X, treatment, y, tau, train_idx, val_idx


def simulate_hidden_confounder(n=2000, p=5, sigma=1.0, adj=0, random_state=42):
    """Synthetic DGP with latent confounder (CausalML-style benchmark)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
    z = rng.normal(size=n)
    X = np.column_stack([z + rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=n) for _ in range(p)])
    e = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(adj + 0.5 * z)))
    w = rng.binomial(1, e)
    b = 2 * z + rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=n)
    tau = 0.5 + 0.3 * z
    y = b + w * tau + rng.normal(scale=sigma, size=n)
    return {"X": X, "y": y, "w": w, "tau": tau, "b": b, "e": e}


def result_table(df_preds, tau_true):
    model_cols = [c for c in ["S", "T", "X", "R", "GANITE", "CEVAE"] if c in df_preds.columns]
    methods = model_cols + ["actual"]
    ate = [df_preds[m].mean() for m in model_cols] + [float(tau_true.mean())]
    mae = [float(np.mean(np.abs(df_preds[m] - tau_true))) for m in model_cols] + [np.nan]
    gain = get_cumgain(df_preds)
    auuc = [float(gain[m].mean()) if m in gain.columns else np.nan for m in model_cols]
    auuc.append(float(gain["tau"].mean()) if "tau" in gain.columns else np.nan)
    return pd.DataFrame({"Method": methods, "ATE": ate, "MAE": mae, "AUUC": auuc})


def synthetic_summary(preds, tau_ref, actual_ate):
    rows = []
    for name, p in preds.items():

            "ATE": p.mean(),
            "MSE": np.mean((p - tau_ref) ** 2),
            "AbsPctErrorATE": abs(p.mean() / actual_ate - 1) if actual_ate != 0 else np.nan,
        })
    rows.append({"Method": "Actuals", "ATE": actual_ate, "MSE": np.nan, "AbsPctErrorATE": np.nan})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

title: 5.1.5 NeuralDML: Neural Double Machine Learning for the Average Treatment Effect
text:
Overview
Observational causal inference from high-dimensional covariates requires two things simultaneously: flexible models for nuisance functions (outcome and propensity) and valid statistical inference for the causal parameter. Classical parametric regression fails when the relationship between covariates and outcomes is nonlinear. Pure deep learning (TARNet, DragonNet) can capture nonlinearity but typically returns point ITE predictions without principled uncertainty quantification for the ATE.
Double/debiased machine learning (DML) resolves this tension. Under the partially linear model
\[Y = \theta T + g(X) + \varepsilon, \qquad T = e(X) + \nu,\]
where \(g(X) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\) and \(e(X) = \mathbb{E}[T \mid X]\), the ATE \(\theta\) is identified as the coefficient in a regression of outcome residuals on treatment residuals:
\[\tilde{Y}_i = Y_i - \hat{m}(X_i), \qquad \tilde{T}_i = T_i - \hat{e}(X_i)\]
\[\hat{\theta} = \frac{\sum_i \tilde{T}_i \, \tilde{Y}_i}{\sum_i \tilde{T}_i^2}\]
NeuralDML in PyDeepCausalML implements this pipeline with MLP nuisance learners and K-fold cross-fitting to avoid overfitting bias from using the same data to estimate nuisances and the treatment effect.

title: 5.1.5 NeuralDML: Neural Double Machine Learning for the Average Treatment Effect
text:
The cross-fitting pipeline
Cross-fitting is the key ingredient that makes DML statistically valid with flexible machine learning. Without it, reusing the same observations to fit \(\hat{m}\) and \(\hat{e}\) and then to estimate \(\theta\) introduces regularization bias that does not vanish with sample size.
The diagram below shows the standard DML workflow: partition the data, fit nuisances on training folds, compute out-of-sample residuals on held-out folds, then aggregate.
