title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 1: Conceptual Foundation

Classical Granger Causality
A variable \(X\) Granger-causes \(Y\) if past values of \(X\) significantly improve the forecast of \(Y\) beyond what \(Y\)’s own past provides. For lag order \(p\):
\[
Y_t = \sum_{k=1}^{p} A_k Y_{t-k} + \epsilon_t
\]
If the coefficient block connecting \(X_{t-k} \rightarrow Y_t\) is nonzero, then \(X\) Granger-causes \(Y\). This is inherently linear and can miss nonlinear dynamics.


Neural Granger Causality: The Big Idea
Replace the linear coefficients with neural networks while preserving sparse input selection logic.

If a neural network trained to predict \(Y_t\) assigns zero (or near-zero) weight to all lags of \(X\), then \(X\) does not Granger-cause \(Y\).

Sparsity is enforced with group LASSO regularization on input weights, grouping all lags of a variable together.
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 2: The Four Models

1) cMLP (Component-wise MLP)
A separate MLP is trained for each target variable \(Y_i\):
\[
\hat{Y}_{i,t} = \text{MLP}_i(Y_{1,t-1:t-p},\ldots,Y_{d,t-1:t-p})
\]
Training objective:
\[
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\text{MSE}}_{\text{prediction}} + \lambda \underbrace{\sum_j \lVert W_j^{(1)} \rVert_2}_{\text{group LASSO on input weights}}
\]


2) cLSTM (Component-wise LSTM)
Uses one LSTM per target variable. Better for sequential/long-lag dynamics:
\[
h_t = \text{LSTM}_i(Y_{1:d,\ t-p:t-1}), \quad \hat{Y}_{i,t} = W_{\text{out}} h_t
\]


3) ECONOMY-SRU
A structurally constrained recurrent unit with a soft gate matrix \(G \in [0,1]^{d\times d}\):

Learns sparse variable interactions
Lower computational cost than full LSTMs



4) NRI (Neural Relational Inference)
NRI (Kipf et al., 2018) is a graph-VAE approach:

Encoder infers latent edge distributions \(q(z\mid X)\)
Decoder predicts trajectories from sampled edges

\[
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q(z\mid X)}[\log p(X\mid z)] - \mathrm{KL}[q(z\mid X)\|p(z)]
\]


In PyDeepCausalML
The four theoretical models above map directly onto package estimators, all with a shared fit(X) → get_adjacency() / get_scores() interface:

Estimator

better for long-lag dynamics

cheap structurally-constrained recurrent unit


NRI

full-vs-reduced test

section: Deep Structural Causal Models and lag-resolved discovery
text:
Deep Structural Causal Models and lag-resolved discovery
Before the attention, RNN, and GNN families, it helps to see the structural view that underlies all of them: a set of equations \(X_i = f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i), U_i)\) that can be queried at all three levels of Pearl’s hierarchy. Two package components implement this view directly — DeepSCM and DECI (in pydeepcausalml.timeseries) — while DynoTEARS (in pydeepcausalml.discovery) brings the NOTEARS acyclicity constraint to time-lagged discovery.

Structural Causal Models with deep components
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 1: Theory
An SCM is \(\mathcal{M}=(\mathbf{S}, P(\mathbf{U}))\) with structural equations
\[X_i = f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i), U_i).\]
SCMs support Pearl’s hierarchy: - Association: \(P(Y\mid X=x)\) - Intervention: \(P(Y\mid do(X=x))\) - Counterfactual: \(P(Y_x\mid X=x', Y=y')\)
Deep SCMs replace hand-crafted \(f_i\) with neural nets:
\[X_i = f_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i), U_i).\]
Variational Deep SCM setup: - Encoder: \(q_\phi(U\mid X)\) - Decoder: \(p_\theta(X\mid U,G)\) - ELBO-style objective with reconstruction + KL
DECI jointly learns graph and structural equations with NOTEARS penalty:
\[h(\mathbf{A}) = \mathrm{tr}(e^{\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{A}})-d.\]

In PyDeepCausalML
DeepSCM fits neural structural equations on a fixed graph and supports interventions via intervene(...); DECI learns the graph and the equations jointly under a NOTEARS acyclicity penalty and exposes the result through adjacency_matrix().
from pydeepcausalml import DeepSCM, DECI

deci = DECI(random_state=0).fit(X)      # joint graph + structural equations
A = deci.adjacency_matrix()


DYNOTEARS — DAG-Constrained Structure Learning
DYNOTEARS extends NOTEARS-style continuous optimization to time-series causal discovery by modeling lagged dependencies while enforcing acyclicity on the contemporaneous graph.
For lag order \(p\), a common formulation is:
\[
X_t = W^{(0)}X_t + \sum_{k=1}^{p} W^{(k)}X_{t-k} + \epsilon_t,
\]
where: - \(W^{(0)}\) captures same-time (instantaneous) effects, - \(W^{(k)}\) captures directed lag-\(k\) effects, - acyclicity is imposed on \(W^{(0)}\) using a smooth constraint such as NOTEARS:
\[
h(W^{(0)}) = \operatorname{tr}(e^{W^{(0)}\circ W^{(0)}}) - d = 0.
\]
A typical optimization objective combines data fit, sparsity, and DAG constraint:
\[
\min_{\{W^{(k)}\}}\; \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_1\sum_{k=0}^{p}\|W^{(k)}\|_1 + \lambda_2 h(W^{(0)}).
\]
Why it is useful in practice: - Produces interpretable directed graphs with explicit lag structure. - Gives DAG-guaranteed instantaneous structure (via acyclicity constraint). - Works well when you need structure-learning rigor beyond purely predictive models.
Limitations: - Sensitive to regularization and optimization hyperparameters. - Optimization can be expensive for high-dimensional or long-lag settings.
In PyDeepCausalML: DynoTEARS lives in pydeepcausalml.discovery (or causal_structure_ml("dynotears", lag=...)). Fit it on a multivariate series and read the contemporaneous and lagged structure via get_adjacency() / get_scores().
from pydeepcausalml import causal_structure_ml
from pydeepcausalml.datasets import make_var_data

X, A_true = make_var_data(n_steps=2000, random_state=0)
dyno = causal_structure_ml("dynotears", lag=5, random_state=0).fit(X)
A = dyno.get_adjacency()

Family 2 — Attention / Transformer Models

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 1: Theoretical Foundation
Why Attention for Causality?
Attention mechanisms compute pairwise relevance scores between all time steps and variables simultaneously. This creates a natural inductive structure for causal discovery:
• Temporal attention → which past time steps influence the present (lag selection) • Variable attention → which variables influence which (causal graph) • Causal masking → structural constraint preventing future information leakage
The self-attention score between query \(q_i\) and key \(k_j\):
\[
\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp\left(q_i^\top k_j / \sqrt{d_k}\right)}{\sum_l \exp\left(q_i^\top k_l / \sqrt{d_k}\right)}
\]
When interpreted causally, \(\alpha_{ij}\) approximates the influence of variable/time \(j\) on variable/time \(i\).
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 2: The Three Models

TCDF — Temporal Causal Discovery Framework
TCDF (Nauta et al., 2019) uses depthwise separable causal convolutions + self-attention to discover time-delayed causal relationships.
Key ideas:
• Dilated causal convolutions: receptive field grows exponentially with depth without data leakage — each output depends only on past inputs • Attention mechanism: scores which input channels (variables) contribute most to each target variable • Causal discovery: for target \(Y_i\), trains a separate network; variables with high attention weights are declared causal parents
The convolution at dilation \(r\):
\[\text{Conv}(x, t) = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w_k \cdot x(t - r \cdot k)\]
Causal mask ensures \(x(t - r \cdot k)\) uses only past values (\(k \geq 0\), never \(k < 0\)).


Causal Transformer
A Transformer with three structural modifications that enforce causal reasoning:

Autoregressive masking: upper-triangular mask on attention so position \(t\) only attends to positions \(\leq t\)
Inter-variable attention head: separate attention heads dedicated to cross-variable influence, whose weights are extracted as the causal graph
Positional encoding: learnable temporal embeddings that encode lag distance

The causal attention output:
\[\text{CausalAttn}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M_{\text{causal}}\right) V\]
where \(M_{\text{causal}}[i,j] = -\infty\) if \(j > i\), else \(0\).


TFT — Temporal Fusion Transformer
TFT (Lim et al., 2021, Google) is the state-of-the-art architecture for interpretable multi-horizon forecasting. Its causal structure comes from:
• Variable Selection Networks (VSN): soft gating that selects which input variables are relevant at each time step — directly interpretable as variable-level causal weights • Gated Residual Networks (GRN): nonlinear transformation with skip connections and gating for stable training • Multi-head attention with interpretable weights: attention across time steps, averaged across heads to produce temporal importance scores • Quantile output: produces full predictive distributions, not just point forecasts
TFT architecture flow:

Input variables
      │
      ▼
Variable Selection Network  ← learns which vars matter (causal weights)
      │
      ▼
LSTM Encoder/Decoder        ← captures local temporal dynamics
      │
      ▼
Multi-Head Self-Attention   ← captures long-range dependencies
      │
      ▼
Gated Residual + LayerNorm  ← stabilize gradients
      │
      ▼
Quantile Output Head        ← p10, p50, p90 forecasts


In PyDeepCausalML

Estimator
Distinctive output

causal delays: discovered_edges, summary(), get_adjacency()


Causal Transformer

attention-derived graph: get_adjacency()

interpretable multi-horizon forecasts: predict()



TCDF is the go-to when you need time-delayed discovery — it reads causal lags off the dilated-convolution kernels after validating candidate causes by permutation importance.
from pydeepcausalml import TCDF
model = TCDF(kernel_size=4, epochs=1000, random_state=0).fit(series)
print(model.summary())        # cause -> effect with estimated delay
A = model.get_adjacency()     # A[i, j] means X_j -> X_i

Family 3 — RNN / LSTM Models
Estimators: CausalLSTM, RETAIN, InterventionAwareRNN, CausalLSTMForecaster  ·  Factory: rnn_causal_model("causal_lstm" | "retain" | "intervention_rnn" | "causal_lstm_forecaster")

Conceptual foundation
The RNN/LSTM family covers three approaches for causal time-series modeling:

Causal LSTM (structure-constrained recurrent modeling)
RETAIN (reverse-time attention with interpretability)
Intervention-Aware RNN (regime + intervention conditioning)

The dedicated tutorial notebook works through each on a multivariate financial series; the theory below motivates them.
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 1: Theoretical Foundation

Why RNNs for Causal Time Series?
RNNs process sequences step-by-step, maintaining a hidden state \(h_t\) that acts as a compressed memory of the past:
\[h_t = f(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)\]
The hidden state \(h_t\) implicitly encodes temporal causal history: which past events shaped the current state. Three architectural extensions turn this into explicit causal machinery.
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 2: The Three Models

1) Causal LSTM
A standard LSTM augmented with an explicit causal adjacency mask \(G \in \{0,1\}^{d \times d}\) that gates which variables are allowed to influence which.
For target variable \(i\):
\[\tilde{x}_t^{(i)} = G_{i,:} \odot x_t\]
and the LSTM transitions are computed on \([h_{t-1}; \tilde{x}_t^{(i)}]\). The mask can be fixed, learned (continuous relaxation + sparsity), or hardened at test time.


2) RETAIN (Reverse Time Attention Model)
RETAIN uses two attention channels in reverse time order:

Temporal attention \(\alpha_t\) (which time step matters)
Variable attention \(\beta_t\) (which variable matters at that step)

\[c = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t \cdot (\beta_t \odot v_t)\]
A practical attribution score is:
\[\text{Contribution}(j,t) = \alpha_t \cdot |\beta_{t,j}| \cdot |w_j|\]


3) Intervention-Aware RNN
To model changing data-generating regimes (policy changes, shocks, treatments), we augment inputs with regime/intervention information:
\[h_t = \text{LSTM}(h_{t-1}, [x_t; r_t; I_t])\]

\(r_t\): learned regime embedding
\(I_t\): intervention indicator
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Interpretation Notes

CausalLSTM yields an explicit, sparse, directed adjacency matrix through a learnable structural mask.
RETAIN gives time- and variable-level attribution, making it useful for interpretability-first workflows.
Intervention-Aware RNN can adapt dynamics when volatility/shock regimes change.

In practice, combining these models is often powerful: 1. Use RETAIN for explanation. 2. Use CausalLSTM for structural constraints. 3. Use Intervention-Aware RNN when regime shifts are expected.

model = CausalLSTMForecaster(pred_len=12, random_state=0)

Family 4 — Graph Neural Network Models
Estimators: GVAR, CausalGNN, CUTS  ·  Factory: gnn_causal_model("gvar" | "causal_gnn" | "cuts")

Conceptual foundation
The GNN family covers three practical approaches to causal modeling for multivariate time series:

GVAR (Graph Vector Autoregression)
CausalGNN / CD-GNN (joint graph learning + dynamics)
CUTS+ inspired model (causal discovery under missing data)

The dedicated tutorial notebook demonstrates them on sector-ETF returns in pure PyTorch (no mandatory torch-geometric); the theory below sets them up.
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 1: Theoretical Foundation

Why GNNs for Causal Discovery?
A GNN treats variables as nodes and causal relationships as edges in a graph
\[\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}).\]
Message passing makes the causal structure explicit and inspectable:
\[
\mathbf{h}_i^{(\ell+1)}=\mathrm{UPDATE}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(\ell)},\ \mathrm{AGGREGATE}\left(\{\mathbf{h}_j^{(\ell)}:j\in\mathcal{N}(i)\}\right)\right).
\]
Unlike RNNs/Transformers where causal effects are implicit in hidden states, in GNN causal models the graph itself is a first-class object that can be regularized, inspected, and interpreted.
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Part 2: The Three Models

1) GVAR — Graph Vector Autoregression
GVAR extends classical VAR with a learned graph and nonlinear feature transforms:
\[
X_i^{(t)}=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{d}A_{ij}^{(k)}\,\phi\!\left(X_j^{(t-k)}\right)+\epsilon_i^{(t)}.
\]

\(A^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\): lag-specific adjacency (learned)
\(\phi(\cdot)\): nonlinear transform (GNN feature map)
sparsity via L1/group-LASSO style penalties



2) CausalGNN / CD-GNN
Two-stage joint learning:

Graph learner outputs soft adjacency \(\hat{G}\) with NOTEARS acyclicity

\[
h(\mathbf{A})=\mathrm{tr}(e^{\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{A}})-d=0
\]

Dynamics learner propagates messages along parents:

\[
\mathbf{m}_{j\rightarrow i}^{(t)}=\mathrm{MSG}(\mathbf{h}_j^{(t)},\mathbf{h}_i^{(t)},e_{ij}),\quad
\mathbf{h}_i^{(t+1)}=\mathrm{UPDATE}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(t)},\sum_{j\in\mathrm{Pa}(i)}\mathbf{m}_{j\rightarrow i}^{(t)}\right).
\]


3) CUTS / CUTS+
Designed for unevenly sampled or missing time series:

causal-aware imputation network
variational posterior over graphs: \(q(G)\approx\prod_{ij}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ij})\)
joint optimization of reconstruction + imputation + graph regularization

A common ELBO form is:
\[
\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}[\log p(X_{\mathrm{obs}}\mid G,X_{\mathrm{miss}})]
+\mathbb{E}[\log p(X_{\mathrm{miss}}\mid G)]
-\mathrm{KL}[q(G)\|p(G)].
\]
crumbs: Introduction to Temporal Deep Causal ML

This model learns lag-specific adjacency matrices jointly with nonlinear temporal dynamics.

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning

Part 4: Model 2 — CausalGNN / CD-GNN
This model learns a soft DAG and uses edge-conditioned message passing for forecasting.
In PyDeepCausalML: CausalGNN (or gnn_causal_model("causal_gnn")) returns the learned soft DAG through causal_matrix().

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning

Part 5: Model 3 — CUTS+ Inspired (Missing Data)
A practical approximation of CUTS+ ideas: learn probabilistic graph edges and jointly impute missing values before forecasting.
In PyDeepCausalML: CUTS (or gnn_causal_model("cuts")) targets irregular / missing series and exposes the recovered graph through causal_matrix().

In PyDeepCausalML
All three GNN models share a fit(X) → causal_matrix() interface and can be built by class or factory:
from pydeepcausalml import GVAR, gnn_causal_model

gvar = GVAR(lag=5, random_state=0).fit(X)
A = gvar.causal_matrix()
# equivalently: gnn_causal_model("gvar", lag=5).fit(X)
Use the GNN family when you want the causal graph itself to be a first-class, regularizable object — GVAR for lag-specific linear-plus-nonlinear structure, CausalGNN for a NOTEARS-constrained soft DAG with message passing, and CUTS for irregular or missing series.

title: 5.4 Time Series Deep Causal Machine Learning
text:
Family 5 — Counterfactual / SCM Forecasting
Estimators: DeepSynth, CRN, GNet, DeepSCM, DECI  ·  Factory: counterfactual_model("deepsynth" | "crn" | "gnet")
The first four families answer structural questions — which series drives which, at what lag. This family answers the interventional question that motivates much applied time-series causal work: given the history, what would the outcome trajectory have been under a different treatment path?

Why a separate family?
Counterfactual forecasting has to handle time-varying confounding: a treatment decision at time \(t\) depends on the history up to \(t\), and also affects future covariates that in turn drive later treatment decisions. Naively regressing outcome on treatment history is biased. These models borrow ideas from the g-methods and representation balancing to break that feedback loop.








Model
Idea
Method




DeepSynth
deep synthetic control — reconstruct the untreated trajectory from donors
predict_counterfactual


CRN
counterfactual recurrent network with balanced representations across treatments
predict_ite


GNet
neural g-computation: simulate trajectories forward under a treatment rule
predict_ite


DeepSCM
neural structural equations, intervene on the SCM directly
intervene


DECI
learn graph and equations jointly, then intervene
adjacency_matrix, intervene



The key output across this family is a counterfactual trajectory or an effect over a horizon, not a single scalar ATE.
from pydeepcausalml import counterfactual_model
from pydeepcausalml.datasets import make_intervention_series

df = make_intervention_series(n_units=500, horizon=24, random_state=0)
crn = counterfactual_model("crn", random_state=0).fit(df)
ite = crn.predict_ite(df)      # per-unit, per-horizon effect

Discovery models should score well on graph_recovery_metrics; effect and forecasting models should recover the known effect within noise. If they don’t at your data’s scale and noise level, tune before drawing conclusions.

title: 5.4.2 Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with Deep Components
text:
Part 1: Theory
An SCM is \(\mathcal{M}=(\mathbf{S}, P(\mathbf{U}))\) with structural equations
\[X_i = f_i(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i), U_i).\]
SCMs support Pearl’s hierarchy: - Association: \(P(Y\mid X=x)\) - Intervention: \(P(Y\mid do(X=x))\) - Counterfactual: \(P(Y_x\mid X=x', Y=y')\)
Deep SCMs replace hand-crafted \(f_i\) with neural nets:
\[X_i = f_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{Pa}(X_i), U_i).\]
Variational Deep SCM setup: - Encoder: \(q_\phi(U\mid X)\) - Decoder: \(p_\theta(X\mid U,G)\) - ELBO-style objective with reconstruction + KL
DECI jointly learns graph and structural equations with NOTEARS penalty:
\[h(\mathbf{A}) = \mathrm{tr}(e^{\mathbf{A}\odot\mathbf{A}})-d.\]

Data Loading and Preprocessing
This cell downloads sector ETF prices, converts them to standardized log-returns, builds lagged input/output pairs, and creates training/validation data loaders.
Note: If online market data is unavailable, this notebook automatically uses synthetic demo data so all downstream cells remain runnable.


Code
TICKERS = {
    "XLF": "Financials",
    "XLE": "Energy",
    "XLK": "Technology",
    "XLV": "Healthcare",
    "XLI": "Industrials",
    "XLY": "ConsumerDisc",
    "XLP": "ConsumerStap",
    "XLU": "Utilities",
}

import yfinance as yf


def fetch_close_prices(tickers, start="2018-01-01", end="2024-01-01"):
    raw = yf.download(
        tickers, start=start, end=end, auto_adjust=True,
        progress=False, group_by="ticker", threads=False,
    )
    close = None
    if isinstance(raw.columns, pd.MultiIndex):
        if "Close" in raw.columns.get_level_values(-1):
            close = raw.xs("Close", axis=1, level=-1)
    elif "Close" in raw.columns:
        close = raw[["Close"]]
        close.columns = tickers[:1]

    if close is None or close.dropna(how="all").empty:
        cols = []
        for t in tickers:
            one = yf.download(t, start=start, end=end, auto_adjust=True, progress=False, threads=False)
            if "Close" in one.columns and not one["Close"].dropna().empty:
                cols.append(one["Close"].rename(t))
        close = pd.concat(cols, axis=1) if cols else pd.DataFrame()
    return close.sort_index().dropna(how="all")

title: 5.4.2 Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with Deep Components
text:
Utilities and Model Definitions (DeepSCM + DECI)
This section defines helper functions (acyclicity penalty, graph thresholding, plotting) and introduces the three structural models used in this notebook.

1) DeepSCM (Fixed-Graph Structural Model)
DeepSCM assumes a known adjacency matrix and learns nonlinear structural equations on top of that fixed graph.
A simplified form is:
\[
X_t = f_\theta\big(X_{t-1:t-p}, A\big) + \epsilon_t,
\]
where \(A\) is fixed (not learned), and \(f_\theta\) is represented by neural components.
Why useful: - Stable training when a credible prior graph is available. - Good baseline for intervention-style analysis.
Limitation: - Performance and interpretability depend on the quality of the fixed graph.


2) DECI (Deep End-to-end Causal Inference)
DECI jointly learns both graph structure and structural equations in a continuous optimization framework.
It uses a soft adjacency matrix and enforces acyclicity with a NOTEARS-style constraint:
\[
h(A) = \operatorname{tr}(e^{A \circ A}) - d.
\]
A common objective combines reconstruction, sparsity, and DAG regularization:
\[
\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_1\|A\|_1 + \lambda_2 h(A).
\]
Why useful: - Learns structure and mechanism together. - Produces interpretable weighted causal graphs.
Limitation: - Hyperparameter-sensitive and can be optimization-heavy.


3) DYNOTEARS (Lagged DAG-Constrained Discovery)
DYNOTEARS extends NOTEARS-style optimization to time-series causal discovery with lagged dependencies.
For lag order \(p\), a common formulation is:
\[
X_t = W^{(0)}X_t + \sum_{k=1}^{p} W^{(k)}X_{t-k} + \epsilon_t,
\]
where: - \(W^{(0)}\) captures same-time effects, - \(W^{(k)}\) captures directed lag-\(k\) effects, - acyclicity is typically imposed on the instantaneous component (or an aggregated proxy) via a smooth constraint.
A typical objective is:
\[
\min_{\{W^{(k)}\}}\; \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_1\sum_{k=0}^{p}\|W^{(k)}\|_1 + \lambda_2 h(\cdot).
\]
Why useful: - Explicitly separates lagged directional effects. - Produces interpretable causal graphs for multivariate time series.
Limitation: - Sensitive to regularization/threshold settings and may be expensive at larger scale.


Code
def plot_dag(adj, names, title, threshold=0.0):
    """Plot a weighted adjacency matrix as a network."""
    G = nx.DiGraph()
    G.add_nodes_from(names)
    for i, tgt in enumerate(names):
        for j, src in enumerate(names):
            w = adj[i, j]
            if w > threshold:
                G.add_edge(src, tgt, weight=float(w))
    pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=42)
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, with_labels=True, node_size=900, font_size=8, arrows=True)
    plt.title(title)
    plt.axis("off")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def threshold_adjacency(w, threshold=0.35):
    a = (w >= threshold).astype(float)
    np.fill_diagonal(a, 0)
    return a

print("Plotting utilities ready.")

text:
Intervention Analysis and ATE Estimation
Intervention analysis is a method used in causal inference to assess the effects of actively changing (intervening on) one or more variables within a system. It typically involves simulating or implementing a “do” operation (e.g., do(X = x)), which forces a variable to take on a specific value, and then evaluating how this change propagates through the system and affects other variables. This approach allows us to understand causal relationships and estimate quantities like the Average Treatment Effect (ATE), which measures the expected difference in an outcome variable due to the intervention.


Code
# Intervention + ATE example
source_name, target_name = "Energy", "Industrials"
source_idx = VAR_NAMES.index(source_name)
target_idx = VAR_NAMES.index(target_name)

x_contemp = data_np[:, :]  # contemporaneous slice for intervention demo
ate = deci.predict_ate(x_contemp, intervention_var=source_idx, n_samples=200)
print(f"Estimated ATE of do({source_name}) on {target_name}: {ate:.4f}")

pred_lo = deep_scm.intervene(x_contemp[:128], var_idx=source_idx, value=-1.0)
pred_hi = deep_scm.intervene(x_contemp[:128], var_idx=source_idx, value=1.0)
delta = (pred_hi[:, target_idx] - pred_lo[:, target_idx]).mean()
print(
    f"Explanation:\n"
    f"Estimated ATE of do({source_name}) on {target_name}: {ate:.4f}\n"
    f"DeepSCM intervention delta on {target_name}: {delta:.4f}"
)

title: 5.4.2 Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with Deep Components
text:
DYNOTEARS - DAG-Constrained Structure Learning
DYNOTEARS extends NOTEARS-style continuous optimization to time-series causal discovery by modeling lagged dependencies while enforcing acyclicity on the learned structure.
For lag order \(p\), a common formulation is:
\[
X_t = W^{(0)}X_t + \sum_{k=1}^{p} W^{(k)}X_{t-k} + \epsilon_t,
\]
where: - \(W^{(0)}\) captures same-time (instantaneous) effects, - \(W^{(k)}\) captures directed lag-\(k\) effects, - acyclicity is imposed through a smooth NOTEARS-style constraint.
A typical optimization objective combines data fit, sparsity, and DAG regularization:
\[
\min_{\{W^{(k)}\}}\; \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}} + \lambda_1\sum_{k=0}^{p}\|W^{(k)}\|_1 + \lambda_2 h(\cdot).
\]
Why it is useful in practice: - Produces interpretable directed graphs with explicit lag structure. - Provides DAG-regularized structure learning in a differentiable framework. - Useful when structure-learning rigor is needed beyond purely predictive models.
Limitations: - Sensitive to regularization and optimization hyperparameters. - Can be expensive for high-dimensional or long-lag settings.


Code
# DynoTEARS — lag-resolved DAG discovery (pydeepcausalml.discovery)
dyno = DynoTEARS(
    lag=5, lambda_l1=0.02,
    epochs=EPOCHS_DYNO, batch_size=256, lr=3e-3,
    device=DEVICE, random_state=42,
)
dyno.fit(data_np)
print(f"[DynoTEARS] final loss={dyno.history_['loss'][-1]:.4f}")

A_dyno = dyno.get_adjacency(threshold=0.05)
W_agg = dyno.get_scores()
plot_dag(W_agg, VAR_NAMES, "DynoTEARS aggregated lag weights")
plot_dag(A_dyno, VAR_NAMES, "DynoTEARS thresholded adjacency")

Summary and Conclusions
In this notebook, we explored structural causal models (SCMs) with a focus on learning and evaluating causal discovery in multivariate time series data. Using a deep learning-based SCM (akin to the DECI framework), we demonstrated steps to:

Represent temporal data for causal discovery.
Learn a causal graph (“who causes whom”) using soft adjacency and regularization techniques.
Visualize and threshold the learned DAG for interpretability.
Perform intervention analysis by simulating “do-operations” on specific variables, enabling the estimation of treatment effects such as the Average Treatment Effect (ATE).

Through these steps, we illustrated how SCMs can move beyond correlation, allowing us to estimate the impact of interventions and support counterfactual reasoning in dynamical systems. The notebook highlights the importance of model assumptions, the tuning of hyperparameters (such as graph sparsity and DAG penalties), and the value of both observational and interventional data in causal inference.
Key Takeaways: - Learning causal structure from time series is feasible and provides interpretable models of temporal influence. - Deep SCMs enable interventional queries, supporting actionable insights in domains like economics and genomics. - Thresholding and proper regularization are crucial for meaningful graphical outputs, but domain knowledge and further validation are needed for robust conclusions.
Overall, this tutorial provides a foundation for practitioners to begin using deep causal models for discovery and decision-making in complex real-world systems.

title: 5.4.4 RNN/LSTM-Based Causal Models
text:
Part 1: Theoretical Foundation

Why RNNs for Causal Time Series?
RNNs process sequences step-by-step, maintaining a hidden state \(h_t\) that acts as a compressed memory of the past:
\[h_t = f(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)\]
The hidden state \(h_t\) implicitly encodes temporal causal history: which past events shaped the current state. Three architectural extensions turn this into explicit causal machinery.

title: 5.4.4 RNN/LSTM-Based Causal Models
text:
Part 2: The Three Models

1) Causal LSTM
A standard LSTM augmented with an explicit causal adjacency mask \(G \in \{0,1\}^{d \times d}\) that gates which variables are allowed to influence which.
For target variable \(i\):
\[\tilde{x}_t^{(i)} = G_{i,:} \odot x_t\]
and the LSTM transitions are computed on \([h_{t-1}; \tilde{x}_t^{(i)}]\). The mask can be fixed, learned (continuous relaxation + sparsity), or hardened at test time.


2) RETAIN (Reverse Time Attention Model)
RETAIN uses two attention channels in reverse time order:

Temporal attention \(\alpha_t\) (which time step matters)
Variable attention \(\beta_t\) (which variable matters at that step)

\[c = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t \cdot (\beta_t \odot v_t)\]
A practical attribution score is:
\[\text{Contribution}(j,t) = \alpha_t \cdot |\beta_{t,j}| \cdot |w_j|\]


3) Intervention-Aware RNN
To model changing data-generating regimes (policy changes, shocks, treatments), we augment inputs with regime/intervention information:
\[h_t = \text{LSTM}(h_{t-1}, [x_t; r_t; I_t])\]

\(r_t\): learned regime embedding
\(I_t\): intervention indicator

title: 5.4.4 RNN/LSTM-Based Causal Models
text:
Summary and Conclusions
In this notebook, we explored causal modeling approaches using temporal deep learning models on time series data. Specifically, we compared three model architectures: CausalLSTM, RETAIN, and an Intervention-Aware RNN. Our objectives were to assess not only their predictive accuracy (in terms of validation MSE), but also their ability to yield interpretable causal or attribution structures regarding variable influence over time.
Key Findings: - All three models achieved comparable validation MSE, with CausalLSTM slightly outperforming others on this run. - CausalLSTM provided a sparse, interpretable adjacency matrix that can reveal directed causal relationships between variables. - RETAIN was able to generate meaningful attribution scores, making it well-suited for interpretation and explanation of sequential model decisions. - The Intervention-Aware RNN effectively captured regime changes and could be especially useful in datasets with known interventions or volatility shifts.
Conclusions and Recommendations: - Causality-aware neural architectures (like CausalLSTM) enhance both transparency and scientific value in longitudinal modeling tasks. - Attribution-based models (like RETAIN) are recommended when explaining predictions to stakeholders is a priority. - In practice, using these models in combination can leverage their complementary strengths: e.g., deploying RETAIN for explanation, CausalLSTM for enforcing causal structural sparsity, and Intervention-Aware RNNs in adapting to changing regimes. - Further work could include benchmarking on more complex interventions, richer synthetic or real-world datasets, and integration with formal causal discovery pipelines.
This workflow demonstrates a robust foundation for causally-informed machine learning on time series, paving the way towards more reliable and interpretable temporal predictive modeling.

title: 5.4.6 Counterfactual / Potential Outcomes Models
text:
Part 1 - Theoretical Foundation

The Potential Outcomes Framework
For binary treatment \(T \in \{0,1\}\), define potential outcomes for unit \(i\):
\[Y_i(1) =  ext{outcome unit } i    ext{ would have under treatment}\] \[Y_i(0) =  ext{outcome unit } i    ext{ would have under control}\]
The Individual Treatment Effect (ITE) is:
\[  au_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\]
The fundamental problem of causal inference: for each unit/time, we only observe one potential outcome (the factual one). The other is counterfactual and must be estimated.
In time series with treatment history \(\bar{T}_t = (T_1,\ldots,T_t)\):
\[Y_t(\bar{a}) = \text{outcome at time } t \text{ under treatment history } \bar{a}\]


Key Estimands








Estimand
Formula
Question




ATE
\(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]\)
Average causal effect in population


ATT
\(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1]\)
Effect on treated units


CATE
\(\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]\)
Effect conditional on covariates


Time-varying ATE
\(\mathbb{E}[Y_t(\bar{a}) - Y_t(\bar{a}')]\)
Effect of treatment strategy over time





The Confounding Problem in Time Series
Time-varying confounders create feedback loops:
\[X_t
ightarrow T_t
ightarrow Y_{t+1}
ightarrow X_{t+1}
ightarrow T_{t+1}
ightarrow \cdots\]
Here \(X_t\) can be both: - a confounder (affects treatment and outcome), and - an intermediate variable (affected by prior treatment).
This breaks naive regression assumptions and motivates causal sequence models.

title: 5.4.6 Counterfactual / Potential Outcomes Models
text:
Part 2 - Model Intuition

1) DeepSynth / Neural Synthetic Control
Classical synthetic control estimates a treated unit’s counterfactual using weighted controls:
\[\hat{Y}_t^{(0)} = \sum_{j \in     ext{controls}} w_j Y_{t,j}, \quad w_j \ge 0,\; \sum_j w_j = 1\]
DeepSynth replaces fixed linear weights with neural representation learning + attention.


2) CRN - Counterfactual Recurrent Network
CRN uses recurrent representations and adversarial balancing to reduce treatment-assignment bias:
\[\min_{    ext{enc, pred}} \max_D \; \mathcal{L}_{ ext{pred}} - \lambda\mathcal{L}_{   ext{disc}}\]


3) G-Net - Deep G-Computation
G-Net learns sequential generative models for covariates and outcomes and rolls forward under interventions:
\[\mathbb{E}[Y_t(\bar{a})] = \int \prod_{k=1}^{t} p(X_k\mid\bar{X}_{k-1},\bar{A}_{k-1}=\bar{a}_{k-1})\,p(Y_t\mid\bar{X}_t,\bar{A}_t=\bar{a}_t)\,d\bar{X}\]

    epochs=EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, lr=LR, device=DEVICE, random_state=42,
)
crn = counterfactual_model(
    "crn", lag=LAG, hidden=32, lambda_adv=0.5,
    epochs=EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, lr=LR, device=DEVICE, random_state=42,
)
gnet = counterfactual_model(
    "gnet", lag=LAG, hidden=32,
    epochs=EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, lr=LR, device=DEVICE, random_state=42,
)

gnet.fit(data_np, treatment, outcome)

Summary and Conclusion
In this notebook, we explored the estimation of individual and average treatment effects (ITE and ATE) in the context of counterfactual reasoning and causal inference, using three different neural modeling approaches: DeepSynth, CRN (Counterfactual Recurrent Network), and GNet. Each model was trained and evaluated on synthetic panel data designed to capture temporal dynamics and complex treatment-outcome relationships.
We demonstrated how to collect both factual and counterfactual predictions from each model, and compared the resulting ITE distributions and overall ATE estimates. Our visualizations showed the diversity in ITE estimates across methods, highlighting how model choice and underlying assumptions may impact causal estimations.
Key Takeaways: - Counterfactual deep learning approaches can efficiently estimate individual- and population-level causal effects, even in the presence of complex time dependencies. - Different model architectures have different strengths: DeepSynth leverages donor similarity, CRN explicitly models treatment-confounding feedback, and GNet supports flexible policy simulations. - Proper interpretation of results requires attention to identification assumptions (such as unconfoundedness and positivity) and model diagnostics.
Practical Recommendation:
When applying these models to real data, it is crucial to supplement them with rigorous domain knowledge, careful feature engineering, and robust sensitivity analyses to ensure credible causal conclusions.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Overview

Why Bayesian A/B Testing?
Traditional (frequentist) A/B testing uses hypothesis testing and p-values. Bayesian A/B testing offers several advantages:

Intuitive probability statements: “There’s a 95% probability that variant B outperforms A” vs. “We reject the null hypothesis at p < 0.05”
Sequential analysis: You can stop experiments early when results are clear, without inflating Type I error
Incorporating prior knowledge: Historical test results or domain expertise can be encoded as priors
Small sample performance: With informative priors, reliable conclusions can be drawn from small samples
Risk-aware decision-making: Posterior distributions enable loss functions and expected value calculations



The Bayesian A/B Testing Framework
In Bayesian A/B testing, we model the outcome for each variant as a random variable with a prior distribution. After observing data, we compute the posterior distribution for each variant’s metric.
For common metrics:

Conversion rate (binary outcome): Beta-Binomial model
Revenue (continuous outcome): Normal-Gamma model
Count data (e.g., transactions): Poisson-Gamma model

The key output is the posterior distribution of the lift (difference between variants), from which we can compute:

Probability that B > A: \(P(\mu_B > \mu_A \mid \text{data})\)
Expected lift: \(E[\mu_B - \mu_A \mid \text{data}]\)
Credible interval for lift: 95% HDI of \(\mu_B - \mu_A\)



Business Setting
Bayesian A/B testing is ideal when:

Sample sizes are limited: Pilot tests, early-stage experiments
Prior knowledge exists: Historical conversion rates, expert judgment
Sequential monitoring: You want to check results continuously
Risk quantification: You need to quantify the probability of negative outcomes
Decision flexibility: Stopping rules based on posterior probabilities

Common business applications:

Website conversion rate testing
Marketing campaign effectiveness
Pricing experiments
Feature rollout impact
Email marketing optimization

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 1: Conversion Rate Testing (Beta-Binomial)
For binary outcomes (convert/don’t convert), we use the Beta-Binomial model:

Prior: Beta distribution for conversion rate
Likelihood: Binomial distribution for observed conversions
Posterior: Beta distribution (conjugate prior)

Let’s simulate an A/B test for website conversion:


Code
# Simulate A/B test data
np.random.seed(42)

# Variant A: control
n_A = 1000
true_rate_A = 0.10
conversions_A = np.random.binomial(n_A, true_rate_A)

# Variant B: treatment (5% relative lift)
n_B = 1000
true_rate_B = 0.105
conversions_B = np.random.binomial(n_B, true_rate_B)

print(f"Variant A: {conversions_A}/{n_A} conversions ({conversions_A/n_A:.3f})")
print(f"Variant B: {conversions_B}/{n_B} conversions ({conversions_B/n_B:.3f})")
print(f"Observed lift: {(conversions_B/n_B - conversions_A/n_A):.3f}")


Variant A: 96/1000 conversions (0.096)
Variant B: 107/1000 conversions (0.107)
Observed lift: 0.011


Now let’s fit a Bayesian model:


Code
with pm.Model() as conversion_model:
    # Priors for conversion rates (weakly informative)
    # Beta(1, 1) is uniform on [0, 1]
    rate_A = pm.Beta("rate_A", alpha=1, beta=1)
    rate_B = pm.Beta("rate_B", alpha=1, beta=1)
    
    # Lift (relative improvement)
    lift = pm.Deterministic("lift", (rate_B - rate_A) / rate_A)
    
    # Likelihood
    pm.Binomial("conversions_A", n=n_A, p=rate_A, observed=conversions_A)
    pm.Binomial("conversions_B", n=n_B, p=rate_B, observed=conversions_B)
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace_conversion = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)








Let’s examine the results:

Example 2: Incorporating Prior Knowledge
One of Bayesian methods’ strengths is incorporating prior knowledge. Let’s use informative priors based on historical data:


Code
# Suppose historical data suggests conversion rates are around 10% with some variation
# We encode this as Beta(10, 90) which has mean 0.10 and moderate uncertainty

with pm.Model() as conversion_model_informative:
    # Informative priors based on historical data
    rate_A = pm.Beta("rate_A", alpha=10, beta=90)
    rate_B = pm.Beta("rate_B", alpha=10, beta=90)
    
    lift = pm.Deterministic("lift", (rate_B - rate_A) / rate_A)
    
    pm.Binomial("conversions_A", n=n_A, p=rate_A, observed=conversions_A)
    pm.Binomial("conversions_B", n=n_B, p=rate_B, observed=conversions_B)
    
    trace_informative = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)

# Compare results
print("Weakly informative priors:")
print(az.summary(trace_conversion, var_names=["lift"], hdi_prob=0.95))

print("\nInformative priors:")

Example 3: Revenue Testing (Normal-Gamma)
For continuous outcomes like revenue, we use a Normal likelihood with a Gamma prior on the standard deviation:

np.random.seed(42)

n_A_rev = 500
n_B_rev = 500

# Variant A: mean $50, std $20
revenue_A = np.random.normal(50, 20, n_A_rev)

# Variant B: mean $55, std $20 (10% lift)
revenue_B = np.random.normal(55, 20, n_B_rev)

print(f"Variant A mean revenue: ${revenue_A.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Variant B mean revenue: ${revenue_B.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Observed lift: ${(revenue_B.mean() - revenue_A.mean()):.2f}")


Variant A mean revenue: $50.14
Variant B mean revenue: $55.64
Observed lift: $5.50

with pm.Model() as revenue_model:
    # Priors for means
    mu_A = pm.Normal("mu_A", mu=50, sigma=20)
    mu_B = pm.Normal("mu_B", mu=50, sigma=20)
    
    # Prior for standard deviation (half-normal)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=20)
    
    # Absolute lift
    lift_abs = pm.Deterministic("lift_abs", mu_B - mu_A)
    
    # Relative lift
    lift_rel = pm.Deterministic("lift_rel", (mu_B - mu_A) / mu_A)
    
    # Likelihood
    pm.Normal("revenue_A", mu=mu_A, sigma=sigma, observed=revenue_A)
    pm.Normal("revenue_B", mu=mu_B, sigma=sigma, observed=revenue_B)
    
    trace_revenue = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Decision Rules
Bayesian A/B testing enables flexible decision rules based on posterior probabilities:


Code
# Decision rule: adopt B if P(B > A) > 0.95 and expected lift > 2%
prob_threshold = 0.95
lift_threshold = 0.02

expected_lift = trace_conversion.posterior["lift"].mean()
prob_better = (trace_conversion.posterior["rate_B"] > trace_conversion.posterior["rate_A"]).mean()

print(f"Expected lift: {expected_lift:.3f}")
print(f"P(B > A): {prob_better:.3f}")

if prob_better > prob_threshold and expected_lift > lift_threshold:
    print("Decision: ADOPT variant B")
else:
    print("Decision: CONTINUE testing or adopt A")

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Sequential Monitoring
One advantage of Bayesian methods is the ability to monitor results sequentially without inflating Type I error. Here’s a simple example:


Code
# Simulate sequential data (cumulative over time)
np.random.seed(42)
n_periods = 10
n_per_period = 100

sequential_results = []

for period in range(1, n_periods + 1):
    # Cumulative data up to this period
    n_cum = period * n_per_period
    conv_A_cum = np.random.binomial(n_cum, 0.10)
    conv_B_cum = np.random.binomial(n_cum, 0.105)
    
    # Fit model (simplified for speed)
    with pm.Model() as seq_model:
        rate_A = pm.Beta("rate_A", alpha=1, beta=1)
        rate_B = pm.Beta("rate_B", alpha=1, beta=1)
        lift = pm.Deterministic("lift", (rate_B - rate_A) / rate_A)
        pm.Binomial("conv_A", n=n_cum, p=rate_A, observed=conv_A_cum)
        pm.Binomial("conv_B", n=n_cum, p=rate_B, observed=conv_B_cum)
        trace_seq = pm.sample(1000, tune=500, chains=2, target_accept=0.95)
    
    prob_better = (trace_seq.posterior["rate_B"] > trace_seq.posterior["rate_A"]).mean()
    expected_lift = trace_seq.posterior["lift"].mean()
    
    sequential_results.append({
        "period": period,
        "n": n_cum,
        "prob_better": prob_better,
        "expected_lift": expected_lift
    })

seq_df = pd.DataFrame(sequential_results)
print(seq_df)

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Peeking with Frequentist Methods
With frequentist methods, checking results repeatedly inflates Type I error. Bayesian methods avoid this, but you should still pre-specify decision rules.
Solution: Pre-specify stopping rules (e.g., “stop when P(B > A) > 0.95 and n > 1000”).


2. Overly Informative Priors
Priors that are too strong can dominate the data, especially with large samples.
Solution: Use weakly informative priors by default, only use informative priors when you have strong justification.


3. Ignoring Model Diagnostics
Poor MCMC convergence can produce misleading results.
Solution: Always check R-hat statistics, trace plots, and effective sample size.


4. Misinterpreting Credible Intervals
Credible intervals are probability statements about parameters, not about future data.
Solution: Be precise in communication: “There’s a 95% probability the true conversion rate is in this interval.”

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
section: When to Use Bayesian A/B Testing
text:
When to Use Bayesian A/B Testing
Bayesian A/B testing is the right choice when:

Sample sizes are limited: Small experiments, pilot tests
Prior knowledge exists: Historical data, expert judgment
Sequential monitoring: You want to check results continuously
Risk quantification: You need probability statements for decision-making
Complex metrics: Multi-variate testing, hierarchical experiments

Consider frequentist methods when:

Large samples with no prior knowledge
Regulatory requirements specify frequentist methods
Simplicity and speed are paramount
Stakeholders are unfamiliar with Bayesian methods

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Summary
Bayesian A/B testing provides a natural framework for analyzing randomized experiments with explicit uncertainty quantification and the ability to incorporate prior knowledge.
Key takeaways:

Bayesian methods give intuitive probability statements (P(B > A) = 0.95)
Use Beta-Binomial for conversion rates, Normal-Gamma for continuous outcomes
Informative priors can improve small-sample performance
Sequential monitoring is possible without inflating Type I error
Always check MCMC diagnostics (R-hat, trace plots)
Pre-specify decision rules to avoid “peeking” bias
Communicate results as probability statements, not just point estimates

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Overview

Why Bayesian DiD?
Bayesian DiD extends the frequentist DiD framework with several advantages:

Full uncertainty propagation: Uncertainty from trend estimation, variance components, and treatment effects all flow through to the final estimate
Prior knowledge incorporation: Historical results or domain expertise about effect sizes can be encoded as priors
Flexible time-series modeling: Bayesian state-space models can handle complex temporal dynamics
Hierarchical structure: Multiple treated units can share information through hierarchical priors
Small cluster performance: With few treated groups, Bayesian methods can stabilize estimates using informative priors



The Bayesian DiD Model
The basic Bayesian DiD model extends the frequentist two-way fixed effects specification:
\[
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau \, D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
\]
In a Bayesian framework, we place priors on:

\(\alpha_i\): Unit fixed effects (can be hierarchical if many units)
\(\lambda_t\): Time fixed effects (can be modeled as random walks)
\(\tau\): Treatment effect (the parameter of interest)
\(\sigma^2\): Error variance

This gives us a full posterior distribution for \(\tau\), not just a point estimate and standard error.


Business Setting
Bayesian DiD is ideal when:

Few treated clusters: Limited number of treated markets/regions
Prior knowledge exists: Historical rollout results, effect size expectations
Complex temporal dynamics: Seasonality, trends, or autocorrelation
Hierarchical structure: Multiple treated units that might share effects
Full uncertainty needed: Decision-makers need probability statements

Common business applications:

Geographic rollout evaluation
Policy impact assessment
Marketing campaign effectiveness across regions
Store format testing

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
section: Example 1: Basic Bayesian DiD with PyMC
text:
Example 1: Basic Bayesian DiD with PyMC
Let’s implement a basic Bayesian DiD model using PyMC:


Code
# Simulate panel data
np.random.seed(42)

n_units = 20
n_time = 50
treat_time = 30
true_effect = 5.0

# Unit fixed effects
alpha = np.random.normal(100, 10, n_units)

# Time fixed effects (trend + seasonality)
time = np.arange(n_time)
lambda_t = 0.1 * time + 5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * time / 12)

# Treatment assignment (first 10 units treated)
treated = np.arange(n_units) < 10

# Generate data
data = []
for i in range(n_units):
    for t in range(n_time):
        D = 1 if (treated[i] and t >= treat_time) else 0
        y = alpha[i] + lambda_t[t] + true_effect * D + np.random.normal(0, 3)
        data.append({"unit": i, "time": t, "treated": int(treated[i]), "D": D, "y": y})

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df.head())


Now let’s fit a Bayesian DiD model:


Code
# Prepare data for PyMC
unit_idx = df["unit"].values
time_idx = df["time"].values
D = df["D"].values
y = df["y"].values

n_units_obs = len(df["unit"].unique())
n_time_obs = len(df["time"].unique())

with pm.Model() as did_model:
    # Priors for unit fixed effects (hierarchical)
    mu_alpha = pm.Normal("mu_alpha", mu=100, sigma=20)
    sigma_alpha = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_alpha", sigma=10)
    alpha_i = pm.Normal("alpha_i", mu=mu_alpha, sigma=sigma_alpha, shape=n_units_obs)
    
    # Priors for time fixed effects (hierarchical)
    mu_lambda = pm.Normal("mu_lambda", mu=0, sigma=10)
    sigma_lambda = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_lambda", sigma=5)
    lambda_t = pm.Normal("lambda_t", mu=mu_lambda, sigma=sigma_lambda, shape=n_time_obs)
    
    # Prior for treatment effect
    tau = pm.Normal("tau", mu=0, sigma=10)
    
    # Prior for error variance
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    # Linear predictor
    mu = alpha_i[unit_idx] + lambda_t[time_idx] + tau * D
    
    # Likelihood
    pm.Normal("y", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y)
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace_did = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)


Let’s examine the posterior of the treatment effect:


Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_did, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95)




Code
# Plot posterior
az.plot_posterior(trace_did, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95, ref_val=true_effect)
plt.title(f"Posterior of Treatment Effect (True = {true_effect})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The posterior should be centered near the true effect of 5.0, with uncertainty reflecting the data.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 2: Bayesian DiD with CausalPy
CausalPy provides a convenient interface for Bayesian causal inference. Let’s use it for DiD analysis:


Code
# Prepare data for CausalPy
df_causalpy = df.copy()
df_causalpy["treatment_time"] = np.where(df_causalpy["time"] >= treat_time, 1, 0)
df_causalpy["group"] = np.where(df_causalpy["treated"] == 1, "treated", "control")

# Use CausalPy for Bayesian DiD
# Note: CausalPy uses PyMC under the hood
result = cp.pymc_experiments.PrePostFit(
    df=df_causalpy,
    treatment="treated",
    outcome="y",
    time="time",
    formula="y ~ 1 + time + treated",
    model=cp.pymc_models.LinearRegression,
    time_variable_name="time",
)

print(result.summary())

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 3: Incorporating Prior Knowledge
Let’s use an informative prior for the treatment effect based on historical knowledge:


Code
# Suppose historical data suggests effects are around 4 with uncertainty ±2
with pm.Model() as did_model_informative:
    # Informative prior for treatment effect
    tau = pm.Normal("tau", mu=4, sigma=2)
    
    # Other priors
    mu_alpha = pm.Normal("mu_alpha", mu=100, sigma=20)
    sigma_alpha = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_alpha", sigma=10)
    alpha_i = pm.Normal("alpha_i", mu=mu_alpha, sigma=sigma_alpha, shape=n_units_obs)
    
    mu_lambda = pm.Normal("mu_lambda", mu=0, sigma=10)
    sigma_lambda = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_lambda", sigma=5)
    lambda_t = pm.Normal("lambda_t", mu=mu_lambda, sigma=sigma_lambda, shape=n_time_obs)
    
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    mu = alpha_i[unit_idx] + lambda_t[time_idx] + tau * D
    pm.Normal("y", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y)
    
    trace_did_inf = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)

# Compare results
print("Weakly informative prior:")
print(az.summary(trace_did, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95))

print("\nInformative prior:")
print(az.summary(trace_did_inf, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95))


With an informative prior, the posterior is “shrunk” toward the prior. This is useful with small samples or strong prior knowledge.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 4: Dynamic Effects (Event Study)
We can extend the model to estimate dynamic effects over time:


Code
# Create leads and lags relative to treatment
df["rel_time"] = np.where(df["treated"] == 1, df["time"] - treat_time, np.nan)

# Bin leads/lags
df["rel_time_binned"] = df["rel_time"].clip(-10, 10)

# Create treatment x time interaction dummies
time_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["rel_time_binned"], prefix="k", dtype=float)
time_dummies = time_dummies.drop(columns=["k_nan"])
df = pd.concat([df, time_dummies], axis=1).fillna(0)

# Select interaction columns
k_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("k_")]

# Event study model
with pm.Model() as event_study_model:
    # Dynamic treatment effects
    tau_k = pm.Normal("tau_k", mu=0, sigma=5, shape=len(k_cols))
    
    # Fixed effects
    mu_alpha = pm.Normal("mu_alpha", mu=100, sigma=20)
    sigma_alpha = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_alpha", sigma=10)
    alpha_i = pm.Normal("alpha_i", mu=mu_alpha, sigma=sigma_alpha, shape=n_units_obs)
    
    mu_lambda = pm.Normal("mu_lambda", mu=0, sigma=10)
    sigma_lambda = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_lambda", sigma=5)
    lambda_t = pm.Normal("lambda_t", mu=mu_lambda, sigma=sigma_lambda, shape=n_time_obs)
    
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    # Linear predictor with dynamic effects
    dynamic_effect = pm.math.dot(df[k_cols].values, tau_k)
    mu = alpha_i[unit_idx] + lambda_t[time_idx] + dynamic_effect
    
    pm.Normal("y", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y)
    
    trace_event = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Extract and plot dynamic effects
tau_post = trace_event.posterior["tau_k"].mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values
time_points = np.arange(-10, 11)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(time_points, tau_post, marker="o")
plt.axvline(0, color="red", ls="--", label="Treatment")
plt.axhline(0, color="gray", ls="-")
plt.xlabel("Time relative to treatment")
plt.ylabel("Treatment effect")
plt.title("Dynamic Treatment Effects (Event Study)")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The event study plot shows:

Pre-treatment: Effects should be near zero (no pre-trend)
Post-treatment: The trajectory of the effect over time

This is a powerful diagnostic for parallel trends and effect dynamics.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Poor Parallel Trends
Even in Bayesian DiD, the parallel trends assumption is critical. Priors cannot fix violated assumptions.
Solution: Always check pre-trends visually and with event-study models.


2. Overconfident Priors
Priors that are too narrow can overwhelm the data, especially with large samples.
Solution: Use weakly informative priors by default; only use informative priors with strong justification.


3. Computational Issues
Hierarchical models with many units can be slow to fit.
Solution: Use non-centered parameterizations, increase target_accept, or use variational inference for exploration.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Overview

Why Bayesian ITS?
Bayesian ITS extends the frequentist ITS framework with several advantages:

Flexible time-series modeling: Bayesian state-space models can handle complex temporal patterns, seasonality, and autocorrelation
Uncertainty propagation: Uncertainty from trend estimation, variance components, and intervention effects all flow through to the final estimate
Prior knowledge incorporation: Historical patterns or domain expertise can be encoded as priors
Probabilistic forecasting: Generate full predictive distributions for counterfactual scenarios
Handles missing data: Bayesian methods naturally handle missing observations



The Bayesian ITS Model
The basic Bayesian ITS model extends the frequentist segmented regression:
\[
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 \, \text{post}_t + \beta_3 \,(t - t^*)\,\text{post}_t + \text{seasonality}_t + \varepsilon_t
\]
In a Bayesian framework, we place priors on:

\(\beta_0\): Intercept (baseline level)
\(\beta_1\): Pre-intervention trend
\(\beta_2\): Level change at intervention
\(\beta_3\): Trend change after intervention
Seasonality parameters
\(\sigma^2\): Error variance

This gives us full posterior distributions for the level and trend changes, not just point estimates.


Business Setting
Bayesian ITS is ideal when:

Company-wide interventions: No control group, just pre/post time series
Complex temporal patterns: Seasonality, trends, autocorrelation
Prior knowledge exists: Historical patterns, expected effect sizes
Probabilistic forecasting needed: Counterfactual predictions with uncertainty
Missing data: Time series with gaps

Common business applications:

Pricing changes (company-wide)
Policy implementations
Website redesigns
Process changes
Regulatory changes

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 1: Basic Bayesian ITS
Let’s implement a basic Bayesian ITS model with a level and trend change:


Code
# Simulate time series data
np.random.seed(42)

n_time = 100
intervention_time = 60

time = np.arange(n_time)
post = (time >= intervention_time).astype(int)
time_post = np.maximum(0, time - intervention_time)

# True parameters
beta0 = 100  # intercept
beta1 = 0.5  # pre-intervention trend
beta2 = -10  # level change
beta3 = -0.2  # trend change

# Generate data with seasonality
seasonality = 5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * time / 12)
y = (beta0 + beta1 * time + beta2 * post + beta3 * time_post
     + seasonality + np.random.normal(0, 3, n_time))

df = pd.DataFrame({"time": time, "post": post, "time_post": time_post, "y": y})

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(df["time"], df["y"], marker="o", markersize=3)
plt.axvline(intervention_time, color="red", ls="--", label="Intervention")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Outcome")
plt.title("Interrupted Time Series")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


Now let’s fit a Bayesian ITS model:


Code
with pm.Model() as its_model:
    # Priors for ITS parameters
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=100, sigma=20)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta2 = pm.Normal("beta2", mu=0, sigma=20)
    beta3 = pm.Normal("beta3", mu=0, sigma=2)
    
    # Prior for seasonality amplitude
    season_amp = pm.HalfNormal("season_amp", sigma=10)
    
    # Prior for error variance
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    # Seasonality
    seasonality = season_amp * pm.math.sin(2 * np.pi * df["time"] / 12)
    
    # Linear predictor
    mu = (beta0 + beta1 * df["time"] + beta2 * df["post"] 
          + beta3 * df["time_post"] + seasonality)
    
    # Likelihood
    pm.Normal("y", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=df["y"])
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace_its = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)


Let’s examine the posterior of the intervention effects:


Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_its, var_names=["beta2", "beta3"], hdi_prob=0.95)




Code
# Plot posteriors
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

az.plot_posterior(trace_its, var_names=["beta2"], ax=axes[0], ref_val=beta2)
axes[0].set_title("Level Change (True = -10)")

az.plot_posterior(trace_its, var_names=["beta3"], ax=axes[1], ref_val=beta3)
axes[1].set_title("Trend Change (True = -0.2)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The posteriors should be centered near the true values, with uncertainty reflecting the data.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 2: Counterfactual Prediction
One advantage of Bayesian methods is the ability to generate probabilistic counterfactual predictions:


Code
# Generate counterfactual predictions (no intervention)
with its_model:
    # Create new data with post = 0 (no intervention)
    df_cf = df.copy()
    df_cf["post"] = 0
    df_cf["time_post"] = 0
    
    seasonality_cf = trace_its.posterior["season_amp"].mean() * np.sin(2 * np.pi * df_cf["time"] / 12)
    mu_cf = (trace_its.posterior["beta0"].mean() 
              + trace_its.posterior["beta1"].mean() * df_cf["time"]
              + seasonality_cf)
    
# Plot with counterfactual
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(df["time"], df["y"], marker="o", markersize=3, label="Observed")
plt.plot(df["time"], mu_cf, "--", label="Counterfactual (no intervention)")
plt.axvline(intervention_time, color="red", ls="--", label="Intervention")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Outcome")
plt.title("Observed vs. Counterfactual")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
section: Example 3: Bayesian ITS with Control Series
text:
Example 3: Bayesian ITS with Control Series
Adding a control series strengthens the design. This is essentially Bayesian DiD with rich time structure:


Code
# Simulate treated and control series
np.random.seed(42)

n_time = 100
intervention_time = 60
time = np.arange(n_time)
post = (time >= intervention_time).astype(int)

# Control series (no intervention)
y_control = (100 + 0.5 * time + 5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * time / 12) 
             + np.random.normal(0, 3, n_time))

# Treated series (with intervention)
y_treated = (100 + 0.5 * time - 10 * post - 0.2 * (time - intervention_time) * post
              + 5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * time / 12) + np.random.normal(0, 3, n_time))

df_control = pd.DataFrame({"time": time, "post": post, "y": y_control, "group": "control"})
df_treated = pd.DataFrame({"time": time, "post": post, "y": y_treated, "group": "treated"})
df_both = pd.concat([df_control, df_treated])

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
plt.plot(df_control["time"], df_control["y"], label="Control")
plt.plot(df_treated["time"], df_treated["y"], label="Treated")
plt.axvline(intervention_time, color="red", ls="--", label="Intervention")
plt.xlabel("Time")
plt.ylabel("Outcome")
plt.title("ITS with Control Series")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Code
# Bayesian ITS with control
group_treated = (df_both["group"] == "treated").astype(int)

with pm.Model() as its_control_model:
    # Priors
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=100, sigma=20)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta2 = pm.Normal("beta2", mu=0, sigma=20)  # group difference
    beta3 = pm.Normal("beta3", mu=0, sigma=20)  # level change
    beta4 = pm.Normal("beta4", mu=0, sigma=2)   # trend change
    
    season_amp = pm.HalfNormal("season_amp", sigma=10)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    seasonality = season_amp * pm.math.sin(2 * np.pi * df_both["time"] / 12)
    
    # Linear predictor with control
    mu = (beta0 + beta1 * df_both["time"] + beta2 * group_treated
          + beta3 * df_both["post"] * group_treated
          + beta4 * (df_both["time"] - intervention_time) * df_both["post"] * group_treated
          + seasonality)
    
    pm.Normal("y", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=df_both["y"])
    
    trace_its_control = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Posterior summary for intervention effects
az.summary(trace_its_control, var_names=["beta3", "beta4"], hdi_prob=0.95)

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 4: State-Space Model
For more complex time series, we can use Bayesian state-space models:


Code
# Simple state-space model with time-varying trend
with pm.Model() as ssm_model:
    # Time-varying trend (random walk)
    sigma_trend = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_trend", sigma=1)
    trend_init = pm.Normal("trend_init", mu=0.5, sigma=1)
    trend = pm.GaussianRandomWalk("trend", mu=0, sigma=sigma_trend, 
                                  shape=n_time, init_dist=pm.Normal.dist(mu=trend_init, sigma=1))
    
    # Level
    level_init = pm.Normal("level_init", mu=100, sigma=20)
    sigma_level = pm.HalfNormal("sigma_level", sigma=5)
    level = pm.GaussianRandomWalk("level", mu=trend, sigma=sigma_level,
                                 shape=n_time, init_dist=pm.Normal.dist(mu=level_init, sigma=20))
    
    # Intervention effect
    tau = pm.Normal("tau", mu=0, sigma=20)
    
    # Error variance
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    # Linear predictor
    mu = level + tau * post
    
    pm.Normal("y", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y)
    
    trace_ssm = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_ssm, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95)

Model Diagnostics
Always check MCMC diagnostics:


Code

plt.tight_layout()

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Co-Interventions
If other events happen at the same time as the intervention, ITS cannot distinguish their effects.
Solution: Maintain an intervention calendar and use control series when possible.


2. Short Pre-Period
A short pre-period makes it hard to estimate the baseline trend and seasonality.
Solution: Use at least 2-3 full seasonal cycles in the pre-period.


3. Autocorrelation
Autocorrelated errors can bias estimates if not modeled.
Solution: Use state-space models or include autoregressive terms.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Overview

Why Bayesian IV?
Bayesian IV extends the frequentist IV framework with several advantages:

Handles weak instruments better: Bayesian methods can incorporate prior knowledge about instrument strength, improving performance with weak instruments
Full uncertainty propagation: Uncertainty from first-stage estimation flows through to the final effect estimate
Natural handling of weak identification: Posterior distributions naturally reflect weak identification through wide uncertainty
Flexible model structures: Can incorporate hierarchical structures, multiple instruments, and non-linear relationships
Prior knowledge incorporation: Domain expertise about effect sizes can be encoded as priors



The Bayesian IV Model
The Bayesian IV model extends the frequentist 2SLS:
First stage: Treatment model \[
D = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 Z + \varepsilon_D
\]
Second stage: Outcome model \[
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D + \varepsilon_Y
\]
In a Bayesian framework, we place priors on all parameters and sample from the joint posterior. The treatment effect \(\beta_1\) is the parameter of interest (LATE).


Business Setting
Bayesian IV is ideal when:

Weak instruments: First-stage F-statistic is borderline
Prior knowledge exists: Expected effect sizes, instrument strength
Complex IV structures: Multiple instruments, hierarchical designs
Full uncertainty needed: Probability statements for decision-making
Small samples: Limited data for reliable frequentist IV

Common business applications:

Encouragement designs (randomized emails, offers)
Supply shocks as instruments
Geographic variation as instruments
Policy changes as instruments

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 1: Basic Bayesian IV
Let’s implement a basic Bayesian IV model:


Code
# Simulate IV data
np.random.seed(42)

n = 1000

# Unobserved confounder
U = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)

# Instrument (randomized)
Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, n)

# Treatment (depends on U and Z)
logit_D = -0.5 + 0.8 * U + 1.0 * Z
p_D = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit_D))
D = np.random.binomial(1, p_D)

# True LATE
true_late = 5.0

# Outcome (depends on U and D)
Y = 50 + true_late * D + 10 * U + np.random.normal(0, 3, n)

df = pd.DataFrame({"Z": Z, "D": D, "Y": Y})
print(df.head())


Now let’s fit a Bayesian IV model:


Code
with pm.Model() as iv_model:
    # First stage: treatment model
    alpha0 = pm.Normal("alpha0", mu=0, sigma=10)
    alpha1 = pm.Normal("alpha1", mu=0, sigma=5)  # instrument strength
    
    # Linear predictor for treatment
    eta_D = alpha0 + alpha1 * df["Z"]
    p_D = pm.math.sigmoid(eta_D)
    
    # Treatment likelihood
    pm.Bernoulli("D", p=p_D, observed=df["D"])
    
    # Second stage: outcome model
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=50, sigma=20)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=10)  # treatment effect (LATE)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=10)
    
    # Outcome likelihood
    pm.Normal("Y", mu=beta0 + beta1 * df["D"], sigma=sigma, observed=df["Y"])
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace_iv = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)


Let’s examine the posterior of the treatment effect:


Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_iv, var_names=["beta1", "alpha1"], hdi_prob=0.95)




Code
# Plot posterior
az.plot_posterior(trace_iv, var_names=["beta1"], hdi_prob=0.95, ref_val=true_late)
plt.title(f"Posterior of LATE (True = {true_late})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 2: Naive OLS for Comparison
Let’s compare with naive OLS (which should be biased due to unobserved confounding):


Code
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# Naive OLS (biased)
ols_naive = smf.ols("Y ~ D", data=df).fit()
print("Naive OLS (biased):")
print(f"Treatment effect: {ols_naive.params['D']:.3f}")
print(f"True LATE: {true_late}")

# Bayesian IV posterior mean
iv_estimate = trace_iv.posterior["beta1"].mean()
print(f"\nBayesian IV estimate: {iv_estimate:.3f}")


The naive OLS is biased upward because high-U units both adopt more and have higher outcomes. The Bayesian IV recovers the true LATE.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 3: Weak Instrument
Let’s simulate a weak instrument and see how Bayesian IV handles it:


Code
# Simulate weak instrument
np.random.seed(42)

n = 1000
U = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)

# Weak instrument (small effect on treatment)
Z = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, n)

logit_D = -0.5 + 0.8 * U + 0.2 * Z  # weak instrument
p_D = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit_D))
D = np.random.binomial(1, p_D)

true_late = 5.0
Y = 50 + true_late * D + 10 * U + np.random.normal(0, 3, n)

df_weak = pd.DataFrame({"Z": Z, "D": D, "Y": Y})

# Check first-stage strength
first_stage = smf.ols("D ~ Z", data=df_weak).fit()
f_stat = first_stage.fvalue
print(f"First-stage F-statistic: {f_stat:.2f}")
print("(F < 10 indicates weak instrument)")




Code
# Bayesian IV with weak instrument
with pm.Model() as iv_weak_model:
    alpha0 = pm.Normal("alpha0", mu=0, sigma=10)
    alpha1 = pm.Normal("alpha1", mu=0, sigma=5)
    
    eta_D = alpha0 + alpha1 * df_weak["Z"]
    p_D = pm.math.sigmoid(eta_D)
    pm.Bernoulli("D", p=p_D, observed=df_weak["D"])
    
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=50, sigma=20)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=10)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=10)
    
    pm.Normal("Y", mu=beta0 + beta1 * df_weak["D"], sigma=sigma, observed=df_weak["Y"])
    
    trace_iv_weak = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_iv_weak, var_names=["beta1"], hdi_prob=0.95)


With a weak instrument, the posterior should be wide (high uncertainty), reflecting the weak identification.

section: Example 4: Informative Prior for Instrument Strength
text:
Example 4: Informative Prior for Instrument Strength
One advantage of Bayesian methods is incorporating prior knowledge about instrument strength:


Code
# Bayesian IV with informative prior on instrument strength
with pm.Model() as iv_informative_model:
    # Informative prior: we believe the instrument is moderately strong
    alpha0 = pm.Normal("alpha0", mu=0, sigma=10)
    alpha1 = pm.Normal("alpha1", mu=0.5, sigma=0.5)  # informative prior
    
    eta_D = alpha0 + alpha1 * df_weak["Z"]
    p_D = pm.math.sigmoid(eta_D)
    pm.Bernoulli("D", p=p_D, observed=df_weak["D"])
    
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=50, sigma=20)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=10)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=10)
    
    pm.Normal("Y", mu=beta0 + beta1 * df_weak["D"], sigma=sigma, observed=df_weak["Y"])
    
    trace_iv_inf = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)

# Compare
print("Weakly informative prior:")
print(az.summary(trace_iv_weak, var_names=["beta1"], hdi_prob=0.95))

print("\nInformative prior on instrument strength:")
print(az.summary(trace_iv_inf, var_names=["beta1"], hdi_prob=0.95))

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Weak Instruments
Weak instruments produce wide posteriors and unreliable estimates.
Solution: Check first-stage strength, use informative priors if justified, or find stronger instruments.


2. Exclusion Violations
If the instrument affects the outcome through channels other than treatment, IV is biased.
Solution: Design instruments where the only plausible channel is treatment. Be honest about uncertainty.


3. Overconfident Priors
Priors that are too narrow can overwhelm the data.
Solution: Use weakly informative priors by default; only use informative priors with strong justification.

When to Use Bayesian IV
Bayesian IV is the right choice when:

Weak instruments: First-stage F-statistic is borderline
Prior knowledge exists: Expected effect sizes, instrument strength
Complex IV structures: Multiple instruments, hierarchical designs
Full uncertainty needed: Probability statements for decision-making
Small samples: Limited data for reliable frequentist IV

Consider frequentist IV when:

Strong instruments with large samples
No prior knowledge
Computation speed is critical
Stakeholders require frequentist methods
