title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Overview

Why Bayesian Propensity Methods?
Bayesian propensity methods extend the frequentist propensity score framework with several advantages:

Uncertainty propagation: Uncertainty from propensity score estimation flows through to the final effect estimate (unlike two-stage frequentist methods)
Prior knowledge incorporation: Domain expertise about treatment assignment can be encoded as priors
Flexible modeling: Bayesian logistic regression can handle complex relationships and regularization naturally
Small sample performance: With informative priors, reliable estimates can be obtained with limited data
Doubly robust estimation: Bayesian implementations of doubly robust estimators that are consistent if either the propensity or outcome model is correct



The Bayesian Propensity Framework
The Bayesian propensity approach has two stages:
Stage 1: Propensity model \[
P(D=1 \mid X) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p)
\]
Stage 2: Outcome model (using propensity scores)
Several approaches: - Bayesian IPW: Inverse probability weighting with Bayesian propensity scores - Bayesian matching: Matching on Bayesian propensity scores - Bayesian doubly robust: Combines outcome regression with propensity weighting


Business Setting
Bayesian propensity methods are ideal when:

Self-selected treatment: Customers/stores choose treatment based on observables
Prior knowledge exists: Expected propensity patterns, effect sizes
Small samples: Limited data for reliable frequentist propensity methods
Full uncertainty needed: Propagating uncertainty from propensity to effect
Complex propensity models: Non-linear relationships, many covariates

Common business applications:

Loyalty program evaluation
Feature adoption analysis
Marketing campaign targeting
Training program assessment

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 1: Bayesian Propensity Score Estimation
Let’s start with Bayesian propensity score estimation:


Code
# Simulate propensity data
np.random.seed(42)

n = 1000

# Covariates
X1 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)  # e.g., tenure
X2 = np.random.normal(0, 1, n)  # e.g., spend
X3 = np.random.binomial(1, 0.5, n)  # e.g., urban

# True propensity model
logit_p = -0.5 + 0.5 * X1 + 0.3 * X2 + 0.4 * X3
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit_p))
D = np.random.binomial(1, p)

# True ATT
true_att = 5.0

# Outcome
Y = 50 + 0.5 * X1 + 0.3 * X2 + 2 * X3 + true_att * D + np.random.normal(0, 3, n)

df = pd.DataFrame({"X1": X1, "X2": X2, "X3": X3, "D": D, "Y": Y})
print(df.head())


Now let’s estimate propensity scores using Bayesian logistic regression:


Code
# Prepare data
X_cov = df[["X1", "X2", "X3"]].values
D_obs = df["D"].values

with pm.Model() as propensity_model:
    # Priors for logistic regression coefficients
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta2 = pm.Normal("beta2", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta3 = pm.Normal("beta3", mu=0, sigma=2)
    
    # Linear predictor
    eta = beta0 + beta1 * X_cov[:, 0] + beta2 * X_cov[:, 1] + beta3 * X_cov[:, 2]
    
    # Propensity score
    p_hat = pm.math.sigmoid(eta)
    
    # Likelihood
    pm.Bernoulli("D", p=p_hat, observed=D_obs)
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace_prop = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_prop, var_names=["beta0", "beta1", "beta2", "beta3"], hdi_prob=0.95)

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 2: Bayesian IPW (Inverse Probability Weighting)
Now let’s use the Bayesian propensity scores for IPW estimation:


Code
# Extract posterior propensity scores
p_posterior = trace_prop.posterior["p_hat"].mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values

# Bayesian IPW using posterior mean propensity scores
# (Note: This doesn't fully propagate uncertainty; see Example 3 for full propagation)
weights = np.where(D_obs == 1, 1.0, p_posterior / (1 - p_posterior))

# Weighted mean difference
y_treated = df.loc[df["D"] == 1, "Y"].mean()
y_control_weighted = np.average(df.loc[df["D"] == 0, "Y"], weights=weights[df["D"] == 0])

att_ipw = y_treated - y_control_weighted
print(f"IPW ATT estimate: {att_ipw:.3f}")
print(f"True ATT: {true_att}")

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
section: Example 3: Full Bayesian IPW with Uncertainty Propagation
text:
Example 3: Full Bayesian IPW with Uncertainty Propagation
A fully Bayesian approach propagates uncertainty from propensity estimation to the effect estimate:


Code
with pm.Model() as full_ipw_model:
    # Propensity model (same as before)
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta2 = pm.Normal("beta2", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta3 = pm.Normal("beta3", mu=0, sigma=2)
    
    eta = beta0 + beta1 * X_cov[:, 0] + beta2 * X_cov[:, 1] + beta3 * X_cov[:, 2]
    p_hat = pm.math.sigmoid(eta)
    pm.Bernoulli("D", p=p_hat, observed=D_obs)
    
    # Outcome model for treated
    mu0 = pm.Normal("mu0", mu=50, sigma=20)
    alpha1 = pm.Normal("alpha1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    alpha2 = pm.Normal("alpha2", mu=0, sigma=2)
    alpha3 = pm.Normal("alpha3", mu=0, sigma=2)
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    # Treatment effect
    tau = pm.Normal("tau", mu=0, sigma=10)
    
    # Outcome likelihood
    mu_outcome = (mu0 + alpha1 * X_cov[:, 0] + alpha2 * X_cov[:, 1] + alpha3 * X_cov[:, 2]
                  + tau * D_obs)
    pm.Normal("Y", mu=mu_outcome, sigma=sigma, observed=df["Y"].values)
    
    # Sample from posterior
    trace_full_ipw = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Posterior summary for treatment effect
az.summary(trace_full_ipw, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95)




Code
# Plot posterior
az.plot_posterior(trace_full_ipw, var_names=["tau"], hdi_prob=0.95, ref_val=true_att)
plt.title(f"Posterior of ATT (True = {true_att})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 4: Bayesian Doubly Robust Estimation
Doubly robust estimators combine outcome regression with propensity weighting and are consistent if either model is correct:


Code
with pm.Model() as dr_model:
    # Propensity model
    beta0 = pm.Normal("beta0", mu=0, sigma=5)
    beta1 = pm.Normal("beta1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta2 = pm.Normal("beta2", mu=0, sigma=2)
    beta3 = pm.Normal("beta3", mu=0, sigma=2)
    
    eta = beta0 + beta1 * X_cov[:, 0] + beta2 * X_cov[:, 1] + beta3 * X_cov[:, 2]
    p_hat = pm.math.sigmoid(eta)
    pm.Bernoulli("D", p=p_hat, observed=D_obs)
    
    # Outcome model (separate for treated and control)
    # Control outcome model
    mu0_0 = pm.Normal("mu0_0", mu=50, sigma=20)
    gamma1_0 = pm.Normal("gamma1_0", mu=0, sigma=2)
    gamma2_0 = pm.Normal("gamma2_0", mu=0, sigma=2)
    gamma3_0 = pm.Normal("gamma3_0", mu=0, sigma=2)
    
    # Treated outcome model
    mu0_1 = pm.Normal("mu0_1", mu=50, sigma=20)
    gamma1_1 = pm.Normal("gamma1_1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    gamma2_1 = pm.Normal("gamma2_1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    gamma3_1 = pm.Normal("gamma3_1", mu=0, sigma=2)
    
    sigma = pm.HalfNormal("sigma", sigma=5)
    
    # Predicted outcomes
    mu0_hat = (mu0_0 + gamma1_0 * X_cov[:, 0] + gamma2_0 * X_cov[:, 1] + gamma3_0 * X_cov[:, 2])
    mu1_hat = (mu0_1 + gamma1_1 * X_cov[:, 0] + gamma2_1 * X_cov[:, 1] + gamma3_1 * X_cov[:, 2])
    
    # Outcome likelihood
    mu_outcome = mu0_hat * (1 - D_obs) + mu1_hat * D_obs
    pm.Normal("Y", mu=mu_outcome, sigma=sigma, observed=df["Y"].values)
    
    # Treatment effect (difference in predicted outcomes)
    tau_dr = pm.Deterministic("tau_dr", mu1_hat.mean() - mu0_hat.mean())
    
    trace_dr = pm.sample(2000, tune=1000, chains=4, target_accept=0.95)




Code
# Posterior summary
az.summary(trace_dr, var_names=["tau_dr"], hdi_prob=0.95)

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Example 5: Bayesian Propensity Score Matching
We can also perform matching using Bayesian propensity scores:


Code
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

# Use posterior mean propensity scores
p_mean = trace_prop.posterior["p_hat"].mean(dim=["chain", "draw"]).values

# Separate treated and control
treated_idx = df["D"] == 1
control_idx = df["D"] == 0

# Match each treated unit to nearest control
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1)
nn.fit(p_mean[control_idx].reshape(-1, 1))
distances, indices = nn.kneighbors(p_mean[treated_idx].reshape(-1, 1))

# Caliper matching (drop matches beyond caliper)
caliper = 0.1 * np.std(p_mean)
good_match = distances.flatten() < caliper

# Get matched outcomes
y_treated_matched = df.loc[treated_idx, "Y"].values[good_match]
y_control_matched = df.loc[control_idx, "Y"].values[indices.flatten()[good_match]]

att_match = (y_treated_matched - y_control_matched).mean()
print(f"Matched ATT estimate: {att_match:.3f}")
print(f"True ATT: {true_att}")
print(f"Match rate: {good_match.mean():.3f}")

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Poor Overlap
If propensity distributions don’t overlap, no method can save you.
Solution: Check overlap plots, trim to common support, or redefine the estimand.


2. Unmeasured Confounding
Propensity methods only adjust for measured confounders. Unobserved confounders can still bias estimates.
Solution: Include rich covariates, especially lagged outcomes. Be honest about limitations.


3. Not Propagating Uncertainty
Using point estimates of propensity scores in downstream analysis ignores uncertainty.
Solution: Use fully Bayesian models that propagate uncertainty through all stages.

title: 6.1 Bayesian Causal Inference
text:
How the Designs Fit Together
Pick the design from the assignment mechanism, then use the posterior to make the decision.

Randomized assignment. Use Bayesian A/B testing. The posterior of the lift is the decision object: adopt the variant when the probability it is better clears a pre-specified threshold and the expected lift is large enough.
Panel of treated and control units. Use Bayesian difference-in-differences. The posterior of \(\tau\) is the effect under parallel trends. An event study checks that leads are near zero before treatment.
One interrupted series. Use Bayesian interrupted time series. Report the posterior of the level change and the slope change, and compare the observed series with the counterfactual path that continues the pre-intervention trend.
Unmeasured confounding with an instrument. Use Bayesian instrumental variables. The posterior of the local average treatment effect should widen when the instrument is weak. Compare it with naive ordinary least squares, which stays biased.
Selection on observables. Use Bayesian propensity methods. A fully Bayesian inverse-probability or doubly robust model carries propensity uncertainty into the effect posterior. Check overlap before interpreting the estimate.

In every case, check R-hat and the trace plots before quoting a probability. A prior can tighten a small-sample posterior. It cannot replace randomization, a control series, a valid instrument, or overlap.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text: Python Banner

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text:
Overview

Why a structural equation, rather than a design dummy?
Difference-in-differences, a cutoff, and a single interrupted series each encode the intervention as a column in one regression. A structural model writes a separate assignment for the treatment and for the outcome, and it states which covariates are allowed in each assignment. That exclusion list is the identifying assumption.
The same idea extends one step in time. A protein, a vital sign, or a price can cause another series within the period and through its own lag. BayesianTimeSeriesSCM gives each series a Gaussian posterior and replaces an equation when the intervention is a hard do.


What this tutorial covers

The two-equation system, the role of \(\rho = \mathrm{Corr}(U, V)\), and the OLS bias it produces
How instruments and outcome_only partition the columns
Recovery of a known \(\alpha\) with simulate_structural_scm, and the failure of the regression that uses every column
Potential outcomes \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) from a homogeneous structural effect
A lagged system with a known contemporaneous coefficient, an impulse response, and a hard intervention
Card’s college-proximity design on the CausalPy schoolReturns file
One patient’s hourly lactate and sepsis-risk series from Data/labs_timeseries.csv

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text:
The algorithms

1. The cross-sectional structural model
Index units by \(i\) and suppress the index. The assignments are
\[
\begin{aligned}
T &= a_T + X_T^\top \beta_T + V, \\
Y &= \alpha T + a_Y + X_Y^\top \beta_Y + U,
\end{aligned}
\]
with \(\mathrm{Corr}(U, V) = \rho\). The parameter of interest is \(\alpha\), the structural coefficient on an endogenous treatment. Substituting the treatment equation into the outcome equation shows the OLS problem. The composite disturbance in the outcome still contains \(V\) whenever \(\rho \neq 0\), and \(V\) is inside \(T\). A regression of \(Y\) on \(T\) and the observed covariates therefore converges to \(\alpha\) plus a term that depends on \(\rho\) and on the variance of \(V\).
simulate_structural_scm builds this system with five standardized covariates:



Columns
Role in the simulation
Where they enter




0 and 1
Confounders
Treatment equation and outcome equation


2 and 3
Instruments
Treatment equation only


4
Outcome-only covariate
Outcome equation only



The treatment and outcome disturbances are bivariate normal with correlation rho. The structural coefficient is the argument alpha. Set binary_treatment=True to threshold the latent treatment index at zero.


2. Exclusion and the estimator
BayesianStructuralSCM.fit partitions the columns of \(X\):

instruments enter the treatment equation only
outcome_only enters the outcome equation only
every remaining column is a confounder and enters both

A column cannot be both an instrument and outcome-only. If instruments is omitted, the treatment is taken to be conditionally ignorable given \(X\) and the fit is a ridge-normal outcome regression. identified_by_ records which of the two routes was used.
When instruments are present the point estimator is two-stage least squares.

Regress \(T\) on an intercept, the confounders, and the instruments.
Regress \(Y\) on an intercept, the fitted treatment, the confounders, and the outcome-only columns.

Posterior draws repeat both stages with Dirichlet weights on the rows (a Bayesian bootstrap). The weight vector treats each unit as exchangeable. First-stage uncertainty is inside every draw of \(\alpha\). There is no separate delta-method correction.
Predictions under \(do(T=t)\) use the outcome equation only. The first-stage residual is an estimation device. It is not part of the intervened assignment. With a homogeneous \(\alpha\),
\[
Y(1) - Y(0) = \alpha
\]
for every covariate row, so the average of \(Y(1) - Y(0)\) equals the structural coefficient. potential_outcomes and predict_interval implement that calculation. The interval is a pointwise credible band from the coefficient draws.


3. The lagged structural model
Let \(X_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) be the vector of series at time \(t\). Contemporaneous parents form a DAG, stored again as CausalGraph. For each series \(i\), with lag \(L \ge 1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_{i,t} = a_i
&+ \sum_{j \in \mathrm{pa}(i)} \beta_{ij} X_{j,t}
+ \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} \phi_{i\ell} X_{i, t-\ell}
+ \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} \sum_{j \in \mathrm{pa}(i)} \psi_{ij\ell} X_{j, t-\ell}
+ \varepsilon_{i,t}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each equation has its own ridge-normal posterior. An empty edge list is a system of independent autoregressions: contemporaneous parents are absent, and each series still depends on its own lags.
A hard intervention replaces the equation for the named series over the forecast horizon. counterfactual rolls the posterior-mean coefficients forward under the intervention and under a baseline. The baseline can be the observational forecast (baseline=None) or a second intervention, for example \(do(X=1)\) against \(do(X=0)\). Draws of the coefficients produce a 95% band on the effect path \(X^{\mathrm{cf}}_t - X^{\mathrm{base}}_t\).
An impulse is a different operation. impulse_response adds a one-period shock to the structural residual and then lets every equation return to its fitted form. The shocked series is free to move on the next date. A hard do is not.
Both rollouts are conditional on the last lag observations of the fitted sample, unless history supplies another window.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text:
Setup
The estimators come from PyCausalML (pycausalml.bayesian_causalML). The schooling file is the CausalPy schoolReturns table, from the CausalPy data directory, Apache License 2.0. The hourly series is Data/labs_timeseries.csv.


Code
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

def _repo_root() -> Path:
    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for cand in [here, *here.parents]:
        if (cand / "pyproject.toml").is_file() and (cand / "src" / "pycausalml").is_dir():

    )

root = _repo_root()

    )

try:
    import pycausalml  # noqa: F401
    print("PyCausalML ready.")
except ImportError:

        [sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "-e", f"{root}[plot]"],
    )
    print("PyCausalML installed.")
print("Data directory:", data_dir)




Code

%matplotlib inline
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from pycausalml.bayesian_causalML import (
    BayesianStructuralSCM,
    BayesianTimeSeriesSCM,
    simulate_structural_scm,
)

plt.rcParams["axes.spines.top"] = False
plt.rcParams["axes.spines.right"] = False
CAUSALPY_FILES = {
    "banks": "banks.csv",
    "drinking": "drinking.csv",
    "risk": "AJR2001.csv",
    "schoolReturns": "schoolingReturns.csv",
    "california_prop99": "california_prop99.csv",
}

def load_causalpy(name: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Load a CausalPy example dataset.

    Uses causalpy.load_data when that package is installed. Otherwise reads
    the same CSV from the CausalPy GitHub data directory.
    """
    try:
        import causalpy as cp
        frame = cp.load_data(name)
        print(f"Loaded {name!r} with causalpy.load_data. Shape {frame.shape}.")
        return frame
    except ImportError:
        url = (
            "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pymc-labs/CausalPy/main/causalpy/data/"
            + CAUSALPY_FILES[name]
        )
        frame = pd.read_csv(url)
        print(f"CausalPy is not installed. Loaded {name!r} from")
        print(url)
        print("Install the package with: pip install 'pycausalml[causalpy]'")
        print(f"Shape {frame.shape}.")
        return frame


def show_posterior(draws, estimate, title, truth=None):
    draws = np.asarray(draws, dtype=float).ravel()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    ax.hist(draws, bins=30, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.9, density=True)
    ax.axvline(estimate, color="#8B1E3F", lw=2, label=f"estimate {estimate:.3f}")
    low, high = np.quantile(draws, [0.025, 0.975])
    ax.axvspan(low, high, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.18, label="95% credible interval")
    if truth is not None:
        ax.axvline(truth, color="black", ls="--", lw=1.5, label=f"known effect {truth:.3f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Structural coefficient")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
section: Getting started: a known structural coefficient
text:
Getting started: a known structural coefficient
simulate_structural_scm draws \(n = 2500\) units with \(\alpha = 3\) and \(\rho = 0.6\). The comparison regression puts the treatment and all five covariates in one equation for \(Y\). That regression is inconsistent for \(\alpha\) because the instruments do not belong in the outcome equation and the shared disturbance remains inside \(T\).


Code

sim = simulate_structural_scm(n=2500, alpha=3.0, rho=0.6, random_state=0)
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(sim["y"])), sim["treatment"], sim["X"]])
ols_slope = np.linalg.lstsq(design, sim["y"], rcond=None)[0][1]

structural = BayesianStructuralSCM(n_draws=80, random_state=0)
structural.fit(
    sim["X"],
    sim["treatment"],
    sim["y"],
    instruments=sim["instruments"],
    outcome_only=sim["outcome_only"],
    feature_names=sim["feature_names"],
)
print("Identified by:", structural.identified_by_)
print("OLS slope on treatment, all covariates included:", round(float(ols_slope), 3))
print(pd.Series(structural.summary()).drop(labels=["identified_by"]).astype(float).round(3))
print("identified_by:", structural.summary()["identified_by"])

y0, y1 = structural.potential_outcomes(sim["X"])
print("Mean Y(1) - Y(0):", round(float(np.mean(y1 - y0)), 4))
print("Structural estimate:  ", round(structural.effect_, 4))
show_posterior(structural.draws_, structural.effect_, "Cross-sectional structural model", truth=3.0)

grid = np.linspace(sim["treatment"].min(), sim["treatment"].max(), 40)
x_mean = np.repeat(sim["X"].mean(axis=0, keepdims=True), len(grid), axis=0)
mean, low, high = structural.predict_interval(x_mean, grid)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.fill_between(grid, low, high, color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.2, label="95% band at mean covariates")
ax.plot(grid, mean, color="#8B1E3F", label="E[Y | do(T=t), mean X]")
ax.set_xlabel("Intervened treatment")
ax.set_ylabel("Outcome")
ax.set_title("Outcome equation under do(T)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The bootstrap interval covers \(3\). The OLS slope is farther from \(3\) than the structural estimate. Because \(\alpha\) is constant, the average of the two potential outcomes differs from the estimate only by numerical error. The band in the figure is the uncertainty in \(\alpha\) and in the intercept at the average covariate row. It is not a prediction interval for a new unit’s disturbance.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
section: Getting started: a lagged system with a known coefficient
text:
Getting started: a lagged system with a known coefficient
The recursion, for \(t \ge 1\), is
\[
X_t = 0.4\, X_{t-1} + \varepsilon^X_t, \qquad
Y_t = 0.8\, X_t + 0.2\, Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon^Y_t.
\]
The contemporaneous structural coefficient of \(X\) in the equation for \(Y\) is \(0.8\). The edge list is (x, y). Lag 1 also enters \(Y_{t-1}\) and \(X_{t-1}\).


Code

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_time = 1500
x = np.zeros(n_time)
y = np.zeros(n_time)
for t in range(1, n_time):
    x[t] = 0.4 * x[t - 1] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.5)
    y[t] = 0.8 * x[t] + 0.2 * y[t - 1] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.3)
series = pd.DataFrame({"x": x, "y": y})

lagged = BayesianTimeSeriesSCM([("x", "y")], lag=1, n_draws=40, random_state=0)
lagged.fit(series)
print(pd.Series(lagged.summary("y")["coef"], index=lagged.summary("y")["feature_names"]).round(3))

impulse = lagged.impulse_response("x", shock=1.0, horizon=12)
held = lagged.counterfactual(8, interventions={"x": 1.0}, baseline={"x": 0.0})

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
axes[0].plot(impulse["effect"][:, series.columns.get_loc("y")], marker="o", color="#4C72B0")
axes[0].axhline(0.8, color="black", ls="--", lw=1, label="contemporaneous coefficient 0.8")
axes[0].set_title("Impulse: one-period shock to x")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Horizon")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Effect on y")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)

steps = np.arange(held["effect"].shape[0])
y_index = series.columns.get_loc("y")
axes[1].fill_between(
    steps, held["effect_lower"][:, y_index], held["effect_upper"][:, y_index],
    color="#4C72B0", alpha=0.2, label="95% band",
)
axes[1].plot(steps, held["effect"][:, y_index], color="#8B1E3F", marker="o", label="do(x=1) minus do(x=0)")
axes[1].set_title("Hard intervention held for 8 periods")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Horizon")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Effect on y")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


The posterior mean of x[t] in the equation for \(Y\) sits next to \(0.8\). The impulse jumps by about that amount on impact and then decays, because the shock lasts one period and \(X\) is allowed to return to its autoregression. The hard intervention holds \(X\) at 1 rather than at 0 for the whole horizon, so the path on \(Y\) stays near the contemporaneous coefficient plus the contribution of \(Y\)’s own lag. The band is coefficient uncertainty along that path.

Key parameters








Parameter
Where
Role




alpha, rho
simulate_structural_scm
Known structural coefficient and disturbance correlation.


instruments, outcome_only
BayesianStructuralSCM.fit
Exclusion restrictions. Other columns are confounders.


n_draws
both classes
Bayesian-bootstrap draws, or coefficient draws in the time-series rollout.


edges
BayesianTimeSeriesSCM
Contemporaneous parents. An empty list leaves independent autoregressions.


lag
BayesianTimeSeriesSCM
Number of lags of the series and of its contemporaneous parents.


interventions
counterfactual
A scalar or a horizon-length sequence that replaces an equation.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text:
Use case: returns to schooling
Card (1995) uses growing up near a four-year college as a source of variation in years of education. The outcome here is log wage. Experience enters both the education equation and the wage equation, so it is a confounder in the partition above. nearcollege enters the education equation only. That exclusion is the identifying assumption: proximity affects wages through schooling and experience, not through a separate channel. The file is CausalPy’s schoolReturns table (schoolingReturns.csv).

Load the schooling table


Code

school = load_causalpy("schoolReturns")
school = school.dropna(subset=["wage", "education", "nearcollege", "experience"]).copy()
school = school.loc[school["wage"] > 0].copy()
school["log_wage"] = np.log(school["wage"].to_numpy(float))
school["near"] = (school["nearcollege"].astype(str) == "yes").astype(float)
print("Rows:", len(school))
print(school[["log_wage", "education", "experience", "near"]].describe().T[["mean", "std"]].round(3))




Data visualization


Code

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
for flag, label, color in [(1.0, "Near a college", "#8B1E3F"), (0.0, "Not near a college", "#4C72B0")]:
    subset = school.loc[school["near"] == flag, "education"]
    axes[0].hist(subset, bins=18, alpha=0.55, label=label, color=color, density=True)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Years of education")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[0].set_title("First stage: proximity and schooling")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
axes[1].scatter(school["education"], school["log_wage"], s=8, alpha=0.15, c="#4C72B0")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Years of education")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Log wage")
axes[1].set_title("Observational wage-schooling cloud")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Fit the structural model
The design matrix carries experience and near. The instrument list contains only near. Experience is then a confounder by the partition rule.


Code

covariates = school[["experience", "near"]]
ols_design = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(school)),
    school["education"].to_numpy(float),
    school["experience"].to_numpy(float),
])
ols_education = np.linalg.lstsq(ols_design, school["log_wage"].to_numpy(float), rcond=None)[0][1]

card = BayesianStructuralSCM(n_draws=80, random_state=0)
card.fit(
    covariates,
    school["education"].to_numpy(float),
    school["log_wage"].to_numpy(float),
    instruments=["near"],
)
print("Identified by:", card.identified_by_)
print(f"OLS coefficient on education, controlling for experience: {ols_education:.3f}")
print(pd.Series({k: v for k, v in card.summary().items() if k != "identified_by"}).round(3))
show_posterior(card.draws_, card.effect_, "Return to one year of schooling")

y0, y1 = card.potential_outcomes(covariates)
print("Mean structural contrast Y(1) - Y(0):", round(float(np.mean(y1 - y0)), 3))


The estimate is a log-wage change for one additional year of schooling under the exclusion restriction. The OLS coefficient that controls for experience answers a different equation: it leaves the education residual correlated with the wage residual. The credible interval is the Bayesian bootstrap of both stages. A wide interval is the sample’s statement about a binary instrument. It is not a failure of the optimizer.
The homogeneous-effect calculation \(Y(1) - Y(0)\) equals the coefficient for every person. The file does not identify a different return for every level of experience unless that interaction is written into the outcome equation.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
section: Use case: lactate and sepsis risk, one hospital stay
text:
Use case: lactate and sepsis risk, one hospital stay
Data/labs_timeseries.csv is an hourly laboratory panel. The series used here is the longest stay, patient 6: lactate and sepsis_risk_score for 72 hours. The contemporaneous edge is lactate into the risk score. Lactate is a clinical marker that moves with perfusion; the risk score is a derived label. The fit is a description of this stay under that one-edge skeleton. It is not an estimate of the effect of treating lactate in a population.


Code

labs = pd.read_csv(data_dir / "labs_timeseries.csv")
stay_id = int(labs.groupby("patient_id").size().idxmax())
stay = (
    labs.loc[labs["patient_id"] == stay_id, ["hour_from_admission", "lactate", "sepsis_risk_score"]]
    .sort_values("hour_from_admission")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
print(f"Patient {stay_id}, hours: {len(stay)}")
print(stay[["lactate", "sepsis_risk_score"]].describe().T[["mean", "std"]].round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(stay["hour_from_admission"], stay["lactate"], color="#4C72B0", label="Lactate")
ax.set_ylabel("Lactate", color="#4C72B0")
ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.plot(stay["hour_from_admission"], stay["sepsis_risk_score"], color="#8B1E3F", label="Sepsis risk")
ax2.set_ylabel("Sepsis risk score", color="#8B1E3F")
ax.set_xlabel("Hour from admission")
ax.set_title(f"Patient {stay_id}")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Code

clinical = stay.rename(columns={"sepsis_risk_score": "risk"})[["lactate", "risk"]]
clinical_model = BayesianTimeSeriesSCM(
    [("lactate", "risk")], lag=1, n_draws=40, random_state=0
)
clinical_model.fit(clinical)
print("Risk equation:")
print(pd.Series(
    clinical_model.summary("risk")["coef"],
    index=clinical_model.summary("risk")["feature_names"],
).round(3))

shock = clinical_model.impulse_response("lactate", shock=1.0, horizon=10)
risk_col = clinical.columns.get_loc("risk")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(shock["effect"][:, risk_col], marker="o", color="#8B1E3F")
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Hours after a one-unit lactate shock")
ax.set_ylabel("Change in sepsis risk score")
ax.set_title("Impulse response along the fitted stay")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()


lactate[t] in the risk equation is the contemporaneous structural coefficient for this stay. The impulse adds one lactate unit to the residual at the first forecast hour and then lets both equations run. Hours after the shock move because of the lags, not because lactate is held at the shocked value. A treatment policy that sets lactate to a target for many hours is the hard counterfactual path, and it needs a baseline policy to subtract. With 72 hours and two series, that band is a description of one trajectory.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text:
Summary and conclusion
BayesianStructuralSCM separates the treatment assignment from the outcome assignment. Instruments identify \(\alpha\) when the treatment disturbance and the outcome disturbance are correlated. The Bayesian bootstrap carries the first stage into the posterior of \(\alpha\). Predictions under \(do(T)\) drop the first-stage residual.
BayesianTimeSeriesSCM uses the same Gaussian equation posterior one lag at a time. A one-period residual shock and a multi-period hard intervention are different experiments, and the two plotting panels keep them apart.
On the simulated cross-section the posterior covers \(\alpha = 3\) and the saturated OLS slope does not. On the simulated lag the coefficient on contemporaneous \(X\) covers \(0.8\). The schooling fit is the same estimator with Card’s exclusion restriction. The lactate fit is the same lagged estimator on one hospital stay.

title: 6.3 Bayesian Structural Causal Models
text:
Scientific terminology







Term
Meaning in this notebook




Structural coefficient
The direct effect written in an assignment, here \(\alpha\) on endogenous \(T\).


Endogeneity
Correlation between a regressor and the disturbance of the equation it sits in.


Exclusion restriction
A covariate is allowed in one assignment and shut out of the other.


Confounder column
A column that enters both the treatment equation and the outcome equation.


Bayesian bootstrap
Dirichlet weights on the sample rows. Each weighted two-stage fit is one posterior draw.


\(Y(1), Y(0)\)
Outcomes under \(do(T=1)\) and \(do(T=0)\). With constant \(\alpha\) their difference is \(\alpha\).


Hard intervention
The structural equation is replaced for the whole horizon.


Impulse response
A one-period shock to a structural residual. Later hours use the fitted equations.

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text: Python Banner

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text:
Overview

From Estimation to Decision-Making
Traditional causal inference focuses on estimating treatment effects (ATE, ATT, CATE). Policy learning goes further by translating these effect estimates into actionable treatment policies.
The key insight is that not everyone benefits from treatment. Policy learning identifies heterogeneous treatment effects and creates rules to assign treatment to those who benefit most.


The Policy Learning Problem
Given: - Covariates \(X\) (features describing units) - Potential outcomes \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) - Treatment \(T \in \{0, 1\}\)
We want to learn a policy function \(\pi(X): \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \{0, 1\}\) that maximizes expected outcome:
\[
\max_{\pi} \mathbb{E}[Y(\pi(X))]
\]
This is equivalent to:
\[
\pi(x) = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \tau(x) > 0 \\
0 & \text{if } \tau(x) \leq 0
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\tau(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X=x]\) is the conditional average treatment effect (CATE).


Methods Covered in This Section









Method
Chapter
Library
Key Features




IRM policy tree
7.1
PyCausalML
Deterministic policies from doubly robust IRM scores


DR policy tree
7.2
PyCausalML
One tree on the sign of the doubly robust score


DR policy forest
7.3
PyCausalML
An ensemble of those policy trees





Business Setting
Policy learning is ideal when:

Targeting is the goal: You need to decide who gets treatment
Heterogeneous effects exist: Treatment effects vary across the population
Resource constraints: Treatment is expensive or limited
Personalization needed: Different groups should receive different treatments

Common business applications:

Marketing: Which customers should receive a promotion?
Pricing: Dynamic pricing based on customer characteristics
Credit: Which loan applicants should be approved?
Healthcare: Which patients should receive a specific treatment?
Education: Which students should receive tutoring?
Retention: Which customers should get retention offers?

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text:
Key Concepts

Deterministic vs. Stochastic Policies

Deterministic policy: Assigns treatment with certainty (0 or 1)
Stochastic policy: Assigns treatment with probability (e.g., 70% chance of treatment)

Most policy learning methods focus on deterministic policies for simplicity and interpretability.


Policy Value
The policy value is the expected outcome under the policy:
\[
V(\pi) = \mathbb{E}[Y(\pi(X))]
\]
Since we never observe counterfactuals, we estimate this using doubly robust estimators or other causal methods.


Regret
Regret is the difference between the optimal policy value and the actual policy value:
\[
\text{Regret} = V(\pi^*) - V(\pi)
\]
where \(\pi^*\) is the oracle optimal policy (knowing true CATEs). Minimizing regret is the goal of policy learning.


Policy Learning vs. CATE Estimation








Aspect
CATE Estimation
Policy Learning




Goal
Estimate \(\tau(x)\) for all \(x\)
Learn treatment assignment rule


Output
Function or value per unit
Binary treatment assignment


Focus
Understanding heterogeneity
Decision-making


Evaluation
RMSE, bias
Policy value, regret



CATE estimation is a stepping stone to policy learning, but policy learning has its own methods and evaluation metrics.

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text:
Advantages of Policy Learning

1. Actionable Output
Instead of just reporting “the effect varies,” policy learning tells you exactly who to treat:

CATE: “Customer A has effect +$10, Customer B has effect -$5”
Policy: “Treat Customer A, don’t treat Customer B”



2. Resource Optimization
When treatment is expensive or limited, policy learning maximizes impact per unit of resource:

Limited budget for marketing → target high-response customers
Limited supply of a product → allocate to high-value customers



3. Robustness to Estimation Error
Policy trees and forests can be more robust to estimation error than point estimates of CATE:

Small errors in CATE may flip treatment decisions at the margin
Policy methods use regularization to avoid overfitting



4. Interpretability
Policy trees provide clear, interpretable rules:

“Treat if age > 30 AND income > $50k”
“Don’t treat if risk score < 0.3”

This is much easier to communicate to stakeholders than complex CATE functions.

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text:
Challenges

1. Estimation Error
Policy learning relies on estimated CATEs, which have error. This error can propagate to the policy:

Overfitting: Policy performs well on training data but poorly on new data
Need for careful validation and regularization



2. Off-Policy Evaluation
Evaluating a policy requires estimating counterfactual outcomes, which is challenging:

Need to estimate what would have happened under the alternative treatment
Requires causal assumptions (unconfoundedness)



3. Sample Efficiency
Learning good policies requires sufficient data:

Need enough treated and control units in each region of covariate space
Sparse data can lead to poor policies



4. Fairness Constraints
Optimal policies may have undesirable distributional effects:

Policy might systematically disadvantage certain groups
May need to add fairness constraints to the optimization

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text:
Connection to Other Sections
Policy learning builds on other causal inference methods in this tutorial:

Tree-Based Models (Section 5.1): Causal trees estimate heterogeneous effects, which can be used for policy learning
Meta-Learners (Section 5.2): Estimate CATEs, which inform policy decisions
DoubleML (Section 5.4): Provides robust CATE estimates that can be used in policy trees
Uplift Learners (Section 5.3): Directly estimate uplift, closely related to policy learning

Policy learning is the decision-making layer on top of CATE estimation.

title: 7. Policy Learners for Causal Inference
text:
What You’ll Learn
By the end of this section, you will:

Understand the policy learning problem and how it differs from CATE estimation
Be able to use PyCausalML’s DRPolicyTree to learn a deterministic policy from doubly robust scores
Be able to compare that tree with a doubly robust CATE fit
Be able to use PyCausalML’s DRPolicyForest when a single tree is too variable
Know how to evaluate policies using policy value and regret
Understand the trade-offs between different policy learning methods
Be equipped to implement policy learning in business settings

text:
Scientific Terminology
Plain-language definitions for the terms in this tutorial are in the scientific terminology glossary.

title: 7.2 DR Policy Tree
text: Python Banner

title: 7.2 DR Policy Tree
text:
Overview

What is DR Policy Tree?
PyCausalML’s DRPolicyTree is a policy learning method that:

Estimates CATEs using doubly robust estimation (combines outcome regression and propensity scores)
Learns a policy tree that partitions the covariate space and assigns treatment to regions with positive expected CATE
Is doubly robust: Consistent if either the propensity model or outcome model is correct



Key Features

Doubly robust: Robust to misspecification of either the propensity or outcome model
Flexible ML models: Can use any scikit-learn compatible model for outcome and propensity
Interpretable: Tree structure provides clear decision rules
Policy evaluation: Built-in methods to estimate policy value and regret
Uncertainty quantification: Optional inference methods for policy estimates



Business Setting
DR Policy Tree is ideal when:

Robustness needed: You want protection against model misspecification
Rich covariates: Many observed confounders to adjust for
Interpretable policies: Clear decision rules for stakeholders
Binary treatment: Treatment is yes/no

Common business applications:

Customer targeting with rich feature sets
Credit scoring with many risk factors
Marketing personalization
Healthcare treatment assignment

Install the required packages:

%matplotlib inline
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.tree import plot_tree

from pycausalml import DRLearner, DRPolicyTree
from pycausalml.policy_learners import policy_value

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")
pd.set_option("display.float_format", lambda x: f"{x:,.3f}")
print("Imported PyCausalML")


def show_policy_tree(model, feature_names, title, tree_index=None):
    """Draw a policy tree. ``tree_index`` selects one tree from a forest."""
    if getattr(model, "policy_", None) is None:
        print(f"{title}: constant policy = {model.constant_}")
        return
    estimator = model.policy_
    if tree_index is not None:
        estimator = estimator.estimators_[tree_index]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))
    plot_tree(
        estimator,
        feature_names=list(feature_names),
        class_names=["control", "treat"],
        filled=True,
        rounded=True,
        impurity=False,
        ax=ax,
        fontsize=8,
    )
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

title: 7.2 DR Policy Tree
text:
Example: Synthetic Policy Learning Data
Let’s create synthetic data with heterogeneous treatment effects:


Code
def create_policy_data(n_samples=1000, n_features=5, random_state=42):
    """
    Create synthetic data for policy learning.
    
    Treatment effect depends on covariates:
    - Positive effect for high values of X1
    - Negative effect for high values of X2
    """
    np.random.seed(random_state)
    
    # Generate covariates
    X = np.random.normal(0, 1, (n_samples, n_features))
    
    # True CATE: heterogeneous treatment effect
    tau = 2 * X[:, 0] - 1.5 * X[:, 1] + 0.5 * X[:, 2]
    
    # Treatment assignment (depends on covariates)
    propensity = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.5 * X[:, 0] + 0.3 * X[:, 1])))
    T = np.random.binomial(1, propensity)
    
    # Outcome
    Y = 10 + np.sum(X[:, :3], axis=1) + tau * T + np.random.normal(0, 1, n_samples)
    
    # Create DataFrame
    feature_names = [f'X{i}' for i in range(n_features)]
    df = pd.DataFrame(X, columns=feature_names)
    df['T'] = T
    df['Y'] = Y
    df['tau_true'] = tau  # true CATE for evaluation
    
    return df

# Generate data
df = create_policy_data(n_samples=1000, n_features=5)

title: 7.2 DR Policy Tree
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Poor Overlap
If propensity scores don’t overlap, doubly robust methods can be unstable.
Solution: Check overlap, trim extreme propensity scores, or use trimming.


2. Overfitting
Deep trees may overfit to noise in the CATE estimates.
Solution: Use shallower trees, increase min_samples_leaf, or use policy forests.


3. Model Misspecification
While doubly robust, if both models are misspecified, estimates can be biased.
Solution: Use flexible ML models, validate model fit, consider ensemble methods.

title: 7.2 DR Policy Tree
section: When to Use DR Policy Tree
text:
When to Use DR Policy Tree
DR Policy Tree is the right choice when:

Robustness needed: Protection against model misspecification
Rich covariates: Many observed confounders
Interpretable policies: Clear decision rules
Binary treatment: Treatment is yes/no

Consider alternatives when:

Multi-armed treatment → Multi-arm policy methods
Complex heterogeneity → Policy forests or neural policies
Weak overlap → Propensity score trimming or alternative methods

title: 8. Quasi-Experimental Methods for Causal Inference
text:
Overview
Quasi-experiments are research designs that aim to estimate causal effects without full randomization — they occupy the space between a controlled experiment (where you randomly assign treatment) and pure observation (where you simply watch what happens). In business settings, true randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are often infeasible due to ethical, practical, or financial constraints. Quasi-experimental methods provide a rigorous alternative when you cannot randomize but still need credible causal estimates.

When to Use Quasi-Experiments
Quasi-experimental methods are particularly valuable in business contexts such as:

Policy evaluations: Assessing the impact of company-wide initiatives (e.g., pricing changes, new return policies)
Geographic rollouts: When new features or programs launch in select markets before nationwide expansion
Natural experiments: Leveraging external shocks or events that create as-if random variation
Historical analysis: Retrospective evaluation of past interventions when RCTs were not conducted



The Key Challenge: Selection Bias
The fundamental problem in observational data is selection bias — treated and control groups differ systematically in ways that affect outcomes. Naive comparisons between treated and untreated units often reflect pre-existing differences rather than treatment effects.
For example, if you compare revenue at stores that adopted a new program versus those that didn’t, the adopters were likely already higher-performing stores. The observed difference mixes the true program effect with this pre-existing advantage.
Quasi-experimental methods solve this by finding structured variation in treatment assignment that allows credible counterfactual construction. Each method makes a different identifying assumption suited to a different assignment mechanism.


Methods Covered in This Section
This section introduces five core quasi-experimental methods, each suited to different business scenarios:









Method
Chapter
Business Setting
Key Assumption




Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
6.1
Treatment assigned to some groups at known time points
Parallel trends: treated and control groups would have evolved similarly absent treatment


Synthetic Control
6.2
One or few treated units with a pool of potential donors
A weighted combination of donors reproduces the treated unit’s pre-intervention path


Regression Discontinuity (RDD)
6.3
Treatment assigned by a threshold on a continuous score
Units just above/below the cutoff are as good as randomized


Instrumental Variables (IV)
6.4
Treatment self-selected with confounding, but an instrument exists
Instrument affects outcome only through treatment (exclusion)


Bayesian quasi-experiments
6.5
Posterior intervals for DiD, synthetic control, RDD, ITS, and IV, plus a linear CATE
The design’s identifying assumption. Uncertainty is a Bayesian bootstrap, or a normal posterior for the linear CATE





The Decision Framework
Choosing the right quasi-experimental method starts from the assignment mechanism — how treatment was actually assigned in your setting:
How was the intervention assigned?
│
├─ By a threshold on a continuous score?  ───────────────► RDD (Chapter 6.3)
│
├─ To some units at known time(s), others never?
│    ├─ Many treated & control units, parallel pre-trends ► DiD (Chapter 6.1)
│    ├─ One/few treated units, many good donors ─────────► Synthetic Control (Chapter 6.2)
│
├─ Self-selected by units with confounding, but instrument exists? ► IV (Chapter 6.4)
│
├─ Need the week-by-week path of an effect? ───────────────► Pre-trend and gap plots (Chapters 6.1 and 6.2)
│
└─ Need a posterior interval for one of these designs? ────► Bayesian quasi-experiments (Chapter 6.5)


Key Concepts

Potential Outcomes Framework
Causal inference relies on the potential outcomes framework. For each unit, define two potential outcomes:

\(Y_i(1)\) — outcome if the unit receives treatment
\(Y_i(0)\) — outcome if the unit does not receive treatment

The individual causal effect is \(\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\). The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we only ever observe one of these — the factual outcome. The other is the counterfactual. Every quasi-experimental method is a strategy for estimating this missing counterfactual.


Common Estimands
Different methods target different estimands (the quantity we’re trying to estimate):








Estimand
Definition
Business Question




ATE
\(E[Y(1) - Y(0)]\)
Average effect if everyone were treated


ATT
\(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid D=1]\)
Effect on the units that actually got the intervention (most common in rollout evaluations)


LATE
Effect on compliers
Effect among those whose treatment status was moved by an instrument


CATE
\(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X=x]\)
Effect for a specific segment — fuel for targeting



Being explicit about the estimand prevents stakeholder confusion: a synthetic control estimates the ATT for one treated market; an IV estimates a LATE that may differ sharply from the ATE.


Identifying Assumptions
Every quasi-experimental method buys identification with an assumption. These assumptions are untestable — they are claims about unobservable counterfactuals. The craft of quasi-experimentation is:

Choosing the assumption that best matches the known facts about how the intervention was assigned
Attacking that assumption aggressively with falsification tests (placebo tests, pre-trend checks, etc.)
Being transparent about limitations with stakeholders




Strengths and Limitations
Strengths of Quasi-Experiments:

Applicability: Can be applied to existing data when RCTs are impossible
External validity: Often use real-world contexts rather than artificial experimental settings
Cost-effectiveness: Leverage data already collected for other purposes
Ethical acceptability: Avoid withholding potentially beneficial treatments

Limitations:

Assumption dependence: Results hinge on untestable identifying assumptions
Design beats estimation: The highest-leverage move is often designing better rollouts (e.g., staggering, holding out controls)
Local effects: Many methods identify effects for specific subpopulations (e.g., units near a cutoff for RDD, compliers for IV)
Susceptibility to confounding: Unobserved confounders can still bias estimates if assumptions fail



Connection to Other Sections
This section on quasi-experimental methods complements other causal inference approaches in this tutorial:

Tree-Based Models (Section 5.1): Focus on heterogeneous treatment effects using decision trees and forests
Meta-Learners (Section 5.2): ML-based wrappers for estimating CATE under unconfoundedness
DoubleML (Section 5.4): Double/debiased machine learning for observational data with rich covariates

Quasi-experimental methods are particularly valuable when:

You have structural variation in treatment assignment (geographic rollouts, thresholds, instruments)
You cannot assume unconfoundedness (treatment assignment depends on unobservables)
You need to evaluate historical interventions that were not designed as experiments



Practical Guidance
When conducting quasi-experimental analysis in business settings:

Start with the assignment mechanism: Understand exactly how and why treatment was assigned
Choose the right method: Match the method to the assignment mechanism, not your preference
Triangulate: When possible, use multiple methods with different assumptions — agreement strengthens conclusions
Attack assumptions: Run falsification tests (placebo dates, placebo units, pre-trend checks)
Be transparent: Report the design, assumption, and estimand — not just the number
Design better next time: Use insights to improve future rollouts (stagger adoption, hold out controls, randomize encouragement)



What You’ll Learn
By the end of this section, you will:

Understand when and how to apply each quasi-experimental method
Be able to implement these methods in Python with PyCausalML
Know how to diagnose and test the identifying assumptions
Be equipped to communicate quasi-experimental results to business stakeholders
Recognize the limitations and be honest about uncertainty

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text: Python Banner

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Overview

The Core Idea
When you have only one treated unit (e.g., a single country, state, or flagship store), standard DiD struggles because you can’t reasonably compare one unit to many controls. SCM solves this by creating a synthetic control unit — a weighted average of untreated donor units that matches the treated unit’s characteristics and pre-treatment outcomes as closely as possible.
The method works in three steps:

Construction: Find nonnegative weights (summing to 1) over donor units such that the weighted combination matches the treated unit’s pre-intervention outcomes (and optionally covariates)
Counterfactual: Project this weighted combination into the post-intervention period to estimate what would have happened without treatment
Effect: The gap between the treated unit’s actual post-intervention outcome and its synthetic control’s projected outcome is the treatment effect



Business Setting
SCM is ideal when:

You have one or a few treated units (a single market, country, or flagship location)
There is a pool of potential donor units that were not treated
You have pre-intervention data on both outcomes and covariates
The treated unit is not an extreme outlier relative to the donor pool

Common business examples:

A new policy tested in one state before nationwide rollout
A store format piloted in a single flagship location
A marketing campaign launched in one city
A product feature tested in one country



The Identifying Assumption
SCM’s identifying assumption is: the pre-period weighting that reproduces the treated unit’s history would have continued to reproduce it absent treatment.
This is more transparent than parallel trends in DiD because you can visually inspect how well the synthetic unit tracks the treated unit in the pre-period. The quality of this pre-period fit is the license to interpret the post-period gap.


Why Business People Like SCM
SCM has several features that make it particularly persuasive to non-technical stakeholders:

Transparency: The counterfactual is interpretable — “Synthetic Chicago = 40% Minneapolis + 35% Detroit + 25% Cleveland”
Visual: The result is a picture (treated vs. synthetic over time), not just a coefficient
Intuitive: If the synthetic unit closely tracks the treated unit before treatment, it’s reasonable to use it as a counterfactual after
Case-study feel: SCM naturally produces compelling narratives about specific interventions



Key Advantages

Handles single treated units: Works when DiD would be inappropriate
Transparent weights: You can see exactly which donors contribute to the synthetic control
No extrapolation: Weights are nonnegative and sum to 1, so the treated unit must lie within the donor pool’s convex hull
Permutation inference: Uses placebo tests (applying SCM to each donor) to construct p-values without distributional assumptions

text:

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Simulated Example: Single Market Intervention
We’ll simulate a scenario where a new program launches in one market only, with several untreated markets available as donors.


Code
def make_market_panel(
    n_markets=12,
    n_weeks=104,
    treated_market=0,
    treat_week=60,
    true_effect=8.0,
    effect_ramp=6,
    seed=42,
):
    """Simulate market-level panel data with one treated market."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    
    # Market fixed effects and trends
    market_fe = rng.normal(100, 15, n_markets)
    market_trend = rng.normal(0.05, 0.03, n_markets)
    
    rows = []
    market_shock = rng.normal(0, 3, (n_markets, n_weeks))
    
    for w in range(n_weeks):
        season = 6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * w / 52)
        for m in range(n_markets):
            treated_unit = (m == treated_market)
            post = w >= treat_week
            
            # Treatment effect ramps in
            if treated_unit and post:
                ramp = min(1.0, (w - treat_week + 1) / effect_ramp)
                tau = true_effect * ramp
            else:
                tau = 0.0
            
            y = (market_fe[m] + market_trend[m] * w
                 + season + market_shock[m, w]
                 + tau + rng.normal(0, 4))
            
            rows.append((m, w, int(treated_unit), int(post), y))
    
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[
        "market", "week", "treated", "post", "revenue"])

# Generate the panel
panel = make_market_panel()
print(panel.head())
print("\nTrue effect at full ramp: $8k/week")

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Fitting the Synthetic Control
We use SyntheticControl from PyCausalML. Weights are nonnegative and sum to one, as in Abadie’s synthetic control.


Code

def _pivot(frame, week_min, week_max):
    subset = frame[(frame["week"] >= week_min) & (frame["week"] < week_max)]
    return subset.pivot(index="week", columns="market", values="revenue").sort_index()

donors = mkt_long[mkt_long["market"].isin(donor_markets)]
treated = mkt_long[mkt_long["market"] == treated_market]
donor_pre = _pivot(donors, 0, treat_week)
donor_post = _pivot(donors, treat_week, 104)
treated_pre = _pivot(treated, 0, treat_week).iloc[:, 0].to_numpy()
treated_post = _pivot(treated, treat_week, 104).iloc[:, 0].to_numpy()

scm = SyntheticControl(n_boot=80, random_state=0)
scm.fit(donor_pre.to_numpy(), treated_pre, donor_post.to_numpy(), treated_post)
weights = pd.Series(scm.weights_, index=donor_pre.columns, name="weight").sort_values(ascending=False)
print("Donor weights:")
print(weights.round(3))
print("\nPost-period average effect:")
print(pd.Series(scm.summary()).round(3))

text:
Visualizing the Results
The most important diagnostic is the path plot, which shows how well the synthetic control tracks the treated unit.


Code

weeks = np.concatenate([donor_pre.index.to_numpy(), donor_post.index.to_numpy()])
synth_path = np.concatenate([donor_pre.to_numpy() @ scm.weights_, scm.synth_post_])
treated_path = np.concatenate([treated_pre, treated_post])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.plot(weeks, treated_path, label="Treated market")
ax.plot(weeks, synth_path, label="Synthetic control")
ax.axvline(treat_week, color="red", ls="--", label="Launch")
ax.set_xlabel("Week")
ax.set_ylabel("Revenue ($k)")
ax.set_title("Treated Market vs. Synthetic Control")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The path plot should show:

Pre-period (weeks 0-59): The synthetic control should closely track the treated market
Post-period (weeks 60-103): A gap emerges between treated and synthetic — this is the estimated treatment effect

If the pre-period fit is poor, stop — the synthetic control is not a valid counterfactual.

gap = treated_path - synth_path
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=1)
ax.plot(weeks, gap, color="#E45756")
ax.axvline(treat_week, color="red", ls="--", label="Launch")
ax.set_xlabel("Week")
ax.set_ylabel("Treated minus synthetic ($k)")
ax.set_title("Treatment Effect: Gap Between Treated and Synthetic")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The gaps plot shows the treatment effect over time. It should be near zero in the pre-period (indicating good fit) and show the effect in the post-period.

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Inference: Placebo-in-Space Permutation
With only one treated unit, standard errors don’t apply. SCM uses permutation inference: apply the same procedure to every donor as if it were treated, then compare the real effect to the distribution of placebo effects.


Code

wide = (
    mkt_long.pivot(index="week", columns="market", values="revenue")
    .sort_index()
)
pre_w = wide.loc[wide.index < treat_week]
post_w = wide.loc[wide.index >= treat_week]

def post_mean_gap(unit):
    others = [column for column in wide.columns if column != unit]
    weights_u = SyntheticControl._weights(pre_w[others].to_numpy(), pre_w[unit].to_numpy())
    return float(np.mean(post_w[unit].to_numpy() - post_w[others].to_numpy() @ weights_u))

placebo_gaps = pd.Series(
    {unit: post_mean_gap(unit) for unit in donor_markets},
    name="placebo_gap",
)
print(placebo_gaps.round(2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.hist(placebo_gaps, bins=8, color="#4C78A8", edgecolor="white", label="Donor placebos")
ax.axvline(scm.effect_, color="#E45756", lw=2, label="Treated market")
ax.set_xlabel("Post-period average gap")
ax.set_title("Placebo-in-space")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

abs_placebo = np.abs(placebo_gaps.to_numpy())
pval = (np.sum(abs_placebo >= abs(scm.effect_)) + 1) / (len(abs_placebo) + 1)
print(f"Treated gap: {scm.effect_:.2f}")
print(f"Permutation p-value: {pval:.3f}")

The p-value indicates how unusual the real effect is compared to the placebo distribution. A low p-value (e.g., < 0.05) suggests the effect is unlikely to occur by chance.

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Diagnostics and Best Practices

1. Pre-Period Fit is Critical
The single most important diagnostic is the pre-period fit. If the synthetic control cannot track the treated unit before treatment, it cannot be trusted as a counterfactual after treatment.
Rule of thumb: Visual inspection should show close tracking in the pre-period. Consider quantitative metrics like pre-period mean squared prediction error (MSPE).


2. No Extrapolation
SCM weights are constrained to be nonnegative and sum to 1. This means the treated unit must lie within the donor pool’s convex hull. A flagship market that is much larger than all donors cannot be synthesized well.
Solutions: - Scale outcomes (e.g., revenue per store) - Use augmented SCM (adds a bias-correcting outcome model) - Exclude extreme outliers from the donor pool - Consider alternative methods (DiD with multiple controls)


3. In-Time Placebo
Test the method by ending the data before the real intervention and imposing a fake treatment date. The “effect” should be near zero.
Implementation: Run SCM with a fake treatment week (e.g., week 40) using only data up to week 50. If you find a significant effect, the method is misspecified.


4. Leave-One-Out
Drop the highest-weight donor and refit. Conclusions should not hinge on a single donor. If results change dramatically, the analysis is fragile.


5. Don’t Cherry-Pick the Donor Pool
Pre-specify the donor pool before seeing results. Changing the donor pool after seeing the effect is a form of p-hacking.
Best practice: Document the donor pool selection criteria in an analysis plan before running the analysis.


6. Include Covariates When Available
While outcome matching is the primary criterion, including pre-treatment covariates (e.g., market size, demographics) can improve the synthetic control’s realism and transparency.

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Common Pitfalls

1. Poor Pre-Period Fit
If the synthetic control doesn’t track the treated unit well before treatment, the post-period gap is meaningless.
Solution: Improve donor pool, add covariates, or use a different method.


2. Treated Unit is an Outlier
If the treated unit is extreme relative to donors (e.g., a megacity compared to small towns), no weighted combination can match it well.
Solution: Scale outcomes, use augmented SCM, or accept that SCM is not appropriate.


3. Too Few Donors
With very few donors, the synthetic control may be unstable or overfit to specific donors.
Solution: Use at least 5-10 donors when possible.


4. Contemporaneous Shocks
If something else affects the treated unit at the same time as the intervention, SCM will attribute the combined effect to the treatment.
Solution: Check for co-interventions and use multiple methods to triangulate.


5. Short Pre-Period
A short pre-period makes it hard to assess fit and may miss pre-existing trends.
Solution: Use at least 2-3 pre-intervention periods (years for annual data, months for monthly data).

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
When to Use SCM
SCM is the right choice when:

You have one or few treated units
There is a pool of untreated donors
The treated unit is not an extreme outlier relative to donors
You have sufficient pre-period data to assess fit
You value transparency and visual communication

Consider alternatives when:

Many treated units → DiD
Treatment assigned by threshold → RDD
Treated unit is extreme outlier → Scale outcomes or use alternative methods
No suitable donor pool → ITS, CausalImpact

title: 8.2 Synthetic Control Method
text:
Summary
Synthetic Control is a powerful method for case-study causal inference with single treated units. Its strength lies in the transparency of the counterfactual construction and the intuitive visual presentation of results.
Key takeaways:

SCM constructs a weighted combination of donors to match the treated unit’s pre-intervention trajectory
Pre-period fit is the critical diagnostic — if it’s poor, stop
Use permutation inference (placebo tests) for statistical significance
Don’t cherry-pick the donor pool — pre-specify it
Be transparent about limitations when the treated unit is an outlier
Combine with other methods (DiD, placebo tests) for stronger conclusions

title: 8.4 Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Overview

The Core Problem: Unobserved Confounding
In many business settings, treatment is self-selected and confounded by factors we cannot measure. For example:

High-ability employees are more likely to participate in training programs and have better performance
Engaged customers are more likely to adopt new features and spend more
Well-managed stores are more likely to try new initiatives and have higher revenue

Even if we control for many observable covariates, unobserved factors (ability, engagement, management quality) can bias our estimates. IV provides a solution when we can find an appropriate instrument.


The Core Idea
An instrument (Z) is a variable that:

Affects treatment (D) — it changes the probability or intensity of treatment
Does not directly affect the outcome (Y) — it only affects Y through D (exclusion restriction)
Is as good as random — it’s not correlated with unobserved confounders (independence)

When these conditions hold, IV isolates the variation in treatment that is “as good as random” and uses it to estimate the causal effect.


Business Setting
IV is ideal when:

Treatment is self-selected and confounded by unobservables
An instrument exists that shifts treatment without directly affecting the outcome
The instrument is credible — stakeholders agree it only affects the outcome through treatment

Common business instruments:

Encouragement designs: Randomly sent emails that nudge feature adoption (randomized encouragement, self-selected adoption)
Supply shocks: Regional shipping delays as an instrument for delivery speed’s effect on repeat purchase
Distance/availability: Distance to the nearest store as an instrument for in-store program exposure
Quasi-random agent assignment: Customers routed to support reps with different propensities to offer discounts
Policy changes: Regulatory changes that affect some firms but not others



The Estimand: LATE
IV identifies the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) — the effect among compliers, defined as units whose treatment status is moved by the instrument.
This is different from ATE (average effect for everyone) or ATT (effect for the treated). LATE is specific to the subgroup that responds to the instrument.
Important: Be explicit with stakeholders about this limitation. “This is the effect for customers whose adoption the email tipped,” not “the effect for all customers.”

title: 8.4 Instrumental Variables (IV)
text:
Implementation in Python
InstrumentalVariable is two-stage least squares. The first stage regresses treatment on the instrument. The second stage regresses the outcome on the fitted treatment. The interval is a Bayesian bootstrap of both stages.
The setup matches the other PyCausalML tutorials: find the repository, import the package, and install the editable checkout only if the import fails.

section: Simulated Example: Email Encouragement for Feature Adoption
text:
Simulated Example: Email Encouragement for Feature Adoption
We’ll simulate an encouragement design: randomly send emails encouraging customers to adopt a new feature. The email is randomized (valid instrument), but adoption is self-selected (confounded by unobserved ability).


Code
n = 10000

# Unobserved confounder: customer ability
ability = rng.normal(0, 1, n)

# Instrument: randomized encouragement email
Z = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, n)

# Treatment: feature adoption depends on ability AND the email
# Higher ability customers are more likely to adopt
# The email increases adoption probability
logit_adopt = -0.8 + 1.2*ability + 1.1*Z
p_adopt = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit_adopt))
D = rng.binomial(1, p_adopt)

# True LATE: effect for compliers (those moved by the email)
TRUE_LATE = 15.0

# Outcome: spending depends on ability AND treatment
# Higher ability customers spend more
# Treatment adds to spending
y = 50 + TRUE_LATE*D + 12*ability + rng.normal(0, 10, n)

iv = pd.DataFrame(dict(Z=Z, D=D, y=y))

print(iv.head())
print(f"\nTrue LATE: ${TRUE_LATE}")

Naive OLS is Biased
Let’s see what happens if we naively compare treated and untreated customers using OLS:


Code

design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(iv)), iv["D"].to_numpy(float)])
ols_effect = float(np.linalg.lstsq(design, iv["y"].to_numpy(float), rcond=None)[0][1])
print(f"Naive OLS effect: ${ols_effect:.2f}")
print(f"True LATE: ${TRUE_LATE:.2f}")
